title_key: leveraging design thinking to tackle contemporary admissions challenges in health professions education|davidson
title: Leveraging design thinking to tackle contemporary admissions challenges in health professions education
abstract: PURPOSE: This study illustrates the use of design thinking (DT) as a structured, participatory approach to explore contemporary complex challenges in health professions admissions, including the rise of generative AI, remote interviews, and the elimination of standardized admissions tests. This work focuses on stakeholder-driven problem framing and idea generation rather than evaluating outcomes. METHODS: A two-hour workshop engaged 15 purposively sampled stakeholders, including faculty, staff, application readers, and student ambassadors, in collaborative problem framing, ideation, and rapid prototyping of admissions concepts. Generative artifacts (brainstorming outputs, reflection worksheets, facilitator notes) and post-session surveys were analyzed using thematic synthesis and descriptive statistics to characterize emergent ideas and participant perspectives. MAJOR FINDINGS: Participants generated ideas that clustered into three major themes: interview restructuring, GenAI integration and compliance, and broadening of admissions criteria, illustrating how stakeholders reframed challenges and proposed diverse solution pathways. Survey responses reflected descriptive indicators of participant experience, suggesting the workshop supported creative problem solving (Mean 4.7 ± 0.5), idea generation (4.8 ± 0.4), and collaboration (4.4 ± 0.5). CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest that DT offers a structured, iterative framework for stakeholder-driven idea generation and problem reframing in an evolving admissions context. The workshop demonstrates the potential of collaborative, reflective processes to surface assumptions and generate diverse perspectives to inform future exploration of admissions practices.
authors: ["Adina O. Davidson", "Wendy C. Cox", "Heather Azzu", "Kelly Womack-Adams", "Jacqueline E. McLaughlin"]

title_key: building critical thinking and ai literacy through the topic development process in kinesiology|lazzarini
title: Building Critical Thinking and AI Literacy through the Topic Development Process in Kinesiology
abstract: The purpose of this teaching and learning resource is to provide a process for developing academic and meta-cognitive skills in students as they engage meaningfully in literature analysis and practice deploying generative artificial intelligence (genAI) effectively and responsibly. Additionally, while gaining critical AI literacy, students will develop the skills needed to advance their critical thinking and avoid overreliance on generative AI. This resource is unique in the specificity of its activities, which promote a healthy perspective on how genAI can be used in the early stages of learning about a topic. It also helps students practice the skills needed to contribute their own value, discernment, and insights to the project development process. This resource is intended for instructors of lower-division courses in a kinesiology program. Depending on students' preparation, some elements may also be useful for upper-division courses. These skills can be supported through out-of-class activities and further developed in online, in-person, or hybrid courses over several weeks.

title_key: research on curriculum system reconstruction of intelligent office ability cultivation from the perspective of industry education integration|liu
title: Research on Curriculum System Reconstruction of Intelligent Office Ability Cultivation from the Perspective of Industry-Education Integration
abstract: The explosive application of generative AI technology has driven profound transformations in corporate office operations toward intelligentization, collaboration, and data-driven approaches. Currently, foundational computer science courses in higher education institutions have failed to keep pace with this industrial revolution in terms of goal setting, content delivery, and teaching methodologies, resulting in structural mismatches between talent supply and industry demands. Grounded in industry-education integration perspectives and incorporating collaborative theory with competency-based education principles, this study analyzes the conceptual characteristics and evolutionary logic of intelligent office capabilities, while examining practical challenges in existing curricula such as goal misalignment, outdated content, and contextual gaps. The research proposes adopting outcome-based education (OBE) principles to reconstruct curriculum objectives, deconstructing typical work tasks to modularize instructional content, and implementing industry-academia collaborative pathways alongside diversified value-added evaluation mechanisms to achieve alignment between educational systems and industrial needs.

title_key: guaranteed dividends why finance and other education law scholars should invest in legal literacy research|decker
title: Guaranteed Dividends: Why Finance And Other Education Law Scholars Should Invest In Legal Literacy Research
abstract: No matter whether you are an education finance scholar or study the myriad of other education law topics, every education law researcher should recognize that legal literacy matters. But are we, as a collective discipline, doing enough to invest in legal literacy research? This article provides persuasive support that we should be doing more to expand current research and offers concrete suggestions to encourage all of us to identify how we could advance legal literacy research. Of course there are personal benefits, but the dividends that enhance our field of education law—as well as society at large—are guaranteed.As education law researchers, we recognize that when university and PK-12 school employees fail to understand how the law impacts their daily lives, it can result in dire situations where students are subjected to discrimination,1 assault,2 abuse,3 or even death.4 When educators are uninformed about the law, it can also result in legal violations affecting students5 and employees.6 Once these errors are made, no matter how skilled and experienced an attorney is, they usually cannot prevent the emotionally draining, expensive, and time-consuming litigation or the many other negative consequences that may result. But when employees are legally literate, they become empowered to influence policies and practices both internal and external to their workplace.7 Legal literacy allows university and school employees to advocate for the changes that they want to see and prepares them to make better decisions which ultimately, improves the overall education system.The purpose of this article is to encourage all education law researchers to reflect on the importance of legal literacy and analyze if collectively, we are prioritizing it enough in our individual research agendas. I conclude that we are not, and propose that if education law researchers will prioritize this topic, our findings can validate the value and impact of our field. Therefore, I argue that we should do more to increase the depth and number of studies focused on legal literacy. Education law is a niche specialization with a relatively small number of scholars. To advance our unique discipline of education law, and also to situate our research in a way where we can have a greater impact on the larger PK-20 educational system, as well as society in general, we must increase our understanding of legal literacy. To put it in finance terms, if we compare education law researchers to shareholders of stocks, then, we as a collective discipline are guaranteed future dividends—or predictable benefits—by investing in legal literacy research now. Education researchers should prioritize this topic because legal literacy research can validate and advance our field in ways that other education law research cannot.To support this proposition, this article begins by providing additional details about what legal literacy is and why it matters. Then, I summarize the relatively few studies that exist about legal literacy. I conclude by offering ideas about how education law researchers should take advantage of opportunities to advance the study of legal literacy. However, my hope is that this article merely initiates a conversation among education law researchers so that we begin to do more to build upon the existing research and as a result, we have an even greater impact on the larger PK-20 educational system.To be legally literate, PK-20 education employees need more than mere knowledge, they must be “able to spot legal issues, identify applicable laws or legal standards, and apply the relevant legal rules to solve legal dilemmas.”8 Therefore, knowing how to define legal terms, identify constitutional amendments, or recite legal standards from court cases is insufficient. Mere knowledge of the law is not enough. To be literate, employees must know how to apply the law. When university and school employees are legally literate, they “have the requisite attitudes to ensure that they will take appropriate action when faced with unfairness, injustice, and inequities.”9 Essentially, education employees do not merely need to know what to do, they need to be prepared to handle the many legal dilemmas that they face.University and PK-12 school employees may not fully recognize how often the law impacts their daily practice, but nearly every aspect of education is governed by the law. Of course, school and university attorneys may be available for consultation, but it is the employees who have direct student contact. They are the ones who are on the front lines and must make split-second decisions about legal dilemmas every day. Many times, these employees are not provided with access to legal advice from an attorney and must respond to situations immediately. For example, a classroom teacher who suspects that a student is vaping must know when it is legally permissible to search the student's backpack. In a college setting, a resident assistant must know the proper procedures to respond to allegations of sexual harassment.When PK-20 employees are legally literate, they are more confident, make better decisions, prevent lawsuits/legal violations, and feel more empowered to influence policy reform at the local, state, and federal levels.10 Without an understanding of the legal system and education law, employees often feel intimidated to advocate for policy changes. However, school leaders, educators, and employees are in the ideal positions to identify problems and offer realistic solutions. Once employees are educated about how the law is enacted, interpreted, and enforced, as well as the interplay between the legislative, judicial, and executive branches of government, they can make more informed decisions.When employees in universities and schools are legally literate, they are also less anxious because this increased knowledge makes them feel better. No one wants to feel unsure and insecure about something as important as the law. Call and O'Brien found that 64% of teachers were concerned about the risk of lawsuits or legal challenges.11 Educators often fear the law, which can “[paralyze] educators such that they fail to act when they should and overreact when they should not.”12 But once employees better understand the legal “complexities, contradictions, and areas of uncertainty,”13 they can recognize how to act in within the gray areas and nuances of the law. Additionally, increasing the legal literacy of employees allows them to better understand how complicated it is to craft policies and attempt to balance diverse needs. This enhanced understanding of the law can “counteract the belief that the scales of justice are tilted against them.”14 Therefore, because legal literacy allows employees to make better decisions, and to understand the legal reasoning behind their decisions, increasing their legal literacy ultimately benefits the overall educational system.On the other hand, when employees are uninformed about the law, they may unintentionally violate the rights of students and coworkers.15 They may fear the law or feel paralyzed to react to legal dilemmas which can exacerbate the problem.16 Once these errors are made, lawyers may be able to help defend universities and school districts, but they cannot erase the facts that have already occurred. Additionally, when employees do not know the law, they cannot use that unfamiliarity with the law as a defense.Further, if a lawsuit is filed, the employees must endure expensive, emotionally draining, and time-consuming litigation—and oftentimes, the distraction of these disputes means the employee may face burnout and find it difficult to balance their other work responsibilities.17 For example, when parents of students with disabilities file lawsuits against school districts, long-term battles over the student's education, accommodations, and placement may result. Specifically, the adults involved become so filled with distrust and resentment that their relationships are irreparably damaged, and they find it impossible to communicate or compromise effectively. Because of all the drama surrounding the lawsuit and allegations of wrongdoing, both school employees and parents may not be focused on the child who ironically, was sole reason for the dispute in the first place! And, like custody battles in divorce cases, these adversarial special education disputes can endure for many years during the precious time when prioritizing the child's needs should be the overarching priority. Therefore, preventing litigation is not only about conserving resources. Avoiding lawsuits is imperative to preserve relationships. No matter who prevails in a lawsuit, “parties on both sides leave feeling disheartened, angry, exhausted, and oftentimes, not fully satisfied with the result.”18 Clearly, when employees are distracted by volatile disputes, toxic environments, or damaged relationships, they are unable to focus on the roles and responsibilities of their jobs.This is why legal literacy matters and education law researchers should care about it. Increasing employees’ understanding of the law will not prevent all legal violations and lawsuits, but it will help to decrease the likelihood of them. Unfortunately, however, we know that a lack of legal awareness often leads to negative consequences and nonetheless, we have not made huge strides in ensuring that employees are adequately educated about the law. On the contrary, the limited existing research has uncovered that most PK-20 employees lack legal training and as a result, are unprepared to accurately respond to legal dilemmas.For 60 years, researchers have repeatedly recommended that more legal training is needed.19 Schimmel and Militello explained that “failure to provide all teachers with [even] a basic understanding of school law, in view of today's demonstrated need, can be considered a form of educational malpractice.”20 But it is extremely rare that future PK-12 teachers or university instructors are required to learn about the law. Additionally, administrators in higher education and schools may be required to only complete one education law course,21 or sometimes, they can complete their degrees without completing any legal training. This section briefly summarizes the relatively few studies about legal literacy by first, discussing PK-12 research and then, higher education research.Despite repeated complaints to prioritize legal training for PK-12 school employees, education law scholars have only produced two large-scale empirical studies to measure legal knowledge of educators.22 Both studies concluded that most teachers and administrators are uninformed or misinformed about the legal rights of students and teachers. In the first study from 2007—which, problematically, is almost 20 years old—Schimmel and Militello surveyed 1,317 elementary and secondary teachers in 17 states.23 They provided a series of true/false statements and found that the over half of teachers provided incorrect responses about students’ and teachers’ legal rights. For example, only 17% accurately answered a question about whether a suspended student has a legal right to be represented by an attorney at a hearing. Only 3% responded correctly to a question about a teacher's liability for student injuries. It makes sense that the teachers were unable to answer the questions correctly, considering that over 75% of the respondents had never completed a school law course and they were getting their legal information from other—presumably uninformed—teachers. But it appears that educators want to know more about the law and explained that they would change their practices if they had more legal training.In the second study from 2009, Militello, Schimmel, and Eberwein similarly found that school leaders lacked legal knowledge.24 They surveyed 493 secondary school principals and found that only 54% of principals correctly answered questions about students’ rights, and only 65% were accurate on questions about teachers’ rights. Many more principals than teachers had completed a school law course—in fact, 87% had received formal school law training. Considering that the great majority had received legal training but appeared uninformed about student and employee legal rights, then, one could question whether their school law training was effective. Additionally, some principals commented that it would be prudent if school leaders were provided with legal updates because the law is constantly evolving and what they learn in a school law course quickly becomes outdated. Similar to the teachers in the previous study, 85% of the school leaders thought that if they were taught more about school law, then they would change their behaviors.In addition to providing a valuable measure of educator legal literacy, the questions used in these two seminal studies about legal literacy were incorporated into a 2023 study by Thomas, McElhattan, and Carlo. These researchers explored how school employees could leverage emerging technology to improve legal literacy. The researchers used the questions from the prior 2007 and 2009 legal literacy studies to prompt ChatGPT and other artificial intelligence (AI) tools and to assess the performance of the AI tools against teacher and administrator performance reported in the 2007 and 2009 studies.25 In comparing the AI responses to educator responses, the researchers found that AI tools outperformed the average educator's performance in every subcategory of issues including school authority, religion, free speech, and disability.26 The researchers stressed the preliminary nature of the research, highlighting that while AI tools may be a useful supplement to educators’ legal literacy, more research needs to be done to ensure the reliability of these tools and the extent to which they can be used to help educators in their daily practice.27More recent scholarship also highlights issues of legal literacy pertaining to specific areas of education law. In 2020, Summers, Kiracofe, and James published the results from their state-level study of 300 teachers where they also concluded that educators lacked important legal knowledge.28 In 2021, Everson measured teachers’ legal literacy pertaining to English Learners. Despite 78% of the teachers had completed a master's degree, they nonetheless scored low on questions measuring legal literacy.29Researchers have also begun to measure legal training and whether it improves educators’ legal literacy. In a 2017 study, Decker, Ober, and Schimmel asked whether educators’ actions and attitudes were impacted in the years after they had completed one graduate-level school law course.30 They found that that legal training did improve educators’ behaviors and attitudes. The large majority of the 123 respondents (88%) stated that their school law course increased their confidence making them less fearful and anxious. Additionally, 85% of respondents reported that the class had changed their behaviors.31 Every single respondent concluded that it was important for future teachers to learn about school law.In addition to research on the value of legal literacy, researchers have also explored the specific legal literacy needs of educators and school leaders. In a survey of Arizona school administrators, Hughes examined their preferred instructional purpose, focus, and delivery of legal literacy trainings.32 Results of the survey demonstrated that administrators overwhelmingly wanted legal literacy trainings that focused on issues “tied to likely administrator challenges” and emphasized how to translate legal requirements to day-to-day situations.33 Based on these results, Hughes recommended that legal literacy trainings be provided in a problem-based approach that emphasizes how to respond to common situations administrators face, Generative artifacts (brainstorming outputs, reflection worksheets, facilitator notes) and post-session surveys were analyzed using thematic synthesis and descriptive statistics to characterize emergent ideas and participant perspectives. Major findings: Participants generated ideas that clustered into three major themes: interview restructuring, GenAI integration and compliance, and broadening of admissions criteria, illustrating how stakeholders reframed challenges and proposed diverse solution pathways. Survey responses reflected descriptive indicators of participant experience, suggesting the workshop supported creative problem solving (Mean 4.7 ± 0.5), idea generation (4.8 ± 0.4), and collaboration (4.4 ± 0.5). Conclusions: Findings suggest that DT offers a structured, iterative framework for stakeholder-driven idea generation and problem reframing in an evolving admissions context. The workshop demonstrates the potential of collaborative, reflective processes to surface assumptions and generate diverse perspectives to inform future exploration of admissions practices.

title_key: ai in the university ethical and strategic diagnosis for a responsible integration in higher education|espinosa
title: AI in the university: ethical and strategic diagnosis for a responsible integration in higher education
abstract: The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is reshaping study practices in higher education, offering opportunities for pedagogical innovation while also raising ethical dilemmas, regulatory tensions, and academic risks. In Ecuador, the institutional integration of AI remains incipient and uneven, making contextualized assessments essential for guiding responsible decision-making. This study evaluates, from an ethical and strategic perspective, the use, perceptions, and AI literacy of students from Universidad Técnica de Cotopaxi (UTC) and Universidad de las Fuerzas Armadas ESPE (Latacunga campus) as a basis for proposing guidelines for responsible integration of AI in higher education. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and comparative design was applied to an intentional sample of 400 students using a validated five-point Likert-type questionnaire (global α > .80) measuring five dimensions: academic use, perceived benefits, ethical risks, perceived literacy and institutional governance, and willingness toward responsible integration. Findings reveal frequent use of AI for information retrieval, writing support, and comprehension of academic content, alongside a generally positive valuation of AI as a learning resource. However, students also express concerns regarding plagiarism, reduced critical-thinking skills, algorithmic biases, and the absence of clear institutional policies. Significant differences were observed between universities in declared AI literacy and awareness of governance frameworks, with ESPE reporting slightly higher levels. Despite these variations, both groups show strong willingness to receive training and engage in responsible AI integration initiatives. Overall, the study concludes that while AI is already embedded in students’ academic routines, ethical and pedagogical governance remains underdeveloped, highlighting the need for explicit institutional policies, critical AI literacy programs, and participatory mechanisms to support responsible integration in Ecuadorian higher education.

title_key: developing learning strategic competence in pre service nglish teachers through artificial intelligence tools|meljnyk
title: Developing learning-strategic competence in pre-service Еnglish teachers through artificial intelligence tools
abstract: The digitalization of modern higher pedagogical education necessitates the integration of advanced artificial intelligence tools into the professional training system of pre-service English teachers to intensify learning and ensure educational autonomy. The purpose of the article is to determine the features ofthe methodological model for developing the learning-strategic competence of pre-service English teachers based on artificial intelligence tools. In the course of the study, a structural-functional model for the development of learning-strategic competence was theoretically substantiated and developed, based on a synthesis of traditional linguodidactic approaches and the adaptive capabilities of generative language models. The structural component ofthe model covers declarative and procedural knowledge, skills for interacting with large language models, as well as a complex of cognitive, metacognitive, socio-affective, and compensatory strategies. The implementation of the model is carried out according to a three-stage algorithm including the phases of awareness and diagnosis, controlled learning, and autonomous application of strategies in the digital space. At the first stage, artificial intelligence tools are used to identify students’ existing strategic experience and overcome the fragmentation of self-assessment by receiving instantaneous intelligent feedback, which contributes to a deeper understanding of individual learning needs. The second stage focuses on mastering prompt engineering methods, in particular the formation of prompt-actions and prompt-scenarios, which ensures the acquisition of relevant content and reduces the level of speech anxiety through the possibility of infinite repetition and prompt error correction. The third stage of the model involves a transition to complete strategic autonomy, where artificial intelligence transforms from a controlling agent into a personal educational partner for solving complex professional tasks, such as designing independent educational routes and preparing for international communication. The conducted analysis confirms that the implementation of the model allows for personalizing learning, yet requires the mitigation of risks associated with threats to academic integrity and the potential loss of critical thinking skills. The development of learning-strategic competence through artificial intelligence tools is a fundamental prerequisite for the readiness of future teachers for professional autonomy and lifelong learning. The scientific novelty of the work lies in the conceptual combination of strategic learning theories with the innovative potential of multimodal language models, which allows for the optimization of teacher training in the context of the digitalization of society.
venue: The scientific and methodological journal Foreign Languages

title_key: chatgpt s quality reliability and validity of concept inventory items|kuchemann
title: ChatGPT's quality: Reliability and validity of concept inventory items
abstract: Introduction: The recent advances of large language models (LLMs) have opened a wide range of opportunities, but at the same time, they pose numerous challenges and questions that research needs to answer. One of the main challenges are the quality and correctness of the output of LLMs as well as the overreliance of students on the output without critically reflecting on it. This poses the question of the quality of the output of LLMs in educational tasks and what students and teachers need to consider when using LLMs for creating educational items. In this work, we focus on the quality and characteristics of conceptual items developed using ChatGPT without user-generated improvements. Methods: For this purpose, we optimized prompts and created 30 conceptual items in kinematics, which is a standard topic in high-school level physics. The items were rated by two independent experts. Those 15 items that received the highest rating were included in a conceptual survey. The dimensions were designed to align with the ones in the most commonly used concept inventory, the Force Concept Inventory (FCI). We administered the designed items together with the FCI to 172 first-year university students. The results show that ChatGPT items have a medium difficulty and discriminatory index but they overall exhibit a slightly lower average values as the FCI. Moreover, a confirmatory factor analysis confirmed a three factor model that is closely aligned with a previously suggested expert model. Results and discussion: In this way, after careful prompt engineering, thorough analysis and selection of fully automatically generated items by ChatGPT, we were able to create concept items that had only a slightly lower quality than carefully human-generated concept items. The procedures to create and select such a high-quality set of items that is fully automatically generated require large efforts and point towards cognitive demands of teachers when using LLMs to create items. Moreover, the results demonstrate that human oversight or student interviews are necessary when creating one-dimensional assessments and distractors that are closely aligned with students' difficulties.

title_key: didactic conditions for implementing innovative technologies in teaching informatics disciplines based on the competence approach in vocational pre higher education institutions|olenyuk
title: Didactic conditions for implementing innovative technologies in teaching informatics disciplines based on the competence approach in vocational pre-higher education institutions
abstract: The article presents a comprehensive analysis and theoretical justification of didactic conditions that ensure the effective implementation of innovative technologies for teaching computer science disciplines in professional higher education institutions (PHCEs). It is substantiated that due to the dynamic transformation of the digital society, the training of future specialists at the junior bachelor's level requires a transition from a knowledge-centric paradigm to a competency-based approach. Within the framework of the study, a set of didactic conditions that contribute to the high-quality implementation of the developed teaching methods has been identified and specified. A comprehensive solution to the first condition includes the creation of an adaptive high-tech educational environment based on virtualization and containerization (for example, Docker and WSL2), which brings the educational process as close as possible to the real working conditions of the IT industry. The second condition is the systemic integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as an interactive assistant for students to promote the development of competencies in independent search, analysis and critical evaluation of information, while strictly adhering to the principles of academic integrity. Third, the fundamental prerequisite is the replacement of teaching aids by introducing practically-oriented cases and professionally-oriented laboratories, which will promote interdisciplinary communication and the application of skills. The study focuses on the issue that the introduction of new technologies is not an end in itself, but a means to achieve certain educational goals. The article substantiates that, provided the proposed conditions are met, the contradiction between the rapid development of IT and the inertia of traditional methodological support in colleges can be overcome. The practical significance of the article is that the proposed approaches can be applied by teachers of vocational pre-university education to update work programs and develop modern didactic content. Opportunities for further research are seen in experimentally testing the effectiveness of each of these conditions in the process of studying individual components of computer science.

title_key: exploring chatgpts potential as a supplementary feedback tool in english writing classes foreign languages education|
title: Exploring ChatGPT’s potential as a supplementary feedback tool in English writing classes. Foreign Languages Education
abstract: This study analyzes students’ use of ChatGPT prompts to explore its potential as a supplementary feedback tool in English writing classes. Thirty-one pre-service teachers participated and were divided into high, middle, and low groups based on their self-evaluation, standardized test scores, and essay scores prior to receiving ChatGPT feedback. The data sources included their two essays, ChatGPT prompts, questionnaires, and transcripts from the second writing conference. The ChatGPT prompts and questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and the writing conference transcripts were examined to understand the participants’ use of prompts. The results showed participants used prompts 40 times in the first assignment and 175 times in the second assignment. The average prompt usage increased from 1.5 times in the first assignment to 6.7 times in the second assignment. In terms of students’ levels, the high group used more prompts (5.58 times) than the middle (5 times) and the low groups (1.75 times). Notably, students who used ChatGPT commands five times or more were mostly from the high and middle groups. Differences in prompt usage patterns were also identified, with the high and middle groups engaging in more continuous and interactive conversations with ChatGPT. Students expressed satisfaction with ChatGPT’s feedback, particularly in vocabulary selection, grammar correction, and sentence generation.

title_key: claude binard md an influential french homeopath pediatrician general practitioner and author who was actively involved with the liga medicorum homoeopathica internationalis|yasgur
title: Claude Binard, MD — an influential French homeopath, pediatrician, general practitioner, and author, who was actively involved with the Liga Medicorum Homoeopathica Internationalis
abstract: Dr. Claude Binard noted for his long tenure and devotion to classical homeopathy and for the roles which he played in the French language versions of Warkentin's Reference Works and van Zandvoort's Complete Repertory , crossed the threshold at the age of 88. Beginning in 1963, Dr. Binard practiced classical homeopathy after having graduated from the Paris Faculty of Medicine. He was president of the Paris Liga Medicorum Homoeopathica Internationalis (LMHI) congress in 2014 and was awarded the “Membres d'Honneur” in 2023. [1] At that 2014 meeting he presented a case, which was well received, titled “Congenital Deformation and Long-term Miracle of the Simillimum?”—it was an Apis case. Previous to that, 19 years before, he submitted a detailed, lengthy discussion and case presentation devoted to Merc. viv . based on Dr. Pierre Schmidt's thought and that masters method of case interrogation—a thorough and excellent instructive piece. Binard received his high school education at Lycée Charlemagne in Paris, where he was from, and studied medicine in Paris choosing to specialize in pediatrics. Upon graduation he practiced at Saint Antoine Hospital in Paris in the 1970s. His chosen specialty, pediatrics, has familial roots as his grandmother was a midwife. She took great care of Claude as a child, and since she had no one to look after him when she was called day or night for a birth (at home at the time), she would take him along. He would wait patiently in the next room and recalled enjoying joyful moments shared with the family when the baby cried, meaning that the wait and birth were over. “He was the first newborn resuscitator in France. He resuscitated babies at home in the family living room! It was truly a different era! He worked with the famous French pediatrician Professor Minkowski. He was deeply traumatized when the latter asked him to perform a baby's autopsy. It was his first encounter with the death of a child.” – Maryvonne Cousin, MD [2] Soon thereafter he became interested in homeopathic medicine and began his training at Saint Antoine Hospital. During one of the initial classes at the hospital, he met a student who advised him to take classes with Dr. Pierre Schmidt (1894–1987). He did so and, in turn, became a disciple of that great master from Switzerland. Since that time he practiced solely homeopathy. As a child, he was cured of eczema of his hand with homeopathy. He left France to settle in Canada, ca. 1972–73, but was unable to practice medicine. This didn't stop him from continuing to practice his art. Soon thereafter he met David Warkentin (1951–2010) and worked with him on the development of the famous MacRepertory and ReferenceWorks software programs, as well as the French versions, which were released in the 1990s (see the group photo). Upon his return to France, ca. 1988–89, he ceased practicing pediatrics and established himself as a general practitioner of homeopathy. Binard taught at ACCE, a classical homeopathy school, in Paris. That is where Dr. Cousin met him, as she attended that school. He became Cousin's family doctor and treated her entire family. [3] David Warkentin's wonderful tool, Reference Works , was updated beginning in 2004 and Drs. Binard and Cousin worked on it until David's death. Binard took care of translating the application into French while Dr. Cousin formatted AFADH materials. They conducted daily software operational tests while remaining in contact with David via daily emails. Warkentin came to Paris to inaugurate this new software, which was met with great success. Claude became a distributor and seller of the French versions of MacRepertory and ReferenceWorks . Unfortunately, David's passing put an end to this collaborative venture. Claude also worked tirelessly with Roger van Zandvoort on translating and updating the Complete Repertory and was responsible for translating annual updates into French. [3] “Claude continued these activities until his last days, always staying up-to-date with current events. He was committed to sharing his knowledge and encouraged young and older homeopaths. He wrote several articles and thus devoted his life to promoting and transmitting homeopathy, a true art of healing.” – Dr. Maryvonne Cousin (email communication September 9, 2025). Yves Maillé, MD, a close friend of Binard (Aix en Provence, France) offered these comments via a July 16, 2025 email communication. Tribute to Dr. Claude Binard (July 17, 1936–July 15, 2025) “An old companion has just left us and 45 years of complicity are flying by. I met Claude in Montreal when I was a beginner in homeopathy. “I called him one day for my 18-month-old nephew who was losing consciousness despite a stay in the hospital. Claude, after a few questions, went to get a dose of China XM and put it under the tongue of the inert child who came back to life before our eyes almost instantly and began to play. I knew that day that homeopathy would be at the heart of my life and Claude would have been one of its ferments. “Claude was one of Pierre Schmidt's last students and was an excellent representative. From that time on, we continued to develop projects together and with my partner Anne-Marie Lacroix we had established a true friendship with Claude and his wife Dominique. Until a few months ago, Claude was present at the LMHI (LIGA) meetings and it was only in his last moments that his voice fell silent, although he had remained present until then despite his many health problems. Claude is for me an example of what homeopathy brings into our lives help and care for our patients, friendship, companionship, loyalty and so on...! Farewell my Friend, may my affection accompany you to the paradise of homeopaths.” Beginning in 1992, Binard worked with Warkentin and did all the translation for MacRepertory (but not Kent's Repertory). David spent a lot of time teaching him in order that it would become useful as a database for Kent Homeopathic Associates (KHA). Later, they began to work on ReferenceHomeo (Reference Works) with Maryvonne Cousin ([ Fig. 1 ]), a physician and friend. They created a database, which was favored and proved useful to their French colleagues. Others such as Drs. Marie Luc and Guy Loutan assisted but most of the work was done by Cousin. Part of Binard's life work was to make the homeopathy world more aware of and understanding of the contributions made by French homeopaths. For example, the works of Petroz and Gallavardin and others are found and referenced in the works of Allen, Hering, and Farrington, et cetera, and, in turn, became a part of Warkentin and van Zandvoort's labors. Fig. 1 Dr. Maryvonne Cousin, David Warkentin, and Dr. Claude Binard. “Claude I knew since 1995. A very amiable man who around that time took it on him to be the translator for Complete Repertory in the French language which he kept doing until very recently, despite his high age. I visited him and his wife a couple of times in Paris, it was always a joy to meet him. I will keep him dear in my memories.” – Roger van Zandvoort (email communication, 7–16–2025). title_key: exploring ai acceptance in higher education data analytics for accounting and auditing a tam driven pls sem analysis|jezovita
title: Exploring AI Acceptance in Higher Education Data Analytics for Accounting and Auditing: A TAM-Driven PLS-SEM Analysis
abstract: The objective of this research is to identify and evaluate the determinants of AI technology acceptance and usage intention in higher education courses focused on data analytics in accounting and auditing. The research sample comprises 281 students from the Faculty of Economics & Business at the University of Zagreb in Croatia. To conduct the analysis, we employed the original Technology Acceptance Model and the Partial Least Square-Structural Equation Modelling analytical approach. A central finding of this study is the dominant role of Perceived Ease of Use. Perceived Ease of Use has a fundamental position in shaping students’ perceptions. Although modifications of Technology Acceptance Model-based models do not include attitude towards use, in our research, this factor serves as an important channel from perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use to behavioral intention to use AI. Furthermore, in our study, behavioral intention to use has the strongest predictive power for actual use of AI. An important contribution of this article concerns the specifics of applying AI in teaching, namely data analytics, which is increasingly significant across various professions, especially in accounting and auditing. Data analytics is an area strongly affected by the development of AI, leading to many new and improved tools and methodologies that leverage generative AI. For university programs to adequately respond to market needs, it is important to understand how students perceive the application of artificial intelligence in learning data analytics, and to what extent they are ready to adopt new technologies that will shape their future professional development.

title_key: estimating the impact of industry 4 0 automation on curricular competence indicators in brazilian vocational education and training a mixed methods ai supported analysis|lima
title: Estimating the Impact of Industry 4.0 Automation on Curricular Competence Indicators in Brazilian Vocational Education and Training: A Mixed-Methods AI-Supported Analysis
abstract: Context: The Fourth Industrial Revolution has accelerated the integration of automation technologies into the world of work, raising important questions about the future of Vocational Education and Training (VET). While existing literature has primarily focused on the labor market impacts of automation, few studies have investigated its direct effects on VET curricula. This article addresses this gap by assessing how automation may influence the structure and content of technical courses offered by Brazil's National Service for Commercial Apprenticeship (Senac), one of the country's largest VET providers. Approach: We implemented a three-stage methodology to estimate the impact of automation on technical education: (i) Technological mapping, (ii) prompt development, and (iii) assessment. In the third stage, we combined human expertise with generative Artificial Intelligence tools (GPT-4 and Claude 2) to evaluate 2,100 Course Competency Indicators (CCIs) across 35 technical courses. This dual approach enabled a scalable yet context-sensitive analysis, leveraging both the depth of human judgment and the efficiency of AI. Findings: The technological mapping identified seven key categories of automation technologies: 3D/4D Printing and Modeling, Applied AI, Data Analytics, Digital Platforms and Applications, Extended Reality, IoT and Connected Devices, and Robotics. The developed prompt provided structured guidance for assessing automation impact on CCIs, including instructions for classifying technologies, estimating impact levels, and justifying the results. The assessment showed that 70.3% of the CCIs are at Medium (39.1%) or Low (31.2%) levels of automation impact, suggesting that the courses remain current and relevant, challenging the narrative of rapid obsolescence in technical education. Digital Platforms and Applications were the most frequently cited technology, appearing nearly three times more often than Applied AI and Data Analytics. In contrast, 3D/4D Modeling and Extended Reality had limited relevance in the current course content. Conclusions: This research contributes to global discussions on the future of VET in the context of rapid technological change. It also highlights how automation risk assessments can support curriculum development by identifying where updates or innovations are most needed. Strengthening the alignment between training programs and emerging labor market demands will be essential to ensuring inclusive, future-oriented vocational education.
venue: International Journal for Research in Vocational Education and Training

title_key: leveraging artificial intelligence enhanced technical and vocational education and training for sustainable skills and economic development in lagos state nigeria|bilau
title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Technical and Vocational Education and Training for Sustainable Skills and Economic Development in Lagos State, Nigeria
abstract: This study assessed the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to transform Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) pedagogy in Lagos State, addressing the persistent skills mismatch that has left over 40% of Nigerian youth unemployed while critical sectors face severe skilled personnel shortages. On the basis of systematic desk review of academic literature, policy documents, and industry reports published between 2015 and 2026, the study identifies five key AI technologies applicable to TVET including adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, virtual/augmented reality, AI chatbots, and predictive analytics. Drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology and Sen's Capability Approach, the study analyzes adoption barriers including unreliable infrastructure, severe shortages of AI-competent instructors, outdated curricula, inadequate funding, and policy fragmentation. The paper presents a conceptual framework linking AI-enhanced TVET to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals, with specific indicators calibrated for Lagos State's industrial ecosystem. Findings indicate that AI can optimize curriculum design through real-time labor market data, provide scalable hands-on training through simulation, and deliver personalized feedback to learners. The study proposes actionable recommendations for digital infrastructure, teacher up-skilling programs, localized AI content development, and ethical data governance frameworks. The study contributes to the literature on digital transformation in education through the development of a context-sensitive framework for the integration of AI integration in Nigerian TVET, with implications for other federating Nigerian states and developing economies facing similar skills challenges.

title_key: edugrader the ai powered grading assistant|ikovic
title: EduGrader: The AI-powered grading assistant
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) is reshaping assessment practices in higher education, particularly in grading open-ended questions. Traditional grading is time-consuming, prone to inconsistency, and difficult to scale for large classes. LLMs offer an opportunity to improve efficiency, consistency, and feedback frequency by leveraging their ability to understand and reason about natural language. This paper introduces EduGrader, an open-source, multi-model grading platform integrating several LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-Chat, GPT-5.1, and DeepSeek-Reasoner. EduGrader supports three grading strictness levels (lenient, neutral, strict) and generates numerical scores with concise explanations highlighting correct reasoning, missing concepts, and errors. The system operates in two modes: a provided reference-answer grading mode guided by instructor solutions and a generated reference-answer grading mode that automatically creates reference answers from course materials. All experiments are conducted in Serbian, a comparatively low resource language underrepresented in mainstream AI training data, extending AI assisted grading research beyond the dominant English-language context. EduGrader is evaluated on 686 real student responses from six university courses across two institutions, including free-text explanations and code-based answers. In its best performing configuration, the system achieves a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.90 with human graders while reducing grading workload and improving reliability, though it is intended to assist rather than replace instructors.

title_key: enhancing control system education through simulation assisted teaching focussing on analogy and pid controller optimization|colaco
title: Enhancing control system education through simulation assisted teaching: Focussing on analogy and PID controller optimization
abstract: This study demonstrated that simulation based experiential learning pedagogy using MATLAB Simscape and Copilot is an effective tool to reduce the theory practice gap in control systems education. Integrating Kolb’s cycle with AI-enhanced, segmented activities allowed students to understand the mechanical–electrical analogies and PID tuning, thereby preparing them for industry skillsets. With engineering curricula changing in the context of AI era, these kinds of pedagogies provide a scalable solution to the issue of rote learning. Due to the strong understanding of fundamental concepts, the students develop critical thinking to solve complex systems and face the challenges of the industry relevant problems with confidence and creativity. Finally, it is not the equations on the blackboard, but hands that transform virtual world into real knowledge, makes true teachers.

title_key: artificial intelligence and marketing education mapping current research and emerging patterns|alenova
title: Artificial intelligence and marketing education: mapping current research and emerging patterns
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing education and to assess the extent to which marketing education addresses technological transformation within education contexts. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a systematic bibliometric review to examine the intersection of AI and marketing education. In accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, 801 records were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection database and screened, resulting in the identification of 66 relevant scholarly articles. Visualization and analytical tools such as VOSviewer, Biblioshiny and Research Rabbit were applied to identify key publication outlets, authorship patterns, co-citation networks and thematic clusters. Findings Analysis reveals rapid growth in AI-related research after 2020, with dominant themes including digital pedagogy, ethical considerations, student competencies and the integration of generative AI tools. Despite this expansion, the literature remains fragmented and primarily conceptual, lacking robust empirical evidence on learning outcomes, cross-cultural dimensions and the long-term effects of AI in marketing curricula. Originality/value This research provides a comprehensive synthesis of the literature on AI in marketing education and outlines critical directions for future inquiry. It offers insights for educators and curriculum designers seeking to align marketing programs with emerging AI-driven practices. This review further emphasizes the need for competency-based and student-centred approaches that reflect the evolving global landscape of AI-enhanced learning. However, as the research domain is at an early stage of consolidation, the findings reflect both the promise and the fragmentations at the intersection of AI and marketing education.

title_key: machine learning based chatbot for enquiries a case study of anchor university lagos|aleburu
title: Machine Learning-Based Chatbot for Enquiries: A Case Study of Anchor University, Lagos
abstract: Effective communication in higher education is essential but often hindered by outdated methods that lead to inefficiencies and frustration. This study presents the development of a machine learning-based chatbot designed to handle university-related enquiries at Anchor University, Lagos. The chatbot was built using the Rasa framework and integrates Natural Language Processing (NLP), Natural Language Understanding (NLU), and the Gemini API to respond to complex student queries in real-time. The system provides quick and accurate responses to frequently asked questions (FAQs), improving the communication flow within the university by providing immediate, accurate information on topics such as admissions, academic programs, and campus services. Key performance metrics, including an intent recognition accuracy of 1.0 and a conversation accuracy of 0.812, illustrate the effectiveness of the chatbot. This paper highlights the design, methodology, performance, and potential improvements of AI-driven chatbot systems in educational settings.

title_key: innovation in teacher education in the artificial intelligence era reimagining pedagogical preparation through adaptive technologies and ethical governance|michael
title: Innovation in Teacher Education in the Artificial Intelligence Era: Reimagining Pedagogical Preparation through Adaptive Technologies and Ethical Governance
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming teaching, learning, and educational decision-making, yet many teacher education programs remain insufficiently prepared to develop the knowledge, skills, and ethical judgment required in AI-enabled classrooms. This conceptual paper reimagines pedagogical preparation as a human-centered, adaptive, and ethically governed process. It examines how adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, generative AI, and simulation environments can personalize teacher candidates’ learning, strengthen reflective practice, and enhance their capacity to design inclusive and responsive instruction. The paper proposes an integrated framework combining AI literacy, pedagogical content knowledge, data literacy, critical digital competence, and professional judgment. It argues that innovation should not be evaluated solely through technological adoption, but through its contribution to teacher agency, educational equity, learner well-being, and instructional quality. Ethical governance is positioned as foundational, with particular emphasis on transparency, privacy, accountability, bias mitigation, accessibility, academic integrity, and meaningful human oversight. The discussion further identifies essential institutional conditions, including faculty development, adequate digital infrastructure, participatory policy design, and continuous evaluation. By connecting adaptive technologies with ethical and pedagogical principles, the paper offers a roadmap for preparing teachers to use AI critically, creatively, and responsibly while preserving the relational and human core of education. Objectives: The study examines transformative innovations emerging at the intersection of artificial intelligence and teacher education, identifies systemic opportunities and ethical challenges accompanying these technologies, and proposes a conceptual framework for their sustainable integration within pre-service and in-service teacher preparation programs. Methods: A qualitative document analysis methodology was employed to systematically review 65 peer-reviewed empirical studies, policy documents, and institutional reports published between 2018 and 2025. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurrent patterns regarding AI adoption, pedagogical transformation, and structural barriers across diverse geographical and institutional contexts. Results: The findings indicate that AI innovations, including adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI conversational agents, and immersive virtual reality simulations, are fundamentally altering the landscape of teacher preparation. While these technologies afford personalized learning pathways, enhanced formative assessment capabilities, and expanded access to clinical teaching experiences, significant challenges persist concerning data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequity, and faculty resistance to pedagogical change. Conclusions: To harness the transformative potential of AI in teacher education, stakeholders must adopt an ethics-centered, equity-driven framework that prioritizes critical digital literacy, continuous professional development, and participatory governance structures. The study recommends the mandatory integration of AI-literacy competencies into teacher education curricula and the adoption of human-in-the-loop pedagogical models that position AI as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, the relational dimensions of teaching. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Teacher education; pre-service training; Digital pedagogy; Algorithmic ethics

title_key: construction and practice of a virtual real integrated practical teaching model driven by aigc and ai agents for higher vocational digital media education|zhou
title: Construction and Practice of a Virtual-Real Integrated Practical Teaching Model Driven by AIGC and AI Agents for Higher Vocational Digital Media Education
abstract: In digital media programs at higher vocational colleges, students usually learn tools in class but rarely carry a project from a client's brief to a delivered work. Generative AI tools and AI agents have entered professional production chains; in most curricula, though, they remain add-on demonstrations, and the virtual-real equipment in the media center is used mainly for demonstration rather than for graded assignments. This paper reports a redesign of the Photography and Videography course at Yibin Industrial Vocational and Technical College, built around a three-loop model that links online AI-assisted planning, offline multi-device shooting and delivery of industrial tasks. The course ran from March to early July 2026 with 180 first-year students in four classes. Evidence came from a pre/post survey with 176 valid responses, a catalogue of student works, and reviews by Sichuan Tourism Investment Group. Self-rated creative skills rose from 2.3 to 4.1 on a five-point scale, the share of works meeting enterprise acceptance standards rose from 52% to 89%, and 91% of students reported that they produced faster. In total the students completed more than 1,000 photographs and 102 videos. The paper describes the model, the course redesign and the empirical findings, and closes with the conditions under which the model can be transferred to comparable colleges.

title_key: cultivating critical thinking in future professionals through advanced information literacy and learning technologies|antonov
title: Cultivating Critical Thinking in Future Professionals through Advanced Information Literacy and Learning Technologies
abstract: In an era defined by information overload, Generative AI-driven content, and sophisticated misinformation, the ability to think critically has shifted from a desirable professional attribute to an essential one. Conventional educational frameworks often reduce information literacy to a procedural skill set for finding and citing sources, inadequately preparing students for the intricate nature of the modern digital landscape. In an attempt to bridge the educational gap, this paper designs and offers support for a new conceptual framework, which we term as Synergistic Framework for Critical Information Engagement (SFCIE). The specific research objective of this study is to develop an integrated and comprehensive framework that synergizes information literacy (IL) capabilities at an advanced level with modern learning technologies in higher education. This study targets higher education curricula and programs which prepare future professionals in a spectrum of fields, including but not limited to management, law, and health science, among many others. This paper follows the research design of a review of the literature and a conceptual development. This research thus reviews the development of IL and its pedagogical tools, the underlying cognitive abilities for critical thinking (CT), and the functional affordances of learning technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence tutors and collaborative digital workspaces to support these dimensions, especially in the case of the recent rise of Generative AI and its paradoxical effect for both supporting and undermining CT. The main finding of this article is an integrative framework of building and supporting CT at the intersection of core literacies, higher-order cognitive skills such as algorithmic thinking, source analysis, and ethical integration of information, and pedagogical methods enabled by learning technologies. SFCIE thus provides teachers and instructors with a principled approach for designing learning experiences that enable and support the development of robust CT. We concluded that higher education programs must progress beyond lower-order learning skills and take an integrative approach, putting pedagogy at the center, to better prepare graduates as professionals who are insightful, analytical, and ethically aware. The article also provides a blueprint for educators and higher education leaders to support CT in a world of increasing integration of AI and AI-powered systems.

title_key: balancing creativity efficiency and ethical practice through use of ai in typography and poster design education|gulacti
title: Balancing Creativity, Efficiency, and Ethical Practice Through Use of AI in Typography and Poster Design Education
abstract: This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in typography and poster design education, focusing on its impact on creative workflows, structural quality, and ethical considerations. Within a graduate Typography course at Yıldız Technical University, original movie posters from the 2023 Academy Awards “Best Picture” category were compared with posters generated by the ChatGPT 4.0 model. Using the Visual Design Principles and Elements Evaluation Form (VDPEEF), expert students evaluated both sets of posters based on design principles, structural features, and typographic elements. Statistical analysis conducted with SPSS revealed that while AI-generated posters demonstrated strong adherence to balance, alignment, and typographic hierarchy, they fell short in emotional depth, originality, and contextual interpretation when compared to human-designed posters. AI outputs showed greater structural variability and repetitive visual patterns, although their rapid generation speed positioned AI as an efficient tool for prototyping and large-scale production. Beyond typography, the study highlights broader educational implications of AI across fields such as language learning, STEM education, architecture, data analysis, and creative writing. It emphasizes the relevance of pedagogical frameworks such as TPACK and SAMR in guiding responsible AI integration. Overall, the findings suggest that AI serves most effectively as a complementary tool that supports—but does not replace—human creativity and cultural intuition. Future research should expand datasets, incorporate diverse evaluator groups, compare multiple AI models, and further investigate ethical, cultural, and cognitive dimensions of AI-assisted design processes. Keywords: AI-Assisted Design, Typography Education, Poster Design Evaluation, Creativity and Efficiency in Design, Educational Technology and Ethics

title_key: embedding ai literacy in philippine higher education a national strategy for workforce readiness in the age of artificial intelligence|baldosano
title: Embedding AI Literacy in Philippine Higher Education: A National Strategy for Workforce Readiness in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Philippine higher education has a problem that keeps getting worse. Students are using AI tools at record rates while their institutions have no real plan for it. Over 83% of Philippine students already use generative AI for academic work, yet fewer than half of all higher education institutions have clear policies on it, and the Philippines ranked last in the 2023 Asia-Pacific AI Readiness Index. This paper argues that embedding structured AI literacy programs across Philippine higher education is not optional. It is an economic and educational necessity. The argument rests on three things: the documented gap between student AI use and institutional readiness, the threat AI disruption poses to the Philippine workforce particularly the IT-BPM sector, and the existence of global frameworks that Philippine institutions can adopt right now. The cost of inaction is a generation of graduates entering labor markets where 39% of existing job skills are expected to become outdated by 2030.

title_key: effects of artificial intelligence chatbot integrated instruction on science positive experiences and attitudes toward artificial intelligence focusing on the unit of stellar types and evolution|
title: Effects of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot-Integrated Instruction on Science-Positive Experiences and Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence: Focusing on the Unit of Stellar Types and Evolution
abstract: This study examined the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot–integrated instruction with embedded scaffolding on high school students’ science-positive experiences and attitudes toward AI in the Earth science unit on stellar types and evolution. To this end, the researchers developed an instructional program grounded in the Exploratory Scientific Data Analysis Inquiry Model and designed an AI chatbot to support students’ inquiry processes and conceptual understanding. The participants were 138 11th-grade students, and a quasiexperimental one-group pre-test–post-test design was employed. The results indicated that the intervention significantly improved students’ science-positive experiences across all subdomains – affective experience in science learning, science self-concept, motivation for science learning, science career aspirations, and attitudes toward science. In addition, students’ attitudes toward AI significantly improved across cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions. Qualitative findings revealed that the AI chatbot’s immediate feedback and hints reduced students’ perceived cognitive burden in science learning and encouraged more active engagement in self-directed problem solving and collaborative inquiry. Students also came to perceive AI as a useful tool for learning, career exploration, and everyday problem-solving.

title_key: estimating the impact of industry 4 0 automation on curricular competence indicators in brazilian vocational education and training a mixed methods ai supported analysis|lima
title: Estimating the impact of industry 4.0 automation on curricular competence indicators in Brazilian vocational education and training. A mixed-methods AI-supported analysis
abstract: Context: The Fourth Industrial Revolution has accelerated the integration of automation technologies into the world of work, raising important questions about the future of Vocational Education and Training (VET). While existing literature has primarily focused on the labor market impacts of automation, few studies have investigated its direct effects on VET curricula. This article addresses this gap by assessing how automation may influence the structure and content of technical courses offered by Brazil's National Service for Commercial Apprenticeship (Senac), one of the country's largest VET providers. Approach: The authors implemented a three-stage methodology to estimate the impact of automation on technical education: (i) Technological mapping, (ii) prompt development, and (iii) assessment. In the third stage, they combined human expertise with generative Artificial Intelligence tools (GPT-4 and Claude 2) to evaluate 2,100 Course Competency Indicators (CCIs) across 35 technical courses. This dual approach enabled a scalable yet context-sensitive analysis, leveraging both the depth of human judgment and the efficiency of AI. Findings: The technological mapping identified seven key categories of automation technologies: 3D/4D Printing and Modeling, Applied AI, Data Analytics, Digital Platforms and Applications, Extended Reality, IoT and Connected Devices, and Robotics. The developed prompt provided structured guidance for assessing automation impact on CCIs, including instructions for classifying technologies, estimating impact levels, and justifying the results. The assessment showed that 70.3% of the CCIs are at Medium (39.1%) or Low (31.2%) levels of automation impact, suggesting that the courses remain current and relevant, challenging the narrative of rapid obsolescence in technical education. Digital Platforms and Applications were the most frequently cited technology, appearing nearly three times more often than Applied AI and Data Analytics. In contrast, 3D/4D Modeling and Extended Reality had limited relevance in the current course content. Conclusions: This research contributes to global discussions on the future of VET in the context of rapid technological change. It also highlights how automation risk assessments can support curriculum development by identifying where updates or innovations are most needed. Strengthening the alignment between training programs and emerging labor market demands will be essential to ensuring inclusive, future-oriented vocational education. (DIPF/Orig.)

title_key: proceedings of the 20th international cdio conference|rytilahti
title: Proceedings of the 20th International CDIO Conference
abstract: Large language models(LLMs) are transforming how teachers work. In this paper, we observe several experimental approaches to generating software programming exercises by utilizing ChatGPT, a popular and open LLM. The generation of these exercises was tightly connected to a large Python programming course that was targeted at students studying in Information Technology, Software Engineering, and Computing. We experimented with three separate approaches. In the first one, we generated new programming exercises with a specific topic using theme injection. In the second one, we generated variations of existing programming exercises by changing the theme or content. In the third one, we generated hybrid exercises by injecting original programming exercises with additional topics or other related exercises. Based on our results, all three approaches showed potential but also revealed limitations. The exercise generation with theme injection can produce fully functional exercises. However, these exercises could appear to students as too generic or erroneous. The exercise variations seem to retain the semantic meaning of the original exercise quite well while still using different context. We also tested the variations in a large introductory programming course and found out that the students could not distinguish them from human-generated exercises in style or quality. The hybrid exercises were built upon the idea of exploring how close we are to fully adaptive learning environments in the field of programming education. The current results of this approach show that we need to do further experimentation to maybe reach the goal. All in all, it was evident that LLMs can be a useful tool in assisting teachers in generating exercises. Even with certain coherent limitations, they are useful in particular cases. We conclude our article by discussing the future possibilities of LLMs, including but not limited to dynamic, automatically generated exercises and fully adaptive learning environments.

title_key: combating brain rot reimagining hr for the distracted generation with ai and adaptive learning systems|v
title: Combating Brain Rot: Reimagining HR for the Distracted Generation with AI and Adaptive Learning Systems
abstract: The main purpose of this research is to achieve employee’s efficiency in organization where efficient employees directly contribute to organizational goals, growth and profits. As people are the driving force behind every organization, it becomes essential to understand their challenges. Especially, in this distracted generation where brain rot, short attention spans, and digital fatigue are common. this study aims to explore how Artificial intelligence (AI) solutions can help human resource (HR) practices adapt to these challenges and support both employee and students, who are future employees. This study uses primary data approach, collecting responses through google forms and in person surveys. Over 124 participants shared their perspectives, and the data was analyzed using chi-square, spearson correlation, descriptive statistics. findings show how strong interest in AI- driven solutions such as gamified daily tasks with rewards, AI- based monitoring tools for detecting early sign of stress (with privacy assured), and adaptive micro-learning platforms that delivers short 2- minute lessons in the forms of videos, quizzes, and reels. Respondents were also open to AI assistants that track work patterns and suggests breaks or reminders. These results highlights that people are not only aware of “brain rot” but are willing to embrace AI solutions to overcome it. Overall, the study spotlight that the employee efficiency is the backbone of any organization. if the employees are distracted and lack focus, organizational reputation and performance will be affected drastically. By combining AI into HR systems, organizations can help foster focus, engagement, and wellbeing of the employees. This research insist that AI-based adaptive systems are not only appealing but also necessary for both current employees and future generations of students.
