title_key: investigating pre service elementary teachers competencies in utilizing digital media and edtech for english instruction|kwon
title: Investigating Pre-service Elementary Teachers’ Competencies in Utilizing Digital Media and EdTech for English Instruction
abstract: The present study implemented Project-Based Learning (PBL) to enhance pre-service teachers’ competencies in using EdTech, focusing on learning and practicing various digital tools for elementary English instruction. Throughout a six-week PBL course, 65 pre-service teachers participated in activities such as creating digital storybooks using text-to-speech (TTS) tools, developing AI chatbots, and designing interactive experiences in the metaverse. Despite the limited timeframe, pre-service teachers effectively developed a strong understanding of new EdTech tools and their classroom applications. Participants self-evaluated their EdTech application skills through preand post-surveys, revealing a meaningful increase in their self-evaluation scores after the course. The results suggest that the digital competence development program experienced through this study significantly improved the participants’ perceived abilities to utilize EdTech in their teaching practices. Additionally, the AI chatbots, metaverse spaces, and digital storybooks produced by the pre-service teachers were deemed suitable for elementary English classes, displaying a high level of completeness.

title_key: re imagining patient safety education global insights and practical pathways for implementation|ashokka
title: Re-imagining patient safety education: Global insights and practical pathways for implementation
abstract: To Err is Human’ by the Institute of Medicine in 1999 was transformational to healthcare, leading to awareness, with an emphasis on patient safety research, healthcare processes, and medical education.[1] Patient harm reported globally, relates chiefly to medication errors (one in every 30 patients), surgical errors (10% of all preventable healthcare harm events), patient misidentification errors (12.3% of all sentinel events), and diagnostic errors (10% of deaths). Multiple interconnected factors (system and organisational factors, technological, human factors and behaviours, patient-related and external factors) are implicated in unsafe practices and the extent of harm that results, with 80% of them being preventable.[2] There is paucity of data from resource poor settings on the prevalence of near misses and near fatal events, and these remain largely under-reported. This makes it hard for global initiatives and patient safety reforms to be designed and contextualised.[3] We discuss the current global patient safety frameworks and the need for patient safety strategies and educational initiatives to be suited for the diverse nature of healthcare settings. We outline an educational strategy to navigate the limitations in implementing the goal of safe healthcare and provide insights for integrating technology to enhance patient safety. PATIENT SAFETY IN HEALTHCARE SYSTEMS The World Health Organisation (WHO), by providing a broad overview, defines patient safety as “a framework of organised activities that creates cultures, processes, procedures, behaviours, technologies and environments in healthcare, that consistently and sustainably lower risks, reduce the occurrence of avoidable harm, make errors less likely and reduce the impact of harm when it does occur.”[4] Patient safety in healthcare systems is based on six core principles: error prevention, transparent reporting and learning, standardisation and best practice, technology and automation, patient engagement, and having an organisational culture of safety. The WHO Global Action Plan (2021–2030) advocates a six-step framework for enhancing patient safety that includes healthcare worker education, enhancing skills and safety.[5] PATIENT SAFETY EDUCATION: OVERVIEW AND COMPETENCIES There are existing frameworks of patient safety competencies that have been in place for more than a decade. The WHO patient safety curriculum, launched in 2009, was originally modelled based on the Australian Patient Safety Education Framework (APSEF) that outlines comparable patient safety goals.[6-8] This curriculum is designed to achieve the core patient safety knowledge, skills, and expected behaviours with levels ranging from foundational patient safety competencies (Level 1) to organisational competencies (Level 4). Entrustable professional activities (EPA) provide an operational construct for ascertaining competence and progression to individual clinical practice.[9,10] Common themes across the majority of frameworks include error prevention, risk management, patient safety culture, and communication [Table 1].Table 1: Summary of patient safety curricular frameworks and guidesThe Canadian Patient Safety Institute (CPSI) prioritises competencies for team safety by optimising human and environmental factors.[11] The European Network for Patient Safety [EUNetPaS] advocates emphasis on context specificity with patient centric and team oriented approaches.[12] The United Kingdom National Health Service (UK NHS) outlines a five-level multi-professional patient safety syllabus, articulating the steps for progression from essential to advanced patient safety.[13] For the developing nations, the priority would be error prevention and reducing communication breakdowns, especially in high acuity and high risk areas. Developed settings, having established a culture of safety, with systems and processes in place, need to be vigilant to identify threats to compliance. The system needs to empower teams to achieve progressively tiered patient safety competencies. For a healthcare system to adopt these patient safety frameworks, there needs to be a good understanding of the diverse nature of these settings and awareness of limitations in implementation. DIVERSE HEALTHCARE SETTINGS AND PATIENT SAFETY PRIORITIES The healthcare systems, even in the developed settings, seem to be variably equipped with a stark contrast between the wealthy metropolises and the impoverished cities. There is a relative sparsity of reforms, health, and manpower resources and supplies. In the undeveloped settings, the concept of patient safety and its implementations, as an integral part of the holistic care of patients, is frequently ill-defined.[14] Meticulously planned patient safety governance, implementation of care pathways, and patient safety systems are imperative. Championing patient safety through education and prevention of harm is vital in differentially resourced settings.[15] LIMITATIONS IN IMPLEMENTATIONS OF PATIENT SAFETY EDUCATION AND CURRICULUM There are inherent difficulties in the implementation of patient safety education at varying levels. These include limited understanding of risk in healthcare and poor stakeholders’ buy in with implementation weaknesses in educational reforms. Suboptimal leadership commitment to patient safety education results in unstructured educational governance and poor curricular coordination and planning. There is limited agility to alter curricula to make them effective and contextually aligned. There is a lack of or insufficient role modelling of patient safety, medical, nursing, and allied health champions, with operational constraints and unfamiliarity of educators and faculty in teaching patient safety. There is limited availability of educators, mentorship, and continued training about evolving safety issues in healthcare.[15] Cultural barriers are a significant limitation to implementation. These include redundant and outdated practices with a resistance to change, or an aversion to newer evidence-based workflows. Socio-cultural practices such as strong hierarchical norms and beliefs affect societal behaviour and result in poor compliance or adherence to recommended safe practice initiatives. IMPLEMENTATION OF GLOBAL PATIENT SAFETY EDUCATION AND STANDARDS The approach to patient safety implementation and education needs to include multiple levels of oversight: government and regulatory bodies, hospitals, health services, and local stakeholders within the healthcare. This will ensure that the standard of care is continuously delivered. The factors or components that may influence patient safety implementation are outlined in Table 2.[13]Table 2: Outline of factors that influence the implementation of patient safety educational initiatives and educational strategiesKey strategies for patient safety education in the setting of clinical management and care include error prevention and management, patient empowerment, education and training, and patient safety administration. For educational interventions to be effective, there needs to be alignment between contextual needs and educational initiatives, with structured implementation in clinical settings, where the impact is meaningful and clinical educator role models are visible. PATIENT SAFETY CONTINUUM AND CONTINUOUS PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT We propose a patient safety educational continuum, where principles of patient safety need to be introduced in foundational years and built upon subsequently [Figure 1]. Layering of past experiences and promoting conceptual learning is enabled with updated patient safety knowledge, skills, and behaviours to eliminate preventable harm that arises from evolving threats.[16]Figure 1: Patient safety education continuum and the various domains across the learning trajectory. Teaching and learning tools and assessment are an integral part of the overall portfolio-based demonstration of attainment of patient safety competencies. UG = undergraduate, PG = postgraduate, CPD = continuous professional development, Sim = simulation, PS = patient safetyThis ‘roadmap’ will help to guide the learner in understanding patient safety essentials while progressing to provide basic and advanced safe patient care. The range of educational tools (lectures, in-person and web-based resources, small-group interactive teaching methods, technology and game-based initiatives) and assessments offer learner-adjusted teaching modalities. These educational initiatives equip and enable error management (error recognition, reporting, mitigation, and prevention). A portfolio-based repository of learning, by embedding formative and summative assessments, self-reflections, and faculty feedback, will improve the effectiveness of patient safety educational endeavours.[17] TECHNOLOGY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN PATIENT SAFETY Technology has enhanced the quality of care through continued efforts to improve diagnostic accuracy, data management, robotics and minimally invasive surgeries, telemedicine, and care in remote settings. Enhancements in wearable technology, continuous monitoring systems, health information exchange, and functionalities that are enabled with Artificial Intelligence (AI) are in place. AI encompasses three approaches: deep learning (complex thinking), machine learning (repetitive tasks), and natural language processing (predictive intelligence from patterns in written language).[18] A review of the potential for AI in enhancing patient safety has shown that AI has the promise for improving outcomes when complex unstructured data are analysed. AI may provide accurate predictions for adverse drug events and diagnostic errors and for the prediction of decompensation and offering safety alerts.[19] AI-driven Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) have shown enhanced quality of care with 30% improvement in medication errors.[20] The addition of sensors and wearables enhances fall for this review included paediatric for metabolic regulations (e.g. blood sugar), and provides a comprehensivew vital signs review. They enhance early predictions, preempt catastrophic events, and prompt the user for time sensitive corrective measures or actions. Introduction of ‘care robots’ when deployed for repetitive tasks like dispensing non-critical supplies and basic interviewing and monitoring has freed the trained professionals to perform complex interactions of caring that cannot be automated. There are inherent biases in AI technology with threats to reliability at the foundational input stage (non-diverse representative data). There are biases in the algorithm coding and construction stage (testing and training for validity) and at the end user human–computer interaction interface.[18] We advocate robust regulatory measures that mandate better transparency in declaring development algorithms that embed AI-based predictive technology. We need legislation for the inclusion of diverse patient profiles and end-user education to reduce these biases. Safety systems, continued vigilance, periodic review of accuracy and quality of outputs of technology, and AI-enabled patient care environments are mandatory. PATIENT SAFETY LEADERSHIP AND EXCELLENCE Excellence in safe patient care requires dynamic leadership that is actively engaged, enabling a culture of safety with proactive problem-solving and resource allocation.[21] The leadership teams need to continuously engage all care facilities through active efforts such as patient safety walkabout programs that help to discover and relay realistic on-the-ground care concerns and operational issues, or resistance to change.[22] The WHO has established frameworks for training healthcare leaders to ensure effective patient safety outcomes. Improvements in patient safety can be achieved through impetus from political and regulatory bodies that enable policies, through institutional strategies for enabling a culture of safety, and by execution at the individual level. Establishing a local, regional, and national network of patient safety professionals, quality and safety specialists would help in steering towards wider acceptance and implementation of patient safety principles. Quality of care can be ascertained and periodically assessed through standards ensured by international (Joint Commission Internationale, JCI) and national accrediting bodies (National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare providers, NABH). These ensure currency in high-quality patient-centred and process-driven safe standard of care that is on par with global benchmarks. We recommend regular accreditation exercises to be considered for healthcare settings. The preparation for achieving accreditation success improves the patient safety culture achieved through rigour in education and stringent quality control measures within the context. We need to encourage patient safety education and research collaboratives across international settings. The aim of this collaborative would be to achieve a repository of safety issues, critical incidents, and pattern recognition across diverse healthcare systems.[23] Stratifying the threats across healthcare systems, while developing and customising teaching and learning modalities, will help overcome knowledge deficits. These initiatives will offer opportunities to learn from untoward events, akin to how the international civil aviation organisation transparently publishes final reports of incidents.[24] Implementation research that provides data on the educational effectiveness of teaching and learning tools needs to evolve beyond the lower levels of Kirkpatrick’s grades (self-reported satisfaction and efficacy) towards translational outcomes of error prevention and reduction of patient harm and conservation of resources.[25] CONCLUSION The WHO patient safety educational initiatives have helped with the global patient safety curricular structure. There are contextual limitations to implementation resulting from disproportionate resources for clinical care, diverse care settings, and priorities. There is a paucity of educational impetus from organisations, leadership, and governing bodies in differentially resourced settings. An overview of the existing patient safety curricular guides and the need for an educational continuum from foundational years to individual and interprofessional clinical care is proposed. Technology and AI-enhanced clinical care are evolving to show clinical effectiveness, with an imperative for better regulation of design, development, inclusion, implementation, and vigilance. There is a need for involvement of all components of the healthcare environment (patient care, staff well-being, resource allocation, patient safety culture, environment, and leadership) for patient safety education to be effective. Establishing patient safety systems with local, regional, national, and international networks, inclusive of patient safety educators and researchers, will help align the priorities, actions, and outcomes. title_key: chatbots as english conversation partners for enhancing academic conversation skills and willingness to communicate in english in china|lei
title: Chatbots as English Conversation Partners for Enhancing Academic Conversation Skills and Willingness to Communicate in English in China
abstract: This study assessed artificial intelligence chatbots as English conversation partners and examined their relationship with the academic conversation skills and willingness to communicate in academic English among EFL learners in China. Specifically, it described the respondents’ profile in terms of year level, self-rated English proficiency, and frequency of AI chatbot use for English learning; assessed the effectiveness of AI chatbots in terms of interaction modality and interface, dialogue management, language understanding, response generation, and feedback functions; determined the level of academic conversation skills and willingness to communicate; tested differences when respondents were grouped according to profile; and examined the relationships among the major variables. The study employed a quantitative descriptive, comparative, and correlational research design. Data were gathered from 100 EFL learners using structured survey and rubric-based instruments. The data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, analysis of variance, and Pearson product-moment correlation. The findings showed that most respondents were 2nd Year students, had Intermediate self-rated English proficiency, and used AI chatbots Sometimes for English learning. AI chatbots were generally assessed as Effective, with an overall mean of 2.83. Interaction Modality and Interface obtained the highest mean of 3.29, while Feedback Functions obtained the lowest mean of 2.41 and was interpreted as Less Effective. The respondents’ academic conversation skills were generally Low, with an overall mean of 2.43. Clarity and Elaboration of Ideas in Academic Interaction was the strongest area, while Effectiveness of Turn-Taking and Topic Management was the weakest. Similarly, willingness to communicate in academic English was generally Low, with an overall mean of 2.40. Engagement in Academic Discussion Tasks was the highest-rated area, while Risk-Taking in English Communication was the lowest. No significant differences were found in the respondents’ assessment of AI chatbots, academic conversation skills, and willingness to communicate when grouped according to profile variables. However, significant positive relationships were found between AI chatbots and academic conversation skills, between AI chatbots and willingness to communicate, and between academic conversation skills and willingness to communicate. The study concluded that AI chatbots have meaningful instructional value as English conversation partners, particularly in providing accessible interaction and response models for academic English practice. However, chatbot use should be guided by teachers because feedback, pragmatic competence, turn-taking, communicative control, and risk-taking remain areas needing improvement. Based on the findings, an AI-supported academic conversation and communicative confidence program was proposed to strengthen learners’ academic conversation skills and willingness to communicate through chatbot-assisted practice, teacher scaffolding, pragmatic feedback, peer interaction, and low-pressure speaking tasks.
venue: International Journal of Social Science and Education Research

title_key: constructing a multidimensional integrated and collaborative education system for cultivating new quality talent in painting majors in the era of ai teachers|yu
title: Constructing a Multidimensional, Integrated, and Collaborative Education System for Cultivating New-Quality Talent in Painting Majors in the Era of AI Teachers
abstract: The rapid iteration of generative artificial intelligence has reshaped the creative modes, aesthetic forms, and industrial ecosystem of the traditional painting industry. The conventional talent cultivation model in painting programs, which emphasizes technical training while paying insufficient attention to innovation and interdisciplinary integration, can no longer meet the developmental needs of the art industry in the AI era. New-quality talent emphasizes creativity and innovation, human–AI collaborative competence, interdisciplinary integration literacy, and industry adaptability, and has become a core orientation for talent cultivation in painting programs at higher education institutions. Against the backdrop of AI-enabled art education, this paper takes multidimensional integration and collaborative education as its central approach, focuses on frontline teaching reform practices, and draws on real cases of curriculum reform, project-based training, and industry–education collaboration in university painting programs. From multiple dimensions, including curriculum integration, teacher–student collaboration, industry–education linkage, and the integration of scientific and technological innovation, this study explores pathways for constructing a new-quality talent cultivation system for painting majors. It aims to address such pain points in traditional painting education as homogenized teaching, rigid skill training, and insufficient innovation, thereby providing practical and implementable references for the digital transformation and high-quality talent cultivation of painting programs in higher education.
venue: Journal of educational theory and practice.

title_key: assessing chatgpts capability as a new age standardized patient qualitative study|cross
title: Assessing ChatGPT’s Capability as a New Age Standardized Patient: Qualitative Study
abstract: Background: Standardized patients (SPs) have been crucial in medical education, offering realistic patient interactions to students. Despite their benefits, SP training is resource-intensive and access can be limited. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly with large language models such as ChatGPT, present new opportunities for virtual SPs, potentially addressing these limitations. objectives: This study aims to assess medical students' perceptions and experiences of using ChatGPT as an SP and to evaluate ChatGPT's effectiveness in performing as a virtual SP in a medical school setting. Methods: This qualitative study, approved by the American University of Antigua Institutional Review Board, involved 9 students (5 females and 4 males, aged 22-48 years) from the American University of Antigua College of Medicine. Students were observed during a live role-play, interacting with ChatGPT as an SP using a predetermined prompt. A structured 15-question survey was administered before and after the interaction. Thematic analysis was conducted on the transcribed and coded responses, with inductive category formation. Results: Thematic analysis identified key themes preinteraction including technology limitations (eg, prompt engineering difficulties), learning efficacy (eg, potential for personalized learning and reduced interview stress), verisimilitude (eg, absence of visual cues), and trust (eg, concerns about AI accuracy). Postinteraction, students noted improvements in prompt engineering, some alignment issues (eg, limited responses on sensitive topics), maintained learning efficacy (eg, convenience and repetition), and continued verisimilitude challenges (eg, lack of empathy and nonverbal cues). No significant trust issues were reported postinteraction. Despite some limitations, students found ChatGPT as a valuable supplement to traditional SPs, enhancing practice flexibility and diagnostic skills. Conclusions: ChatGPT can effectively augment traditional SPs in medical education, offering accessible, flexible practice opportunities. However, it cannot fully replace human SPs due to limitations in verisimilitude and prompt engineering challenges. Integrating prompt engineering into medical curricula and continuous advancements in AI are recommended to enhance the use of virtual SPs.

title: 생성형 AI와 교육용 로봇을 연계한 초등 실과 수업 모형 탐색: 블록기반 코딩에서 바이브 코딩으로
abstract: The purpose of this study is to explore and propose Vibe Coding as an alternative instructional approach suitable for elementary Practical Arts education in response to the limitations of grammar-centered coding education in the era of generative AI. In this study, vibe coding refers to natural language–based programming practices, whereas Vibe Coding denotes the instructional approach conceptualized for classroom use. As an initial phase of design-based research, this study employed a combination of literature review and implementation research. Based on these analyses, the study designed an instructional sequence based on V–I–B–E (Visualize–Input–Bridge– Execute/Edit) as a structured framework that integrates natural language, generative AI, and educational robots, and examined its feasibility through implementation scenarios. Expert content validity verification (CVI) provided preliminary support for the appropriateness and classroom feasibility of the proposed the V-I-B-E procedural framework and the four-lesson plan. The findings indicate that Vibe Coding demonstrates strong educational potential by lowering grammatical barriers to programming through a natural language–AI–robot execution structure, while repositioning learners as designers of problem-solving solutions rather than mere code writers. Furthermore, the V-I-B-E procedural framework aligns closely with the 2022 revised Practical Arts curriculum, particularly in its emphasis on technical problem-solving processes, artificial intelligence understanding, and creative and convergent competencies. By conceptualizing generative AI as a cognitive agent that mediates and extends learners’ thinking, the proposed model offers high applicability for elementary Practical Arts education.
venue: Journal of Korean Practical Arts Education

title_key: the innovation of college english multimodal teaching from the perspective of artificial intelligence literacy an empirical analysis based on 127 questionnaires|li
title: THE INNOVATION OF COLLEGE ENGLISH MULTIMODAL TEACHING FROM THE PERSPECTIVE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE LITERACY--AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS BASED ON 127 QUESTIONNAIRES
abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the college English teaching ecosystem. The challenge of how to maintain the core value of language teaching in the face of the widespread integration of AI has become a new, urgent imperative for college English education. Based on survey data from 127 college students, this paper analyzes the current status and deficiencies of students' Artificial Intelligence Literacy (AIL) across four dimensions: AI knowledge, AI skills, AI attitude and values, and AI ethics. The results indicate significant shortcomings among students in prompt engineering and the critical evaluation of AI-generated content. Addressing these issues, this paper proposes an innovative model for college English teaching based on GenAI applications, promoting the synergistic development of students' language proficiency and AI literacy. AI literacy education (AILE) should be embedded in the language learning process, activating learners' meaning construction and creativity through multimodal tasks to achieve technology-enabled innovation in college English multimodal teaching.
venue: Trends in Social Sciences and Humanities Research

title_key: data driven precision diagnosis and personalized learning practice for data structureshybrid intelligent teaching exploration based on pta and xuexitong|
title: Data-Driven Precision Diagnosis and Personalized Learning Practice for Data Structures—Hybrid Intelligent Teaching Exploration Based on PTA and Xuexitong
abstract: 针对《数据结构》课程教学中长期存在的“指针恐惧症”、“递归理解难”、“调试效率低”、“分层教学缺失”四大核心痛点，本研究构建了“PTA数据感知–混合智能诊断–学习通平台干预”三位一体的智能化教学体系。通过PTA平台自动化采集学生学习行为数据，运用聚类分析与开源大语言模型(如ChatGLM-6B)进行学习困境诊断，依托学习通平台实现精准化教学干预。在一项为期16周的准实验研究中，实验组(60人)采用上述模式，对照组(60人)接受传统教学。结果显示：实验组调试时间缩短33.3%，指针与递归题型正确率从55.3%和49.7%分别提升至76.8%和71.2%，教师重复答疑工作量减少41.7%。大语言模型在153个代码错误样本上的诊断准确率达86.9%，K-Means聚类将学生划分的三个学习群体特征可解释性良好。半结构化访谈显示，实验组学生普遍认可诊断推送的针对性和实用价值。本研究为计算机类专业课程的教育数字化转型提供了可复制的实践案例。To address the four long-standing core pain points in the teaching of the Data Structures course—namely “pointer phobia,” “difficulty in understanding recursion,” “low debugging efficiency,” and “lack of tiered instruction”—this study constructs a three in one intelligent teaching system that integrates “PTA data perception, hybrid intelligent diagnosis, and Xuexitong platform intervention.” By automatically collecting students’ learning behavior data through the PTA platform, employing clustering analysis and an open source large language model (e.g., ChatGLM 6B) to diagnose learning difficulties, and relying on the Xuexitong platform for precise instructional intervention, a 16 week quasi experimental study was conducted with an experimental group (60 students) adopting the above model and a control group (60 students) receiving traditional teaching. The results show that the experimental group reduced debugging time by 33.3%, increased accuracy on pointer and recursion related problem types from 55.3% and 49.7% to 76.8% and 71.2%, respectively, and cut teachers’ repetitive question answering workload by 41.7%. The large language model achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 86.9% on 153 code error samples, and the K Means clustering produced three learning groups with good interpretability. Semi structured interviews indicated that students in the experimental group generally recognized the relevance and practical value of the diagnostic feedback and resource recommendations. This study provides a replicable practice case for the digital transformation of education in computer related programs.

title_key: pelatihan pembuatan komik ai dan dampaknya terhadap hasil belajar|kurnia
title: Pelatihan Pembuatan Komik AI dan Dampaknya terhadap Hasil Belajar
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates new opportunities for teachers to design learning materials that are more visual, contextual, and efficient. Digital comics are a promising medium because they integrate text, images, dialogue, and narrative into a coherent learning experience. This Community Service Program (PkM) aimed to improve elementary school teachers’ competence in producing AI-assisted educational comics and to examine their implications for learning-material quality and student learning outcomes. The program was conducted at SDN 01 Pagi on May 23, 2026, involving 10 teachers: six classroom teachers, two subject teachers, and two supporting teachers. The activities consisted of needs identification, conceptual instruction, demonstration, hands-on practice, mentoring, product presentation, and evaluation. Evaluation used pretest-posttest scores, a participant satisfaction questionnaire, and product observation. The mean pretest score increased from 57.2 to 84.6 in the posttest, representing a 27.4-point gain (47.9%). Participant satisfaction reached 92.1%, while the quality of the resulting comic products reached 92.0%. All participants produced at least one AI-assisted digital comic. These results indicate that the training effectively strengthened teachers’ readiness and competence in using AI to develop innovative learning media. However, because the program did not directly measure students’ test scores before and after using the comics, the impact on student learning outcomes should be interpreted as a pedagogical implication supported by previous research rather than direct causal evidence. Further mentoring and classroom trials are recommended to establish stronger evidence of effects on learning outcomes.
authors: ["Heri Kurnia", "Aeng Muhidin", "Abd. Chaidir Marasabessy", "Ainayya Fathiyyaturrahma", "Zulkarnain Arif"]

title_key: eesd special issue ai and datadriven methods in earthquake engineering part 2|lu
title: EESD special issue: AI and data‐driven methods in earthquake engineering – (Part 2)
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in earthquake engineering research, as it offers new possibilities for understanding, predicting, and mitigating the effects of earthquakes and related hazards. In the coming years, there will be continued research in AI-informed earthquake engineering that is focusing on ground motion modeling, geotechnical engineering, structural analysis, seismic design, health monitoring, multi-hazard assessment, and other areas, to enhance the safety and resilience of buildings and infrastructure. This is Part 2 of the special issue, whose topics include geotechnical engineering, structural analysis, design, health monitoring, damage evaluation, and seismic risk assessment. The first three articles in the Part 2 issue examine the application of AI and data-driven methods to geotechnical earthquake engineering. Hudson, Ulmer, Zimmaro, Kramer, Stewart, and Brandenberg propose an automated method for discretizing soil layers in cone penetration test (CPT) profiles using unsupervised machine learning (ML). The method aims to overcome the limitations of manual approaches that heavily rely on the analyst's experience and subjective judgment, which may lead to unrealistic results. Automated layer detection is achieved using a combination of agglomerative clustering and two cost functions to identify the optimal number of layers. The proposed algorithm is tested using 272 CPT profiles from the next generation liquefaction (NGL) database and is currently being used to develop liquefaction triggering and manifestation models. The results indicate that the proposed method has the potential to eliminate the bias induced by engineers. In spite of this, the authors recommend that the results from the automated detection be visually reviewed to ensure their validity. The paper by Hu, Xiong, Zhang, and Wang develops an approach to enhance the prediction accuracy of Bayesian network (BN) models used to evaluate earthquake-induced liquefaction settlement. The study deals with a specific limitation in existing BN models that require discretization of continuous variables, which limits predictions to categorical outcomes or ranges of settlement values. The authors address this challenge by proposing a hybrid approach that integrates domain knowledge with the hill-climbing algorithm in the formulation of a continuous BN regression model. The required conditional probability distributions of the parameters that define the BN model are computed based on historical liquefaction-induced settlement data and a Gaussian process learner. Using five-fold cross-validation, the authors show that the continuous BN model provides better generalization performance compared to previous approaches including those that employ the discrete BN classification strategy, simplified estimators such as the Tokimatsu–Seed and Ishihara–Yoshimine methods as well as an artificial neural network (ANN) model. Zhang, Ayello, Honegger, Bozorgnia, and Taciroglu develop an ML -based approach to predict the seismic response of fault-crossing natural gas pipelines, with the aim of improving the efficiency of time-consuming simulations. The study used the results from 217K nonlinear finite element analyses (FEA) for training and testing. Regression models based on ANNs are used as surrogate models for prediction. The input features cover various combinations of soil, structure, and fault attributes, and the output variable is the pipeline response under fault rupture displacement. The results from a case study indicated that the ANN method performs well, with the coefficient of determination R2 > 0.95. Based on the trained model and 14.5 million Monte Carlo-generated inputs, a large number of response predictions are obtained, forming a dataset that supplemented the missing input-output points in the 217K FEAs and improved the prediction accuracy. The following four articles aim to apply AI and data-driven methods to the advancement of structural seismic design and evaluation. Note that five more articles were published in Part 1 regarding the application to seismic design and analysis. Issa, Silva-Lopez, Baker, and Burton formulate an ML based optimization framework to support resilience-based design. More pointedly, an ML-driven surrogate model is used to capture the highly nonlinear relationship between the set of input variables used in the design and the building recovery performance. The surrogate model uses 43 design-related features as inputs and generates recovery time predictions, enabling (i) rapid estimation of recovery performance under a range of user-defined improvements, and (ii) implementation of complex and informative optimization techniques. The results from an application to a 3-story steel moment resisting frame office building showed that the surrogate model had a high prediction accuracy with the coefficient of determination R2 > 0.99, and reduced the computation time from 300 to 0.0002 s, further supporting the evaluation of the relationship between nonstructural and structural improvement strategies on recovery-based design. Liao, Wang, Fei, Huang, Xie, and Lu developed a physics-rule-co-guided self-supervised generative adversarial network (GAN) for determining the layout and mechanical properties of seismic isolation bearings. The self-supervised GAN addresses the limited availability of isolation design information that is needed to develop data-driven models. Four models comprise the intelligent design model including a physics estimator, rule evaluator, discriminator, and design generator. A deep neural network (DNN)-based surrogate model that predicts the response of the isolator is at the core of the physics estimator. A tensor operation-based loss calculator serves as the rule evaluator by ensuring that the design parameters are specified in accordance with the governing code or standard. The physics estimator and rule evaluator work together to guide the learning process of a GAN model without requiring ground truth data. A series of case studies were conducted using varying seismic intensities and building geometries. The results showed that the GAN design was consistent with the engineers’ design and was approximately 60 times more efficient than traditional engineering methods. A critical aspect of the design and performance assessment of base-isolated structures is ensuring that the axial pressure and shear deformation of the rubber bearings are within reasonable limits. Unlike pressure studies which consider the two loading mechanisms individually, the paper by Zeng, He, and Pan considers the coupling effect of axial pressure and shear deformation. Specifically, the authors develop a DNN to simultaneously detect the axial pressure and shear deformation in the rubber bearing of base isolators. Named pressure and deformation neural network (P&D-Net), the proposed model integrates wavelet packet decomposition with a fully connected neural network. The data set used to train the P&D-Net was derived from a series of full-scale physical tests performed on smart rubber bearings. By implementing a series of data-driven experiments, the study showed that the ability to accurately detect the axial pressure in the bearing is strongly influenced by the shear deformation and vice versa, thus highlighting the importance of considering the interaction between the two mechanisms. Furthermore, compared to a prior method which only used wave-let packets, the P&D-Net significantly improved the predictive performance. Guan and Burton formulate a computationally efficient method for performing collapse fragility assessment of building structures using the collaborative filtering (CF) technique. The CF-based collapse performance assessment procedure reduces the number of explicit simulations when conducting incremental dynamic analyses. The method randomly selects and runs a subset of the required nonlinear response history analyses (NRHAs) and uses CF to estimate the structural performance of the omitted cases. The results estimated by the CF are combined with that of the explicit NRHAs to obtain the corresponding fragility curves. The proposed method is applied to three archetype steel moment frame structures, and the results showed that the CF-based approach could reduce the required NTRAs by up to 50% while providing reliable collapse fragility estimates. Further, a series of sensitivity analyses showed that the method is robust to variations in key input parameters and the record-set used in the analyses. The following three articles apply AI and data-driven methods to advancing monitoring technologies for evaluating the behavior and performance of building structures. Note that four more articles on this sub-topic were published in Part 1. Eltouny and Liang present an uncertainty-aware early warning system that is specifically designed to avoid deep learning model mistakes and can provide near real-time structural health monitoring (SHM). The system utilizes a deep composite encoder-decoder network that combines elements from convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and variational inference to provide damage index distributions. The framework can detect anomalies in the structural system during seismic events and provide a measure of uncertainty that can be used to question the model's predictions. They apply their proposal to three real structures, two of which suffered damage during the 1994 Northridge earthquake. The framework is able to send a warning whenever damage is present. The results of the case study show that the number of warning signals sent correlates well with actual damage. In a comparative study, the proposed method is superior to two recently developed variational autoencoder (VAE)-based damage detection methods. Long-term SHM systems for large structures are known to suffer from data loss which reduces the reliability of near-real-time performance assessments. The paper by Zheng, Li, Li and Hao [Correction added on 2nd of August 2023, replaced author from Chou, Liu and Chang to Zheng, Li, Li and Hao.] implements a transformer-based GAN to reconstruct response measurements that are lost in SHM systems. Within the GAN, a multi-level wavelet-based discriminator is used to determine the degree of realism in the spectra of the reconstructed signals that are produced by the generator. The response reconstruction model was evaluated on two bridges at very different scales (pedestrian bridge and long-span vehicular traffic bridge), both equipped with SHM systems. The performance of the model was evaluated by establishing a relationship between the number of lost SHM channels and the response reconstruction error. For the pedestrian bridge, the error in the reconstructed response was limited to less than 25% even when five of the six channels were lost. When applied to the vehicular traffic bridge, the GAN limited the response reconstruction error to less than 30% despite losing half of the 16 channels that comprised the SHM system. Wang, Xu, Jing, Cui, Zhang, and Li formulated a deep learning model to automatically classify post-earthquake building damage from optical remote sensing images. Recognizing that several prior studies have developed image-based earthquake-induced building damage assessment models, the authors introduce a unique loss function that combines geometric consistency constraints (GCCs) with cross-entropy (CE). The GCC-CE-based loss function enhances the segmentation capability of the image classification model for buildings with complex geometries while providing superior overall performance at multiple scales. The GCC loss was designed to measure split line lengths, curvature, and area which facilitated more precise extraction of the complex geometries in damaged buildings. Compared to image-based damage detection models developed only using CE loss, the GCC-CE model reduced the duration of the training process which provided more accurate predictions. In terms of prediction accuracy, the GCC-CE-based loss model achieved the highest mean intersection over the union (mIoU) (86.98%). The specific improvements in segmentation capabilities include more reliable recognition of edge closures, removal of internal, and reduction of both false-positive and false-negative predictions. The last five articles apply AI and data-driven methods to seismic risk assessment at the regional scale and post-earthquake damage assessment of building structures. Kang, Kim, Kwon, and Song propose two frameworks for regional seismic loss assessment based on DNNs to extend the applicability of engineering demand parameter (EDP) residual estimation and improve its accuracy. The first framework estimates the EDP residuals of buildings by combining the EDP residuals of various single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) systems through modal combination rules. Three DNN models are constructed to predict the EDP residuals of SDOF systems. The second framework predicts the EDP residuals of buildings directly using the two DNN models. The accuracy of the two DNN-based frameworks is tested by comparing the results to those obtained from explicit response history analysis and the regression-based models. The numerical example demonstrated the importance of considering EDP residual correlation and the successful performance of the proposed frameworks in regional seismic loss assessment. Li, Farrar, and Yang develop a deep generative learning framework that achieves efficient regional seismic risk assessment. The method constructs input–output surrogate models of regional seismic risk by learning the underlying complex relation between earthquake source parameters and site-specific infrastructure performance at many locations from data. The learned deep surrogate models directly output the ground motion intensity map and the risk map of a region given the earthquake source parameters, circumventing the massive amounts of computation and data access that would be needed for site-specific assessments. They validate the presented framework on the bridge network risk assessment using simulated scenario earthquakes in the San Francisco Bay Area. They observe that the deep surrogate models perform well without the need for data access to locations and structures and are time-efficient (approximately 0.015 s). Galvis, Hulsey, Baker, and Deierlein presented a methodology to identify and evaluate relevant damage indicators that can be quantitatively related to safety thresholds using numerical simulations of damage. Ideally, these indicators should be insensitive to variability in the structural materials and model parameters. As such, the damage indicators are selected based on their reliability in estimating structural safety and the sensitivity to modeling uncertainty. The safety threshold for each damage indicator is selected to maximize accuracy in post-earthquake building assessments. The methodology is demonstrated through an application study of ductile reinforced concrete frame buildings. Results show that aggregated indices of structural component damage (e.g., aggregated over the floor of a building) have a level of accuracy of approximately 80% and outperform other damage indicators based on peak or residual drifts or simpler percentages of damaged components. It is noted that the methodology can be applied to a wider variety of structures to improve post-earthquake evaluation guidelines. Ahmed, Mangalathu, and Jeon proposed a stacked long short-term memory network to consider the influence of ground motion and structural characteristics on post-earthquake building damage assessment. Unlike previous studies, acceleration history and the number of stories are utilized to generalize the results for the same plan building frames with different numbers of stories. Three different approaches are presented in this work to link the ground motion history with the number of stories (2, 4, 8, 12, and 20 stories) in a reinforced concrete building frame, and the networks were tested using unseen ground motions. Of the three tested approaches, those providing good results were selected for further analysis. For the approaches chosen, the network architectures were changed to a diamond shape and an autoencoder-like shape with more hidden units (to obtain higher accuracy), which were tested on frames with unseen plan layouts. The adopted approaches produced high predictive accuracy (80%−90%) and low training time. The proposed model shows superior performance relative to previously developed techniques. Bhatta and Dang perform ML-based seismic damage prediction of RC buildings, while considering both seismic and structural parameters. The paper first evaluates the feasibility of using ML techniques such as K-nearest neighbor, random forest, decision tree, support vector machine, and ANN to rapidly predict earthquake-induced reinforced concrete building damage considering both the structural properties and ground motion characteristics. Then, the ML models are trained using the simulation results. Due to a lack of real earthquake damage datasets, most prior related studies utilized simulation data to develop ML-based earthquake damage prediction models. In contrast, this study uses real earthquake damage data for RC buildings collected after the 2015 Nepal Earthquake. An overall accuracy of more than 62% is obtained for the test set. The study demonstrates that ML algorithms are capable of rapidly predicting the seismic damage of reinforced concrete buildings with reasonable accuracy. Based on the 28 articles published in Part 1 and Part 2 of the special issue and a review of the broader literature, we present the following brief outlook on how AI can be further integrated into earthquake engineering research and practice: It is expected that there will be an increased focus on developing hybrid models that combine physics-based simulations with AI-based approaches to improve the accuracy of ground motion prediction models while reducing computational costs. AI-based methods will also continue to improve our understanding of geotechnical earthquake engineering such as soil-structure interaction and liquefaction potential. AI-infused structural analysis and performance assessment models will be trained on increasingly larger and more generalizable datasets and used to predict structural response, damage, and collapse, and develop optimal retrofit schemes and smart materials. AI has the potential to revolutionize SHM by providing real-time assessment of buildings and infrastructure during and after earthquakes. Additionally, AI-based methods will be implemented to evaluate the combined effects of earthquakes and other hazards, such as tsunamis, landslides, and floods, by modeling their complex interactions and impacts on the built environment. It is noteworthy that Generative AI, or AI Generated Content (AIGC), offers numerous opportunities to revolutionize many fields, including earthquake engineering. For example, AIGC can automate the generation of structural layout designs that use appropriate materials and maintain desired performance levels under earthquake loading. Additionally, AIGC can facilitate rapid digital prototyping by automatically populating design spaces and identifying the solution(s) that minimizes cost and environmental impacts while achieving the desired performance objectives. The integration of AI into earthquake engineering is poised to transform the field, enabling more accurate predictions, innovative designs, and enhanced infrastructure resilience to seismic hazards. However, as AI techniques continue to develop, researchers and practitioners must collaborate closely to ensure the successful implementation of these methods. It is through this collaboration that the full potential of AI will be leveraged to mitigate the risks associated with earthquakes and related hazards. The guest editors would like to thank Masayoshi Nakashima, the Executive Editor, for his leadership of the journal and the support and guidance provided for this Special Issue. Additionally, the overwhelming response of the earthquake engineering research community to the call for papers as part of this special issue is acknowledged. Finally, this issue, as well as all refereed journals, would not be possible without the diligent reviews provided by peers within the earthquake engineering community. As such, the guest editors wish to thank the individuals that participated in the review process.

title_key: an experimental study exploring humanai complementarity in early social emotional learning|raave
title: An experimental study exploring human–AI complementarity in early social-emotional learning
abstract: Many children are not receiving crucial social-emotional learning (SEL) support due to systemic constraints, such as high educator workload and training burdens. Pedagogical conversational agents (PCAs)—generative AI-powered virtual characters trained to converse with students like a teacher—offer promising solutions that could extend to SEL. However, the current affective-computing capacities of PCAs may be limiting, as SEL facilitation requires deeper emotional and relational attunement than cognition-heavy subjects (e.g., literacy, numeracy). The emotional and relational skills of human educators likely confer benefits beyond those of PCAs in SEL instruction. Despite this potential complementarity, no studies have experimentally assessed the relative performance of PCAs and educators in SEL contexts. It remains unclear if and how PCAs can help educators close the SEL gap. In this study, we used a controlled comparison to reveal complementary strengths, comparing the performance of a PCA to that of human educators when independently facilitating story-based SEL activities with a static AI child. We used a static AI child to help ensure that any performance differences could be attributed to facilitator type. The PCA ( n = 18 simulations) and educators ( n = 18) each delivered three SEL activities ( N = 108 observations). Expert raters, blind to facilitator type, coded dialogue excerpts for evidence-based SEL support techniques and indicators of pedagogical quality. A mixed ANOVA and t -tests revealed significant differences. The PCA showed strengths in basic relational and instructional domains, maintaining respectful tone and routinely providing procedural scaffolding. Educators showed strengths in deeper SEL instruction, guiding reflection and promoting social-emotional knowledge. We discuss implications for SEL through the lens of human–AI complementarity.
authors: ["Doris Kristina Raave", "Tyler Colasante", "Eric Roldan-Roa", "Juan Carlos Ramos Martinez", "Hongtao Li", "Sayan Mukherjee", "Tina Malti"]

title_key: ste ai ming across disciplines and into the future|caines
title: STE(AI)ming across disciplines and into the future
abstract: This paper shares the results of a research creation study, examining GenAI use in interdisciplinary STEM/STEAM classrooms. It outlines curricular examples developed for a university education setting and discusses the potential for the use of GenAI tools in wider, community-engaged research. The author argues that careful implementation of these tools can help teachers and learners to engage with questions of ethics in technology contexts and offer new forms of access to technical and creative training in cross-disciplinary learning environments. The paper proposes that informed and careful use of GenAI tools can contribute to helping grow “improvisatory” STEAM skillsets for both teachers and students including self-directed learning, collaboration, responsibility, curiosity, and play.

title_key: evaluating web frameworks for personal learning decision making a comparative analysis|hyseni
title: Evaluating Web Frameworks for Personal Learning Decision-Making: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: Nowadays with rapid evolution of World Wide Web, the web frameworks of different programing languages are crucial for development standardization, but the huge type of web frameworks makes challenges for chosen the appropriate one for personal learning therefore, this study evaluates and compare the PhP and Python popular web frameworks in terms of their job market trends, web performances, learning resources and community support.Findings of job market trends shows that PhP web frameworks such as Laravel and Slim are being widespread in Europe region, while the python web frameworks such as Django and Flask are being more widespread in the United States. Whereas the findings of performance testing shows that Laravel outperform better in loading speed comparing to the other web frameworks treated in this study, while Django perform better in visual stability and Flask is better than Slim in responsiveness. As well, the survey findings shows that Online tutorials and ChatGPT are most used learning resources comparing to traditional community forums. These findings offer valuable understanding for developers and students in choosing the appropriate web framework for their personal learning based on job market demands and project requirements and can be used by educators and policymakers in curriculum adaption and teaching strategy to meet the industry needs.Moreover, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of Laravel, Django, Slim and Flask framework adoption in professional and academic settings considering the gap in the literature regarding the comparison of frameworks especially for performances, learning resources and job market trends.

In recent years, renamed as “integrative biology”, the study of organisms appears to be regaining strength. This talk will celebrate the joys of spending your scientific energy studying an organism – in my case, the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus). I'll discuss four traits (twinning, small body size, cooperative parental care and chimerism) that are central to the marmoset puzzle. I'll explore how what we've learned has shaped those puzzle pieces into a picture of what a marmoset is as well as the practical implications of developing “a feeling for the organism”.
