title_key: chat generative pretrained transformer a disruptive or constructive technology|deshmukh
title: Chat Generative Pretrained Transformer: A Disruptive or Constructive Technology?
abstract: There is a lot of buzz going around the word Chat Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) and artificial intelligence (AI) in dentistry. The interpretation on this topic is wide and diverse because of the diversity in the thought process of dentists, the varied age groups, and ChatGPT or AI applications in different dental specialties. AI in general and AI in dentistry or medicine, in particular, started gaining its foothold with the advent of data computing as well as cloud computing ability and availability of the vast amount of data collected. With the vast amount of data, for example, in the field of radiology, a specific algorithm was created, which further helped for diagnosing and suggesting probable treatment options.[1] As an avid Sci-fi Movie buff, I recently came across the movie Ex Machina. Ex Machina is a science fiction movie that explores the relationship between a young programmer, Caleb Smith, and an advanced humanoid robot named Ava, who is created by Caleb’s employer, Nathan Bateman. In this movie, the protagonist is selected to test the advanced humanoid AI robot for its efficacy of human-like behavior. As the conversations unfold, the AI machine learning takes over in humanoid, faster than the human mind and adapts to the Turing test, a measure of a machine’s ability to exhibit human-like intelligence. What unfolds is exciting and chilling at the same time. So what is ChatGpt? ChatGPT is a sibling model to InstructGPT, which is trained to follow an instruction in a prompt and provide a detailed response. ChatGPT is an AI program that generates text based on written prompts; this program has gained a great deal of popularity as evidenced by its web-based accessibility through OpenAI.[2] ChatGPT is a natural language processing model with 175 billion parameters that uses deep learning algorithms to generate responses similar to those of humans. As a versatile conversational agent, it can handle various topics, making it useful for customer service, chatbots, and other applications. Although it has received a lot of attention for exceptional features such as generating Shakespearean sonnets, its inability to answer straightforward math questions has also been noted.[3] There are several versions of ChatGPT as it is evolving continuously. The following versions were given as a prompt to ChatGPT. There are several versions of the GPT language model developed by OpenAI, which are designed to perform a range of natural language processing tasks, such as text completion, summarization, and translation. Here are some of the notable versions of GPT: as answered by ChatGPT: GPT-1: This was the first version of the GPT language model, released by OpenAI in 2018. It was trained on a large corpus of the text and had 117 million parameters GPT-2: Released in 2019, GPT-2 is a larger and more powerful version of the GPT model, with 1.5 billion parameters. It generated controversy due to its ability to generate coherent and realistic-sounding text that some felt could be used for nefarious purposes GPT-3: Released in 2020, GPT-3 is currently the largest and most powerful version of the GPT model, with 175 billion parameters. It has demonstrated impressive performance on a range of natural language processing tasks, including language translation, question answering, and even creative writing GPT-Neo: This is an open-source implementation of the GPT model developed by EleutherAI, a community-driven research organization. It is designed to be more accessible and transparent than the original GPT models and has been trained on large-scale datasets using distributed computing GPT-J: Released in 2021, GPT-J is a variant of GPT-3 with 6 billion parameters, developed by EleutherAI using open-source tools and distributed computing resources. It is intended to be more accessible than GPT-3, which is only available through OpenAI’s API. These are just a few examples of the versions of the GPT language model that have been developed. As natural language processing continues to evolve, it is likely that we will see further advancements in this technology, including even more powerful versions of the GPT model. Thus, now as we understand what it is and what can be done with this advanced AI interface, the further question of its importance in dentistry is eminent. Another prompt about the use of ChatGPT in dentistry gave us the following answer. As a language model, ChatGPT can provide assistance to dentists in various ways, such as: Patient communication: Dentists can use CatGpt to generate responses to commonly asked questions by patients, including procedures, aftercare instructions, and dental hygiene advice. This can save time and effort for the dental team while improving patient satisfaction Diagnosis and treatment planning: CatGpt can help dentists with diagnosing conditions and planning treatments by providing relevant information and suggestions based on the patient’s symptoms, medical history, and other factors Education and research: CatGPT can assist in creating educational materials and conducting research by generating accurate and relevant content for various dental topics Electronic health records (EHRs): CatGPT can assist in recording patient data and generating EHRs, which can help dentists make informed decisions and provide better care to patients Marketing and patient outreach: CatGPT can help dental practices create marketing materials and outreach campaigns by generating content that resonates with potential patients. Overall, CatGPT can provide a valuable tool for dentists to improve patient care, enhance their practice, and advance the field of dentistry. ChatGPT is indeed a very useful chatbot that can be helpful in many applications in dentistry and health care. We have already seen the use of AI in orthodontics, radiology, and 3D imaging. What we have to be careful of when dealing with this technology is the monitoring of its interpretations? However, it comes with its own disadvantages and limitations. The use of ChatGPT can place the patient’s privacy at risk because it needs to collect and store the patient’s data and medical history to perform its required task.[4] When it comes to privacy risks, ChatGPT contains personal information from all over the Internet.[5] This raises concerns regarding patients’ confidentiality. ChatGPT has greatly impacted dental education and higher education. Hence, students can use ChatGPT to write assignments without fully comprehending them and putting in their full effort. Therefore, traditional efforts to write an essay may need to be changed. People, mostly nonnative speakers, have used ChatGPT to make their scientific writing more fluent and to reach standards. However, when it comes to interpreting graphs and tables, it fails to give relevant information. However, when it comes to writing, ChatGPT has demonstrated flawed and fabricated research and even plagiarism has been noted.[6] Thus, the answer to the question, is ChatGPT is disruptive or constructive, is like a movie Ex Machina. It is an open-ended interpretation, which depends on who is answering it and who understands it. It seems that all these AI-driven technologies will surpass the human intelligence, but it is nice to remember that, at the helm of it, all is a human with intelligence and emotional quotient.
venue: Journal of the International Clinical Dental Research Organization

title_key: research on an intelligent training system for highway construction safety based on cloud edge end collaboration and knowledge graph|gao
title: Research on an Intelligent Training System for Highway Construction Safety Based on Cloud-Edge-End Collaboration and Knowledge Graph
abstract: The highway construction environment is complex, with high personnel mobility and numerous potential hazards. Traditional safety training models commonly suffer from issues such as being overly formalized, having dull content, lacking specificity, and missing a closed loop for effectiveness evaluation, making it difficult to effectively enhance the safety awareness and skills of practitioners. To address the above problems, this paper proposes and develops a "Cloud-Edge-End Integrated Multimedia Safety Training Management System," similar to the system adopted in Shaanxi Province's highway construction projects. This system is based on a "cloud-edge-end" collaborative architecture and deeply integrates knowledge graph technology, AI recommendation algorithms, and IoT hardware technologies. On the cloud side, a highway construction safety knowledge graph covering the five-dimensional elements of "personnel, machinery, materials, methods, and environment" is constructed, and a personalized assessment and course recommendation engine is developed based on the Transformer model; this achievement is supported by research on the construction and application of a multimodal safety knowledge graph for construction based on large language models, while the application of BIM technology in highway construction safety management also provides a technical background for this work. On the edge side, a portable intelligent training toolbox integrating identity verification, multimedia teaching, and paperless assessment is developed, and seamless collection of training process data is achieved through a PPT plugin. On the terminal side, a WeChat mini-program for trainees is developed, supporting pre-/post-training assessments, personalized learning path recommendations, and interactive learning. This study elaborates in detail on the system's overall architecture, key technologies (including automatic knowledge graph construction, AOV-optimal learning path generation, and edge device integration), and business processes. The system has been successfully applied in the Hu-Zhou-Mei Highway project in Shaanxi Province. Practice demonstrates that the system effectively achieves precise, dynamic, and closed-loop management of safety training, significantly improving training efficiency and outcomes, and provides an innovative technical model and practical reference for safety production management in the field of transportation infrastructure construction.
venue: Journal of computer technology and electronic research.

title_key: the future of universities in the digital world expert foresight from leading global universities|larionova
title: The Future of Universities in the Digital World: Expert Foresight from Leading Global Universities
abstract: The article examines universities’ strategic responses to the key challenges of the digital era, including rising stakeholder expectations, competition with EdTech companies, misalignment with labor market demands, and the need to rethink the university mission in the context of generative AI. The relevance of the study stems from the need of universities at an early stage of transformation for reference points to inform long-term strategy development. The methodology combines an analysis of academic literature (25 selected articles) with 30 in-depth interviews conducted with internationally recognized experts from leading universities (Stanford University, the University of Arizona, HSE University, the University of Reading, among others), as well as representatives of EdTech companies and the business sector. The study identifies five priority thematic areas for development, reflecting a consolidated expert consensus. The findings demonstrate that digital transformation has become a necessary condition for closing the gap with labor market requirements and requires close cooperation with business and EdTech providers. Practical recommendations for university leadership are formulated based on global best practices, including the transition to hybrid models, the implementation of project-based learning, the development of systems for recognizing micro-credentials, and a focus on fostering a new type of student mindset. Specific solutions are also proposed for resource-constrained universities.
authors: ["V. A. Larionova", "N. V. Goncharova", "L. V. Daineko", "V. A. Sokolova"]

title_key: the signals that matter resumes cover letters and success on the job search|wingate
title: The Signals That Matter: Resumes, Cover Letters, and Success on the Job Search
abstract: ABSTRACT Although organizations commonly collect resumes and cover letters to screen job applicants, the features of these materials that affect hiring remain unclear. The current study tracked 183 students applying for full‐time, paid jobs in their field, in connection with a postsecondary co‐operative education program in Canada. We found that applicants whose cover letters and resumes were written with more detail, clarity, and structure secured substantially more interviews (relative to the number of applications submitted) and took less time to secure a position. These effects remained strong after controlling for content factors (work experience and achievement) and tailoring of materials, suggesting that organizations may be hiring applicants based on compositional factors that can be easily produced by new technologies like ChatGPT.
authors: ["Timothy G. Wingate", "Chet Robie", "Deborah M. Powell", "Joshua Steven Bourdage"]
venue: International Journal of Selection and Assessment

title_key: the impact of digitization fostering media news digital critical data and ai literacies|miltenoff
title: THE IMPACT OF DIGITIZATION: FOSTERING MEDIA, NEWS, DIGITAL, CRITICAL DATA, AND AI LITERACIES
abstract: This paper examines the challenges and opportunities in fostering AI literacy within Bulgaria and the broader Central and Eastern European (CEE) region. It emphasizes the importance of foundational literacies—media, news, digital, and critical data—as critical enablers for developing comprehensive AI literacy. The paper highlights key initiatives, including workshops at the University of Economics – Varna, AI-enhanced teaching tools like ChatGPT, and microcredentialing programs aimed at preparing students for AI-driven job markets. Despite these efforts, challenges such as institutional resistance, limited funding, and language barriers persist. Recommendations for coordinated strategies to address these gaps and build sustainable frameworks for AI literacy education are shared, aiming for an effective engagement by academia and society with the opportunities and challenges of an AI-integrated future.
venue: THE LAW AND THE BUSINESS IN THE CONTEMPORARY SOCIETY

title_key: the relational triangle of objectives process and evaluation in ai assisted arabic writing pedagogy|zubaidi
title: The Relational Triangle of Objectives, Process and Evaluation in AI Assisted Arabic Writing Pedagogy
abstract: Abstract: The purpose of this study was to conceptualize and examine the effectiveness of the Relational Triangle of Objectives, Process, and Evaluation in AI-assisted Arabic writing pedagogy. While previous research on generative AI and digital platforms has shown potential for supporting Arabic learners, studies often treated objectives, learning processes, and evaluation as separate domains. This study sought to address this gap by introducing and empirically validating a triangulated framework that integrates the three components into a single pedagogical cycle. Employing a Research and Development (R&D) design based on Borg and Gall’s model, the study combined quantitative and qualitative approaches. Expert validation confirmed the feasibility of the relational triangle, followed by a preliminary trial with 32 students and a field test with 64 students enrolled in an Islamic Religious Education program. Instruments included expert validation sheets, pre- and post-tests, questionnaires, and reflection sheets, all validated through factor analysis and tested for reliability. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, inferential measures, and thematic analysis of student reflections. The findings revealed consistent improvements in students’ Arabic writing competence, with notable gains in grammar, morphology, iʿrāb, vocabulary, and especially in coherence and cohesion. Expert evaluations rated the model as highly feasible, while student responses confirmed its clarity, fairness, and effectiveness. The study demonstrated that improvement was not merely the result of AI use, but of the systematic triangulation of objectives, structured processes, and evaluation feedback. The novelty of this research lies in articulating the Relational Triangle of Objectives, Process, and Evaluation as a dynamic pedagogical framework. By embedding AI tools within a structured instructional design, the model bridges the gap between technological affordances and pedagogical integrity. Its theoretical contribution lies in extending constructivist principles into the digital era, while its practical implication is offering educators a replicable approach for integrating AI responsibly into Arabic writing instruction. Abstrak: Tujuan penelitian ini adalah untuk mengkonseptualisasikan dan menguji efektivitas Segitiga Relasi Tujuan, Proses, dan Evaluasi dalam pedagogi penulisan bahasa Arab berbantuan kecerdasan buatan (AI). Penelitian sebelumnya mengenai AI generatif dan platform digital menunjukkan potensi dalam mendukung pembelajar bahasa Arab, namun umumnya memperlakukan tujuan, proses pembelajaran, dan evaluasi sebagai domain yang terpisah. Penelitian ini berupaya mengisi kesenjangan tersebut dengan memperkenalkan serta memvalidasi secara empiris sebuah kerangka triangulatif yang mengintegrasikan ketiga komponen ke dalam satu siklus pedagogis. Dengan menggunakan desain Research and Development (R&D) berbasis model Borg dan Gall, penelitian ini memadukan pendekatan kuantitatif dan kualitatif. Validasi ahli mengonfirmasi kelayakan segitiga relasi, diikuti dengan uji coba awal kepada 32 mahasiswa dan uji coba lapangan kepada 64 mahasiswa program Pendidikan Agama Islam. Instrumen yang digunakan meliputi lembar validasi ahli, tes awal dan akhir, kuesioner, serta lembar refleksi, yang divalidasi melalui analisis faktor dan diuji reliabilitasnya. Data dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif, ukuran inferensial, dan analisis tematik dari refleksi mahasiswa. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan peningkatan yang konsisten dalam kompetensi menulis bahasa Arab mahasiswa, dengan peningkatan signifikan pada aspek tata bahasa, morfologi, iʿrāb, kosakata, dan terutama koherensi serta kohesi. Evaluasi para ahli menempatkan model ini pada kategori sangat layak, sedangkan tanggapan mahasiswa menegaskan kejelasan, keadilan, dan efektivitasnya. Penelitian ini membuktikan bahwa peningkatan tersebut bukan hanya hasil penggunaan AI, melainkan buah dari triangulasi sistematis antara tujuan, proses terstruktur, dan umpan balik evaluasi. Kebaruan penelitian ini terletak pada artikulasi Segitiga Relasi Tujuan, Proses, dan Evaluasi sebagai kerangka pedagogis dinamis. Dengan menempatkan alat AI dalam desain instruksional yang terstruktur, model ini menjembatani kesenjangan antara potensi teknologi dan integritas pedagogis. Kontribusi teoretisnya adalah memperluas prinsip konstruktivisme ke era digital, sementara implikasi praktisnya adalah menawarkan pendekatan yang dapat direplikasi bagi pendidik dalam mengintegrasikan AI secara bertanggung jawab ke dalam pembelajaran menulis bahasa Arab.

title_key: training efl pre service teachers in using ai tools to create digital narrative teaching materials|nikmah
title: Training EFL Pre-Service Teachers in Using AI Tools to Create Digital Narrative Teaching Materials
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been increasingly used to support EFL material development, yet many pre-service teachers often lack the skills to integrate it effectively. In response to this need, this study examines the implementation and impact of a structured AI-integrated training session to develop digital storytelling (DST) competencies. Using a mixed-methods approach, the research involved 90 EFL pre-service teachers participating in AI training sessions that followed a five-stage workflow: prompting, voice-over creation, image generation, video editing, and lesson planning. Data were collected from training observations, analysis of 23 DST projects, and a 10-item Likert-scale satisfaction survey. Findings show that participants successfully produce multimodal narrative DST using 4-7 AI tools per project, such as ChatGPT, Canva AI, AI Video Cloud, and Magic School AI, to produce diverse digital narrative materials. The digital products targeted students and designed pedagogically aligned lesson plans for Grades 2 to 12 that assessed multiple English skills, with listening and reading being the most frequently integrated. Fables were also the most selected genre, followed by romance, fantasy, and fairy tales. Survey results indicate a high level of satisfaction (M=4.25), confidence, and perceived usefulness of AI tools for EFL material development. The study highlights the pedagogical potential of integrating AI-driven tools in EFL teacher preparation and suggests practical implications for curriculum design in teacher education programs.
venue: Issues in Applied Linguistics & Language Teaching

title_key: pemanfaatan artificial intelligence sebagai media pembelajaran bahasa inggris di sdn 15 padang genting|amin
title: Pemanfaatan Artificial Intelligence Sebagai Media Pembelajaran Bahasa Inggris di SDN 15 Padang Genting
abstract: Abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology offers substantial potential for providing interactive educational media, yet its implementation at the elementary education level is frequently impeded by educators' limited digital literacy. This situation was observed at SDN 15 Padang Genting, where English language instruction remains dominated by conventional methods with minimal utilization of adaptive digital media. Therefore, this community service program aims to enhance teachers' competencies and skills in utilizing AI technology as a medium for English language learning. The implementation adopted a Capacity Building approach comprising three structured stages: initial evaluation (pre-test), hands-on practice training, and final evaluation (post-test). The training focused on introducing text and visual generative AI, along with basic prompt engineering techniques. The results demonstrated a highly significant increase in teachers' capacity; comprehension of basic AI concepts surged from 15% to 85%, and the perceived ease of using the technology rose from 20% to 85%. Furthermore, the program successfully facilitated participants in independently producing educational media, such as interactive vocabulary flashcards and bilingual short stories. The hands-on training approach proved effective in overcoming the anxiety of non-technical teachers while accelerating their creativity in designing English learning materials that are relevant and engaging for digital-generation students. Keywords: artificial intelligence; capacity building; english language; learning media; teacher training. Abstrak: Perkembangan teknologi Artificial Intelligence (AI) menawarkan potensi besar dalam penyediaan media pendidikan yang interaktif, namun implementasinya di tingkat pendidikan dasar seringkali terhambat oleh keterbatasan literasi digital pendidik. Kondisi ini ditemukan di SDN 15 Padang Genting, di mana pembelajaran Bahasa Inggris masih didominasi oleh metode konvensional dan minimnya pemanfaatan media digital adaptif. Oleh karena itu, kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan kompetensi dan keterampilan guru dalam memanfaatkan teknologi AI sebagai media pembelajaran Bahasa Inggris. Pelaksanaan kegiatan ini mengadopsi pendekatan Capacity Building yang mencakup tiga tahapan terstruktur: evaluasi awal (pre-test), pelatihan berbasis praktik langsung (hands-on practice), dan evaluasi akhir (post-test). Pelatihan difokuskan pada pengenalan AI generatif teks dan visual serta teknik rekayasa prompt dasar. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan peningkatan kapasitas guru yang sangat signifikan; pemahaman konsep dasar AI melonjak dari 15% menjadi 85%, dan persepsi terhadap kemudahan penggunaan teknologi meningkat dari 20% menjadi 85%. Lebih lanjut, kegiatan ini berhasil memfasilitasi peserta untuk memproduksi luaran media pembelajaran secara mandiri, seperti flashcard vocabulary interaktif dan naskah cerita dwibahasa. Pendekatan pelatihan berbasis praktik terbukti efektif meruntuhkan kecemasan guru non-teknis, sekaligus mengakselerasi kreativitas mereka dalam merancang materi Bahasa Inggris yang relevan dan menarik bagi siswa generasi digital. Kata kunci: artificial intelligence; capacity building; media pembelajaran; bahasa inggris; pelatihan guru

title_key: on the use of the term philosophy|aloia
title: On the Use of the Term Philosophy
abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) beyond the sciences has not only ushered in a wave of controversy amongst the humanists but the humanities in general—more stridently than when Wittgenstein did it with his infamous Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus. That language can ultimately be (pre)determined algorithmically (a notion, I am sure, that Wittgenstein himself would take no small pleasure in availing his interpretation of language as a calculus), wherein the essence behind the meaning of a word is simply a dictionary’s definition away from complete and total erasure. Indeed, “one can calculate whether a proposition belongs to logic”, as Wittgenstein puts it, “by calculating the logical properties of the symbol … . And this is what we do when we ‘prove’ a logical proposition. For, without bothering about sense or meaning, we construct the logical propositions out of others using only rules that deal with signs” (76-77). It remains to be seen whether or not consciousness can arise on this basis, as in a truly Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and by only using those same rules that seem to emerge from their own, inherent complexity; themselves just another form of statement, to recall Wittgenstein, and those statements caught “in an eternal relation to a proposition about a constituent of the complex” (15). But for me to even acknowledge Wittgenstein in some respects, and in some circles, is to contemplate the end of philosophy itself, or at the very least to dwell on the significance of the sense or meaning of the end. Karl Popper might have us refrain from stoking this fire altogether, although neither Popper, nor Wittgenstein for that matter, could have ever anticipated the extent to which the sciences, let alone the computer sciences, would eventually go on to ‘prove’ that a reductionist approach towards language does, in fact, work; in light of, and in spite of, Leibniz’s postulation of a giant brain the size of a windmill, fundamentally reducing the thinking and experiencing capacity of an individual to a series of cogs and wheels; Lawrence Davis’s duplication of the brain’s own synapses using telephone wires (no doubt an early precursor to neural networks and machine learning); Ned Block’s description of a Chinese brain (as being somehow different from any other brain); and finally John Searle’s Chinese room argument, perhaps the most recognisable variation of and to a thought experiment in which an individual is placed inside a room and asked to associate a symbol in Mandarin with another in English without knowing Mandarin, and in much the same way an input parses through a computer that is none the wiser about its output (Cole). The computer does not think, that is to say, about what any of these inputs or outputs are supposed to mean, least of all the use of the term philosophy. I, however, want to focus on the sense and meaning behind the use of this term, in particular, and for two main reasons. Firstly, because the sense and meaning of philosophy tends to differ from philosopher to philosopher, in as much as someone like Locke contiguously builds upon the likes of Descartes, and Descartes on Plato, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, and their ideas. Secondly, because the difference between the one and the other philosopher is also demonstrative of a (con)temporality to language, especially when the use of the term philosophy itself does not strictly imply existentialism, or existential nihilism, or, as in the case of Wittgenstein, analytic philosophy, any more than it does phenomenology, or Socratic method, or film philosophy. Of course, if we were to define and differentiate these terms, like analytics from technics from aesthetics, say, well might we then go on to ‘prove’ their logical propositions as statements (analytics is this, technics is that, etc.), but that is entirely my point: in the absence of the presence of any logic, any curation, and without bothering about sense or meaning at all, well might LLMs then go on to construct their own predominantly English rooms out of rules that deal with only one philosophical statement to the exclusion of all others. Moreover, even if we were to curate such statements, well might these propositions lack the capacity (re: empathy) to sense or mean anything beyond the sign of the times in which they were produced—well might the affect of this time come into play as part of another, eternal relation to propositions about time and affect themselves as exponential functions in the arrangement of these terms caught in another eternal relation between their past and present meaning. Long have we outgrown Cartesian dualism, for example, with regard to Locke and Hume, but the philosophy of the one is meaningless without the other; instead, we should try to imagine the intelligence of a machine caught in an eternal relation between mind and body without body, and in light of a more than likely Christian interpretation of God, or, as is more popularly the case with the likes of James Barrat, a self-styled Busy Child that is just as omnipotent as it is superintelligent. Would the machine judge us on the basis of Cartesian dualism, or Locke’s social contract, or Hume’s empiricism, as they are understood and reflected upon now, or in the past—or, in the past of the future, which is become now? I must admit that Barrat’s rather hyperbolic use of language when it comes to AGI gets us little to no traction with the Ray Kurzweils of this world, which is why I think a much more innocuous consideration of the use of the term philosophy paves the way with a series of similarly good intentions. No philosopher, no good scientist, sets about in earnest to create a means by which to act against their own best interests, but then again: “here is this tendency to think that well-intentioned people create nice Ais [sic],” according to Eliezer Yudkowsky, “they themselves assume that if they are good-intentioned people the Ais [sic] they make are automatically good intentioned, and this is not true” (qtd. in Barrat, 53). Let us take, for example, Jianqiu Zhang’s article "Should We Fear Large Language Models? A Structural Analysis of the Human Reasoning System for Elucidating LLM Capabilities and Risks through the Lens of Heidegger’s Philosophy". As well-intentioned though it may very well be, it begs the question: why Heidegger? What is it about Heidegger’s philosophy as opposed to Wittgenstein’s that someone like Derrida has not already elucidated through Writing and Difference about language through its meaning-making? “Heidegger’s framework illuminates the dual nature of entities; ‘ready-to-hand’ entities are appreciated for their practical utility”, according to Zhang, “while ‘present-at-hand’ entities are scrutinized for their intrinsic qualities from a scientific attitude. This duality forms the basis of what we term our Faculty of Knowledge, delineating the intricate structure by which we perceive and engage with our surroundings” (3). My emphasis on the use of the term duality here is that Zhang’s choice of Heidegger’s philosophy not only forms the basis for a convenient, if not computationally binary, interpretation of language, and by again calculating the logical properties of a symbol no less, this same scientific attitude would sooner relegate than ‘prove’ another logical kind of proposition algorithmically, away from the subjectivity of the ostensibly clunky rules that deal with signs, as well as the consequences of those rules, that have been up for debate across the humanities, and to a greater extent philosophically, since time immemorial. These properties, I might add, are in no way restricted to just Wittgenstein, or to just Heidegger, or even to just Derrida, but unlike Wittgenstein’s Tractatus, Heidegger’s framework—in Zhang’s case, Being and Time—is fraught with its own problems, the least of which concern its translation from German into English. By Heidegger’s own admission, he considers this framework a failure, and to such an extent that he abandons “the second half … . After a quarter of a century”, leaving Being and Time effectively unfinished (17). There are also the rather pragmatic, if not proto-fascistic, tendencies to these so-called ‘ready-to-hand’ entities that are only really being appreciated for their practicality in much the same way that a being might only be considered human in terms of their usefulness—at first to certain roles, to applications, and finally to society at large, in a slippery slope towards an abject (and utterly objective) utilitarianism that even now threatens to outmode swathes of the population under the guise of innovation, automation, and business agility (Baron). To Zhang’s credit, this utilitarian approach is clearly not what they intended when invoking someone like Heidegger, but, again, this is entirely my point: philosophy, as it is understood nowadays, can often be confused for, and conflated with, one’s own worldview not unlike a business philosophy. The goal of any business, any good business, and I use the term ‘good’ not in the sense of what is morally right or righteous, but effectively good for business, is to make a profit. Of course, there are going to be various businesses that would claim that their business philosophy, in particular, is more or less agile, sustainable—ethical—than others, but this only goes to show that the use of the term philosophy is itself up to interpretation. So, what philosophy means for us today, it may or may not mean for us tomorrow. “When we make something present by bringing it close from its ‘thence’ [seinem Dorther], the making-present forgets the ‘yonder’ [das Dort] and loses itself in itself. Thus it comes about that if ‘observation’ of entities within-the-world commences in such a making-present”, according to Heidegger, “the illusion arises that ‘at first’ only a Thing is present-at-hand, here of course, but indefinitely—in space in general”

title_key: application of artificial intelligence in clinical pharmacology literature revew|
title: APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY (LITERATURE REVEW)
abstract: Background. Clinical pharmacology is a scientific discipline that covers all aspects of the interaction between drugs and humans. Aim: to review current data on the possibility of using artificial intelligence (AI) to optimize scientific research, practical application and education in clinical pharmacology. Materials and methods. Analysis of data presented in PubMed, using the keywords "clinical pharmacology", "artificial intelligence". Results. It was found that AI is used at all stages of drug development from molecule discovery to real clinical practice. In particular, AI provides prediction of the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs, the need for monitoring therapy, and the risk of drug interactions. The introduction of AI-based programs (for example, ChatGPT) into the activities of modern clinics allows to increase the accuracy of prescriptions (up to 50%), reduce repeat hospitalizations (up to 58%) and reduce administrative costs. AI models allow to individualize the dose, in particular for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (for example, vancomycin); determine the dose taking into account pharmacogenetic reactions; accurately identify the risk of drug interactions and offer clinical solutions. In the educational sphere, the use of ChatGPT allows to simulate clinical situations, accelerating the creation of cases and test tasks (although almost 30% of the generated tasks were unsuitable without expert revision); promotes the development of clinical thinking in students; forms decision-making skills. Among the problems of using AI in clinical pharmacology, in addition to the need for expert assessment of data quality, issues of ethics, confidentiality and dual use of technologies (for example, the risks of developing bioweapons) are of great importance, therefore it is important to combine the capabilities of AI with the experience of specialists. Conclusion. Artificial intelligence has great potential for organizing clinical trials; optimizing the therapeutic effects of drugs, taking into account the risk of pharmacogenetic reactions and drug interactions, improving clinical decision-making and patient safety; and learning personalized drug use. It is important to use AI tools in conjunction with expert judgment from healthcare professionals, and to properly consider regulatory considerations, data privacy, and ethical implications.

title: News
abstract: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has expanded its statistical activities by creating a centralised statistics office, the Office of Homeland Security Statistics (OHSS). The OHSS (dhs.gov/ohss) replaces the Office of Immigration Statistics (OIS) – which, as its name suggests, collected only immigration statistics – and is responsible for gathering and reporting data from more than a dozen agencies within its scope, including on cybersecurity, emergency management, infrastructure protection, maritime safety, screening, terrorism and targeted violence, and chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear security. The new office has pledged to release more detailed data regularly and with greater transparency, and support “evidence-based” policies, programmes, and decision-making. For the current fiscal year, it plans to release data on law enforcement, international trade, cybersecurity, airport screening, emergency response to federal disasters, and maritime response operations. It will also oversee the development of department-wide data standards and help bring the DHS – formed in 2003 in response to the September 11 attacks two years earlier – in line with the 2018 Evidence Act, which requires agencies to make their data accessible and support their policy-making with statistical evidence. The OHSS is led by former OIS director Marc Rosenblum, who joined the DHS in 2016 and has a background in immigration policy. Launching the new office at DHS headquarters last November, Rosenblum said demand for immigration data governance, processing, modelling and reporting had “exploded in the last few years,” adding that “DHS does incredibly important work, and the OHSS team is 100 percent committed to our piece of the mission, which is to foster transparency and data-driven homeland security decision-making by analyzing and disseminating timely, objective DHS data and statistics. “OHSS differs a bit from most existing statistical agencies because our reporting is mainly on DHS activities, rather than external data, and because a major part of our work is to support leadership decision-making. “In establishing this new office, we'll begin releasing data more quickly, with greater granularity and covering a broader scope of DHS activities. “Simply growing the reporting and data governance that accompanies that will be a big undertaking. “This is a big step forward for an office that until recently published data annually, a few years late, so we're really upping our game.” Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas (pictured) said: “Data-driven decision-making is an integral part of everything we do … Our increased transparency will inform the American people as we work to fulfil our security and safety mission, while safeguarding privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties.” The first systematic study of how ChatGPT might affect the white-collar workplace has found that AI may be more useful for creative tasks than analytical ones. Currently under review at a scientific journal, the study (tinyurl.com/yc25bkbs) examines the performance implications of AI on “realistic, complex, and knowledge-intensive” professional tasks at Boston Consulting Group, one of the world's largest management-consulting firms, which had previously banned its consultants from using AI bots in their work. A total of 758 consultants were randomly assigned to carry out typical work-related tasks with either no AI access, GPT-4 AI access (i.e. ChatGPT), or GPT-4 AI access after 30 minutes of training. The findings showed that consultants assisted by ChatGPT for creative tasks, including brainstorming and writing persuasively, produced work that independent human evaluators rated about 40% better on average – and that they did so over 20% faster. However, when tasks required evidence-based reasoning such as interpreting data from spreadsheets, AI was more of a hindrance than a help. Consultants not using ChatGPT were correct about 84.5% of the time, compared to 70% of those using the bot, and 60% of those using the bot after training. Authors said their findings “bring in a nuanced response to the ongoing debate on whether organizations should adopt AI for high-end knowledge work.” The Office for National Statistics (ONS) has begun quarterly publication of the Household Cost Indices (HCIs), after over a decade of campaigning from the Royal Statistical Society (tinyurl.com/ynyu4dvm). Before the introduction of HCIs, the ONS published only the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), the Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers’ housing costs (CPIH), and the soon-to-be-discontinued Retail Price Index (RPI), which measure changes in the cost of goods and services. The RSS has promoted the case for HCIs, an additional and alternative measure of household inflation devised by two RSS Fellows, Jill Leyland and John Astin, since around 2012. The HCIs are an attempt to reflect more accurately the true rises in the cost of living for different UK households, and include interest payments such as mortgages and student loans. They also weight households equally, whereas the CPI gives greater weight to higher-spend (usually higher-income) households. The first release estimates that, in the year to September 2023, the cost of living for the average UK family rose by 8.2%, which is higher than the 6.7% recorded by the CPI. “The data shows exactly why we've been pushing for development of the HCIs,” Jill Leyland told the BBC. “CPI is fine for broader economic purposes but over the past two years, it has not reflected the true extent of the cost of living crisis.” In response to the latest figures, RSS chief executive Sarah Cumbers encouraged policy-makers to “take into account the Household Cost Indices, now published quarterly by ONS, as the best way to understand people's experiences of inflation, particularly those on lower incomes.” Former Stanford University president Marc Tessier-Lavigne has retracted a contested paper on Alzheimer's research after a decade of criticism. The authors have acknowledged the study contained image anomalies and biostatistical errors, but deny it includes falsified data. Data from the National Center for Education Statistics has shown large increases in the numbers of undergraduate and master's degrees awarded in the recently introduced categories for data analytics and data science. The number of bachelor's degrees in statistics also grew but there was a 15% drop in the number of master's degrees in statistics (tinyurl.com/yp4wb3u2). Former RSS executive director Hetan Shah, now chief executive of the British Academy, has warned the UK government it faces losing statisticians at a time they are most needed. “Everyone – every company in the country – wants to hire a data scientist, and most statisticians are rebadging themselves as data scientists,” Shah told the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee. “How will the government hold onto talented people?” Streaming giant Netflix has announced it will now release audience statistics every 6 months (tinyurl.com/3xzzxjyd). “What We Watched: A Netflix Engagement Report” will report hours viewed for every title – original and licensed – that has been watched for over 50,000 hours, over a period of 6 months. Top of the list in the first data drop was thriller The Night Agent, which viewers spent 812 million hours watching. Among the most interesting findings of the first 6-monthly report is that non-English stories received 30% of all viewing. “This is a big step forward for Netflix and our industry,” said the company. “We believe the viewing information in this report – combined with our weekly Top 10 and Most Popular lists – will give creators and our industry deeper insights into our audiences, and what resonates with them.” Netflix added: “Success on Netflix comes in all shapes and sizes, and is not determined by hours viewed alone.” Got a view on any of this issue's news stories? Let us know at [email protected] and we might publish it on our Letters page.

title_key: pembekalan guru dengan teknologi masa depan kecerdasan artifisial|elly
title: PEMBEKALAN GURU DENGAN TEKNOLOGI MASA DEPAN: KECERDASAN ARTIFISIAL
abstract: Abstrak: Di tengah pesatnya perkembangan teknologi AI, guru-guru SMA Panglima Polem Rantauprapat menghadapi tantangan berupa kesenjangan pengetahuan dan keterampilan teknologi. Kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (PkM) ini bertujuan untuk memberikan pembekalan komprehensif guna meningkatkan pemahaman konseptual AI dan keterampilan praktis guru dalam memanfaatkan platform AI seperti ChatGPT untuk menunjang kualitas pembelajaran. Metode pelaksanaan kegiatan ini melibatkan 23 orang guru sebagai peserta. Tahapan kegiatan yang ditempuh meliputi identifikasi kebutuhan dan persiapan, pengembangan bahan ajar dengan Canva, pengisian pre-test, pemaparan materi kecerdasan buatan untuk pendidikan, diskusi tanya jawab, pengerjaan studi kasus praktik (pemanfaatan ChatGPT dan program Python sederhana untuk analisis sentimen), pengisian post-test, serta penyusunan laporan akhir. Sistem evaluasi diukur secara kuantitatif melalui perbandingan hasil pre-test dan post-test yang mencakup uji pemahaman dan uji persepsi hasil kegiatan. Hasil kuantitatif menunjukkan adanya peningkatan persentase jawaban benar pada seluruh indikator uji pemahaman peserta. Selain itu, terjadi penguatan pada persepsi positif peserta dengan peningkatan skala 'sangat setuju' yang konsisten, terutama pada aspek keberlanjutan penerapan IPTEK (meningkat dari 57,9% menjadi 69,6%) serta efektivitas kegiatan dalam memberikan solusi terhadap permasalahan pembelajaran (meningkat dari 36,8% menjadi 56,5%). Dapat disimpulkan bahwa kegiatan ini berhasil meningkatkan literasi digital guru serta memberikan solusi konkret dalam integrasi AI di sekolah.Abstract: Amid the rapid development of AI technology, teachers at Panglima Polem High School in Rantauprapat are facing the challenge of a gap in their technological knowledge and skills. This Community Service (PkM) activity aims to provide comprehensive training to enhance teachers’ conceptual understanding of AI and their practical skills in utilizing AI platforms such as ChatGPT to support the quality of learning. The activity involved 23 teachers as participants. The stages of the activity included needs assessment and preparation, developing teaching materials using Canva, administering a pre-test, presenting material on artificial intelligence for education, a question and answer session, working on a practical case study (using ChatGPT and a simple Python program for sentiment analysis), administering a post-test, and preparing a final report. The evaluation system was measured quantitatively by comparing pre-test and post-test results, which included comprehension tests and perception tests of the activity’s outcomes. The quantitative results showed an increase in the percentage of correct answers across all indicators of participants’ comprehension. In addition, there was a strengthening of participants’ positive perceptions, with a consistent increase in the “strongly agree” rating, particularly regarding the sustainability of science and technology application (rising from 57.9% to 69.6%) and the effectiveness of the activity in providing solutions to learning problems (rising from 36.8% to 56.5%). It can be concluded that this activity successfully improved teachers’ digital literacy and provided concrete solutions for integrating AI in schools.
authors: ["Elly Elly", "Erwin Setiawan Panjaitan", "Yuni Marlina Saragih", "Sabrina Adela Br Sibarani", "Fandi Presly Simamora"]

title_key: schedio an ai driven unified academic portfolio platform for verified campus recruitment|kumar
title: SCHEDIO: An AI-Driven Unified Academic Portfolio Platform for Verified Campus Recruitment
abstract: Campus recruitment processes still rely heavily on traditional resumes, yet they rarely give a complete picture of what a student is actually capable of technically. On top of that, student projects end up spread across multiple repositories with no single place to find them all, which makes things genuinely difficult for recruiters trying to evaluate candidates. Schedio addresses these problems by offering a centralized platform for academic project portfolios, combined with automated verification and AIpowered code explanation features. The system is built on the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js) and operates on a three-tier user structure made up of Students (T1), Colleges (T2) and Recruiters (T3), with each group having clearly defined responsibilities in the recruitment process. On this platform, colleges take care of uploading student project artifacts such as ZIP files, videos and documentation, while also verifying originality through plagiarism detection tools. Colleges also get access to analytical insights covering different domains and skill categories. Students can look through their own portfolios, check out projects from others and use AI-generated explanations when they want to understand the code without digging through it manually. Recruiters get search and filter options to find candidates by domain, skill set and institution. They get access to verified project details along with explanations and can save profiles for later. This setup allows even non-technical recruiters to understand what a project does without having to go through the actual code. The platform is built using the MERN stack, with authentication handled through JSON Web Tokens (JWT). GridFS manages large files while MongoDB handles session storage. The system also connects with the Google Gemini API to produce simplified code explanations using structured prompts. What also sets Schedio apart is how it organizes projects by domain, grouping them into areas like Web Development, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning and Healthcare, with each project tagged to specific skills. This structure makes finding the right candidate far less tedious. At its core the platform is about making academic work count in the job market.
authors: ["T Aditya Kumar", "Arepalle Neha Sri Reddy", "B Manikanteshwara Reddy", "Mathi Florence Angelina", "Pinninti Reeni Reddy", "Sanjeeva Sanku"]

title_key: navigating the artificial intelligence frontier on cataloguing and metadata work in libraries an interview with getaneh alemu|alemu
title: Navigating the artificial intelligence frontier on cataloguing and metadata work in libraries: an interview with Getaneh Alemu
abstract: Getaneh Alemu is an experienced Cataloguing and Metadata Librarian with over two decades of experience in higher education and libraries. He specialises in ensuring that metadata is accurate, consistent, usable and standardised. His expertise covers several key metadata standards and tools, including MARC21, MarcEdit, Dublin Core, AACR2, RDA, LCSH, DDC, Alma and Primo. These standards aim to maximise the visibility, discoverability, accessibility and utilisation of library resources.Getaneh has an impressive academic background that includes a PhD in Metadata for Digital Libraries from the University of Portsmouth, earned in 2014. He also holds an MA in Digital Library Learning from Oslo University College, Parma University and Tallinn University, obtained in 2009. Additionally, he earned an MA in Knowledge and Information Management from Ghent University in 2005 and a BA in Library and Information Science from Addis Ababa University in 2001.His research on metadata is well-documented through key publications such as “Metadata Standards and Models” (2024), “The Future of Enriched, Linked, Open and Filtered Metadata” (2022) and “An Emergent Theory of Digital Library Metadata: Enrich then Filter” (2015).Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to automate repetitive, data-intensive and pattern-recognition tasks, thereby freeing human cataloguers for more complex work. What impact will this have?We interviewed Getaneh Alemu because his current work demonstrates a proactive engagement with AI in cataloguing. He is actively involved in exploring, testing and evaluating various AI tools. This exploration extends to discussions with colleagues to understand AI’s practical applications in metadata creation, enrichment and the enhancement of library catalogues and discovery systems.Q1.How does Artificial Intelligence currently impact your work as a cataloguer?Currently, the impact of AI on my cataloguing work is mainly in the exploratory phase. I am actively exploring, testing and evaluating various tools, including the new AI Metadata Assistant from Ex Libris, as well as Copilot, ChatGPT and Gemini. Additionally, I am engaged in ongoing discussions with colleagues in the library to gain a better understanding of the practical applications of these technologies in metadata creation and enrichment, as well as in improving the library catalogue and discovery.We are entering an exciting phase and we must engage as active participants rather than as complainers or passive observers. It’s important to remember that AI is not an external force intruding upon our lives; rather, it is a human innovation that we must use wisely, ethically and responsibly. AI is no longer a distant concept, relegated to the realm of science fiction; it is a reality. The emergence of large language models like ChatGPT and Copilot has made AI increasingly relevant to our work, transforming it from an abstract idea into a practical tool for organising and managing bibliographic data. This process is ongoing and requires continuous learning, critical reflection and experimentation, but is happening at a fast pace.I stay informed about the latest developments in Artificial Intelligence by reading authoritative sources, including “New Horizons in Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” (Balnaves et al., 2025), as well as peer-reviewed journal articles and professional discussions on platforms like LinkedIn. In my workplace, a dedicated team of information librarians regularly updates us on new AI tools and innovations. In this regard, my university shows significant proactivity and remains at the forefront of technological advancement. The university has provided a concise online training module covering the fundamental principles of artificial intelligence, which I have successfully completed.Currently, the impact of AI on my professional responsibilities is limited but overall positive. Although its use is not yet widespread, I am involved in a small-scale experimental project that explores the use of AI-generated metadata for subject headings. We plan to provide further updates as this project progresses.Q2. What are some examples of successful AI implementations in metadata management and cataloguing?We’re observing some promising developments, although they are still in the experimental stages. I utilise the Copilot and Gemini AI tools to check Dewey Decimal numbers and to suggest appropriate subject headings. Ex Libris has introduced an AI assistant called “Metadata Enrichment using AI,” which aids in the ongoing enhancement of bibliographic records. It’s essential to note that Ex Libris emphasises the need for human cataloguers to validate the outputs generated by AI to ensure accuracy and trustworthiness.I tested the AI Assistant with both new and existing records to evaluate its capability to create MARC 21 bibliographic records from minimal input. The tool can handle basic bibliographic elements (such as title and author) or visual sources (like a book cover or an image of the table of contents) and generates a draft record that is sent to the Metadata Editor (MDE).For this test, I supplied an image sourced from a publisher’s website, providing the main title, author and year but deliberately omitting the subtitle. The AI inferred and correctly populated the title along with the subtitle, inserted the correct MARC21 245 field, auto-assigned some basic (generic) subject headings (in the 650 LCSH field) and generated a summary note (520). It also embedded provenance metadata via a note indicating: “Part of the metadata in this record was created with the help of the AI Metadata Assistant.” However, some essential metadata elements were missing such as physical description (300), classification numbers (082 / 050), standard identifier and richer (granular) subject access. ISBD punctuation (e.g. colons, commas) and subfield spacing in 245 and elsewhere were also inconsistent. While effective for generating core descriptive metadata, the Assistant requires cataloguer input to ensure full bibliographic control, structural accuracy and standards compliance.AI has significant potential to improve metadata and cataloguing. While it offers powerful capabilities, integrating AI with existing standards and tools requires effort. AI can enhance metadata, providing users with more intuitive access to information through linked subject systems. Additionally, it can address historical biases in classification systems and improve data quality by conducting consistency checks and detecting anomalies in bibliographic records.Q3.What are your thoughts on the risks and ethical considerations of using AI in metadata and cataloguing?AI-augmented metadata must adhere to established ethical principles by prioritising user-centred access and non-discrimination, reflecting IFLA’s emphasis on “user convenience.” This requires actively addressing the inherent biases present in both AI algorithms and the socio-cultural biases that are built into historical metadata standards. As noted by Gartner (2016) and Bowker and Star (1999), metadata is never completely neutral; every standard and category reflects a particular viewpoint while silencing others. This can result in historical classification schemes that represent colonial perspectives or lack appropriate terminology for diverse cultural expressions.To combat these entrenched biases, it is essential to continuously and critically examine, diversify and decolonise metadata practices to ensure inclusivity and equitable representation.Thus, transparency and accountability in the metadata decisions made by AI are crucial. It is important to highlight the vital role of human oversight and the need for collaborative efforts among all metadata professionals to ensure ethical and responsible information practices.Q4.To what extent can AI automate cataloguing tasks and what tasks are best suited for automation?AI holds significant potential to automate various cataloguing tasks, thereby increasing efficiency and freeing up human cataloguers for more complex, nuanced work. The tasks best suited for automation generally involve repetitive, data-intensive, or pattern-recognition processes.One key area is data remediation and normalisation. AI can effectively identify and rectify common errors or inconsistencies present in legacy metadata records, particularly useful for older data, such as pre-RDA records created under AACR2, which often contain numerous abbreviations and display inconsistencies that can be automatically corrected. Similarly, AI excels at format conversion, efficiently transforming metadata from one standard to another, for instance, from MARC21 to BIBFRAME, XML, or compatible formats for archival metadata.AI can also significantly enhance record enrichment and cross-linking. It can automatically augment bibliographic records by adding granular details and establishing crucial connections. This involves incorporating URIs from authoritative sources such as Wikidata, LCNAF and VIAF, thereby ensuring accurate and unique identification of entities like authors, editors, agencies and events, which is vital for achieving full Linked Data compliance. Furthermore, given the exponential growth of e-book, database and e-journal collections, AI is invaluable for identifying defunct links by scanning e-resource records to flag broken or outdated URLs, proactively resolving access issues and ensuring consistent full-text access for users.Other highly suitable tasks for automation include bulk updates and imports, allowing for large-scale changes on bibliographic records or efficient ingestion of new records. AI can also assist in comparing bibliographic record sets, automatically finding common or differing records, similar to an Excel VLOOKUP function. For the initial stages of cataloguing, AI can be instrumental in automatic record generation, creating preliminary bibliographic records directly from full-text books and documents, which human cataloguers can then review.Beyond structured data, AI’s capabilities extend to deciphering illegible texts, extracting information from old handwritten archival materials. It can also assist with intellectual analysis by suggesting relevant subject headings based on content analysis. Finally, AI can ensure records adhere to specific presentation standards like ISBD through automated formatting and indentation and provide initial translations of metadata from one language to another, requiring subsequent human review for accuracy and nuance.Q5. How can AI enhance the discoverability and accessibility of library resources?When integrated with existing standards, systems and practices, AI enhances bibliographic records, improving discoverability and accessibility. It strengthens the core functions of metadata as defined by standards like FRBR, IFLA LRM and RDA. These standards are designed to help users find information, identify relevant resources, select appropriate materials, gain access and explore related content (Riva, Le Boeuf and Žumer, 2017). By harnessing enriched, linked, enhanced and open metadata, AI amplifies these capabilities. It achieves this through automating processes such as content indexing, metadata creation, labelling and summarisation, which makes resources more accessible across various disciplines and contexts. AI also improves information retrieval and analysis, allowing users to find and analyse relevant information within large and complex data sources more effectively. This facilitates better access to extensive collections of data through advanced techniques like intelligent grouping and filtering.Ultimately, AI enables large-scale global access through automated classification, organisation and retrieval. It also offers multi-dimensional subject access through innovations like topic modelling and AI assistants, fostering a richer, interconnected and more equitable learning environment for users.Q6.How can libraries ensure data quality and accuracy when using AI for cataloguing?Ensuring data quality and accuracy is crucial. AI models rely on exceptionally large data sources to learn patterns, highlighting the importance of providing high-quality input data. Discussions about algorithmic bias, as well as the need for transparency and explainability in machine learning, are highly relevant; AI requires accurate provenance metadata. Consequently, librarians must verify metadata for accuracy and consistency. To achieve this, specific targets should be set, quality metrics established and human oversight implemented to maintain the accuracy and consistency of AI-generated metadata.Q7. Can technology replace the cataloguer? Why or why not?My answer is no, and here is why. Technology and innovation are not threats to librarianship but rather indispensable allies in its ongoing evolution. As a profession, we stand on the shoulders of visionary librarians such as Panizzi, Ranganathan, Dewey, Cutter, Garfield, Avram, Otlet and many others, each of whom embraced innovation and the tools of their time to reimagine new ways of thinking, working and information organisation. Their work exemplifies the dynamic and adaptive spirit at the heart of librarianship.Today, with the advent of AI, we are charting a new horizon, one marked not by displacement but by transformation. I am unequivocally in favour of AI, not as a replacement for human expertise but as a catalyst for efficiency, enrichment and improved discovery. We, like our predecessors, must embrace adaptation, readily adjusting our approaches with ethical discernment and unwavering professional integrity. In doing so, we perpetuate librarianship’s legacy as a field that is both profoundly humanistic and dynamically responsive to technological advancements.The future of metadata creation is evolving, blending human expertise with the computational efficiency of AI, as discussed in “New Horizons in Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” (Balnaves et al., 2025). This integration fosters richer and more inclusive metadata ecosystems. In this model, metadata creators, users and AI will collaborate closely. The hybrid approach of co-creating metadata is essential, as human judgement is crucial for maintaining trust and accuracy in light of the limitations of AI, such as bias and factual errors. Instead of viewing technology as a replacement for cataloguers, we should embrace a future where human insight and machine capabilities work together to enhance bibliographic metadata.Q8.What skills will be essential for cataloguers in an AI-driven environment?We must continually explore, learn and better understand AI, actively engaging with it rather than remaining on the sidelines. Being proactive and hands-on involves mastering prompt engineering, delving into the logic behind algorithms and fostering a richer, more engaging research and learning environment. Therefore, essential skills for cataloguers in an AI-driven environment will undoubtedly include comprehensive AI literacy, encompassing prompt engineering and a foundational grasp of AI principles. Deep subject analysis and cataloguing skills will remain paramount, enabling cataloguers to strategically cede repetitive tasks to AI. Furthermore, a strong knowledge of the ethical considerations surrounding AI, coupled with developed technical skills in digital and algorithmic literacy and competencies in developing and applying various AI approaches, will be crucial.Q9.What training or resources should be provided to cataloguers to prepare them for AI integration?To effectively prepare librarians and cataloguers for AI integration, training, development and resources are essential. This includes providing opportunities for direct experimentation with AI tools, such as chatbots, to build hands-on understanding of their capabilities and limitations. Access to open-source toolkits with guides and examples for recommender systems should be made available for those keen to explore coding applications. Furthermore, robust educational resources, like online courses covering AI basics and ethical implications, alongside current research reports on AI’s impact on information professions, are vital. Finally, encouraging and supporting proof-of-concept projects will allow cataloguers to develop crucial technical and business skills in a practical, real-world context. I believe we can all come together to teach one another, continuously experiment and improve our processes. We can achieve this through seminars, conferences, magazines, articles and books.Q10.What role does human oversight and intervention play in AI-assisted cataloguing?Human oversight and intervention are crucial, especially in AI-assisted cataloguing. This situation is reminiscent of the outdated belief that paperless offices would render libraries obsolete. Such hype often overlooks the importance of traditional institutions. Just as physical libraries, archives and museums remain vital despite decades of technological advancements, human involvement will continue to be central in the age of AI.In this era, cataloguers play an essential role in subject analysis and metadata creation. They interpret the content, context and purpose of resources, selecting appropriate subject headings while upholding the principles of Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI). While AI can assist with tasks like keyword extraction, the nuanced process of subject analysis demands human judgement, cultural sensitivity and an understanding of complex standards such as Resource Description and Access (RDA) and IFLA’s Library Reference Model (LRM).Cataloguers are adept at distinguishing between different works and editions, often requiring professional judgement and background knowledge. Although AI can enhance efficiency, it lacks the critical thinking and ethical awareness that skilled cataloguers possess.Q11.How might AI change the future of metadata standards and practices?Efforts are being made to transition from outdated data formats such as MARC and AACR2 to modern standards like BIBFRAME and RDA. Similarly, we must envision and adapt our metadata standards and practices to keep pace with advancements in AI.AI’s influence on metadata is significant, as it will both utilise existing metadata and drive the creation of new standards. Metadata will be essential for establishing trust and authenticity in AI-generated content, ensuring provenance and integrity.Our standards will facilitate interoperability, fostering Linked Data environments, while also guiding ethical AI practices by incorporating usage rights and privacy considerations. As cataloguers, we must strategically integrate AI, recognising its potential for efficiency alongside the necessity for human oversight to address current imperfections like inaccurate data. This moment reflects a “paradigm shift” in how we approach metadata in light of AI’s capabilities.

title_key: scientific mapping of the field of artificial intelligence and information seeking behavior analysis of trends and topic clusters in the web of science|dastar
title: Scientific Mapping of the Field of Artificial Intelligence and Information Seeking Behavior: Analysis of Trends and Topic Clusters in the Web of Science
abstract: IntroductionInformation seeking behavior (ISB) is a complex, multidimensional process at the intersection of cognitive, affective, and technological dimensions. Traditional models describe ISB as a conscious, goal-oriented process. However, the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI), including large language models, recommender systems, and conversational agents, has fundamentally transformed this paradigm. AI has shifted ISB from reactive, keyword-based searching to proactive, conversational, and algorithm-driven interactions. Despite these shifts, there is a lack of comprehensive, quantitative mapping of the global scientific structure at the intersection of AI and ISB. This study addresses this gap by employing scientometrics to map the intellectual structure, evolutionary trends, and emerging thematic clusters of this domain.Research Questions1. Which countries, institutions, authors, and journals have the highest scientific output in the domain of “AI in the transformation of ISB”?2. What are the temporal trends, language distribution, and annual growth of publications from 1976 to 2025?3. What is the conceptual structure, keyword co-occurrence network, and thematic clustering of this research field?Literature ReviewFoundational ISB models emphasize cognitive and affective stages, highlighting uncertainty and information anxiety. Later systemic models incorporated social and organizational barriers. In the digital era, scholars note that AI introduces new concepts such as “hidden information needs” and “conversational information interaction.” While previous studies have qualitatively explored specific AI systems, they lack a macro-level quantitative analysis. Scientometric approaches, utilizing databases like Web of Science (WoS), offer robust tools for mapping knowledge domains, identifying core contributors, and revealing hidden evolutionary patterns in scientific production, which this study leverages.MethodologyThis applied research utilized a scientometric approach. The statistical population comprised all documents indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) core collection, extracted on January 15, 2025, covering the period from 1976 to 2025. The search strategy combined AI-related terms with ISB terms. The initial search yielded 2, 147 records. After data cleaning (including removing duplicates, non-research documents, and standardizing author names) 1, 902 records were retained. Data analysis and visualization were conducted using Excel and R software with the bibliometrix package, employing co-word analysis, co-authorship networks, and citation analysis.ResultsThe United States led scientific production with 392 records, followed by China (324) and the UK (162). Harvard University was the top institution (33 articles), followed by the University of Toronto (28). “IEEE” and “Lecture Notes in Computer Science” were the most prolific sources (56 articles each). Trend Analysis: English dominated the literature (98.26%). The publication trend exhibited two distinct phases: a slow growth phase (1976–2020, comprising 31% of outputs) and an exponential acceleration phase post-2020. The peak occurred in 2024 with 393 documents. Conceptual Structure: Computer Science was the dominant subject category (965 articles), while Information Science accounted for only 161. Co-word analysis revealed seven distinct thematic clusters. Cluster 1 focused on AI in digital health, trust, and bias. Cluster 2 covered deep learning. Cluster 3 centered on natural language processing. Cluster 4 (16 keywords) related to data mining applications, precision, feature extraction, machine learning, neural networks, information retrieval, and visualization. Cluster 5 highlighted generative AI and ethics. Cluster 6 (5 keywords) focused on recommender systems and personalization techniques such as collaborative filtering and case-based reasoning. Cluster 7 (3 keywords) related to algorithms and the music information retrieval process.DiscussionThe findings revealed that AI is no longer merely a retrieval tool but an active agent shaping user behavior, trust, and cognitive processes. The exponential growth post-2020 aligned with the rise of conversational AI. However, a significant disciplinary imbalance exists; the field is heavily dominated by computer science and engineering, while the human, cognitive, and ethical dimensions (traditionally the domain of information science and psychology) are marginalized. This technological determinism risks creating systems that are highly efficient but lack human-centric design. Furthermore, the geographical concentration of research in Western institutions highlighted a global scientific divide. The emergence of clusters focusing on “ethics” and “bias” indicated a growing awareness of socio-technical challenges.ConclusionThe intersection of AI and ISB is a rapidly evolving, interdisciplinary field transitioning from traditional search to proactive, generative interactions. To ensure these technologies serve humanity effectively, future research must pivot towards three main axes: developing ethical frameworks for transparent AI systems, investigating the long-term cognitive impacts of AI on vulnerable groups like students, and fostering deep interdisciplinary collaborations. Only by integrating computer science with information science, psychology, and ethics can we design AI-driven information systems that are not only technologically robust but also socially equitable and human-centric. Ethical ConsiderationsAuthor ContributionsAll authors contributed equally to the conceptualization of the article and writing of the original and subsequent drafts.Data Availability StatementData are available upon request from the authors.AcknowledgementsNot applicable.Ethical ConsiderationsThe authors avoided data fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, and misconduct. As this study utilized publicly available, anonymized bibliometric data, no ethical approval was required.FundingThis research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.Conflict of Interest“The authors declare no conflict of interest.”
authors: ["Yeganeh Dastar", "mohammadreza khorramabadi arani", "Ahmad Shabani", "Fatemeh Darestani Farahani"]
