title_key: large models in transportation infrastructure a perspective|du
title: Large models in transportation infrastructure: a perspective
abstract: In late 2022, OpenAI launched ChatGPT and quickly came into the spotlight based on the development of large language modeling technology. ChatGPT is regarded as a new breakthrough in artificial intelligence technology, marking a major advancement in AI technology, stimulating global attention to the application of AI products, and opening up the ‘large model era’ of AI. Large models are also reshaping tasks and achieving impressive results in a wide range of complex downstream tasks (Li et al., 2023). The rapid development of large models provides new solution possibilities for the challenges faced by the transportation infrastructure industry. For the complicated industry specifications, design standards, feasibility study reports, and other textual data, large models can help them to study and integrate to better cope with the complex and changing application scenarios. At the same time, data management and analysis with the help of large language models in the era of big data can facilitate the study and formulation of data standards and processing procedures applicable to the transportation infrastructure industry and promote the scientific application of data in program decision-making and planning. Large models refer to deep neural network models with billions, tens of billions, or even more parameters (Lu, 2019). As shown in Fig. 1, such models are usually pre-trained on massive corpora and can learn complex patterns, linguistic nuances, and semantic relationships, but they are not targeted at a specific downstream task per se but rather gain an understanding of the training data. The application of large models means that the pre-trained large models are used to integrate and migrate the acquired knowledge to each specific downstream task through transfer learning. The training basis of large models The success of large models is inseparable from the application of its key technologies, such as self-attention mechanisms (Vaswani et al., 2017), self-supervised learning (Raffel et al., 2020), prompt engineering, etc. Transformer can model the context relationship in data (text, image, etc.) to obtain rich and effective data representation. Large language models, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and GPT (Radford et al., 2018), are trained using the Transformer architecture. After the establishment of large models, their downstream applications are based on self-supervised learning. This learning mode avoids the mapping relationship between only fitting data and simple and highly abstract annotations in supervised pre-training and enables the model to learn data representations with rich semantic expression ability and strong generalization ability, so as to better transfer ‘knowledge’ to specific downstream tasks. Hint engineering is regarded as a catalyst to guide the model to output expected answers (Kirillov et al., 2023). Through well-designed inputs, the model can be guided to complete specific tasks, not only in text, but also in modalities, such as images. According to the training data and the type of modality output, large models can be mainly divided into language, visual, and multimodal large models. Language large models learn general features from massive texts, while visual large models focus on giving computers human-like visual processing abilities for understanding, identifying, and processing images and videos. Multimodal large models integrate multi-source data, such as text and images, which is the key to general artificial intelligence (AGI) (Blum and Blum, 2023), and have shown potential in biomedical (Li et al., 2023), scientific research (Beltagy et al., 2019), and other fields. The development of the GPT series models has heralded the era of large pre-trained language models. In addition to the GPT series, companies, such as Google and Microsoft, have also been continuously releasing large models with parameters ranging from hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions. Due to the high dependence of large models on massive computational power and data resources, the research forces are mainly from the industrial community. However, with the release of open-source large models of different parameter sizes by universities, such as Berkeley and Tsinghua, the academic community has also been able to actively participate with limited computational resources. This article summarizes the basic situations of the current mainstream 10 open-source large models, as shown in Table 1 (research time up to April 2024, arranged in ascending order of release time). Representative open source large models basic situation. Representative open source large models basic situation. As shown in Table 1, in the process of the development of open-source large models, the decoder architecture has dominated. The emergent abilities (i.e. abilities that are not explicitly programmed during training but are unexpectedly acquired, which can be understood as the creativity of large models) of the large models based on the decoder architecture with ‘big data + big parameters’ are also more pronounced, highlighting that large models with decoder architecture often possess stronger and more versatile performance. This paper provides a summary of the research status related to large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, as reported in publicly available research papers and patents. The study is organized into four stages: planning and design, project management, operation and maintenance, and safety control. As illustrated in Table 2, the number of literature related to the stage of safety control is the highest, followed by the stages of planning and design and project management. In contrast, the stage of operations and maintenance has the fewest number of literature. This distribution shows the hotspots and focal points of academic research at different stages, while it also highlights some area, particularly operations and maintenance, that may require more research attention, to ensure the overall success and long-term benefits of transportation infrastructure projects. These methodologies and models hold significant guidance and reference value for the establishment of specialized large models within the domain of transportation infrastructure. Literature on large models in transportation infrastructure industry. Literature on large models in transportation infrastructure industry. As depicted in Fig. 2, transportation infrastructure projects encompass a multitude of engineering data, industry standards, and local or national policies, the complexity of which necessitates interdisciplinary research to ensure successful integration (Uddin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). Moreover, the various stages of transportation infrastructure, from planning and design to construction and maintenance, demand a diverse array of specialized skills and knowledge. This integration process relies on the collaborative efforts of a multidisciplinary team comprising designers, engineers, and other professionals, presenting significant challenges for the research and development of large models in transportation infrastructure. The construction process of a large model for transportation infrastructure Large models hold the potential to play a pivotal role in design assistance and inspiration. By analyzing extensive datasets encompassing geographical and economic information (Roberts et al., 2023), these models can aid transportation infrastructure engineers in gaining a more profound understanding of the natural environment and socio-economic conditions of the project site, thereby facilitating the formulation of more rational plans. This is particularly crucial for applications involving environmental data, such as the alignment design of railways and highways, the site selection and planning of stations and bridges, and geospatial analysis, among others. Furthermore, large models can be integrated into the design process to generate design options and recommendations. By incorporating AI-based blueprint review technologies that have been developed over the years, it is possible to achieve intelligent interactions between large language models and engineering drawings (Chen et al., 2022). This capability can be utilized for understanding, querying, and manipulating various architectural domain data, including drawings, models, and specifications, thereby significantly enhancing the efficiency of project design communication. Large models are capable of conducting real-time analysis of various data throughout the project implementation process, thereby offering decision support for project management. Leveraging large language models can assist in the analysis of railway bid documents and the requirement analysis of railway-related software (Abbas et al., 2023; Bashir et al., 2023), which aids in advancing project progress and enhancing the efficiency of project completion. In the realm of operations and maintenance, a comprehensive perspective that considers the viewpoints of designers, civil engineers, and AI programmers can be employed. Utilizing large models for project planning, operational management, design enhancement, and risk mitigation (Rane, 2023) can foster collaboration, effective communication, and the integration of interdisciplinary expertise. In the context of safe control for transportation infrastructure, research on the application of large models mainly involves training and fine-tuning the base models using accident images and textual reports. For instance, by integrating GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) with stable diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), and incorporating relevant knowledge about foreign object intrusions on railways, high-quality and highly realistic samples of railway intrusion images can be generated, achieving the goal of preventing railway disasters (Chen et al., 2023). Alternatively, effective action plans can be rapidly generated by including disaster response and planning guidelines in the initial prompts (Goecks and Waytowich, 2023). Similarly, large models can be utilized to analyze aviation safety (Chandra et al., 2023) by mining accident sample data. Looking ahead, the development and research of large models for transportation infrastructure will not be confined to the current domain of professional knowledge querying but will also integrate multimodal technologies. By fine-tuning pre-trained large models toward the field of transportation infrastructure, there is an expectation to create an AIGC (AI-Generated Content) platform specific to this domain, aiming to achieve artificial substitution in engineering processes. Leveraging in-depth industry expertise and relying on AIGC technology, the planning and design of transportation infrastructure is anticipated to achieve intelligent breakthroughs at the forefront. In particular, preliminary design, which relies heavily on industry experience, requires the development of more sophisticated algorithmic models based on professional knowledge. This process entails a longer development cycle and is challenging to realize in the short term. Conversely, construction drawing design is relatively procedural, but it encompasses numerous specialized sub-fields that need to be tackled one by one. In the long term, as model algorithms continue to mature, large models are expected to become involved in various stages, including conceptualization, preliminary design, three-dimensional model output, and drawing review. This integration aims to establish a complete closed-loop system from ‘demand input’ to ‘AI design’, ‘demand feedback’, and ‘design updates’, thereby significantly enhancing design efficiency and optimizing business models. Furthermore, in the field of structural health monitoring, research related to large models barely exists. However, given the robust text data analysis capabilities of large models, there is potential for their application in real-time data analysis of sensors through training and fine-tuning. This could lead to the monitoring of the structural health conditions of transportation infrastructure. Taking the professional intelligent Q&A of railway line selection as a starting point, a professional knowledge Q&A platform case was constructed by combining a large model with a knowledge base to achieve the resolution of issues related to railway line selection. This application not only reflects the practical application value of large models in the field of transportation infrastructure but also demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence technology in enhancing decision-making efficiency and accuracy. From the perspective of document processing, the working principle of the railway line selection knowledge Q&A platform is shown in Fig. 3. The realization principle of railway line selection knowledge Q&A The case study first examines the Langchain framework and its application in the construction of a professional knowledge base for railway line selection. By employing the data extraction methods of Langchain as well as text embedding techniques, a professional vector data knowledge base for railway lines is established. Subsequently, as shown in Fig. 4, a web-based intelligent Q&A platform for railway line selection is established. It integrates retrieval-enhanced generation technology, text embedding technology, semantic retrieval technology, and prompt engineering. The platform utilizes the BGE embedding model and the ChatGLM2-6B large language model and integrates them into the Q&A system, designing a user-friendly web interface. Langchain+LLM professional Q&A WebUI of railway route selection The case study uploads the document ‘TB 10098-2017 Code for Design of Railway Line’ as the knowledge file and poses questions regarding this specification. The responses obtained from the test are consistent with the content of the provisions recorded in the design specification, as shown in Fig. 5, and are not fabricated. Example of professional Q&A on railway line selection The case study illustrates the strengths of large models in the field of knowledge Q&A. By drawing on this example, knowledge-based Q&A platforms can be established for other specific segments within the field of transportation infrastructure. Looking further into the future, industry-specific algorithms can be integrated into the web platform for invocation, allowing for the modification of algorithm parameters through interaction with the large model. Additionally, a knowledge base can be constructed using engineering case data, enabling the large model to refer to the case database to make suggestions for new tasks. Despite the encouraging achievements made by artificial intelligence in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development of large models within this domain still faces significant challenges, with numerous technical difficulties and issues. The problems shown in Fig. 6 are particularly pronounced. Difficulties and Challenges in developing large models for transportation infrastructure The data within the transportation infrastructure domain encompasses a variety of document types, such as engineering technical forms and design drawings, which include both structured and unstructured elements. To effectively process such data, large models must comprehend their structure and the relationships among them. Documents in the transportation infrastructure field are typically lengthy. As document length increases, large models face challenges in locating key information segments and processing the internal semantic relationships within the documents. Concurrently, there is an urgent need to integrate specialized domain knowledge. The retrieval augmented generator (RAG) architecture (Lewis et al., 2020) is designed to address this challenge, but its integration with the transportation infrastructure context is currently insufficient. In the context of sensitive engineering and topographical information, data privacy protection and security precautions are critical issues for the use of large model technology in the transportation infrastructure sector. It is imperative to implement robust security measures, such as encrypted transmission and enhanced activity monitoring. Additionally, adherence to industry standards and regulations is essential to circumvent potential data privacy and security issues that may arise during the development and application of large models. Due to the nature of large models as black-box models, their internal decision-making processes are hardly interpretable. However, in the context of transportation infrastructure work, explaining the decision-making process of models is not only crucial for overall planning and architectural design stages but also essential for each phase of transportation infrastructure to comply with relevant standards and industry norms. Therefore, the interpretability of the model is equally important. Large models exhibit stability issues, where the model’s output may vary significantly in response to minor changes in the input data, potentially impacting the system’s reliability and consistency. Additionally, managing the connectivity and correlation between different tasks within transportation infrastructure projects represents a significant challenge for large models. Transportation infrastructure projects typically encompass multiple stages, such as pre-feasibility studies, feasibility studies, preliminary designs, and so on. However, large models often tend to provide direct answers, neglecting the records of previous steps and lacking comprehensive and effective explanations and reasoning regarding the future steps and their sequence. As the technology of large models rapidly advances and the quality of their generated content progressively approaches human-level performance, this poses challenges for model evaluation. Currently, the assessment of large models primarily revolves around evaluation metrics (for instance, BLEU and ROUGE are utilized to assess the model’s generative capabilities) and datasets for evaluation. However, in the field of transportation infrastructure, the development and application of large models are still in their infancy, and there is a particular lack of established indicator systems and organized datasets for evaluation. To realize the practical application of large models in transportation infrastructure, the research and development of reliable evaluation methods has become an urgent task. Finally, in the human-centered process of transportation infrastructure construction, decisions at each stage are made by human agents who assume corresponding technical responsibilities. However, with the application of AI technologies, such as large models in the field of transportation infrastructure, the decision-making process will introduce an element of ‘machine will’. Given the large model technology’s capabilities for continuous self-learning and evolution, its decision outcomes may become unpredictable, leading to potential inconsistencies between user intent and model output. In such cases, the attribution of decision-making responsibility and the mechanisms for accountability become complex and difficult to clearly define. The intelligentization of transportation infrastructure largely depends on the integration of diverse AI technologies. Large models, machine learning, deep learning, and big data analytics are all critical components in this field. They work in concert to enhance aspects, such as planning and design, project management, operations and maintenance, and safety control. The integration of large model technology paves the way for the construction of safer, more efficient, and more human-centered transportation infrastructure. The solutions to the difficulties and challenges discussed in Section 4 rely on these artificial intelligence technologies previously mentioned. This includes the standardized construction of professional datasets specific to the transportation infrastructure field, the development of more coherent long-text segmentation techniques, and the creation of more concise and efficient text vectorization technologies. Additionally, it involves the establishment of external information retrieval technologies, evaluation datasets, and assessment metrics. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies centered around large models is imperative. Finally, data privacy protection measures and multi-party accountability mechanisms urgently require enhancement and refinement. Looking ahead, to achieve enhanced specialization, robustness, and generalizability in dynamic, interference, and non-prior complex environments, transportation infrastructure large model technology must make leaps in several areas. These include the transition from purely machine learning models to structurally interpretable models, from offline learning to continuous autonomous learning, and from rote learning to associative inference. Efforts should be concentrated on promoting interdisciplinary innovative research between artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science within the field of transportation infrastructure, striving to make breakthroughs in areas, such as interpretability, high security, and low power consumption. title_key: artificial intelligencedriven surgical innovation a catalyst for medical equity|chiu
title: Artificial intelligence‐driven surgical innovation: A catalyst for medical equity
abstract: Dr. Takeuchi and Kitagawa1 described the importance of artificial intelligence (AI) in surgical innovation. AI is rapidly gaining ground in various surgical fields worldwide. The current trajectory indicates that harnessing AI technologies can significantly improve patient care by reinforcing established practices and accelerating surgical innovation, offering a distinctive chance to explore potential advantages in providing health services to low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) globally. Large language models hold immense promise in revolutionizing medical education and emerging as indispensable assets in surgical practice. Medical students and surgeons could easily access a wealth of educational materials and clinical insights presented intuitively, enriching their understanding and proficiency.2 AI technologies have demonstrated their effectiveness in tailoring surgical training, streamlining administrative duties, and creating practical and affordable simulation training programs tailored to the specific needs of diverse individuals.3 Integrating machine learning algorithms in areas like big data analysis, computer vision, and operative robotics promises to revolutionize surgical patient risk assessment, surgical treatment, and postoperative monitoring, potentially enhancing patient outcomes through reductions in morbidity and mortality.4 More importantly, immediate intra-operative suggestions can assist surgeons in providing better evidence-based treatment to surgical patients. As the key players in this transformation, surgeons have the power to grasp the basic principles of AI, understand its implications in healthcare, and explore avenues for integrating this technology. Collaboration with data scientists to capture comprehensive data and provide clinical context is pivotal to optimizing surgical care quality. In the upcoming AI-driven era, it is crucial to prioritize AI's conscientious and ethical utilization. This should be underscored by vigilant monitoring of data governance and potential patient safety risks during deployment. The implementation process must also address usability, pathway feasibility, and the crucial need for thorough evaluation of healthcare technology and evidence generation. When these may be perceived as obstacles to AI adoption, holistic implementation strategies promise to establish a robust framework for the widespread integration of AI across healthcare systems, ensuring its responsible and ethical use. Global surgery encompasses a swiftly growing interdisciplinary domain dedicated to enhancing and ensuring fair access to quality surgical care within global healthcare frameworks. Initiatives within global surgery predominantly concentrate on bolstering capabilities, advocating for equitable access, facilitating educational programs, conducting research, and crafting policies tailored to the context of all countries. This is particularly significant for LMICs, where AI can potentially address deficiencies in surgical, anesthetic, and postoperative care, and is estimated to prevent 18 million mortalities annually, mainly in LMICs.5 It holds promise in providing insights for governance, infrastructure development, and logistics prediction, bolstering the foundational pillars of global surgery. The expansion of the interdisciplinary domain of AI in surgery brings with it a beacon of hope, aiming to bridge the gap in access to equitable quality of surgical care globally. Further research is imperative to ensure optimal and equitable AI utilization, overcoming obstacles such as data representativeness, training deficiencies, human hesitancy, and ethical considerations. Dealing with these challenges through a targeted, evidence-driven strategy could assist LMICs in surmounting bureaucratic inefficiencies and establishing improved surgical systems. N/A. title_key: sat119 artificial intelligence mediated assistants will they educate the public about health disparities in diabetes|zhao
title: SAT119 Artificial Intelligence Mediated Assistants: Will They Educate The Public About Health Disparities In Diabetes?
abstract: Abstract Disclosure: W. Zhao: None. G. Wu: None. E. Cheng: None. J. Lee: None. A. Wong: None. Background: In 2022, 37 million US adults had diabetes and 96 million had pre-diabetes. Diabetes and prediabetes affect 49.3% population in America. In the diabetic population, 12.1% are non-Hispanic blacks, 11.8% of Hispanics, and 9.5% of Asian Americans. 54% of Americans read at or below the sixth-grade level. ChatGPTTM, launched 11/30/22, has the newest Artificial Intelligence (AI) software versus Google AssistantTM, launched 05/2016. Purpose: Can ChatGPT use its natural language software to educate the lay public about diabetes and health disparities? Methods: Evaluate the readability of responses after five questions were posed to ChatGPTTM and Google AssistantTMQuestions: 1. Do African Americans have a higher risk of complications with Type 2 Diabetes? 2. Do Hispanic Americans have a higher risk of complications with Type 2 diabetes? 3. Do Asian Americans have a higher risk of complications with Type 2 diabetes? 4. Do women get Type 2 diabetes more than men? 5. What is pre-diabetes vs diabetes? Word count and Dale-Chall score assessed the readability level of both ChatGPT and Google Assistant responses. The Dale-Chall readability formula is calculated based on the percentage of difficult words and average sentence length in words. The U.S. Department of Education used the Dale-Chall formula to adjust the text to grade-level readability. Result: Word count: CHAT:Q1=104; Q2=135; Q3=136; Q4=133; Q5=232 vs GOOGLE: Q1=38, Q2=49, Q3=16; Q4=50; Q5=42. CHAT Word Count Avg=148, SD=48.81; GOOGLE Word Count Avg=39, SD=13.7; P-value=0.003908 Dale-Chall: CHAT: Q1=8.4; Q2=8.6; Q3=9.8, Q4=8.6, Q5=8.7 vs. GOOGLE: Q1=6.7, Q2=9, Q3=9.4, Q4=6.3, Q5=9.1. CHAT Dale-Chall Score Avg=8.82, SD=0.56; GOOGLE Dale-Chall Score Avg=8.1, SD=1.47; P-value=0.1306. ChatGPT has nearly the same grade level of comprehension as Google Assistant, including statistics about health disparities. However, ChatGPT was trained using information and transforming it into paragraphs, and google assistant extracts the data from websites and the variability is higher with a higher standard deviation than ChatGPT. Conclusion: ChatGPT with its artificial intelligence software is able to provide answers to our patients. While the answers may require a high school reading level and beyond, this is an excellent beginning for health education. Presentation: Saturday, June 17, 2023

title_key: dr blair bowers a pioneer in biological electron microscopy|jerome
title: Dr. Blair Bowers: A Pioneer in Biological Electron Microscopy
abstract: Dr. Mary Blair Bowers is a pioneer in the use of biological electron microscopy (EM) for the study of cell cytoskeleton and motility. As part of the second generation of biological electron microscopists trained by the early pioneers, she played an important role in adapting specimen preparation techniques for studying biological samples under an electron beam. Prior to the 1940s, biological transmission EM was limited to observing small objects like viruses, extracellular filaments, and intracellular objects isolated from intact cells and tissue. Observation of these particles was normally done using negative stains for contrast. However, in 1945, Keith Porter, Albert Claude, and Ernest Fullam published the first electron micrograph of an intact cell showing a very thin edge of a spread-out and osmium tetroxide (OsO4)-fixed fibroblast [1]. The edges of the cell were thin enough for the electron beam to penetrate, although the more central areas of the cell were too thick to be imaged successfully. Over the ensuing years, these same individuals, along with other early biological EM pioneers, developed methods for fixing, embedding, and thin sectioning whole cells to allow high-resolution imaging of the cell interior. Notable among these methods was the introduction of glutaraldehyde as an EM fixative by Sabatini, Bensch, and Barrnett in 1963 [2]. Dr. Porter heard of this innovation in advance of publication and immediately had his lab begin using glutaraldehyde for EM ultrastructure studies. The many advances during this nascent period began the field of ultrastructural cell biology. It was the students of these pioneers, including Blair Bowers, who helped to develop and use the new EM techniques to further explore cell structure and function. Blair Bowers grew up in Jackson, NC, a small town in the northeastern part of the state (Figure 1). She received her BA and, in 1956, her Master of Arts degree from Duke University. After obtaining her master’s degree, she took a research assistant position at the National Heart Institute of NIH (now the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute) working for Frederic C. Bartter, MD, an internationally recognized endocrinologist and Chief of the Endocrinology section of the National Heart Institute. During her tenure with Dr. Bartter, she was part of groundbreaking studies on the role of adrenal steroids on patients with Addison’s disease [3,4]. In 1957 she left NIH to pursue her doctoral degree at the Biological Laboratories of Harvard University under the tutelage of Dr. Carroll Williams, a pioneer in insect physiology (Figure 2). In 1961, Blair received her Ph.D. from Radcliffe College of Harvard University for her work on DNA synthesis during the metamorphosis of the Cecropia silkworm. It was during these studies that Dr. Bowers adapted the new technique of autoradiography to the light microscopy study of the timing of DNA synthesis in the developing wing of Cecropia [5]. The receipt of her Ph.D. degree coincided with the arrival of Keith Porter to Harvard’s Biology Department. Dr. Porter offered her a post-doctoral fellowship in his laboratory, and later she was promoted to Instructor in the Department of Biology, where she assisted in teaching undergraduate courses. During this period, Dr. Porter was developing electron microscopy within the Biology Department at Harvard and influenced many young researchers, including Blair. An electron micrograph from her 1963 article on neurohormone transport in insects was the cover art for that issue of Science [6]. Her passion for electron microscopy developed during this time and remained with her throughout her career. Blair Bowers (on left) at 16 in Jackson, NC. Blair Bowers at Harvard. In 1966, Dr. Bowers left Harvard to join the intramural research branch of the National Heart Institute of NIH, working in Dr. Edward Korn’s laboratory. Dr. Korn was doing groundbreaking research on cell movement, combining structural and biochemical approaches. In 1968, Drs. Bowers and Korn published a series of papers describing the fine structure of Acanthamoeba castellanii, establishing Acanthamoeba as an extremely useful organism to study cell structure and function relationships [7]. Throughout her career, Blair continued to return to Acanthamoeba as a model system to study cell functions such as cell motility, membrane dynamics, endocytosis, exocytosis, and organelle dynamics for which she is best known. In addition, in a multiyear collaboration with NIH biochemist Enrico Cabib, she helped unravel the mystery of chitin synthesis in yeast and the role of chitin in the formation of the septum of dividing yeast cells. A paper from this work was chosen for the cover of a 1991 issue of the Journal of Cell ­Biology [8]. Her published work also includes microscopic studies of insects, bacteria, protozoa, and mammals. She remained at NIH until her retirement in 1995. Blair was always highly active in the microscopy community. She held membership in the Microscopy Society of America (and the MSA local affiliate Chesapeake Society for Electron Microscopy), American Society of Zoologists, American Society for Cell Biology, American Association for the Advancement of Science, and The Histochemical Society. She served on the MSA Certification Board, MSA Publications Committee, MSA Nominations Committee, and was the MSA Treasurer from 1983–1987. As Treasurer, she had the daunting task of converting the MSA Membership roster from index cards to digital format. In 1981, she was part of the committee proposing the concept of the Technologists’ Forum. Soon thereafter, the Technologists’ Forum became a mainstay organization within MSA and served as a model for the development of other interest groups within MSA. For her continued service to MSA, Blair was awarded the MSA Distinguished Service Award in 1992. Outside of MSA, she served on the Editorial Board for ­Molecular and Cellular Biology and in 1994 was elected Treasurer of the Histochemical Society, where she is credited with helping to bring the Histochemical Society’s financial ­situation back into the black and working with the rest of council to expand publication of the Journal of Histochemistry and ­Cytochemistry to a monthly journal. Blair has always been an active educator. In the early days of biological EM, there were no authoritative textbooks on biological specimen preparation for EM, and books on imaging using EM were geared to those with a physics degree. To counter this and to spread the biological EM gospel, Blair and Mort Maser ran workshops on electron microscopy in the biological sciences. These two-week, intensive, residential workshops covered specimen collection, specimen preparation, negative staining, replica production, resin embedding, glass knife breaking (the old-fashioned way with glazier’s pliers), and thin sectioning. Beginning in 1964, these courses were conducted at Northeastern University’s Conference Center, Henderson House, located in the suburbs of Boston. Henderson House had an EM facility in the basement (Figures 3 and 4). After the Henderson House EM facility closed in 1974, the annual courses were conducted at the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole, where Mort had taken a position to oversee educational activities. The courses continued at Woods Hole until 1982. Many electron microscopists, including me, got their introduction to EM through these courses and the talented instruction of Blair and Mort. Thus, I can speak firsthand about Blair Bowers as an extraordinarily gifted and patient educator. Besides what she, Mort, and others taught me at the workshop, her guidance and encouragement continued and has been central to my career. Meeting with Blair during the Microscopy & Microanalysis meetings (Figure 5) or the annual American Society for Cell Biology conferences was always the highlight of my year. We had similar scientific interests and, so, getting Blair’s take on my harebrained ideas and hearing what she was working on were always enlightening experiences and never failed to energize my enthusiasm for cell biology. During one such discussion, she indicated that a stereology approach to quantification of cellular ultrastructure was a much more efficient approach than the laborious one I had chosen to employ. That simple comment led me down a whole new avenue of exploration that yielded significant results. It was also Blair who encouraged me to volunteer for a position in MSA and suggested that I join the Education Committee. As a member of the Education Committee, I programmed the in-meeting tutorials for a number of years. This was an incredible opportunity to meet many senior scientists and develop friendships within MSA. Without that small push from Blair, I doubt that my scientific horizon would be as broad as it has become. I went on to chair the Education Committee and serve in a number of other positions within MSA, including the honor of being its President in 2006. My association with MSA leadership has opened access to unbelievable resources, provided incredible friendships, and generated wonderful memories. And it all started with a prompt from Blair Bowers. Blair Bowers demonstrating block trimming at Henderson House workshop, 1973. Blair Bowers, with coffee, supervising specimen preparation at Henderson House workshop, 1973. Blair Bowers with Jay Jerome enjoying ice cream at Microscopy & Microanalysis 2003 in San Antonio, TX. For all the reasons above, I was very pleased and honored to be asked to write this tribute to Dr. Blair Bowers’ achievements as a pioneer in microscopy and as a microscopy educator. For full disclosure, however, I must confess that in addition to counting Blair as a mentor, colleague, and friend, she is also my first cousin, a connection of which I am very proud.

title_key: assessing fairness in ai assisted writing scoring developing fairness measures to detect predictive bias in automated essay scoring|chen
title: Assessing fairness in AI-assisted writing scoring: Developing fairness measures to detect predictive bias in automated essay scoring
abstract: Automated essay scoring (AES) is increasingly utilized in educational settings, yet concerns about its fairness persist. This study reviews current fairness measures in AES and summarizes their respective strengths and weaknesses. Drawing on principles from educational and psychological testing, we introduce two measures for detecting potential predictive bias: conditional disparity ratio and conditional disparity difference. Our method emphasizes two key principles: first, that bias should be assessed among students with comparable proficiency levels, and second, that evaluations should be conducted on a test set independent of the AES training set. We demonstrated this approach using writing samples from the Facial Action Coding System task within the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus to assess potential predictive bias related to sex and race. Four AES models were evaluated for predictive bias: ordinal logistic regression using TF–IDF features, fine-tuned BERT, and ChatGPT in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. The findings indicated that, without accounting for proficiency, subgroup differences remained ambiguous, making it difficult to detect potential predictive bias. In contrast, conditioning on proficiency revealed clearer and more interpretable patterns of bias. The discussion addresses key factors and the extension of the bias detection framework and outlines future directions for bias mitigation.

abstract: Recently, Quantitative Biology (QB) held a discussion on "AI (artificial intelligence) for Life Science" among editorial board members and interested scholars in anticipation of rapid development of this growing area after AlphaGo and ChatGPT mania.Many young people tend to get confused between facts and fictions; heated debates are unavoidable even among their mentors.When deep learning as represented by convolutional neural networks and LSTM (long shortterm memory) was made available for bioinformatics students, many of them rushed into this research field and tried to adopt these methods in all their projects without knowing the history that these tools were becoming successful consistently with Moore's Law (relating to rapid computer technology advances), but more importantly due to new structural/ functional understanding of vision and auditory circuits in the brain.Recently, some young people have claimed "LSTM is dead, long live transformer" (which is somewhat like saying "the bike is dead, long live the car"), and have amplified the threat that ChatGPT could wipe out human jobs.They believe transformer is the "silver bullet" for all learning tasks, clearly reflecting their lack of basic knowledge (i.e."No Free Lunch Theory," the trade-off of such global "attention network" is to pay the price for complexity: difficulty of training and high memory costs).There is no doubt ML (machine learning) and AI have brought a new revolution in science and technology, and will deliver huge unforeseeable impact to human everyday life as well as to social relationships.In this context, QB journal could be a great platform for encouraging intellectual discussions and for promoting AI for Life Science.Here, I would like to use the DIALOG to "抛砖引玉" (make some initial remarks to get the ball rolling), although it is my personal opinion which is inevitably subject to bias and limitations.

title_key: travel into my future perceptions of generation z along a fictive journey|miskolczi
title: Travel into my future: perceptions of Generation Z along a fictive journey
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to reveal Generation Z’s perspectives on their distant (2070s) future considering technological, socioeconomic and environmental challenges. This approach reveals latent fears and expectations of this generation and thus highlight key paths for further scientific analysis and strategy development in the tourism sector (e.g. keeping AI development under control, adapting to climate change). Design/methodology/approach The relevant literature was reviewed using the rapid evidence assessment (REA) framework. The empirical research follows a hybrid approach, employing Grounded Theory (GT) to analyze self-reflective narratives of Generation Z university students (n = 150). Subjects imagined themselves in 50 years and reported a fictive journey’s technological, sociodemographic and infrastructural characteristics. For the analysis, the three-phase coding process of Corbin and Strauss (1990) was applied to identify patterns in respondents’ future perceptions. Findings are validated by employing a cluster analysis using the NVivo software. Findings The GT-based analysis resulted in a six-variable model identifying key technological (e.g. the rise of AI and smart tourism services), social (e.g. anticipated health challenges) and environmental factors shaping future travel behavior. This study also brings attention to previously underexplored concepts, such as the negative perceptions of technological advancements and Generation Z’s concerns about aging, leading to the introduction of new theoretical perspectives (e.g. AI detoxification tourism, negative perceptions of seniority) that could shape the future of consumer behavior. Research limitations/implications The analysis is based on a sample of Hungarian university students, which may limit generalizability to other cultural or socioeconomic contexts. While the research offers theoretical contributions to future tourism studies, further quantitative validation is recommended, particularly through cross-cultural comparisons and longitudinal studies tracking possible generational attitude changes. Practical implications Our findings provide valuable insights for tourism stakeholders. In destination management, the integration of AI-based tourism services should prioritize hybrid solutions, ensuring that human interactions remain available for travelers seeking authenticity. Future marketing strategies should balance high-tech convenience with nostalgia-driven travel preferences, acknowledging Generation Z’s growing demand for AI detox experiences. In terms of policymaking, regulations should promote sustainable AI adoption in tourism, ensuring ethical data use, accessibility and intergenerational inclusivity. By incorporating these insights, tourism professionals can better align future strategies with the evolving preferences of Generation Z travelers. Social implications With a deeper understanding of Generation Z’s concerns and expectations, this research highlights emerging generational differences in tourism consumer behavior. Findings suggest that digital literacy, climate awareness and AI skepticism will play crucial roles in shaping future travel decisions. This knowledge can boost educational initiatives, policy frameworks and intergenerational travel planning strategies, ensuring that tourism remains inclusive and adaptable to evolving consumer expectations. Originality/value Our findings provide novel insights into the relationship between tourism, technological development and generational shifts, offering a long-term perspective on how Generation Z envisions travel in an AI-driven world. Unlike previous studies that primarily examine short-term technological adoption in tourism (e.g. AI chatbots, smart hotels or VR experiences), this research explores deeper psychological and sociocultural influences, including climate anxiety, nostalgia-driven travel and AI skepticism. Through the application of GT methodology, this study not only identifies emerging travel behaviors and concerns but also introduces new conceptual frameworks, such as AI detoxification tourism and the paradox of high-tech vs traditional travel preferences.

title_key: ai assisted medicine possibly helpful possibly terrifying|brandt
title: AI-Assisted Medicine: Possibly Helpful, Possibly Terrifying
abstract: ChatGPT and Google Bard have great potential that could simplify ED tasks—if used appropriatelyFigure: artificial intelligence, AI, medicine, ChatGPT, Google Bard, ED, emergency medicine, emergency physicians, EM, EPs, technology, patients, HPIs, physical exams, diagnosisFigureWe emergency physicians strive to stay on the cutting edge of new technologies and tools for patient care. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology such as ChatGPT and Google Bard offer significant potential. Of course, many have rightfully raised concerns. Give these programs a try. ChatGPT and Google Bard are free to use and can provide answers to any question you can ask. They can also provide recipes, help with editing, or instantly create a unique fairy tale about a grumpy porcupine and a pineapple named Bonzo. (True story: I tried it; the porcupine's name is Quillbert.) AI-assisted technology has tremendous potential, but it also has challenges. I asked both programs about the potential hazards of using them. The programs responded similarly, stating they may unintentionally provide inaccuracies and misinformation. Both may have biased responses because they base their information on selections from the internet. ChatGPT used data up until 2021 for training, while Bard is ongoing. ChatGPT even explained a risk of dependence, where users could become reliant on it for decision-making, leading to a reduction in critical thinking and decision-making skills. Obviously, results provided by these programs must be carefully weighed. Leon Gussow, MD, explained how ChatGPT problematically recommended syrup of ipecac while describing the dangers of gastric lavage. (EMN. 2023;45[3]:19; https://bit.ly/3YfQB8C.) Another article I read talked about how a physician provided HPIs and physical exams to see if the program could correctly diagnose patients. Given a presentation of a young woman with abdominal pain, ChatGPT did not even suggest the possibility of ectopic pregnancy, the actual diagnosis. Weigh Answers Carefully Even with these limitations clearly branded in our brains, what benefits could this cutting-edge technology provide? ChatGPT “passed” the USMLE licensing exam. These programs are excellent at answering questions with clearly defined answers, and they can suggest guidance with next-step management once the diagnosis is established. Again, answers must be weighed carefully for accuracy. These programs can also be quite helpful for providing patient education. We all have discharge instructions for common diagnoses, but this can be especially beneficial for patients with a unique or less typical diagnosis. I asked both to act as an emergency physician and provide simple-to-understand discharge instructions for a patient diagnosed with rickets. I did the same with Raynaud syndrome and Alice in Wonderland syndrome. The programs provided excellent, accurate, and simple instructions each time, explaining and outlining the diseases and what can be done for each. These programs could be huge time-savers when used appropriately. Here to Stay AI also provided excellent information when asked about healthy eating advice for a newly diagnosed diabetic. I then asked for advice for a patient with a new diagnosis of celiac disease. The programs provided a variety of gluten-free ideas and options as well as advice for healthy living. I also inquired about recipes, and they instantly came up with a wide variety of gluten-free options and support. The prompts provided can be tailored to the individual. AI can generate meal plans for a week (or month) for a patient who had gastric bypass that he must have 1100 calories a day with 110 grams of protein. Interestingly, ChatGPT added a note at the bottom saying, “It is important to consult with a healthcare provider or registered dietitian to determine the appropriate calorie and nutrient intake for your individual needs.” Similarly, the programs provided detailed exercise schedules for a wide variety of stretches and exercises. The programs will tailor to individual needs, weights, diets, and desires. Queries can be extremely specific, giving differing advice based on the inputs provided. Ultimately, these programs are tools. Like it or not, responsive AI is here to stay. It will continue to improve and will likely become embedded into various aspects of our lives. This technology has amazing potential and may aid and simplify tasks in and out of the ED as long as we remain vigilant to use it appropriately. DR. BRANDT is an emergency physician currently working in New Zealand (after 12 years in Michigan). Read his blog and other articles at http://brandtwriting.com, follow him on Twitter @brandtwriting, and listen to his humorous ED podcast, EpineFriends, which can be found at http://apple.co/3d9Nco2. Read his past EMN columns at http://bit.ly/EMN-BrandtsRants.

title_key: ai native value creation beyond labor substitution the economics of difference personalized therapeutics and the rise of ai native life infrastructure|guo
title: AI-Native Value Creation Beyond Labor Substitution: The Economics of Difference, Personalized Therapeutics, and the Rise of AI-Native Life Infrastructure
abstract: AI-Native Value Creation Beyond Labor Substitution: The Economics of Difference, Personalized Therapeutics, and the Rise of AI-Native Life Infrastructure Civilization Physics - Series: Economy This article develops a theory of AI-native value creation beyond labor substitution. The first commercial wave of generative AI has focused on faster drafting, coding, search, customer support, and administrative execution, but these gains remain bounded by inherited workflows. The deeper economic shift begins when AI changes what institutions can represent, coordinate, verify, and deliver. The central claim is that industrial scale made sameness cheap, while AI-native systems may make difference economically manageable. Instead of measuring value only as a task completed more cheaply, the article shifts the unit of value toward a person, case, learner, patient, client, or environment served at higher resolution. This requires more than model capability: it requires longitudinal data, modular production, expert judgment, validation, coordination, and responsibility architecture. The article develops this argument through several linked mechanisms: The economics of difference names the shift from lowering labor cost to lowering the full-stack cost of preserving useful heterogeneity across cases. AI-native production systems use standardized lower-layer infrastructure so that upper-layer outputs can become individualized without losing coherence. The individualization ratio compares value gained from case-specific adaptation against the additional full-stack cost of acquisition, representation, design, verification, coordination, responsibility, and production. Intismeran autogene provides a threshold case: patient-specific sequencing, computational target selection, individualized mRNA design, and standardized manufacturing have reportedly reached positive Phase 3 topline results in high-risk melanoma, while important effect-size, cost, survival, and generalization questions remain unresolved. AI-native life infrastructure describes a persistent service stack that coordinates sensing, memory, analysis, expert judgment, consent, audit, escalation, and feedback around a person over time. Human amplification becomes an architecture of task allocation, visibility, escalation, and learning, with humans governing goals, exceptions, standards, ethics, and accountability rather than merely approving model output. This article reframes AI’s economic role as resolution expansion: raising the granularity at which civilization can act responsibly. Medicine can move from population averages toward individualized interventions; education can move from standardized pacing toward governed developmental adaptation; professional services can move from episodic transactions toward continuous, context-rich support. The scarce resource is the ability to preserve useful difference without losing truth, control, access, or accountability. Keywords: AI-native economy, economics of difference, labor substitution, resolution expansion, personalized medicine, individualized therapeutics, intismeran autogene, neoantigen therapy, AI-native life infrastructure, mass customization, precision education, human-AI augmentation, responsibility architecture, full-stack cost, premium-first protocolization, expert-governed AI

title_key: artificial intelligence for ophthalmology ai 4 o within ai for vikshit bharat 2047|senjam
title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmology (AI-4-O) within AI for Vikshit Bharat 2047
abstract: Today, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the fastest growing technological fields of the twenty-first century. The term AI was first coined by John MaCarthy in 1956, an American computer scientist of Dartmouth College, The United States.[1] AI is a computer technology that is capable of imitating human behaviors and can execute tasks in a way that is considered intelligent or that normally require human intelligence, such as speech recognition, decision-making process, and language translation. It makes possible for machines to interact with humans and thereby obeys commands and performs activities that resemble human actions. The development of AI relies on vast amounts of external data and cloud computing technologies, and its applications now extend across various fields. As of today (September 28, 2025), AI technology is used in numerous areas, including the medical field. Advancements in AI technology such as computer vision (CV), natural language processing (NLP), and various methods of deep learning have enabled machines to recognize and analyze images with remarkable accuracy. As a result, AI incorporation in the context of medical field has increased dramatically, including within ophthalmology practices in recent years. For instance, AI is widely applied for medical imaging for screening, diagnosis, and even classification of ocular diseases. At the same time, AI-based wearable assistive technology for low vision and vision rehabilitation services have gained significant attention worldwide.[2] In the screening and diagnosis of eye disease, the images of fundus are collected from an external dataset, either newly acquired or from the open access sources that fed into a deep learning model, a subset of machine learning, which is further trained to have the ability to screen or diagnose ocular diseases. A type of AI deep learning method, named CNN (Convolutional Neural Networks), frequently is employed that helps in image feature extraction and processing. To date, the most common application of AI technology in ophthalmology has been the screening of retinal problems like diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma. For instance, a CNN variant, called CNN-UNet, is used to identify the presence or absence of hemorrhage in retina, aiding in the early diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy.[3] Additionally, another deep learning model variant, named GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks), is used for the improvement of the quality of medical or fundus images. For example, RF-GAN is used to synthesize retinal fundus images, thereby improving the performance of diabetic retinopathy grading.[4] Additionally, the integration of AI-powered medical technology can assist eye care professionals in performing faster and more accurate screening and diagnosis, while reducing repetitive manual tasks and supporting the clinical decision-making process. Furthermore, AI-based approaches offer a noninvasive and cost-effective method for screening eye diseases, making them particularly valuable in large-scale or resource-limited settings. Similarly, AI has recently revolutionized assistive technology (AT) for vision impairment (VI), benefiting persons with low vision and blindness. Such advanced AI-powered devices have surpassed all limitations associated with traditional AT for vision impairment, such as white cane, Braille books, and optical magnifiers. In fact, these AI-enabled vision ATs have transformed previously inaccessible environments into the accessible ones among users. Therefore, such innovations have the potential to reshape the paradigm of low vision care and vision rehabilitation services in the future. These AI-powered ATs for vision use CV techniques based on deep learning models and NLP, enabling a computer to perceive, interpret, and understand objects, text, and scene while providing audio outputs for the users. For example, apps such as Be My Eyes or Seeing AI app leverage CV and NLP to recognize objects, faces, and currency. The envision smart glasses, equipped with advanced cameras, use CV technology and NLP to help visually impaired individuals interact more effectively with their surrounding and facilitate them in their daily living activities. These smart glasses often combine CNN and OCR (Optical Character Recognition) technology to support in executing independent living activities. A few AI-powered ATs also enhance navigation and mobility, for example, app like Seeing AI and DeepNAVI that provides detailed information on obstacle location and distance from the user, whereas AI-enabled DAISY WIBORD audiobooks help access to many educational books.[5,6] A study reported that DAISY-WIBORD are very useful and satisfactory for blind students. Such AI-based solutions can provide additional benefits to those persons with low vision and total blindness for whom the traditional AT cannot address the challenges. There are also other AI-powered ATs that equipped NLP technologies to help blind users to communicate, interact, and access the digital content, including images description. Examples include JAWS (Job Access with Speech) with Picture Smart AI, which provides AI-enhanced screen reading and audio output of images descriptions on the screen. Another rapidly advancing AI-powered technology is Large Language Model (LLM), such as ChatGPT, Gemini, incorporated with voice output and screen reading software, which offers new and novel opportunities to enhance the learning process for visually impaired individuals. Furthermore, integrating AI technology into the home (smart home) environment, although still in the development stage, has the potential to further enhance autonomy and efficiency in executing daily tasks among low vision and blind persons. Such AI integration will have huge potential to revolutionize the daily lives of individuals with low vision and blindness. Following the IndiaAI Mission in 2024, NITI Aayog, Government of India, launched an initiative, “AI for Vikshit Bharat,” in September 2025 to leverage AI across various disciplines, including healthcare.[7] The focus is on advancing AI-based cutting-edge Research and Development, as well as promoting adoption to enhance productivity and service efficiencies across all fields. Such a transformative national initiative creates a significant opportunity to accelerate research on AI-powered ophthalmology. To maximize the benefits in the years to come, the ophthalmological community and academia should be encouraged for AI-enabled technology research projects. At the same time, the government can be urged to prioritize funding for advanced AI-driven research targeting ophthalmological applications under the umbrella of AI for Vikshit Bharat 2047. About the authorDr. Suraj Singh Senjam is Professor-in-Charge of Vision Training and Rehabilitation and Professor of Community Ophthalmology at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. He currently serves as an Associate Editor for Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology (Taylor & Francis) and as an Academic Guest Editor for Frontiers in Public Health and Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences. He has also previously served as an Academic Editor for PLOS ONE. In research, Dr. Senjam has been recognized among the world’s top 2% of scientists in 2024 and 2025 by Stanford University and is a contributor to Oxford Bibliographies in Disability Studies. Since 2017, he has worked extensively in the field of assistive technology, particularly vision assistive devices, in collaboration with national and international organizations including the World Health Organization (WHO), Geneva. He served as an expert member of WHO’s technical working group that redesigned the Rapid Assistive Technology Assessment (rATA) tool and led the first-ever rATA study in India, supported by WHO. He has also spearheaded a twinning Low Vision Rehabilitation Program in Southeast Asia with support from the WHO Regional Office. Academically, Dr. Senjam earned his MBBS from the Regional Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS), Imphal, Manipur, and completed his MD in Community Medicine at PGIMER, Chandigarh. He holds a Master’s in Public Health for Eye Care from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), UK, and has received training in medical device development and its social implications at Osaka University, Japan.

title_key: genwise an all in one ai toolkit|khanum
title: GenWise – An All-in-One AI Toolkit
abstract: GenWise is a cross-platform intelligent mobile suite designed to unify diverse AI-driven utilities into a single, cohesive application experience. Developed in Flutter for multi-device compatibility, GenWise integrates Google Generative Language Models (Gemini) for natural-language reasoning, understanding, and text generation; Vertex AI Imagen 2 for prompt-based visual synthesis; and Firebase for secure user authentication alongside lightweight cloud data persistence. The system is targeted toward learners, educators, content creators, and software developers who often rely on fragmented AI tools that lack interoperability and consistent workflows. GenWise consolidates these capabilities into modular, extensible components such as Chat-with-PDF for document question answering, Code Explainer for static code understanding, AI UI Designer for rapid prototyping of interfaces into structured HTML/CSS, and Communication Practice using speech-to-text and text-to-speech for conversational skill development. Additional creative and productivity features—such as Resume Builder, Question Paper Generator, Knowledge Duel, Image-to-Story transformation, Poster Generator, Lyrics/Recipe assistants, and image compression/upscaling—demonstrate the system’s breadth. This paper presents the architecture, design decisions, and implementation strategies that enable GenWise to function as a unified AI toolkit. We describe the chunking and retrieval mechanisms used for document Q&A, the conversational pipeline for speech-based interactions, and the modular plugin-style design pattern that supports rapid tool integration. Security considerations, performance optimizations, and limitations—such as dependency on cloud inference and variability in generative outputs—are discussed. Finally, we outline future directions including vector-store-based retrieval augmentation, partial offline inference via ONNX Runtime, advanced analytics, and adaptive personalization. GenWise illustrates how emerging AI capabilities can be orchestrated into a stable, production-ready platform suitable for educational, creative, and productivity-oriented tasks.

title: Journal of Applied Informatics and Technology (Editorial Note)
abstract: The Journal of Applied Informatics and Technology (JIT) has published Volume 8, Number 1 (2026): January-June, comprising a total of 13 research articles. Each article has undergone peer review by at least three experts from different institutions. The authors revised their articles based on the reviewers’ comments until they were approved for publication. The editorial team also verified the accuracy of the content, references, and language usage to ensure the highest quality. We sincerely thank all the reviewers for their valuable feedback and thoughtful recommendations.
venue: Journal of Applied Informatics and Technology

title: ШЕТ ТІЛІН ОҚЫТУДЫ ҰЙЫМДАСТЫРУДАҒЫ ЦИФРЛЫҚ ТРАНСФОРМАЦИЯ ЖӘНЕ ЖАСАНДЫ ИНТЕЛЛЕКТ
abstract: Мақалада жоғары оқу орындарында шет тілдерін оқыту үдерісінде жасанды интеллект мүмкіндіктерін пайдаланудың өзекті мәселесі қарастырылады. Білім берудің цифрлық трансформациясы жасанды интеллектті оқу үдерісін жаңғыртудың негізгі құралдарының бірі ретінде айқындайды. Мақалада тілдік мамандықтарды оқытудағы жасанды интеллекттің негізгі артықшылықтары мен педагогикалық әлеуеті талданып, сондай-ақ оны білім беру ортасында қолданудың мүмкін шектеулері мен тәуекелдері қарастырылады. Зерттеуде чат-боттардың оқу контентін студенттердің тілдік дайындық деңгейіне, білім беру қажеттіліктері мен қызығушылықтарына бейімдеу мүмкіндіктеріне ерекше назар аударылады. Сонымен қатар жасанды интеллекттің жазбаша және лексика-грамматикалық дағдыларды дамытудағы рөлі айқындалады. ChatGPT, Duolingo, Babbel, Mondly және Replika.ai сияқты ағылшын тілін үйренуге арналған ең танымал жасанды интеллект платформаларына жасалған шолу олардың функционалдық және педагогикалық мүмкіндіктерін талдауға мүмкіндік берді. Зерттеудің эмпирикалық бөлігі «Шетел тілі: екі шетел тілі» білім беру бағдарламасы бойынша оқитын екінші курс студенттері арасында жүргізілген сауалнама нәтижелеріне негізделген (Орталық Азиа инновациялық университет, Шымкент қ.). Сауалнама ағылшын тілін меңгеру барысында жасанды интеллект құралдарын қолдану деңгейі мен сипатын анықтауға бағытталды, соның ішінде кәсіби лексика мен грамматиканы меңгеру, жазбаша тапсырмаларды (эссе және іскерлік хаттар) орындау, ауызша сөйлеу дағдыларын дамыту және үй тапсырмаларын орындау үдерістерінде қолданылуы қамтылды. Алынған деректер сандық әдістерді қолдану арқылы өңделіп, пайыздық көрсеткіштер түрінде ұсынылды. Зерттеу нәтижелері негізінде жоғары білім берудің цифрлық трансформациясы жағдайында чат-боттар мен басқа да ЖИ-құралдарын шет тілдерін оқытуда көмекші құрал ретінде қолданудың мақсатқа сай екендігі туралы қорытындылар жасалды. В статье говорится об актуальной проблеме использования возможностей искусственного интеллекта в процессе обучения иностранным языкам в высших учебных заведениях. Цифровая трансформация образования определяет искусственный интеллект как ключевой инструмент модернизации учебного процесса. В работе рассматриваются основные преимущества и педагогический потенциал искусственного интеллекта в обучении языковым специальностям, а также анализируются возможные ограничения и риски его применения в образовательной среде. Особое внимание уделяется возможностям чат-ботов, способных адаптировать учебный контент к уровню языковой подготовки, образовательным потребностям и интересам студентов. Предложенное исследование акцентирует внимание и на роль в развитии письменных и лексико-грамматических навыков. Обзор наиболее популярных платформ искусственного интеллекта, используемых для изучения английского языка, таких как ChatGPT, Duolingo, Babbel, Mondly и Replika.ai, позволил проанализировать их функциональные и педагогические возможности. Эмпирическая часть исследования основана на результатах анкетного опроса среди студентов второго курса образовательной программы «Иностранный язык: два иностранных языка», Центрально-Азиатский Инновационный Университет (г. Шымкент). Опрос был направлен на определение уровня и характера использования средств искусственного интеллекта в процессе изучения английского языка, в том числе при освоении профессиональной лексики и грамматики, выполнении письменных заданий (эссе и деловых писем), развитии устной речи и выполнении домашних заданий. Полученные данные обработаны с применением количественных методов и представлены в процентном соотношении. На основе результатов исследования делаются выводы о целесообразности применения чат-ботов и других AI-инструментов в качестве вспомогательных средств обучения иностранным языкам в условиях цифровой трансформации высшего образования. The article addresses the relevant issue of using the capabilities of artificial intelligence in the process of teaching foreign languages in higher education institutions. The digital transformation of education defines artificial intelligence as a key tool for modernizing the learning process. The paper examines the main advantages and pedagogical potential of artificial intelligence in teaching language-related specialties, as well as analyzes the possible limitations and risks of its application in the educational environment. Special attention is paid to the capabilities of chatbots that can adapt educational content to the level of language proficiency, educational needs, and interests of students. The survey also emphasizes the role of artificial intelligence in the development of written and lexical- grammatical skills. A review of the most popular artificial intelligence platforms used for learning English, such as ChatGPT, Duolingo, Babbel, Mondly, and Replika.ai, made it possible to analyze their functional and pedagogical potential. The empirical part of the study is based on the results of a questionnaire survey conducted among second-year students of the educational program “Foreign Language: Two Foreign Languages” at the Central Asian Innovative University (Shymkent). The survey aimed to determine the level and nature of the use of artificial intelligence tools in the process of learning English, including the acquisition of professional vocabulary and grammar, completion of written tasks (essays and business letters), development of speaking skills, and performance of homework assignments. The collected data were processed using quantitative methods and presented in percentage terms. Based on the research findings, conclusions are drawn about the feasibility of using chatbots and other AI-based tools as supplementary means of teaching foreign languages in the context of the digital transformation of higher education.
