title_key: opening a new chapter in health care reporting on the inauguration of the international conference on ai in medicine|chotirmall
title: Opening a new chapter in health care: reporting on the inauguration of the International Conference on AI in Medicine
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) continues to transform society in ways beyond the revolutions that foreshadowed it, namely the industrial, internet and digital revolutions. While being unique, the ‘AI revolution’ offers significant opportunities and presents inimitable challenges with important ethical considerations different to the eras preceding it. This is best exemplified by its emerging role in medicine, transforming healthcare delivery, improving patient outcomes and changing the way we diagnose and treat disease. Through advanced algorithms and machine learning, AI enables more accurate imaging analysis, earlier disease detection, better risk assessment, more personalised treatment and management, and many other breakthroughs such as robotic surgery and drug discovery. It facilitates the use of virtual assistants and chatbots, enhancing patients’ and care providers’ accessibility to healthcare information. With predictive analytics, it empowers healthcare providers to optimise scarce resource allocation. Excitement, discoveries and applications around AI in medicine continue to increase, progressing at a breakneck speed, with nobody being able to accurately predict what the future holds. Despite the uncertainty, AI in medicine possesses the power to alleviate some of the field’s grand challenges: containment of healthcare costs, more efficient diagnosis, precise individualised treatment, and prevention of clinician shortages and physician burnout. Many healthcare systems globally see imminent opportunities to reduce administrative burden and enhance operational efficiency, citing improving clinical documentation, structuring and analysing data, and optimising workflows as key priorities. The greatest hurdles to keeping up with rapid technology development include resource and cost constraints, acquiring acceptance and trust of healthcare providers and recipients, and deliberations and consensus of ethical, regulatory and legal considerations. To address this myriad of questions, facilitate debate and mutual understanding, and foster collaboration, Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine (LKCMedicine), Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore, in partnership with College of Engineering, NTU, and National Healthcare Group (NHG), Singapore, held the inaugural International Conference on AI in Medicine (iAIM) in August 2023 [Figure 1]. Over 3 days, more than 600 delegates from Singapore and international institutions participated in robust discussion and debate on the latest transformative research and applications of AI in medicine, including regulatory and ethical implications. The congress included 12 keynote lectures, two panel discussions, several parallel symposia and numerous abstract poster presentations. Here, we summarise the key points from iAIM keynote presentations.Figure 1: International Conference on AI in Medicine.IMPENDING CHANGE OF CULTURE IN HEALTH CARE The conference opened with Professor Chin Jing Jih (Chairman Medical Board, Tan Tock Seng Hospital [TTSH], Singapore) addressing ‘Medical practice in the era of AI: a rapidly changing landscape’. In his talk, Prof Chin spoke about AI representing a ‘marathon without a finishing line’ and its already transformative impact in radiology, emergency and cardiovascular medicine, sepsis and diabetes mellitus in hospital care. He also emphasised the importance of developing intelligent healthcare systems, including the need for an ‘AI culture’ within the medical workforce, and having a fundamental change in workflow and professional culture, more than technological advancement, for successful implementation. This was followed by a fireside chat with Dr Andrew Ng (Founder of DeepLearning.AI). Dr Ng depicted AI as a general purpose technology in recent future, with omnipresence and omnipotence much like electricity, and suggested that a timeline to its full adoption needs to be carefully considered, balancing rapid developments with the need for ‘thoughtful, responsible and transparent’ applications. He also outlined the required alignment of values among academic development, scientific discovery and patient care, and emphasised that while randomised controlled trials (RCT) remain the gold standard evidence for medical interventions, it may not be practicable to insist on RCT for all AI technologies due to the fact that AI systems are increasingly complex, with change so rapid that RCT may not be completed by the time another advancement emerges. The ‘ethics of ChatGPT’ was addressed by Professor Julian Savulescu (Director, Centre for Biomedical Ethics, National University of Singapore [NUS], Singapore), who impressed upon the audience the importance of justifying credit for the use of AI in academic publications and the importance of transparency. He also emphasised that while the model of a doctor–patient relationship may evolve with use of AI, the ethics of delegating medical decisions to a large language model must be tackled. TRANSFORMATIONS FROM DRUG DISCOVERY, CLINICAL SERVICE TO MEDICAL EDUCATION Dr Le Song (Chief Technology Officer and Chief AI scientist, BioMAP, USA) spoke on ‘Pretrained AI models for target discovery and drug design’, outlining the rapid increase in model sizes, data volume, complexity and diversity, as well as how AI is demonstrating key capabilities in identifying drug targets, protein and antibody structure, with efficiency in exploration of complex biological systems in high-dimensional space. Professor Kendall Ho (Medical Director, Healthlink-BC emergency iDoctors in Assistance [HEiDi], University of British Columbia, Canada) pointed out the importance of ‘Digitalisation of Emergency Medicine’ to reduce health inequity and empower patients who require emergency hospital service. Citing HEiDi as an exemplar, he outlined the immense success the programme has brought to the Canadian health system, especially in relation to optimal telehealth, its hospital at home programmes and contactless sensing for vital signs, with the system having been proven to reduce over 60% emergency service requirements without jeopardising patient outcome. Professor Wong Tien Yin (Founding Head of Medicine, Tsinghua University, China) spoke on ‘Transforming medical education and physician training in the era of AI’. He spoke about the need to transform current curricula to be ‘fit for purpose’, potentially including AI as a new academic subject, as future doctors will need to know how to use, interpret and potentially explain AI. With its potential to democratise health care and education, AI represents an important global opportunity. A talk on ‘State of the art in AI for gastroenterology/endoscopy’ was delivered by Professor Prateek Sharma (President-Elect, American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy), who demonstrated the use of new technology in endoscopy while emphasising that digitalisation is key in all current applications of AI in gastroenterology practice. He further showed that AI can assist in locating lesions, perform optic biopsies for diagnosis, assess the risk of endoscopic treatment, provide quality assurance of endoscopy and generate reports for endoscopists to streamline procedures for efficiency. A fresh concept of using a patient’s own data to optimise care through AI was the focus of Professor Dean Ho (Director, The institute for Digital Medicine, NUS) in his keynote entitled ‘Medicine made for you’. He provided case examples using digital avatars and digital therapeutics in the fields of transplant medicine and cancer. This new perspective bypasses the need for large data volume and circumvents concerns of data privacy, with the patient’s own physiological data (i.e. blood biomarker for cancer) possibly guiding individual therapy and determining the best medicine and the optimal dosage. Professor Tao Da Cheng (University of Sydney, Australia) spoke on ‘Foundational models and opportunities in medical image analysis’, illustrating the practical example of his studies on human posture for development tracking, elderly care, sport optimisation and rehabilitation. SETTING THE BOUNDARIES AND FRAMEWORK FOR AI TECHNOLOGIES IN HEALTHCARE SERVICES In view of the disruptive impact of AI in medicine, values, ethics and legal issues need to be resolved. Collaboration among the three medical schools and three hospital clusters across Singapore has produced a series of position statements from the Singapore Working Group on the use of AI in medicine. This was delivered by Professor Joseph Sung (Dean, LKCMedicine, NTU), who outlined the 14 statements in eight categories devised by the multidisciplinary group, including explainability, feedback, provider and receiver autonomy, values, equity, affordability, accessibility, engagement, doctor–patient relationship, trust, legality, evidence and governance. Professor Tan Chorh Chuan (Executive Director, Office for Healthcare Transformation, Ministry of Health, Singapore) further elaborated on the use of ‘AI in future healthcare systems’ by discussing data revolution, digitalisation and the future healthcare system, both in Singapore and beyond the country’s borders. Prof Tan emphasised that facilitating AI applications in health systems will necessitate firm foundations, interoperability, integration, scalability and trust while ensuring data privacy and security. Across continents from North America, Dr Aleksandra Mojsilovic (IBM Research, USA) emphasised the need for ‘Trustworthy, safe and beneficial models’. She pointed out that trust in foundation models may be different from trust in other traditional data science: hallucinations, lack of factuality or faithfulness, lack of source attribution, inability to reason, privacy leakage and misinformation are just some of these new challenges. To build trust, different detectors, guardrails and mitigators will be required for system monitoring. To govern AI effectively, the systems must ensure that trust and safety remain multifaceted and include multiple stakeholders. This includes the following: (a) establishing policy and regulation to define what AI should or should not do; (b) setting up industrial standards to establish common definitions, guardrails and standards; (c) defining frameworks and best practices to encode policies into business rules and guidelines; and (d) adding tools and technologies to support them. ENSURING THE JOB SECURITY OF HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS The iAIM included two panel discussions. The first panel addressed the question, ‘Will AI affect the lives and jobs of medical professionals?’ and was chaired by Professor May Lwin (Chair, Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information, NTU). It included a distinguished panel consisting of Dr Tan See Leng (Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry, Singapore), Professor Kenneth Mak (Director-General of Health, Ministry of Health, Singapore), Professor Miao Chun Yun (Chair, School of Computer Science and Engineering, NTU) and Dr Zhou Lihan (Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer, MiRXES, Singapore). The increased opportunities for healthcare manpower with AI were discussed, including its acceptance among healthcare professionals and the observation that technology was ahead of policy. Industry perspectives were shared, including the view that costs of generating data are increasingly less than those associated with storing it. It is important to heed prudence when assessing AI’s benefits, but these technologies should be embraced but should never replace the ‘human’ aspect of medicine. Both Dr Tan See Leng and Prof Kenneth Mak reassured participants that healthcare providers’ roles within the system will not be replaced or displaced. The second panel, chaired by Dr Ng Yih Yng (Director, Digital and Smart Health Office, TTSH and Central Health Region, Singapore) and comprising Associate Professor Michelle Jong (Group Chief Education Officer, NHG), Professor Wong Tien Yin and Professor Simon Kitto (Visiting Professor, LKCMedicine, NTU), discussed the importance of ‘Medical education for future healthcare providers’, with a focus on what will be needed in medical education in relation to AI, separating the ‘must knows’ from the ‘good to knows’ when designing curriculum for future healthcare professionals. To stay in the loop and ensure centrality of the doctor–patient relationship, we need to start training doctors, allied health workers and even medical students now, before system change ensues. While it is hard not to catch AI ‘fever’, there are significant challenges, known and unknown, that lie ahead. We hope that future iterations of the iAIM meetings will continue to serve as a key global platform to address new opportunities, emergent challenges and collaboration across institutions for better patient outcomes. Financial support and sponsorship Nil. Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts of interest.

title_key: bernard charpentier md|
title: Bernard Charpentier, MD
abstract: You graduated from the Paris University School of Medicine in 1975. What sparked your interest to go into Medicine?BC: Medicine had just left the “stone ages” by the early 1960s, moving forward into an innovative “scientific age” with clinically the most relevant‚ novel techniques, including novel ultrasound, an imaging technique; fascinating biology; DNA sequencing; efficient therapeutics; and novel surgical approaches. I was thrilled to see this exciting development with many opportunities and wished to play a modest part in this medicine revolution! You have been heading the Department of Nephrology, Dialysis, and Transplantation at the University Hospital Bicêtre for almost 20 y (1992–2011). During that period, your institution performed >4000 transplants. What were the most memorable experiences? BC: When I started my job in 1970, transplant outcomes were very poor: the mortality rate after 1 y was 20%. By 5 y, only 40% of grafts continued to work even with loads of immunosuppression, including kilos of IV steroids, 150 mg azathioprine per day, and crude anti-lymphocytes serum portions, all coming with major side effects! Fast forward 40 y: the mortality rate rarely exceeds 4% by 1 y after transplantation. Some centers show graft survival rates of 90% by 5 y, all achieved in more challenging and older patients! A complete revolution! One more comment: deceased organ procurement has always been a challenge in France linked to a tremendous psychological burden. In 1976, we saw a legal revolution in France when the Caillavet Law was approved by the French parliament, introducing the concept of presumed consent, putting into law that everyone was considered a potential organ donor unless there has been an active and documented refusal. At least in France, organ procurement advanced greatly with that legal decision, another revolution! You have been involved in transplantation for more than half a century. What strikes you as the most relevant progress that the field has achieved during this time? BC: There has been a significant amount of progress. Let me mention 6 areas that I found of particular significance: (1) prophylactic antibiotic treatment pre- and peritransplantation; (2) therapies for cytomegalovirus, herpes, and other relevant viral infections; (3) the prophylactic treatment of Pneumocystis carinii infections; (4) structured training of transplant surgeons‚ including novel minimally invasive, robotic, and endoscopic approaches‚ reducing the rate of surgical complications while providing a rapid recovery; (5) novel and precise techniques of tissue typing; and, last but not least, (6) novel immunosuppressive agents predominantly introduced in the 1970s and 1980s with a few additional‚ more recent advancements. All together, those were significant improvements that changed the field. You have been a most prolific researcher covering a broad field of clinical and basic science. What do you consider your most relevant academic contribution and publication? BC: Immunoregulation in a broad sense. When I started in the laboratory, T and B cells had just been discovered, and tissue typing was in its infancy. Antibody-mediated immune responses were neither understood nor targetable. My work for 40 y has delineated the negative regulation of the immune response (regulatory T cells, viruses, bio reactants, immunosuppressive drugs, cytokines, etc), either in transplant recipients or autoimmune diseases. A centerpiece of those contributions has been the delineation of the mechanistic underpinnings of belatacept, a costimulating blocker, and introducing this agent into the clinic. You have been the Director of numerous Centre National de Recherche Scientifique-Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale research units. What has been at the heart of those projects, and what is your advice in making collaborations in research successful? BC: I do believe that organ transplantation is a perfect model of collaboration between surgeons, physicians, basic researchers, and other disciplines working in a cooperative bed-to-bench-bedside approach aiming to provide a better, safer, and optimal treatment for patients with irreversibly damaged organs. Successful translational medicine is a challenge and requires effective and ethical collaboration with support from the industry and big pharma. The main challenge has been and continues to be to synergize divergent goals of maximizing returns with the best, equitable, accessible, and affordable treatment. In my opinion, professional societies, including The Transplantation Society, the European Society of Organ Transplantation (ESOT), and many others around the world, together with the input from scientific journals, have, for the most part, found and created ways to synergize efforts between participants, facilitating collaborations that provided productive outcomes for patients. Moving forward, it will be important to get expert feedback from professional societies on the feasibility and ethical soundness of clinical trials that may be moved into emerging countries. You have mentored numerous young clinicians and investigators. How would you describe your mentoring style? Has that approach changed during the course of your career? BC: This is both a most interesting and relevant question. I enjoyed mentoring so many students during 40 y! In my opinion, several steps need to be implemented: (1) how do we convince a young medical student to choose Transplant Immunology over the many other interesting fields of biology? (2) Is my laboratory able to help the young researcher publish the sufficient amount of articles in high-ranked journals required to obtain a PhD thesis? (3) Is there a complementary laboratory where can I send the young researcher abroad for a postdoctoral fellowship with the expectation to produce several high-ranked publications? (4) Last but not least‚ am I able to recruit this individual after a productive research time into a permanent position at a research institute or university? Unfortunately, there have not been enough complementary positions in France‚ and many (approximately 50% of my postdoctoral students) stayed in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, or Switzerland. Of additional relevance‚ the student’s profile has changed over time with a stronger focus on “quality of life” and being immersed in the “digital world” in every sense (research, laboratory activity, bibliography, publications, business, job, love…!). It was long time ago that I saw the blackboard at the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology meetings in the United States full of handwritten offers for jobs! Guiding young individuals with an interest in transplantation, how would you advise them for their clinical and research career? BC: I have been fortunate to have worked during a time when transplantation teams, at least in Europe, have been able to assemble their own staff, promoting clinical and research careers aiming to meet the societal demand of establishing transplantation as a lifesaving procedure. Being part of this movement appeared to me as most exciting and interesting, and I have communicated this to young researchers and health providers in our field. At the same time, international professional societies, including The Transplantation Society, ESOT, and others, facilitated communication in an interconnected world, exchanging information on all levels during scientific conventions, providing young individuals an insight into the relevance of our work worldwide. Among the many leadership roles in academic societies, you have been President of the ESOT (2005–2007). What are memorable recollections and major achievements? BC: ESOT had a particular focus on playing an active teaching role. The society invested a lot of money, at least during my time, in teaching students and young doctors. The so-called Hesperis course offered 66 seats for participants from all European countries. The entire course was funded by ESOT and, therefore, free of charge for all participants. The so-called Top Courses were designed for postgraduates to gain additional experience in surgical techniques, organ procurement, or immunology offered in approximately 20 different courses/y. Teaching was more than an educational success and also a cultural immersion among all European nationalities, facilitating connections across geographies and cultures in Europe. In addition to promoting research and science, ESOT publishes Transplant International. ESOT was also involved in the accreditation of European transplant teams through classical on-site visits, providing evaluation and recommendations. Prof N. Hakim was the father of this activity, and I must say that‚ as ESOT President, I was more than thrilled with this very original approach with the goal of harmonizing transplant activities in Europe and improving patient care. Most recently (2021), you have been President of the French Academy of Medicine. This organization has a broad agenda in health care, education, and science. What have been key accomplishments, and where do you see pressing needs in the future? BC: After having been President of the French Academy of Medicine, a society that is >2 centuries old, I was elected President of the Federation of European Academies of Medicine, an organization across 21 countries and 3 disciplines: Medicine, Pharmacy, and Veterinarian Science. With the support of Jean-Claude Juncker, President of the European Commission at the time‚ and his desire to get the advice of European Academies, I was elected Chairman of Science Advice for Policy by European Academies, an organization that includes 110 European Academies with 15 000 Academy Fellows! That was a heavy lift with the goal to respond to top-down topics imposed by the Commission and also with bottom-up matters, topics that originated from the National Academies. The Europe of the 27 countries has a population of 350 million with the highest Gross Domestic Product worldwide! During my tenure, we published around 20 statements on a broad spectrum of topics ranging from “Food from the Oceans” to “Transforming the Aging Societies.” My mandate for the French Academy took place during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic‚ during which we published 140 statements advising the French Government during the crisis. I started an online assessment of our weekly plenary sessions, including speakers. Moreover, we did an internal Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats analysis and have embarked on an external international assessment of the French Academy with a jury consisting of foreign Presidents of National Academies. In Brussels, the Federation of European Academies of Medicine and Science Advice for Policy by European Academies urged the commission to launch Health Emergency and Preparedness Response Authority comparable with the US Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority. This was the first time that the European countries delegated the regulation of health activities from the national to a European level, aiming for an effective response to the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic and the next crisis to come. You have received many most prestigious awards, including Commander in the Order of the Legion of Honor, Officer in the National Order of Merit, Knight in the Order of Academic Palms, and the Medal of the Honor of the French Army Health Service. What award makes you particularly proud? BC: In many countries, national decorations are not strictly following your service to the nation, and I believe that some of the prestigious awards have been given to me as the Dean of the large University of Paris-Saclay, listed 14th in the Jia Tong ranking. Other recognitions I have received for my role as President of the French Dean’s Council, encompassing 39 Faculties of Medicine and >100 University Hospitals. It is not an easy task at all to have clinical, research, teaching, and administrative responsibilities at the same time. My grandfather fought during the bloody battles of the First World War, including “Verdun” in 1916 and the “Chemin des Dames” in 1917 when young French and German soldiers killed each other from a distance of 50 m. It was also when German was the first language taught to French pupils and French to German students. Thus, those young and innocent men understood each other in the trenches! My grandfather was fortunate having survived this terrible war, awarded “only” with the Military Medal with Palm; however, he was not awarded the Legion d’Honneur that he deserved as a military hero in the middle of a bloody and awful war between 2 very similar countries that share so many interests in fine arts, literature, music, and friendship! I feel that I received the recognition as Commander in the Order of the Legion of Honor in his place, and I’m sure that there are many similar stories for generations of French and Germans. I can say that I am proud of my awards but know that many more deserve comparable recognition in previous generations and those to come. You are an emeritus professor of exceptional class living in an exceptionally beautiful city. What excites you most now that you are less restricted by clinical, administrative, and research responsibilities? BC: I am thankful for my long life, during which I have focused on academic work, family, sport, with art playing a central role. I never developed a major interest in food, wine, tobacco, or fast cars. I continue to run along the banks of the Seine. Horseback riding, skiing in the winter, and sailing in the summer are additional hobbies! Like many medical doctors, I greatly enjoy listening to music from J.S. Bach to the Stones and admiring paintings in many museums. N. de Staël of France, M. Rothko of the United States, D. Hockney of the United Kingdom, and the German M. Beckman are favorites. Reading (not only science) is another much-loved interest. All those hobbies provide a wonderful balance to the, at times, stressful and challenging life of transplant physicians and surgeons!

title_key: the line ai and the future of personhood|drayson
title: The Line: AI and the Future of Personhood
abstract: OpenAI’s release of ChatGPT, an impressively functional large language model, in November 2022—among much else—prompted a flurry of new academic publications on the topic of artificial intelligence. ChatGPT was interesting because it offered a convincing imitation of human language, at times impossible to discern from a human writer, as well as an eerie sense of sentience. In keeping with a long intellectual tradition, the ability to use complex language was, until 2022, considered a bastion of what makes human beings special. It was the logic behind Alan Turing’s [1] suggestion of an imitation game now known as the “Turing Test” to answer the question “Can machines think?” However, the intuition that the ability to listen and respond—at least verbally, with the appearance of understanding and abstract thought—is one of the attributes that makes human beings special, no longer holds the same weight. Stephen Wolfram’s [2] summation is gratifying in how succinctly he puts it: “The reason a neural net can be successful in writing an essay is because writing an essay turns out to be a ‘computationally shallower’ problem than we thought.”The necessary reassessment of the relationship of complex language to sentience as a general attitude is just one example of the difference between (sometimes carefully reasoned out) philosophical positions used to understand problems posed by complex technologies like machine intelligence, and how things turn out in practice. In his book The Line, James Boyle offers many generous insights into this as he considers how human society may navigate the ethical and legal questions raised by machine intelligence over the coming years. He charts the factors that shape “the line” that separates things—entities like machines, animals, and objects, which can be considered property—from persons, with moral and legal rights. However, while he gives a very well-synthesized overview of the capacity-based debates that have surrounded these questions, which focus on attributes like intelligence, consciousness, or language use, that attempt to worry out the specific criteria by which we might confer a particular kind of rights on machine intelligence, Boyle’s book also looks at the circumstances in which these questions have already been answered, focusing particularly on the legal system. Considering the precedents set by corporations, nonhuman animals, and transgenic entities, he explores how personhood and its rights are already conferred upon, advocated for, or denied to a whole range of non- and semi-human entities.While he gives many generous explanations of the theoretical discussions of “the line,” as in his opening chapters on the questions in the history of AI so far, Boyle questions the overall usefulness of moral philosophy for reasoning out what is coming, and instead shows the expected impact that the lived experience of using new technologies can have on the ethical judgments that might be made about them. As he argues in the example of large language models, we have trouble imagining things that then seem completely obvious when they happen; the fact that countless humans across the planet have now had the experience of talking with a large language model like ChatGPT, the idea that we might grant sentience or personhood to something that can generate convincing humanlike language no longer seems even a faintly viable way to draw a line. In a matter of months, one of the bastions of complex intelligence and human exceptionalism was demolished, and these kinds of surprises should be counted amongst our expectations.Of course, the current excitement over AI is something that many scholars wish would go away, particularly those who find themselves faced with marking endless “computationally shallow” AI-generated essays in the coming academic year [3]. But Boyle cautions us against overlooking the potential for dramatic and unpredictable technological change, for which we best not find ourselves unprepared. In his opening arguments to the book he is careful to address the natural skepticism of “singularist” claims that at some point in the near future, advancements in technology will result in an exponential explosion of autonomously self-advancing and generating machine intelligence, the results of which will be the end of humanity, in one way or another— through extermination, evolution, or basic irrelevance (which sounds faintly inviting and potentially rather comfortable). Dismissing the entire discussion in the face of this rhetoric is certainly tempting. However, Boyle is careful to point out the extent to which shifts in the performance of many AI systems over recent years suggest that even the most conservative view of the pace and potential of developments in machine intelligence should not simply dismiss the possibility of a need to deal with the questions surrounding machine personhood. In fact, he suggests that it is not unfeasible that complex autonomous systems may at least attempt to secure rights to legal autonomy or make claims of self-awareness or some form of complex sentience.While it is easy to point to the fact that the real issue in many cases is that AI systems are “not intelligent enough,” it is still the case that the development and application of neural networks trained with reinforcement learning and large data sets have resulted in remarkable advances in a number of fields—not just chess, but useful things like genomics—with machine learning techniques developing algorithms able to perform certain tasks and provide insights that have been a shock to their own designers. Boyle points to examples from the history of technology showing how the conditions for the emergence of an innovation can be in place for a considerable period, decades even, before some crystallizing factor makes application feasible. For example, internet technologies were in place for some time before the innovation of HTML made the sudden emergence of the web possible. If we can learn anything from the history of technology, it is that firm prediction isn’t possible, but we can get better at keeping our balance, reading the weather, and perhaps not falling out of our proverbial boats.Particularly interesting, instructive, and disturbing is the chapter on corporate personhood, which explores the somewhat accidental ways in which it became legally feasible for U.S. companies to be granted constitutional rights. These range from the ability to sue and be sued—something arguably practical for the conduct of business—to First Amendment rights such as free speech that perhaps should not be granted to beings who cannot die, feel pain, or have any moral investment. As Boyle points out, the legal rights granted to U.S. corporations offer a well-established precedent for similar rights being potentially sought for (or by!) AIs, regardless of their status as sentient or not—although he also points toward the debates around the ontological questions about what we might understand is incorporated together when a corporation is created. As well as offering a model for what AIs might request, corporations themselves could offer vehicles for AIs to act as autonomous persons. A corporation controlled exclusively by an AI could serve as a “sock puppet” offering the forms of legal personhood that corporations are already granted. Boyle’s discussion of corporate personhood focuses less on why this might be a problematic scenario and instead digs back into the story of how companies have been granted these rights in the first place. Central to this is the case study he presents, of how the Fourteenth Amendment to the American constitution—made to guarantee equal treatment of previously enslaved people—was coopted and invoked in numerous legal proceedings that sought to instead grant corporations personhood. The story reveals a tangle of what seems to be a very poorly supported historical accident at best and at worst outright conspiracy. Artificial persons have already been granted legal rights in the United States, and the lack of genuine debate that preceded this is quite alarming given the implications of the decision. One lesson here is simply that we are not on firm ground, and that there are already problems built into the systems that we might have hoped would help us navigate this new territory.Two further chapters turn to debates around the definition of sentience and rights in nonhuman animals and in transgenic and hybrid organisms. Boyle considers the tangled way in which different sets of values become connected to one another. In his discussion of the debates around chimeric and transgenic beings, and technologies that make them possible like genetic engineering and stem cell research, Boyle’s analysis of the debates around what kind of entities it is acceptable to create reveals that the criteria by which the line is drawn are numerous and often contradictory. In many cases, these values come to influence judgments about novel developments through recourse to what is often experienced as “intuition” about what is natural. Popular discourse may have more influence on decisions about where lines will be drawn than ethicists may expect. Underlying political allegiances and predispositions toward interpretations of what is “natural,” and moral influence, will likely affect how new technologies are interpreted. Boyle also points out how quickly these allegiances may shift. For example, anti-vaccination sentiments have switched from one side of the American political spectrum to the other, and evangelical support of anti-abortion legislation suddenly increased when not so long ago, state interventions interfering with the sanctity of the family’s private hierarchy and relationship with God would have been opposed.Boyle’s book is, by his admission, limited in its scope to the cultural, political, and legal context of the United States and other countries closely affected by developments there. This is a story that is too complex to be told globally in one text, but a similar study written about the Chinese context would be a welcome complement and likely fascinating. In addition to offering many useful ideas on the problem posed by “the line,” this book offers a lot as a case study of the impossibility of firmly predicting the development of complex technologies. It is the kinds of lessons that Boyle shares with us that make the claims of AI doom-mongers, salesmen, and accelerationists alike sound so confused. A long view of how technology and culture construct one another as well as attention to social, legal, historical, and technological precedents and contexts can arm us with a perspective on what is happening while it is happening. These dimensions contain insights that offer to help navigate, and perhaps even steer events as they unfold. Rather than offering predictions, Boyle draws attention to the expectations and counterintuitive developments that might likely wrong-foot us; he offers perspectives that both orient our attention in this developing story and help us see past the surface of events. I am happy to confirm that as far as I can tell, The Line is the result of processes with computational depth.

title_key: disclosure is not destigmatization rethinking ai and mental health stigma|chen
title: Disclosure is not destigmatization: rethinking AI and mental health stigma
abstract: The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated the integration of conversational agents into mental health support systems (Abd-alrazaq et al., 2019;Boucher et al., 2021;Cho et al., 2023;He et al., 2022;H. Li et al., 2023;Vaidyam et al., 2019). Large language model (LLM)based tools are increasingly used for emotional support, psychoeducation, symptom discussion, and helpseeking guidance (Alanezi, 2024;Boucher et al., 2021;Cho et al., 2023;Lawrence et al., 2024;H. Li et al., 2023;Siddals et al., 2024). Existing evidence suggests that some users perceive AI systems as less judgmental and emotionally safer environments for discussing stigmatized or psychologically sensitive concerns (Pauw et al., 2022;Siddals et al., 2024;Stamatis et al., 2026). This trend has contributed to growing optimism regarding the anti-stigma potential of AI-assisted mental health support. In particular, recent studies suggest that individuals may feel more comfortable disclosing distress, symptoms, or emotionally sensitive experiences to AI systems than in some interpersonal contexts, including clinical or peer-based interactions (Lee et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2025;Lucas et al., 2014;Lucas et al., 2017;Siddals et al., 2024). Consequently, greater willingness to engage with AI tools has often been interpreted as evidence that AI may alleviate stigma-related barriers and facilitate psychological help-seeking (Liu et al., 2025;Lucas et al., 2017;Miles et al., 2021;Stamatis et al., 2026). Such interpretations, however, depend on how stigma is conceptualized and measured. Mental health stigma is a multidimensional construct encompassing public stigma, self-stigma, structural stigma, and anticipated stigma. Among these forms, anticipated stigma, defined as expectations of being judged, rejected, or devalued by others, is particularly relevant to disclosure decisions and help-seeking behavior (Fox et al., 2017;Link et al., 2015). Here, disclosure refers to the voluntary communication of mental health concerns to another person or system, including AI-mediated interactions (Chaudoir & Fisher, 2010).Importantly, increased disclosure does not necessarily imply reduced stigma. Individuals may become more willing to discuss mental health concerns with AI systems while continuing to anticipate judgment, conceal symptoms, or avoid disclosure in human social contexts. Existing research suggests that AI systems may reduce some interpersonal barriers to disclosure by providing environments perceived as less judgmental, less socially evaluative, and more comfortable for discussing sensitive concerns (Lee et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2025;Lucas et al., 2014;Lucas et al., 2017;Miles et al., 2021;Pauw et al., 2022;Stamatis et al., 2026). The distinction between increased disclosure and stigma reduction is consistent with both disclosure theory (Goffman, 1964;Link, 1987;Vogel & Wester, 2003) and the Disclosure Process Model (DPM; Chaudoir & Fisher, 2010). The DPM conceptualizes disclosure as an ongoing interpersonal process rather than a single event, emphasizing that disclosure outcomes depend on contextual and interpersonal factors, including disclosure goals, characteristics of the disclosure target, and social responses following disclosure. From this perspective, AI-assisted disclosure may represent changes in the conditions under which disclosure occurs rather than reductions in underlying stigmatizing attitudes or expectations. Consequently, evidence that AI facilitates disclosure should not be automatically interpreted as evidence that AI reduces mental health stigma.A person may feel comfortable disclosing depressive symptoms to an AI chatbot while still avoiding disclosure to clinicians, family members, employers, or peers. This possibility is consistent with broader disclosure research showing that disclosure decisions and outcomes vary substantially across social contexts and intended audiences (Chaudoir & Fisher, 2010;Pachankis, 2007). Prior research has shown that anonymous or less identifiable online environments can facilitate self-disclosure by reducing social risks and concerns about negative evaluation (Joinson, 2001;McKenna & Bargh, 2000;Bargh et al., 2002). Consistent with this, individuals frequently use online platforms to discuss stigmatized experiences, mental health concerns, and other sensitive issues that may be difficult to disclose in offline settings (Andalibi et al., 2017;Naslund et al., 2014). Taken together, these findings may be more consistent with the interpretation that increased disclosure to AI systems reflects the availability of a lower-risk disclosure environment rather than genuine reductions in mental health stigma.A relatively small but coherent group of studies provides evidence that AI systems can reduce certain forms of mental illness stigma when they are explicitly designed as anti-stigma interventions (Cui et al., 2024;Kim et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2023;Song et al., 2025). These interventions typically incorporate mechanisms such as guided social contact, empathy induction, perspective taking, emotional engagement, or educational framing rather than simply providing a private AI conversation partner.Across chatbot-based social contact interventions, vulnerable social bots, and embodied conversational agents, studies have reported reductions in blame, fear-related stigma, and desired social distance, alongside increases in helping intentions and other supportive attitudes toward individuals with mental illness (Cui et al., 2024;Kim et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2023;Song et al., 2025). However, these findings also suggest that the active mechanism is not AI exposure itself. Rather, stigma reduction appears most evident when AI systems are intentionally designed to deliver contact-based, educational, or emotionally guided interventions. Such approaches differ fundamentally from ordinary AI-mediated emotional disclosure, and their effectiveness should not be generalized into the broader claim that AI inherently reduces stigma.Outside these purpose-built interventions, much of the AI mental health literature examines a different outcome: increased willingness to disclose distress to AI systems. For example, Lucas et al. (2017) found that service members reported more mental health symptoms to a virtual human interviewer than during standard post-deployment mental health assessments. This finding suggests that AI-mediated interactions may facilitate disclosure, although the study did not directly assess changes in stigma-related attitudes or beliefs. More recent studies suggest that AI systems become especially attractive in contexts characterized by stigma-related concerns, including shame, anticipated judgment, embarrassment, and fear of social evaluation (Branley-Bell et al., 2023;Hannah et al., 2025;Kosyluk et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2025;Miles et al., 2021;Stamatis et al., 2026). Individuals who fear negative evaluation from others may perceive AI systems as emotionally safer disclosure environments because such systems are often experienced as less judgmental, less socially evaluative, and more accepting than many interpersonal interactions (Abdalrazaq et al., 2020;Lee et al., 2020;Lucas et al., 2014;Lucas et al., 2017;Siddals et al., 2024).Collectively, these findings suggest that AI systems may reduce the interpersonal costs of disclosure by providing emotionally safer interaction environments. However, reduced disclosure burden should not automatically be equated with reduced stigma. Individuals may become more willing to disclose distress to AI systems while continuing to conceal these experiences from clinicians, family members, or peers. In this sense, AI systems may function less as direct anti-stigma tools and more as low-risk alternatives to interpersonal disclosure.Several conceptual and methodological considerations suggest that disclosure alone should not be treated as a direct proxy for stigma reduction. First, the outcomes measured in many AI mental health studies differ substantially from traditional stigma outcomes. Existing studies frequently assess willingness to disclose, emotional openness, acceptability, or intention to engage with AI systems (Abd-alrazaq et al., 2019;Branley-Bell et al., 2023;Cho et al., 2023;Hannah et al., 2025;Kosyluk et al., 2023;Lee et al., 2020;L. Li et al., 2023;Miles et al., 2021;Rackoff et al., 2025;Stamatis et al., 2026). While clinically relevant, these outcomes are not equivalent to reductions in self-stigma, public stigma, discriminatory attitudes, or desired social distance.Second, much of the current evidence remains correlational or cross-sectional. Although shame-related barriers, anticipated stigma and concerns about social evaluation are associated with greater willingness to use AI support tools (Hannah et al., 2025;Kosyluk et al., 2023;L. Li et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2025;Stamatis et al., 2026), such findings cannot determine whether AI interactions actually reduce stigma over time. Third, the same characteristics that facilitate AI-based disclosure may leave the social roots of stigma largely unchanged. Although AI systems provide private and low-risk interaction environments (Alanezi, 2024;Boucher et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2020;Lucas et al., 2017;Pauw et al., 2022;Rackoff et al., 2025;Siddals et al., 2024;Stamatis et al., 2026), these features do not necessarily alter how mental illness is perceived within families, workplaces, schools, peer groups, or healthcare systems (Corrigan et al., 2004;Corrigan & Watson, 2002;Fox et al., 2017;Hatzenbuehler, 2016;Link et al., 2015).For this reason, AI systems may currently function more accurately as stigma buffers than as direct stigma-reduction tools, reducing exposure to stigmatizing interactions without necessarily changing stigma itself. Such systems may create lower-friction pathways into emotional disclosure, screening, or referral while leaving broader social attitudes toward mental illness relatively intact.Strong claims regarding the anti-stigma potential of AI must also account for evidence that current AI systems may themselves reproduce stigmatizing content. Studies evaluating large language models in mental health contexts have reported stigmatizing responses, problematic therapeutic interactions, and negative judgments toward individuals with mental illness, including borderline personality disorder and substance use disorders (Heinz et al., 2023;Lauderdale et al., 2025;Lawrence et al., 2024;Moore et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2025). These findings suggest that stigma may emerge not only from users' concerns about disclosure but also from the content generated by AI systems themselves (Lawrence et al., 2024;Weiner & Wakeman, 2023).Ease of disclosure and quality of representation are therefore distinct properties. A chatbot may lower barriers to disclosure while simultaneously reinforcing harmful assumptions, biased language, or stigmatizing narratives. Consequently, increased user comfort should not be interpreted as evidence that AI systems promote psychologically safer or less stigmatizing understandings of mental illness.The current literature does not yet fully support the broad claim that AI-assisted mental health disclosure reduces stigma itself. A more conceptually precise interpretation is that AI systems may play two distinct roles.First, carefully designed AI interventions can reduce stigma through structured social contact, empathy induction, perspective taking, and educational framing. Second, and more commonly, AI systems appear to reduce the interpersonal cost of disclosure by providing privacy, anonymity, reduced social evaluation, and emotionally safer interaction environments. The first process reflects genuine anti-stigma intervention. The second may be better understood as stigma buffering or stigma avoidance, in which AI systems reduce the interpersonal burden of disclosure without necessarily changing underlying social attitudes toward mental illness. We suggest that distinguishing between stigma reduction and stigma buffering may provide a more precise framework for evaluating the role of AI in mental health support. While stigmareduction interventions aim to change stigmatizing attitudes, beliefs, or social structures, stigma-buffering tools primarily reduce the interpersonal costs associated with disclosure and help-seeking. Recognizing this distinction may help researchers more accurately interpret the benefits and limitations of AI-assisted mental health support.Future mental health interventions may benefit from integrating traditional stigma-reduction approaches, such as contact-based interventions, psycho-education, and perspective-taking programs, with AI-based support tools that reduce disclosure barriers and facilitate initial help-seeking. Such an approach may help combine the strengths of stigma-reduction and stigma-buffering strategies within a single intervention framework. From a research perspective, future studies should move beyond disclosure willingness alone and more directly examine whether AI-assisted interactions reduce fear of human judgment, improve realworld help-seeking behavior, and produce durable changes in interpersonal and institutional attitudes toward mental illness.As AI systems become increasingly integrated into mental health care, distinguishing between stigma reduction and reduced interpersonal exposure may become essential for evaluating AI-assisted support and defining meaningful anti-stigma progress in the digital era.

title_key: wapor news 2024|research
title: WAPOR News 2024
abstract: In this section, the International Journal of Public Opinion Research will publish briefs about past and future activities of the World Association for Public Opinion Research (WAPOR) and its members, as well as previews of forthcoming conferences and seminars that might be of interest to its readers. The Managing Editor and the chair of the WAPOR Publications Committee appreciate any information provided by the journal’s subscribers and readers that might help make this section as relevant and interesting as possible. A total of 408 participants from 51 countries attended the 77th WAPOR conference in Seoul, Republic of Korea. WAPOR extends its heartfelt gratitude to Sungkyunkwan University and the Survey Research Center for their invaluable support in organizing and hosting the event. We would also like to thank our co-hosts and co-organizers, including the National Research Council for Economics, Humanities and Social Sciences; the Korean Sociological Association (KSA); the Korean Association of Party Studies; the Korean Association for Survey Research; Korea Social Science Data Archive (KOSSDA); the Institute of Social Development and Policy Research (ISDPR) at Seoul National University; and PMI. Our sincere thanks also go to our sponsors for their exceptional support, which helped make the conference such a memorable experience. Special appreciation goes to the Seoul Metropolitan Government; the Ministry of Unification; the Center for Social Value Enhancement Studies; D3: Designs Data Decisions; Gallup Korea; Hankook Research; K-stat; Jason TG; Langer Research Associates; the Survey Research Center at the University of Michigan; Gallup International; NORC at the University of Chicago; Research & Research; Survey Research Lanka (SRL); Westat; KODAQS; and the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research. The conference program included 60 sessions where 272 papers and 21 posters were presented. Highlights included eight training workshops by renowned international public opinion experts (two more than in 2023), 15 featured panels, and an awards banquet at the Floating Island Convention Center at Seoul’s Han River. The conference theme “The Soul of Public Opinion Research: Liberty, Quality and Humanity” set the stage for three impressive keynote events. The opening keynote—on liberty—was given by Kathleen Frankovic (Independent Consultant, USA) who addressed the importance of polling and ways to protect the freedom to poll. The second keynote addressed the aspect of quality in survey research: Tom W. Smith (NORC at the University of Chicago, USA) spoke about the need to maintain data quality amid measurement disruptions. The closing keynote was an engaging roundtable discussion on the role humanity plays in the survey profession, moderated by WAPOR President (2023–2024) Robert Chung (Hong Kong Public Opinion Research Institute, Hong Kong). Speakers included Eun-Ju Lee (Seoul National University, Republic of Korea), Colin Irwin (University of Liverpool, UK), Christof Wolf (GESIS-Leibniz Institute of Social Sciences, Germany), and Lai Sim Fong Zoe (On&On Theater Workshop, Hong Kong; presenting for Daniel Wetzel, Rimini Protokoll, Germany), thus bringing academic, practitioner and artistic perspectives together. All three keynote events nicely aligned with the conference theme: If liberty reminds us of all people’s right to be heard, and quality urges all of us to adopt the highest standards when serving the people, then humanity must provide us with the ultimate purpose for upholding liberty and quality. WAPOR especially thanks Jibum Kim (Sungkyunkwan University, Republic of Korea), the 2024 Local Conference Chair, and Wolfgang Aschauer (Paris-Lodron University of Salzburg, Austria), the 2023-2024 WAPOR Conference Chair, for all their hard work with planning and organization of the conference. In 2024, WAPOR decided to give the Helen H. Dinerman Award for lifetime career contributions to innovative public opinion research and methodology to Ineke Stoop (Netherlands). A renowned survey statistician, Professor Stoop has significantly advanced the understanding of non-response in surveys and has been instrumental in developing and consolidating survey research infrastructures. Her dedication, expertise, and innovative contributions make her a deserving recipient of the Dinerman Award, celebrating her lasting impact on survey research and methodology. The esteemed Robert M. Worcester Prize, given annually to an outstanding paper published in the International Journal of Public Opinion Research, was awarded to Seungsu Lee and Jaeho Cho (both University of California, Davis, USA) for their paper “Communication Mediation in an Era of Partisan Selectivity: Modeling Effects of Information and Discussion on Participation.” The award committee commented that their study developed a theoretical framework for exploring polarization, political discussions, and participation. It is analytically rigorous, uses high-quality survey data, and creates a framework for examining this important issue in the future. The 2024 Alexis de Tocqueville Award for the best paper on democracy and public opinion was given to Alexis Jan Patacsil (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila, Philippines) and Reginald G. Ugaddan (University of the Philippines, Quezon City, Philippines) for their paper “Power in Numbers: Defining Democracy in the Philippines through Social Capital, Citizen Empowerment and Political Support, and Trust in Political Institutions.” This paper merits recognition for its insightful analysis of the interplay between social capital and democratic perception in the Philippines during Duterte’s administration. By leveraging Putnam’s social capital theory and using Asia Barometer survey data, the study reveals that social capital’s impact on democratic understanding is not direct but fully mediated by political support and trust. This research stands out for its rigorous methodology, theoretical innovation, and significant contributions to understanding democracy in Southeast Asia’s unique sociopolitical landscape. The Naomi C. Turner Prize for the best student paper was given to Yin Wu (University of Wisconsin-Madison, USA) for “The Words We Choose to Believe: Comparing the Influence of Press, Valence, Nationalism, and Emotion on Trust in Foreign Media Coverage of the U.S. on Facebook.” The award committee noted that the paper tackles an important topic, deals with a range of significant concepts, and has the potential to advance our understanding of trust, ideology, and cultural alignment. The Janet A. Harkness Award, jointly awarded by AAPOR and WAPOR for the best student paper that employs 3MC research (survey methods in multi-cultural, multi-lingual, multi-country contexts), was given to Mao Li, Stephanie Morales, and Kaidar Nurumov (all University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA) for their paper “Probing on Self-Rated Health and Autocoding Its Responses through Large Language Models (LLM): Strengths and Weaknesses under Multilingual Survey Contexts.” The study evaluates the innovative use of LLMs to automate the coding of open-ended survey responses, which is traditionally labor-intensive and costly. The committee was impressed by the students’ work, and the study underscores the potential of LLMs to streamline survey research and calls for further exploration in diverse linguistic contexts. An interview with the winners can be found here. The 2024 conference featured a new ad hoc award—the Best Conference Poster Award. The 2024 Best Poster Award was given to Yul Min Park (University of Pittsburgh, USA) for the poster “Issue Ownership, Electoral Accountability, and Politicians’ Social Media Posts: Evidence from the George Floyd Protests in the United States.” This poster featured an insightful exploration of the interplay between technology and political communication, revealing critical drivers behind politicians’ social media behavior. Through a rigorous case study of the 2020 George Floyd protests, the research elucidates how race, party affiliation, and constituency demographics influence the frequency and framing of political issues on Twitter. Additionally, the 2024 Best Student Poster Award was given to Sujin Song (Chung-Ang University, Republic of Korea) for the study “Does Political Participation Buffer Depression of the Discriminated? Application of Anomic Depression Theory.” This poster featured a profound investigation into the impact of discrimination on mental health. The findings provide vital insights for practitioners and policymakers, emphasizing the importance of fostering political engagement to enhance mental health in marginalized populations. Given that the 2024 conference was also a joint conference of WAPOR and its Asia Pacific regional chapter, the WAPOR Asia Pacific Chapter 2024 Lifetime Achievement Award was given to Emeritus Professor Hyunho Seok (Sungkyunkwan University, Republic of Korea). A true pioneer in the realm of social science research methodology, his extensive work and dedication have not only profoundly impacted the understanding and development of social indicators and survey statistics in Korea but have also inspired a generation of researchers to push the boundaries of their field. WAPOR thanks all award committee members for taking their time to review and evaluate all papers submitted for consideration.1 Compared to previous years, WAPOR has increased the frequency of webinars, offering a total of 11 digital events in 2024. With the exception of summer, they are now conducted monthly. In 2024, WAPOR implemented, via a software license, automated two-way translated captions between approximately 30 languages for our webinars. Sessions with a strong regional focus included the following: “Elections and surveys in Argentina and Chile” (March 2024) by Ana Iparraguirre (Argentina), Carlos Fara (Argentina), and Ricardo González (Chile). “Public opinion research in Iraq and Syria” (April 2024) by Johnny Heald (UK), Munqith Dagher (Jordan/Iraq), and Firas Al Kayal (Syria). “Public opinion on the Gaza War: A cross-national perspective” (October 2024) by Munqith Dagher (Iraq/Jordan), Nader Saeed (Palestine), and Samir Abu Rumman (Kuwait/USA). “Understanding the 2024 Asian elections and what they mean for the future of democracy” (December 2024) by Yashwant Deshmukh (India), Agus Nurudin (Indonesia), Bilal Gilani (Pakistan), and M Saidul Haq (Bangladesh). Webinars with a methodological focus or on substantive matters of public opinion research included: “A new way to think about and measure water insecurity: The Water Insecurity Experiences Scales” (January 2024) by Sera Young (USA) and Pablo Paras (Mexico). “Comparative cross-national surveys in Afrobarometer” (February 2024) by Boniface Dulani (Malawi). “CATI and SMS surveys in Sub-Saharan Africa” (June 2024) by John Paul Murunga (USA) and Charles Lau (USA). “Perceptions and communication on climate change” (June 2024) by Marija Verner (USA), Manuel Hermelo (Argentina), and Perla Marvell (USA). “Generalizable nonresponse prediction and machine learning-based adaptive designs” (October 2024) by John “Jack” Collins (Germany) and Christoph Kern (Germany). WAPOR’s Education and Conference Committees also offered a joint webinar on “Writing a successful abstract for the 2025 WAPOR conference: Practical guidance” in November 2024. More information can be found on WAPOR’s website. The webinars are open to the public and can also be found on WAPOR’s YouTube channel. WAPOR sought to fill four offices in elections in autumn: Vice-President & President-Elect, Chair of the Conference Committee, Chair of the Education Committee, and Chair of the Professional Standards Committee. Voting took place between November 1 and November 28, 2024. According to the results, Christian Haerpfer was elected as Vice-President & President-Elect, Wolfgang Aschauer was re-elected as the Chair of the Conference Committee, Alice Siu was elected as the Chair of the Education Committee, and Sunghee Lee was elected as the Chair of the Professional Standards Committee. Their 2-year terms begin on January 1, 2025. WAPOR thanks all candidates who stood for the election and the 33% of the membership who voted. Additionally, following the resignation of the WAPOR Vice-President and incoming President for the 2025–2026 term David Jodice, and after a consultation with the WAPOR membership and a vote of the WAPOR Council, the winning candidate for the election of the Vice-President, Christian Haerpfer, has been appointed Vice-President to fill the vacancy left by David Jodice and shall serve as the WAPOR President in 2025–2026. More information on the leadership transition can be found on our website. We thank outgoing Chair of the Education Committee Chase Harrison, outgoing Chair of the Professional Standards Committee Ignacio Zuasnabar, Past President Timothy Johnson, and WAPOR President in 2023–2024 Robert Chung for their outstanding service to the association these past 2 years. The 78th Annual WAPOR Conference will take place on May 12–15, 2025, in conjunction with the 80th Annual AAPOR Conference, in St. Louis, Missouri, USA. This joint event is a leading forum for discussing advancements in public opinion and survey research, providing an opportunity for networking, learning about the latest research trends, and engaging with diverse experts from across the globe. The venue for the conjoined AAPOR and WAPOR conferences is the St. Louis Union Station. The call for papers for the WAPOR conference opened on October 1, 2024, encouraging submissions on a variety of topics related to public opinion and survey research. More information about the conference, including the call for abstracts, is available at our website. Last but not least, WAPOR’s regional chapters can look back at a successful year 2024—and forward to an exciting 2025. In April 2024, WAPOR’s Sub-Saharan African (SSA) chapter hosted its first regional conference in Mombasa, Kenya. You can find an in-depth interview with the SSA leadership team here. WAPOR Latinoamerica will hold its next conference in Florianópolis, Brazil, on April 28–30, 2025. In November 2025, WAPOR’s Asia Pacific chapter will host its eighth annual conference at Rikkyo University, Tokyo, Japan. You can find more information about the different chapters on our website.
