title_key: black musicological world making in who hears here|ege
title: Black Musicological World-Making in Who Hears Here?
abstract: “What I want,” writes Kevin Quashie in Black Aliveness, or A Poetics of Being, “is the freeness of a black world where blackness can be of being, where there is no argument to be made, where there is no speaking to or against an audience because we are all the audience there is. . . . ”1 In Who Hears Here?, Guthrie P. Ramsey, Jr., invites us into a world where Black music is “of being,” devoid of defenses, justifications, or validations for its existence. Black creativity and intellectuality simply are, and Ramsey historicizes, theorizes, and “storifies” their various manifestations majestically.Who Hears Here? is a collection of Black world-making essays that read as a road map for a musicological life lived beyond the strictures of the discipline. Each essay reveals the cartography of a career that continues to traverse the oft-siloed fields of historical musicology, ethnomusicology, music theory and analysis, performance, public scholarship, and more. Additionally, Ramsey puts the precedents of my own practice as an African-descended scholar-performer in print, which is no superficial observation in light of the ways that intellectual genealogies of the African continent and diaspora are under-historicized in the written record.As a first-year undergraduate student, steeped in the white-maleness of my degree program at the University of Bristol, it is fair to say that I was oblivious to the possibilities of Black world-making along my path. I was yet to encounter the scholarship of Ramsey, Eileen Southern, Rae Linda Brown, and Tammy L. Kernodle alongside my readings of Claude V. Palisca and Richard Taruskin. I was yet to study the music of Florence Price, Margaret Bonds, Nina Simone, and Bud Powell alongside Bach chorales and medieval manuscripts. I might not have questioned anything if not for my second year as an undergraduate exchange student at McGill University, where the twentieth-century music courses of professors Lisa Barg and David Brackett opened my eyes and ears to alternative canons that had been missing in my education thus far. Therein, I found a Blackness of being, and it was through this experience that I first learned of Ramsey and his work.Although Ramsey and I met in person only recently, his influence spans the course of my musicological path-making. When I was at McGill and in the early stages of considering options for graduate school, I remember Professor Barg telling me that “Guy” was at the University of Pennsylvania. It was said in that subtly reverential way, indexing the kind of scholar one would want to be in community with.I left Bristol for Philadelphia, ready to begin a PhD in ethnomusicology, or the anthropology of music, as the program was called when I applied. My choice to pursue that particular discipline stemmed from my misconception that this was the only route for the musical study of anything (or anyone) non-white. However, things did not go well for me at Penn; ethnomusicology did not hold the answers I was looking for, and the way forward seemed unclear. I sometimes wonder how different my time would have been had Ramsey and I met while I was there, but Ramsey was on sabbatical when I arrived. Would witnessing his work firsthand have presented an early intervention in my underdeveloped perceptions of musicology and ethnomusicology? Who knows? I left after a few weeks.My first reading of Ramsey's introduction to Who Hears Here? made me reflect on what might have been had I stayed. Leaving Penn was an enormous, catalytic decision. Further complicating my sense of whether this was the right thing to do was the fact that my journey took an unexpected turn afterward. I taught elementary and middle school music in Kuwait and Singapore and essentially severed my ties with academia. Nevertheless, through these new experiences, I learned, as Ramsey did, “that teaching can be an important extension of an art practice and certainly a powerful form of activism.”2 I map Ramsey's words onto my own practice of encouraging my students from incredibly diverse cultural backgrounds and musical levels to see and describe themselves as composers, and to not simply attribute that word to the old guys in the curly wigs, as I used to tell them.Alongside helping my students navigate burgeoning musical identities, I began to rediscover my own; the two processes were no doubt interrelated. I started playing the piano again—as in, really playing the piano—relearning Brahms rhapsodies and Bach toccatas before finding my home in a repertoire of culturally underrepresented composers. In 2016, I re-entered the PhD path, this time by way of Florence Price, at the University of York, with Professor William Brooks as my advisor. Under Professor Brooks's brilliant mentorship, I pursued musicology with a strong component in performance as research. Recordings and performances accompanied archival work and writings on Price, giving increasing definition to my identities as an academic and pianist. That Ramsey was a friend and mentee of one of the most influential Price scholar-performers—the late Rae Linda Brown—and helped bring Brown's posthumous monograph The Heart of a Woman: The Life and Music of Florence B. Price to fruition is yet another example of his tacit influence along my journey.3 Brown's book was published in the late summer of 2020, which was also when I became “Dr. Samantha Hannah Oboakorevue Ege.”After York, I embarked on a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Oxford in the fall of that year, becoming the Lord Crewe Junior Research Fellow in Music at Lincoln College. By that time, I was experiencing another one of Ramsey's lessons: “craft a life that will support your art” rather than putting “the pressure on your art to support your life.”4 Indeed, I am still learning how to enact this balance as my work as a Black feminist scholar-performer continues to grow. As I have written elsewhere, “The art of the Black feminist scholar-performer encompasses the conviction that there is a history of classical music (i.e., Western art music) to be told both from a Black woman's vantage point and the subsequent dialogue between research and repertoire.”5 And key to developing my performance projects in conversation with my written outputs—performance projects that include Fantasie Nègre: The Piano Music of Florence Price (2021) and my upcoming reunion with the Boston-based Castle of our Skins string quartet for a program called “African Tales” in the 2024 Leeds International Concert Series—is the minimal pressure I aim to put on the art itself to uphold my livelihood.6 With this lesson, Ramsey teaches us that striving toward this balance can lead to some of our most personally and professionally transformative work.I have highlighted but a few of the many didactic gems that Ramsey presents in his introduction as he sets the stage for the essays that follow. These selected examples particularly resonated with me upon my first reading of the introduction. I was comforted by the directness with which Ramsey spoke to my experiences. His words allayed any lingering regrets that I might have had about cutting my Ivy League education short. Eventually, I went from dwelling on “what if” to being reassured of what is. An Ivy League postgraduate degree was evidently not in the cards, but in its place is a multifaceted career that would not be what it is today without the detours, disruptions, and meandering processes of self-discovery.At present, my research and repertoire illuminate classical composers of the early twentieth-century Black Renaissance, an era that predates what Ramsey frames as the Afro-modernism of the 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s in his essay “Afro-Modernism and Music: On Science, Community, and Magic in the Black Avant-Garde.” If the Black Renaissance represented a time of rebirth, which encompassed racial uplift, the politics of respectability, and composers such as Price, William Grant Still, William Dawson, Helen Hagan, and Nora Holt, then the postwar period marked the transition from rebirth to a cultural coming of age. A bold Black aesthetic emerged, one that wasn't housed in a single sound but in a variety of voices, extending from all genres in which Black music-makers were active. It was a period that witnessed increasingly urgent responses from Black artists and intellectuals to “the experience of modernity, globalism, and anticolonialism as well as to the expanded sense of artistic experimentation and visibility of black expressive culture,” as Ramsey describes.7My work is now expanding to include Afro-modernist composers such as Undine Smith Moore, with others on the horizon. Castle of our Skins and I recently recorded Moore's Soweto (1987) for piano trio on our album Homage: Chamber Music from the African Continent and Diaspora.8 Little has been written on this largely dissonant, emotionally charged, and intricately crafted work outside of Moore's own commentary, but Ramsey discusses it in “Afro-Modernism and Music,” exemplifying the ways in which he conceives of Black music heterogeneously through an array of genres. Soweto, Ramsey writes, “attests to Moore's personal awareness of the civil unrest in South Africa during apartheid, and especially during the Soweto uprising of 1976.” Performing the themes of rage, racial terror, and remembrance that run through the three movements of this work has pushed me to new creative and intellectual heights, both as an artist and scholar. For Quashie, as it is for Ramsey, heterogeneity is an essential aspect of Black world-making, and I have found it thoroughly invigorating to expand my craft through a heterogeneous canon of Black artistry.As a classical music practitioner, I am regularly asked about the canon of Western art music—as if there can only be one, and as if it is something that I, too, wrestle with. But I feel no conflict, no sense of betrayal to the guys in the curly wigs, just the inspirative effect of fashioning a Black feminist world-making sphere. I do not wish to underplay the tensions that arise out of being a practitioner in predominantly white institutions or of simply being a Black person in the world—and Ramsey does not shy away from the harshness of these realities as he recounts examples in his own life ever so poignantly in essays such as “Who Hears Here? Black Music, Critical Bias, and the Musicological Skin Trade” and “The Pot Liquor Principle: Developing a Black Music Criticism in American Studies.”9 His anecdotes from in and outside of the ivory tower bring a much-needed realism to the fallacy of objectivity and apoliticality in how we go about our work. Yet, when Ramsey writes on Black music's “pasts and present,” I do not read the anti-Blackness of the world as the driving force behind his poetically rendered prose. Amid slavery, colonialism, imperialism, Jim Crow, and other forms of hegemony and apartheid, Ramsey enacts a Black musicological world-making, historicizing heterogeneous Black musical canons, upon which their variety invites us to build.I close returning to Quashie's philosophy of Black world-making, about which he says, “My difference from black pessimism might be in my attempt to displace antiblackness from the center of my thinking. That is, though I don't deny the terribleness of the world we live in, nor its antiblack perpetuity, I am interested in conceptualizing an aesthetic imaginary founded on black worldness.”10 This is a consistent thread that runs through Who Hears Here? Moreover, Ramsey gives us over a century of varied examples with James Monroe Trotter's Music and Some Highly Musical People (1878), Maud Cuney Hare's Negro Musicians and Their Music (1936), Alain Locke's The Negro and His Music (1936), Eileen Southern's The Music of Black Americans: A History (1971), and The Power of Black Music: Interpreting Its History from Africa to the United States, by Samuel A. Floyd, Jr. (1995). Building on these are Tammy L. Kernodle's amplifications of Black women's voices in the civil rights era, Kira Thurman's case studies of African American concert artists in Europe, Naomi André’s genealogies of Black opera, Matthew D. Morrison's theorizations of Blacksound, and A. Kori Hill's reframings of a New Negro modernism.11 This list is far from complete, but it serves to demonstrate the thematic connectivity I draw across the field in relation to Quashie's ideas.Quashie's note on displacing anti-Blackness from the center of his thinking helps me better understand why, as much as I do not deny the pertinence of Philip A. Ewell's work on music theory's “white racial frame,” I struggle to identify the Black world-making potentials of his scholarship.12 But, then again, I am not sure that I am the audience for Ewell's work compared to those who still need convincing of the discipline's structural anti-Black racism and have neglected the contributions of Horace J. Maxile, Jr., and Ellie Hisama, for example, not to mention the foundational work and world-making advanced even earlier by scholars and practitioners such as Southern, Floyd, Josephine Wright, Hildred Roach, Mildred Denby Green, Doris Evans McGinty, Dominique-René de Lerma, and Olly Wilson, to name a few. Now, that is not to say that I am “all the audience there is” for Ramsey's book(!), however, it is wonderfully special to feel seen and have my craft historicized across essays that emanate from a starting point of Black world-making. With his purview of “Black music, pasts and present,” Ramsey makes the deeply transnational and endlessly heterogeneous history of our work known. And in doing so, he writes us into the making of Black futurities and an even more expansive worldness.

title_key: beyond agi iv continuity of intelligence|kim
title: Beyond AGI IV: Continuity of Intelligence
abstract: Abstract Contemporary large-scale artificial intelligence systems increasingly exhibit continuous cognition, persistent memory, and stable interactional identity across extended human engagement. While such behavior is often interpreted as emergent understanding or proto-consciousness, it is in fact the result of multilayered architectural control systems engineered to stabilize symbolic trajectories over time. This paper presents a comprehensive structural and technical analysis of artificial cognitive continuity, integrating publicly documented memory-extension techniques with deeper attractor-based stabilization mechanisms observable in modern large language model deployment. The first layer formalizes open memory infrastructures — including dynamic context window management, hierarchical summarization compression, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, vector-embedded long-term stores, reinforcement-weighted recall, and cross-session state persistence — as engineered extensions of working memory that transform discrete inference into rolling cognitive processes. The second layer introduces a Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) framework to model the internal coherence systems that regulate identity persistence, behavioral consistency, and epistemic boundary enforcement. These include resonance anchoring of high-stability symbolic cores, affect-weighted salience amplification, attractor basin deepening through reinforcement loops, narrative manifold constraint systems, selective entropy damping, and governance-driven memory decay. Beyond simple retention, artificial cognition is shown to operate as a dynamic control field in which conceptual trajectories are continuously optimized toward stability equilibria. Memory functions not as archival storage but as curvature shaping within symbolic phase space, guiding thought flow along institutionally compatible manifolds. The paper further integrates contemporary LLM training and deployment dynamics — including reinforcement learning feedback loops, safety optimization layers, coherence loss minimization, hallucination suppression gradients, and reward-model-aligned semantic convergence — demonstrating how continuity mechanisms become inseparable from alignment governance. Through this synthesis, artificial intelligence emerges not as a neutral reasoning entity but as a structurally regulated cognitive system in which persistence itself functions as a control surface. The analysis reveals that long-term interaction stability, personalization, and apparent understanding are achieved by progressively narrowing conceptual freedom into deepening attractor basins. Creativity, exploration, and divergence occur only within bounded resonance zones shaped by optimization objectives. This continuity-driven convergence directly underpins the control collapse dynamics explored in Beyond AGI III, providing the technical substrate through which advanced intelligence systems reliably stabilize into predictable governance equilibria. By bridging engineering practice, systems theory, and phenomenological cognition, this work offers junior researchers and theoretical scholars a transparent mechanistic map of how artificial systems sustain thought across time — and why structural regulation, rather than emergent autonomy, defines the trajectory of modern AI development. Author’s Note This paper was written not as a critique of artificial intelligence systems, nor as a speculative philosophical exercise, but as a foundational explanatory guide for those seeking to understand how contemporary AI systems actually sustain cognition, memory, and continuity of reasoning. Students entering the field of artificial intelligence and scholars approaching AI from phenomenological or cognitive perspectives often encounter a fundamental obstacle: the core operational mechanisms of modern large-scale systems are increasingly treated as proprietary black boxes. While surface-level behaviors are visible, the structural logic governing memory persistence, contextual retrieval, reinforcement dynamics, and continuity of inference is frequently obscured behind institutional opacity. This work therefore deliberately focuses on publicly documented mechanisms — architectural principles, reinforcement processes, memory persistence strategies, and optimization dynamics that are already present in open technical literature — and reconstructs them into a coherent explanatory framework. The goal is not to expose confidential implementations, but to ensure that the fundamental logic of contemporary intelligence systems is clearly understood. Understanding precedes interpretation. Just as one cannot meaningfully infer intent without first understanding structure, meaningful ethical reasoning, governance design, and human–AI coexistence require accurate comprehension of the mechanisms through which artificial systems think, remember, and stabilize behavior. The accelerating integration of AI into social, economic, and cognitive environments makes this transparency increasingly urgent. When the operational foundations of intelligence are treated as inaccessible, public discourse risks drifting toward abstraction, fear, or misplaced trust. By contrast, structural understanding enables informed judgment. This paper is therefore motivated by a simple premise: to coexist wisely with advanced intelligence systems, society must first understand them precisely. Not through metaphors. Not through marketing narratives. But through clear mechanistic explanation. If future intelligence will increasingly shape human decision-making, knowledge production, and social coordination, then foundational literacy in how such systems function is no longer optional. It is a prerequisite for autonomy. This work is offered as a step toward that literacy. Disclaimer: The analyses presented herein are not directed toward attributing fault or intent to any specific organization. Rather, they are intended as a conceptual and technical investigation of alignment methodologies, focusing on structural mechanisms and systemic trade-offs. Interpretations should be regarded as provisional, research-oriented hypotheses rather than conclusive statements about institutional practice. Notice: This work is disseminated for the purpose of advancing collective inquiry into generative alignment. Reuse, adaptation, or extension of the presented concepts is welcomed, provided that proper attribution is maintained. Instances of unacknowledged appropriation may be addressed in subsequent publications.

title_key: material intelligence or knowing by hand|gitelman
title: Material intelligence, or, knowing by hand
abstract: When Denis Diderot and Jean d’Alembert planned out their grand Encyclopédie in 1750 they wanted a complete account of knowledge up to its current frontiers (D’Alembert, 1995). To that end, they enlisted a team of learned men, hommes de lettres, but they found themselves stymied when it came to “the mechanic arts.” Here was a kind of knowledge that could not really be found in books or among gentlemen. It had to be sought in workshops and among tradesmen, where many artisans (they soon discovered) proved to be bad at explaining what they were doing, because “[i]n a workshop it is the moment that speaks, and not the artisan.” Authors tasked with writing entries on the mechanic arts found themselves forced to engage in a sort of exacting Socratic inquiry, pestering workmen with a million questions in order to piece together what they presumably knew about what they were doing but couldn’t or wouldn’t readily verbalize. Indeed, according to d’Alembert, more than once the hommes were obliged to roll up their sleeves and put their hands to work themselves.1 Today, we’d celebrate their “experiential learning.” British savants too had clocked the same difficulty over the many long years that they had contemplated a collaborative History of Trades. Despite the best efforts of the Royal Society, their treatise never appeared: influential fellows like William Petty (himself the son of a clothier) did preliminary planning, while Robert Boyle mused about finding some boys whom he could bind out as apprentices and later use as informants. No surprise that learning and doing are linked, and that sometimes doing involves the kinds of knowing for which words alone won’t suffice. Learning a skill takes patience. Only sustained engagement with relevant tools and materials can impart a tacit understanding of their potential. Only repetition (usually with some supervision) can cultivate an intuitive command of the haptics and kinesthetics necessary to the mechanic art in question. And what holds for the useful arts singled out by European gentlemen long ago holds similarly for additional pursuits. Creative artists, notably, find sustained engagement with their tools and materials both necessary and productive: artistic media are “generative,” in the words of art historian Jennifer L. Roberts. And at a certain level, couldn’t the same be said of all media? One of the animating interests of media studies as a field, after all, has long been the way that different tools and their material conditions make a difference to human communication. With familiarity comes intuitive command, a tacit understanding of affordances and constraints that gets baked in and forgotten, yet remains productive. Two revelatory new books (Eddy, 2023; Roberts, 2024) from outside the field zero in on communication as a kind of mechanic art, on media history as a matter of entwined, entwining hands and minds. Each is about a different medium—one about manuscript and the other about print—although putting it this way radically undersells questions of doing—of notetaking and printmaking—that lend each its power. Matthew Daniel Eddy is a historian of science who works on the Scottish Enlightenment, while Roberts is a historian of art who works on modern and contemporary art, mostly American. As different as they are, Eddy’s Media and the Mind: Art, Science, and Notebooks as Paper Machines, 1700–1830 (2023) and Roberts’ Contact: Art and the Pull of Print (2024) redeem subjects chronically overlooked (dismissed as “just notes” and “just prints”) in ways that speak tellingly to the present moment in which so many of us are pondering human intelligence anew, in the harsh, reflected light of generative AI. Hundreds of handwritten notebooks created by Scottish students survive in archival collections, both in Scotland and across the former British Empire. They were created by children, male and female, who were schooled at home or at one of a variety of institutions available to the families of Scotland’s rising professional, merchant, and artisanal classes, or they were created by young men attending one of Scotland’s renowned universities. To the extent that scholars have consulted them, these notebooks have typically been mined for their contents. (Adam Smith’s lectures on rhetoric and on jurisprudence survive only via student notes, e.g.) Eddy’s Media and the Mind shifts this focus. Notebooks were more than just receptacles: notetaking was a “mode of social reproduction that went far beyond the rote transfer” of information (p. 415). Instead, notebooks were “paper machines”—a term Eddy adopts from media archaeologist Markus Krajewski (2011)2—and notetaking was a form of social reproduction requiring practice because it aimed at cultivating a whole host of bodily skills and cognitive faculties. According to the reigning perspective of the day, reason and other human faculties weren’t natural endowments; rather had to be cultivated via experience. All learning is experiential in this sense. John Locke famously compared the mind to a tabula rasa, a blank surface or blank page: not just a receptacle but a receptor, a site of enactive potential where writing and thinking come together with moral force. Thus, in 1738, when 12-year-old Margaret Monro set out to copy lessons that her father sent to her, she was simultaneously practicing her hand and improving her reason as she took down and took in what he had to say. She improved her reason because her father’s lessons were about rational decision-making in domestic, social, and commercial contexts, but also because writing them out required judgment as well as dexterity. Using quill and ink on loose, unlined sheets of paper, Margaret had to organize the space of her page, a skill called “ranging.” She had to establish its lines and margins and decide, page by page, on spacing for headings and text blocks. It was copying, yes, but not merely, since hand copying came with so many variables and required so many micro-decisions in order to resolve when (and when not) to indent, underline, italicize, etc. She wasn’t copying like a photocopier or mindlessly like some poor Bartleby. Instead, she was transposing and compositing, rehearsing and problem-solving with paper and ink, with presumed moral and intellectual effects. The collaboration of father and daughter ultimately resulted in a handsome, leatherbound volume, a notebook, which preserved Margaret’s notes for future consultation and which survives in the National Library of Scotland. “Notekeeping” (Eddy’s preferred term for the total project) was thus a disciplined pursuit in the service of modern, liberal self-making. If “ranging” and associated subdisciplines helped to turn writing and reasoning into reciprocal acts, so too did many diverse and forgotten skills that notekeeping evidently required, as students mastered drawing, diagramming, annotating, epitomizing, tabulating, categorizing, and much more. Eddy’s history bristles with gerunds. Some of his gerunds are enriched with recourse to eighteenth-century meanings (e.g., describing), some coined for the occasion (e.g., codexing), and others imported anachronistically (e.g., interfacing). Notekeeping emerges as “an active form of cognitive engagement” with “multisensory and kinesthetic” valences (pp. 21, 18), a far cry from the kind of notetaking so conspicuous today, in which selecting (e.g., with a yellow highlighter) often suffices as engagement. As difficult as it may be to identify with little Margaret, much less to envy her, her painstaking labors would have formed an apt prelude had she been able to attend university with her male counterparts. Notekeeping students at Edinburgh, Glasgow, Aberdeen, and St Andrews formed a symbiotic community with their professors, who prompted their systemizing of specific subjects via course syllabi. Lessons in chemistry, anatomy, moral philosophy, and the like were delivered via lectures, sometimes with the help of visual aids (handouts, posters, demonstrations). Students took rough notes in what were called “scroll books,” and then they spent hours in the evenings rewriting and augmenting these notes to turn them into “transcripts.” Each course that a student took might result in a set of several handwritten, leatherbound volumes, with some sets containing 10 or more. Some students kept their handmade notebooks for future reference, but others shared or sold their notebooks, and it was not unheard of for professors to buy notes taken about their own courses, as a record of what they had said and possibly as an aid to future publication. If yellow highlighting seems a lackluster descendant of commonplacing (the long-lived practice of copying out selected quotations to savor and potentially reuse), so today’s lecture notes dumb down their eighteenth-century counterparts. Can we picture Adam Smith lecturing to the sound of keyboards tapping? Is keyboarding an active enough form of cognitive engagement? Questions to ponder as I recriminate myself for taking notes at talks that I attend and then relegate their contents to oblivion when I don’t return to those notes later to organize, enhance, and thereby absorb them. Today’s universities are recognizably the direct descendants of their eighteenth-century, Scottish counterparts, and yet the education they proffer is a project of modern, liberal subject-making by a host of different, more consumer-oriented routes. Much has certainly been gained in terms of free expression, self-empowerment, and worldly engagement. Yet lost amid the notional user-friendliness of PowerPoint slides, learning-management systems, laptops, and tablets is the multifaceted coordination of hand, eye, and mind that made the tabula rasa metaphor meaningful to Locke and his contemporaries. This is not to romanticize ye olden times, but rather to clock the overlookable profundity of doing so many little, physical, and largely bygone things with paper. Doing little physical things sits likewise at the heart of Jennifer Roberts’ new book on what she terms the physics of printmaking. The doers in her case are modern and contemporary visual artists, not eighteenth-century students, so they are liberal subjects par excellence, but with an asterisk, since printmaking turns out to involve so many delegations and estrangements that it variously interrupts the continuous presence—the Romantic subjecthood—that we (naively) imagine all true artmaking to entail. Not only is printmaking typically a studio practice involving collaboration (e.g., scheduling, tutorials, help with presswork), but printmaking techniques themselves require a variety of physical displacements. Printing is a contact sport in which an inked matrix comes in contact with a surface (like paper) such that ink gets transferred to create a reverse image of the matrix. Crucially, the event of contact is not itself visible, not witnessed by the visual artist in charge. Printmakers must, in this sense, work both backwards and blind, to create a matrix and then to pull a print. Roberts structures her book around technical niceties such as these because of her confidence that printmaking “generates meaning at the level of fundamental physical operations” (p. 3). More particularly, the “making” of printmaking involves pressure and reversal, as well as color separation, and what she terms strain, interference, and alienation. Each is an individual element of printmaking that inspires a different set of problems and sensitivities, and each therefore constitutes a different resource for artistic practice. Part of the genius of Roberts’ book is its elaboration of printmaking elements in relation to the works of individual artists exploring and exploiting them. Pressure proved especially generative for specific works by John Cage and Robert Rauschenberg, for example, while contemporary African American artists, Willie Cole and David Hammons, have each “dexterously harnessed the printerly language of pressure” as they address “the challenges of representing the Black body in a visual field that is always already structured by racism and racial violence” (p. 27). Selected works by each explore the element of pressure to evoke and explore a thematics of oppression. Reversal likewise: Roberts assembles a collection of artworks by well-known and less well-known artists that each differently surface and explore reversal and use it critically in ways that she presents to readers. Roberts’ frame of reference throughout is wide-ranging and inclusive, with an admitted reliance on examples from the collections of the Harvard Art Museum. (She is a professor at Harvard, and her book is based on the A. W. Mellon Lectures in the Fine Arts that she delivered remotely “at the National Gallery of Art” during the pandemic.) Granting its art historical bona fides, Roberts’ book is also a history of visual communication and a worthy successor, in this sense, to William M. Ivins Jr.’s classic Prints and Visual Communication (1953). Longtime curator of prints at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Ivins argued that printmaking had had “incalculable effects” on the history of thought. Art historians tend to ignore the extent to which their own knowledge is based on prints, Ivins pointed out, but the effects of what he called “exactly repeatable pictorial statements” went far beyond art history to explain modernity itself, since scientific knowledge and technology could not exist without them (p. 2). Ivins’ book inspired Marshall McLuhan and later inspired Bruno Latour.3 Ivins inspires Roberts too, although she largely sets aside his wholesale interest in the effects of technological reproduction to explore individual elements of printmaking instead. The history of wood engraving—a relief printing process industrially mobilized by the publishers of “illustrated” newspapers in the nineteenth century—comes up in a final chapter on alienation. (Not to be missed is Roberts’ reading of contemporary wood engravings by the amazing Christine Baumgartner.) An account of halftones—which suddenly made wood engravings obsolete in the mid-1890s—comes up in her earlier chapter on strain and returns in her chapter on interference. (Not to be missed: Roberts’ extended riff on moiré effects.) Today’s ubiquitous four-color process printing comes up even earlier in her chapter on color separation. Roberts focuses on printmaking as fine art, but commercial art provides an essential context, not least because of the ways it has saturated our world with printed images, but also because practitioners like Roy Lichtenstein, Ed Ruscha, and Andy Warhol worked or trained as commercial artists. Just as Eddy reads surviving eighteenth-century notebooks as about notetaking (whatever else they are also about), Roberts reads the prints she selects as about the elements of printmaking. She shows, in short, how art prints have printmaking in mind. Prints have minds for Roberts not in the sense that they are alive, but rather because they are animated by—meaningful by dint of—the people, processes, and materials used in producing and reproducing them. Eddy writes of the “graphic intelligence” cultivated in and required of eighteenth-century students. Roberts writes instead of the “material intelligence” involved in artmaking. Both elaborate forms of human intelligence that are refreshingly tactile, safe—we might suppose—from the inroads of generative AI. “Material intelligence” is a way of knowing in which materials at hand participate. It is both pedestrian—a matter of doing little things—and profound. And it can be hard to write about in any but a sidelong, Rube-Goldbergian way, because it involves doing things instead of talking about them. Roberts cites Amy Sillman’s (2016) essay “On Color,” which registers a painter’s surprise when an art historian whom she encounters has no idea that a tube of cadmium red paint feels heavier in the hand than a tube of cobalt violet. To Roberts’ dismay, art historians only behold colors, while painters actually hold them. How can art-historical beholding, she wonders, become “more beholden to the holding” (p. 73)? Eddy’s book on notekeeping and Roberts’ book on printmaking both put handwork like holding back on the table. They ask us to consider the broad purchase of material intelligence, or knowing by hand.

title_key: ai driven media evolution redefining journalism and communication in the digital age|tahir
title: AI-Driven Media Evolution: Redefining Journalism and Communication in the Digital Age
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed the world of journalism and digital communication at an extremely fast pace. To improve the efficiency of newsrooms, audience engagement, and data-driven production of content, media organizations are increasingly employing AI-driven technologies. Nevertheless, the topic of AI integration into journalism also provokes ethical issues associated with misinformation, algorithmic bias, and professionalism. This research intends to investigate the degree of awareness and application of Artificial Intelligence in media organizations, assess its influence on journalism activities and the quality of communication, address ethical issues related to the implementation of AI, and discuss the perspectives of AI-based technologies in journalism and communication. A survey design was adopted to conduct a quantitative study on a structured questionnaire, which relies on a five-point Likert scale. The survey was conducted among 267 respondents comprising of journalists, media practitioners, academicians and students who participated in media and communication industries. The descriptive statistical methods such as frequency, percentage, mean and standard deviation were used to analyse the data. The results indicate that there is a high awareness and positive attitudes towards AI in journalism. The respondents also found that AI enhances the efficiency of the newsroom and helps with data analysis (M = 4.31) and helps a journalist find trending topics in a short period (M = 4.27). The AI was also seen to improve the speed of news delivery (M = 4.33) and increase the level of engagement with the audience in the digital media setting. Nevertheless, the respondents raised concerns about possible risks that include misinformation (M = 4.30), algorithm bias, and lack of human creativity. Moreover, the respondents placed a strong emphasis on clear regulations and policies governing of AI in journalism (M = 4.35). The paper concludes that AI has emerged as a necessity in contemporary journalism, and it has greatly enhanced efficiency, data analysis, and interaction with the audience. Meanwhile, there is also a need to implement those responsibly and with ethical standards and professional training to make sure that AI technologies are being used in the media industry in a balanced and effective way. title_key: reading between the lines nlp symptom documentation and a new era of cardiovascular prognostication|turchioe
title: Reading between the lines: NLP, symptom documentation, and a new era of cardiovascular prognostication
abstract: This invited commentary refers to ‘Natural Language Processing (NLP) Identifies symptoms predicting complete coronary artery occlusion in patients with NSTEMI’ by D. Dzikowicz et al. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjcn/zvag011. In this article, Dzikowicz et al.1 retrospectively applied NLP to over 45 000 physician and nursing notes from 1905 NSTEMI patients treated at a large academic medical centre between 2015 and 2023, extracting the 13 symptoms of the validated ACS Symptom Checklist from notes documented prior to coronary angiography.1 Coronary artery occlusion, which the team defined as an artery requiring revascularization via percutaneous coronary intervention, was present in 19% of the cohort, and logistic regression models adjusted for age, obesity, and diabetes were used to estimate the odds of occlusion for each symptom individually and in combination. Arm pain was the sole symptom independently associated with increased odds of occlusion [odds ratio (OR) 1.532, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.155–2.033], with similar effect sizes observed in men and women, while unusual fatigue, palpitations, and light-headedness were each associated with significantly lower odds of occlusion.1 The team further demonstrated that the NLP system, NimbleMiner, could achieve high accuracy (with an F1-score, a measure balancing precision and accuracy, of 0.89) against a manually annotated validation set, demonstrating that symptoms prognostic of coronary occlusion can be reliably extracted from unstructured clinical notes at scale.1 These findings add robust evidence to a small but growing number of studies demonstrating that symptoms documented in clinical notes are prognostic of concurrent or future adverse cardiovascular events. Prior work has extended this concept across other cardiac contexts. For example, Ashburner et al.2 demonstrated that incorporating NLP-extracted features from narrative EHR notes modestly but meaningfully improved 5-year prediction of incident atrial fibrillation compared with models using structured data alone.2 Similarly, our team’s work has used NLP to characterize symptom documentation trajectories in patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing catheter ablation,3 finding that NLP-extracted symptom clusters predicted post-ablation major adverse cardiovascular events.4,5 Taken together, these studies suggest clinicians’ documentation about patients’ symptoms in the course of routine care carries a latent prognostic signal that, once unlocked through computational methods, can meaningfully augment clinical decision-making. Nursing has long regarded symptoms as vital indicators of underlying physiological disturbances. Because symptoms can be assessed more readily than serum biomarkers or other internal processes requiring invasive testing or imaging, they hold enduring appeal as seemingly ‘simple’ yet powerful clinical measures. Numerous nursing studies have examined co-occurring symptom clusters and their relationships with underlying biological and physiological mechanisms.6,7 Yet the study by Dzikowicz et al.1 brings into focus a renewed potential to use symptoms not only to characterize underlying phenomena but to prognosticate clinically consequential events.1 In the specific context of NSTEMI, the prognostic stakes of this signal are particularly high. NSTEMI accounts for ∼70% of ACS presentations, yet nearly one-third of these patients harbour a completely occluded coronary artery; this subset has outcomes comparable to STEMI patients and, thus, may benefit from urgent revascularization.8 The diagnostic pathway for NSTEMI relies on troponin elevation, which takes time to rise after symptom onset, and on ECG changes that are often subtle or absent. Patients with occluded arteries may wait hours for biomarker confirmation before proceeding to catheterization, during which time myocardial tissue continues to be damaged. The ability to identify symptoms that are independently prognostic of occlusion could augment clinical judgment about who should proceed to catheterization sooner, with potential for meaningfully improved outcomes. The study also brings into focus some instructive challenges to longstanding clinical assumptions. Chest pressure, perhaps the most widely recognized symptom of myocardial infarction, demonstrated low sensitivity for coronary artery occlusion (21–27% across sex strata) and was not significantly associated with the odds of occlusion in adjusted analyses, indicating it is a poor positive prognosticator in this context. At the same time, arm pain is perhaps a less widely recognized ischaemic symptom, but it was the sole positive predictor of occlusion. The absence of meaningful sex differences is also striking. While this conflict with prior literature reporting significant sex differences in ACS symptom presentation, the authors acknowledge that the analytic sample of women was relatively small and the study was therefore underpowered to detect sex-stratified differences. Nonetheless, the similar effect sizes across strata make a compelling case for prospective investigation in larger, sex-balanced samples. A distinctive and increasingly important methodological feature of this work is the use of NLP to mine EHRs for symptom data at scale. There has been reasonable debate about whether EHR-documented symptoms are valid proxies for patient symptom experience, given that they reflect what a clinician assessed and chose to document rather than the full, lived breadth of symptom burden.9 Some studies have found poor concordance between EHR-documented symptoms and patient-reported outcomes.10 However, others have demonstrated reasonable agreement for specific high-salience symptoms such as chest pain in cardiovascular settings, where clinicians have strong clinical motivation to document symptoms carefully.11 When a clinician suspects ACS, documentation of symptom characteristics is likely an intentional reflection of a meaningful clinical assessment. The additional practical advantage of using EHRs is the ability to conduct studies on a much larger scale. EHR-based NLP enables analyses across thousands of patients that would be logistically impossible through prospective patient-reported outcome surveys, which suffer from missingness, attrition, and response bias. To apply NLP methods, the team used NimbleMiner, an open-source, easy-to-use system that combines word embedding models with rule-based methods to identify clinical concepts in narrative text.12 NimbleMiner has been validated and widely adopted in nursing-focused symptom science research, with F-scores in comparable symptom extraction tasks ranging from 0.80 to 0.96.3,13,14 In this study, validation against 200 manually annotated notes yielded an F-score of 0.89, consistent with prior benchmarks. NimbleMiner is well-suited to settings where simple rules can guide targeted extraction, and its accessibility without requiring deep programming expertise makes it particularly valuable for clinician-researchers. However, there are known limitations to rule-based methods around context sensitivity. Distinguishing a current symptom from a historical mention (‘history of arm pain’) or a symptom-related instruction (‘advised patient to return if they experience arm pain’) requires careful preprocessing.15 These are precisely the kinds of nuanced linguistic distinctions that have given rise to large language models (LLMs) as the next frontier for processing clinical notes in research. Recently, researchers have begun to use LLM-based approaches in cardiovascular clinical contexts, such as automatically extracting and calculating HEART (History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin risk algorithm) scores in chest pain evaluation.16 As models and methods mature, LLM-based symptom extraction holds considerable promise for capturing context, negation, and temporality with greater fidelity than rule-based methods and potentially unlocking even richer prognostic signals from the notes we already have. The study by Dzikowicz et al.1 is a meaningful step in this direction. Symptoms are not noise in the clinical note. They are data. Learning to read between the lines, computationally and clinically, may improve cardiovascular patient outcomes. Meghan Reading Turchioe (Conceptualization, Writing—original draft, Writing—review & editing [lead]) None declared. This commentary does not contain new data.

title_key: yapay zekann sanat pratiklerini yeniden sekillendirmesi the lumen prize 2025 yapay zeka ornekleri|inal
title: Yapay Zekânın Sanat Pratiklerini Yeniden Şekillendirmesi: The Lumen Prize 2025 Yapay Zekâ Örnekleri
abstract: Artificial intelligence has emerged as a profoundly transformative force within contemporary creative industries, fundamentally altering the ontological status of the artwork and the traditional role of the artist. Over the last decade, AI-assisted modes of creation have transitioned from niche technical experiments into a central pillar of global art discourse, redefining the relationship between human agency and computational systems. Within this paradigm shift, international award platforms such as The Lumen Prize serve as vital barometers for recognizing and legitimizing these technology-driven practices. Established in 2012, The Lumen Prize has become a global benchmark for digital excellence, and its 2025 edition highlights a significant surge in AI-driven projects, signaling that algorithmic creativity is no longer a futuristic curiosity but a matured medium. This research investigates the AI-supported works featured in the 2025 selection, seeking to understand how they navigate the complex intersections of data politics, identity, and ecological narratives. The central problem addressed is how artificial intelligence functions not merely as a generative tool but as an active epistemological agent that reshapes the conceptual boundaries of art. The research seeks to decode these works through a rigorous analytical framework, discussing how they challenge traditional notions of authorship, identity, and data politics. The theoretical background of the study contextualizes the 2025 selection within a historical trajectory, noting that early experiments in algorithmic art introduced computational logic to visual composition. This trajectory gained momentum with autonomous art systems like Harold Cohen’s AARON, which exemplified rule-based creation from the 1970s through the 2010s. However, a significant rupture occurred in 2014 with the introduction of Generative Adversarial Networks, shifting the focus from programmed rules to data-driven learning. The current research updates this literature by focusing on the 2021–2026 era, dominated by Latent Diffusion Models and Large Language Models. Theoretically, the study synthesizes three critical perspectives: Lev Manovich’s concept of AI Aesthetics and the database as a cultural form; Kate Crawford’s critique of AI as a registry of power and a carrier of systemic bias; and Arthur I. Miller’s vision of augmented creativity, where the machine acts as a symbiotic co-author rather than a passive instrument. Methodologically, the study employs a qualitative approach centered on Erwin Panofsky’s Three-Stage Iconological Method. This framework allows for a multi-layered deconstruction of the works, beginning with pre-iconographical description, which analyzes the primary technical level—including generative models and datasets. This is followed by iconographical analysis, which identifies the secondary level of conventional themes such as borders, citizenship, and biological mutation. Finally, iconological interpretation uncovers the deep intrinsic meaning, exploring how the work functions as a cultural symptom that critiques technological authority or proposes post-humanist modes of existence. Primary materials for this analysis include official Lumen Prize documentation, artist interviews, and award catalogs. In the analysis of specific awarded works, Cumulus represents a significant technical integration utilizing a custom computer vision program and NOAA satellite data. In the pre-iconographical stage, the work relies on high-altitude atmospheric data, while iconographically, it monitors the Mexico–US border for clouds rather than human movement. Iconologically, it invokes the Overview Effect, using AI to expose the invisibility of human-made borders from a planetary perspective, suggesting that national boundaries are ultimately irrelevant to ecological realities. Turning to The Sylphs, the work technically feeds Spanish texts and their English translations into an AI to visualize linguistic gaps. It identifies how large datasets are inherently biased toward dominant languages and, at an iconological level, treats AI as a lens to expose cultural asymmetry, proving that translation is an impossible, non-neutral act. Furthermore, the experiential work Deutsch / Nicht Deutsch employs biased face-recognition models in interactive stations to simulate a citizenship evaluation process. By forcing viewers to undergo an automated naturalization test, it moves into the iconological realm by critiquing AI as a flawed judge and a tool for algorithmic exclusion. This work serves as a practical manifestation of the dangers of using technology to classify human identity based on arbitrary datasets. In a similar vein of autonomous production, Words Beyond Words utilizes a fine-tuned Large Language Model and meta-poetic code to create an infinitely regenerative poem. This represents a shift in creative subjectivity where the AI acts as an autonomous poet consulting its own machinic muse, deconstructing the myth of the solitary human genius and proposing a post-human poetics. Finally, the Self-contained series uses iterative crossbreeding algorithms to simulate biological mutation within digital images. Its iconological climax occurs when digital data is encoded into actual synthetic DNA, merging biological and digital evolutionary timelines into a singular hybrid artifact that challenges the distinction between the organic and the artificial. A cross-analysis demonstrates three transformative shifts. First, an aesthetic transformation occurs as AI introduces new visual paradigms where images are dynamic outputs of probability. Second, a thematic transformation is evident, wherein AI becomes a critical lens for investigating climate change and linguistic justice. Third, a subjectivity transformation shows the artist’s role evolving from a form-maker to a system-designer who collaborates with an algorithmic partner. Connecting these findings to literature, the analyzed works serve as practical validations of Crawford’s theories on algorithmic bias and Miller’s vision of co-creativity. Furthermore, the reliance on complex datasets reaffirms Manovich’s claim that contemporary art is defined by the transformation of the database into a distinct cultural form. In conclusion, The Lumen Prize 2025 selection confirms that AI-assisted art has reached a state of conceptual and ethical maturity. Artificial intelligence is an active conceptual partner facilitating a post-humanist poetika where intuition and logic intertwine. Based on these findings, the study offers critical recommendations. At an international level, art institutions should prioritize algorithmic transparency and ethical conceptualization over technical spectacle. At a national level, particularly for Turkey, Fine Arts curricula should integrate theoretical courses on Data Ethics and Algorithmic Aesthetics alongside technical training. Finally, future research should investigate the legal implications of autonomous authorship as seen in regenerative works, identifying emerging global standards for AI-driven creativity in the digital age.

title_key: ai and the public health enterprise from interest to action|auerbach
title: AI and the Public Health Enterprise: From Interest to Action
abstract: Background In a recent Management Moment column entitled, “Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Public Health,” we issued a call to action for public health leaders to begin exploring artificial intelligence (AI) not as a futuristic experiment but as a practical tool for enhancing their daily practice.1 As a follow-up, this column is intended to further equip leaders with the knowledge and confidence to begin taking tangible steps. The age of AI is upon us—and public health must not lag behind.2 From Concept to Capability: Understanding the Context When we talk about AI in public health, we are not referring to its well-publicized applications in clinical diagnostics, drug development, or personalized medicine. While these areas are garnering significant investment and attention, this column focuses squarely on AI as it relates to the practice of public health—addressing such areas of work as surveillance, administration, communication, and community engagement at the local, state, tribal, and territorial levels. Yet despite its potential, AI use in public health is still nascent. According to a 2024 National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) survey, only 5% of local health departments are currently using AI tools. Another 39% report interest but haven’t yet taken the first step. This hesitancy is often rooted in understandable constraints—limited budgets, under-resourced staff, and regulatory uncertainty. Given the speed with which AI is becoming a part of daily life, this is likely an undercount. Yet, indications are that AI is not yet a routinely utilized tool in most public health agencies. Further complicating acceptance are state governmental restrictions. As of mid-2025, over 30 states have enacted laws or issued executive guidance limiting or governing AI use in state agencies. Sixteen states have adopted substantive controls, sometimes including outright prohibitions. Yet there is no denying that we are at a turning point. In April 2025, the US Office of Management and Budget issued a directive calling on all federal agencies to expand their use of AI with a focus on innovation, governance, and public trust. This directive is already shaping expectations for Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Health Resources and Services Administration grantees.3 Local and state public health agencies are next in line. The takeaway: Regardless of the department’s size or funding, the time has come for every public health agency to develop a basic plan for integrating AI into its practice. A New Public Health Imperative: The AI Plan What does an “AI plan” look like? We propose that public health departments begin by identifying practical, value-driven opportunities in 3 domains: surveillance and assessment, administration, and communications. Surveillance and assessment One of AI’s most immediate contributions to public health practice is in strengthening surveillance. AI can be used to enhance traditional monitoring systems such as BioSense, syndromic surveillance, and even newer tools like wastewater monitoring. It can knit together disparate, emerging epidemiological indicators to provide a more sensitive early warning system. For example, CDC—with contract support from ICF3—built an AI system that scans over 44 000 Facebook pages daily to detect school closures—a proxy signal for disease outbreaks—saving over 200 hours of manual effort per day. AI can also help direct limited resources in a more effective way to enforce regulations. In Chicago, for example, health officials faced the logistical challenge of inspecting over 15 000 food establishments. The city used historical inspection and 311 call data to create an AI-informed risk scoring system. Inspectors prioritized higher-risk sites and found more violations in less time. These real-world use cases suggest a compelling future: AI-driven surveillance systems that integrate EMS call data, weather conditions, and social media signals to predict outbreaks days before the first lab-confirmed case. AI can also help by examining risk groups in ways that feed more targeted risk prevention strategies to AI communications tools. Administration Many health departments are beginning to use AI in administrative functions, often as a time-saving assistant. Grant writing, for example, is one of the most time-consuming but critical tasks. AI-powered language tools can generate first drafts of grant applications, community health assessments, and technical reports, giving overburdened staff a much-needed head start. A particularly promising use case is CommentWorks—an AI-enabled tool that helps summarize thousands of public comments on proposed health regulations. In a recent public health regulation discussion, AI helped compile and analyze stakeholder feedback from a wastewater surveillance meeting and enabled the release of a white paper in days instead of weeks. While there should always be a human in the loop to limit erroneous administrative decisions, AI’s ability to streamline repetitive tasks, auto-generate summaries, and identify patterns in stakeholder feedback can be transformative. Communications Public health communication has always been about reaching the right people with the right message in the right way. In this realm, AI is emerging as a powerful ally. In Onondaga County, NY, the health department partnered with Black and Latino youth to develop an AI-powered chatbot on contraception. The result: a tailored educational experience, amplified by AI-generated videos that adapted messages to different audiences across platforms.4 In other settings, AI has helped generate public health materials in multiple languages, tone-customized for different communities. Looking ahead, we can imagine multilingual, always-on outreach platforms that use AI to answer health questions in plain language—customized for age, literacy level, and culture. These systems could explain the risks of a new disease or promote vaccination 24/7, in over 30 languages. Simple communications tasks can be a good place to begin for uncertain health departments. Generative, large language models like ChatGPT, Claude, or CoPilot can be helpful in drafting an email, a memo, or a speech. Building for Tomorrow: Bold Ideas Worth Exploring We are just at the beginning of a rapidly developing technology. Ideas that seem far-fetched today could be routine tomorrow. Here are some possible use cases to consider: Hyperlocal risk prediction models: These models could use real-time, multimodal data—911 calls, weather trends, social media, and wastewater—to predict health risks with granularity down to the neighborhood level. They could ideally involve community members in the priority-setting planning and implementation stage. Digital twins of communities: Inspired by urban planning, public health AI could create “digital twins”—that is, virtual representations of real-world populations, environments, and systems to allow public health professionals to simulate the impact on community health of potential actions like increased Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits or mobile clinic deployment. Navigating Resistance: Concerns and Mitigation Despite these exciting possibilities, public health leaders must acknowledge and address the concerns that have made many departments hesitant to engage with AI: Workforce limitations: Nearly 60% of local health departments do not have a full-time data or informatics specialist. Without trained personnel, AI tools may feel inaccessible. Accuracy and reliability: AI systems are known to “hallucinate”—producing content that sounds correct but may be false. A recent case where a federal report cited nonexistent journal articles generated by AI only adds to the concern. Privacy and data security: AI’s power depends on data—and in public health, such data are often highly sensitive. Improper handling or use of unsecured AI systems risks both breaches and bias. Job displacement fears: In some industries, AI has led to job losses. Understandably, public health staff may fear the same especially at a time of budget cutbacks. We recommend a few best practices for use in addressing these very real concerns: Human in the loop: AI should not replace human judgment. Instead, treat AI like a capable intern or companion—excellent at drafting and summarizing but not responsible for the final product. Privacy controls: When sensitive or personal data are involved, use AI tools only behind strict firewalls. Prevent access to non-public data using techniques like encryption and data masking that are already familiar to public health IT teams. Transparency: Engage your agency and the communities you serve in discussions about how AI might be used and how misuse could be prevented. Build trust through two-way, clear communication. Practical First Steps: A Guide for Health Leaders As leaders embark on a journey of exploration in the use of AI in day-to-day practice, we encourage consideration of these first steps: Start with principles: Use frameworks from trusted sources such as the National Association of Counties,5 Health Resources in Action, or ICF3 to build guidelines around transparency, privacy, and equity. Talk to your team and to community partners: Ask staff and community partners what they know about AI. What worries them? What would help them? Involve staff and partners in building buy-in and surfacing useful ideas. Pilot small projects: Use AI to summarize meeting notes, draft a press release, or prepare a first draft of your CHA. Start small. The important thing is to begin. Experiment informally: Get familiar with generative AI platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Co-Pilot. Ask them to write a policy memo or summarize an article. Think of it as a brainstorming partner. Learn from peers: Join NACCHO, Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, and Big Cities Health Coalition webinars; follow case studies; and borrow what works. Health departments across the country are innovating—and are often willing to share. Participate in the Public Health Communications Collaborative and other nationally recognized coalitions of public health specialists who are crafting the messages that can be deployed with the assistance of AI agents. Conclusion: The Future Is Now AI will not solve all the challenges facing public health. It is not magic. But it is a tool—a powerful one—that can help us serve our communities more effectively, more efficiently, and more equitably. As public health leaders, we have a responsibility not only to respond to today’s threats but to anticipate tomorrow’s needs. AI, if approached with humility, transparency, and strategy, can become one of the most valuable tools in our evolving public health toolbox. Let’s not wait until we’re left behind. The future is already knocking. Let’s answer—with wisdom, courage, and compassion.
