abstract: AI in Precision OncologyAhead of Print InterviewFree AccessFace to Face with Douglas B. Flora, MDDouglas B. Flora and Damian DohertyDouglas B. FloraEditor-in-Chief, AI in Precision OncologySearch for more papers by this author and Damian DohertyEditor-in-Chief, Inside Precision MedicineSearch for more papers by this authorPublished Online:17 Oct 2023https://doi.org/10.1089/aipo.2023.29000.intAboutSectionsPDF/EPUB Permissions & CitationsDownload CitationsTrack CitationsAdd to favorites Back To Publication ShareShare onFacebookXLinked InRedditEmail Douglas B. Flora, MDDr. Douglas B. Flora is the Executive Medical Director of Oncology Services at St. Elizabeth Healthcare in northern Kentucky. He is also the founding Editor-in-Chief of AI in Precision Oncology, the new peer review journal published by Mary Ann Liebert Inc., dedicated to advancing the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in precision oncology to a global community of oncologists.In this exclusive interview with Damian Doherty (Editor-in-Chief of Inside Precision Medicine magazine), Dr. Flora discusses his clinical and leadership role at St. Elizabeth and his conviction that AI will revolutionize the practice of oncology.This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.Damian Doherty: Douglas, tell me about the mission at St. Elizabeth and the work you're doing for your community in northern Kentucky.Douglas B. Flora: I'm a practicing medical oncologist, so I see patients in our clinic. I have an administrative role for our healthcare system as the Chief Clinical Officer over our cancer programs and help lead a large team over six different facilities taking care of cancer patients.This region is really ground zero for cancer in America. Kentucky is a hotbed — it's number one in the country for colon cancer and lung cancer in both deaths and late-stage presentations. We have our hands full but we're doing a lot of good work here at St. Elizabeth.I've been in clinical practice for almost 20 years, but in this role for about 6 years. It's been a real treat to work at St. Elizabeth — it's a very mission-driven place, a very kind place.Doherty: How has this cancer center enabled you to scale this new precision oncology approach and the quality of care you're providing to a region that has such a high incidence of cancer?Flora: We have thrown ourselves into screening and prevention. We have a prevention cancer clinic. We have an emphasis on hands-on demonstration, teaching people that food is medicine. We have a very avid center for precision medicine and genomic health with about a dozen genetic counselors, pharmacogenomic pharmacists, and other support staff.Doherty: As a cancer survivor yourself, Douglas, and an oncologist, you are acutely aware of the importance of getting an early diagnosis so we can treat cancers more precisely, which of course is where the power of AI joins this narrative. When did you have your “Road to Damascus” moment with AI's potential and when did you realize this was something that you had to bring to St. Elizabeth's?Flora: Probably 5–6 years ago. Many of us recognized the problem — health care had become purely transactional, and I felt like damage was done over the past 5–10 years to the doctor-patient relationship, where it became more of a conveyor belt. That's not how I or the doctors in my system are wired. But in a fee-for-service system, where there are more patients than doctors or providers, it creates a stressor. We don't have the staff that we need and that's not likely to get better as the number of cancer patients rises exponentially.With over 18 million cancer survivors in the United States and 13,000 cancer doctors I realized we had to find a new approach to this. The math doesn't work. So I started looking into technology solutions that would help scale our nurses, social workers, dieticians and others. I was impressed with how fast AI was accelerating this field and the number of tools that were becoming available. Tech is a very reasonable solution to take away some of the more mundane tasks from them. AI is an exceptional example. So I started to lean into that and it's only accelerated lately.Doherty: Did you have like-minded colleagues that felt the same way? Who inspired you?Flora: I'm a tech enthusiast, so I read everything including Eric Topol's 2019 book, Deep Medicine, which was illuminating. Some of the themes in his book resonated with me in terms of repairing that doctor-patient relationship and using these tools to make care more human. As I learned more about AI and started to speak around the country on this, I realized this was a real opportunity that we needed to grab quickly — to rebuild the patient-doctor relationship by removing those other stressors that weren't productive for doctors or patients.Doherty: I remember reading Deep Medicine, it was a seminal book. Generative AI has come crashing into our world recently, but it's going to be incredible to see what these models can do in pulling all that disparate data together. That's going to be the key, isn't it, to create that more comprehensive picture?Flora: We're in this unimodal phase where it's really good at pattern recognition and reading digital pixelated slides for pathologists or image recognition for CT scans or chest X-rays and so on. But as we get into this next generation — well beyond chatbot and into clinical decision making — I think we're going to see more cures. We're going to find earlier identification and more patients saved. That's just music to my ears.Doherty: It is very hard for the clinical policy and regulatory frameworks to keep pace with this exponential change. We've had a recent call for a moratorium on AI and there's talk of these large language models being prone to hallucinations. How are we going to keep all these stakeholders aligned and ensure that we're creating robust, unbiased and safe AI systems?Flora: I think that's the sweet spot. That was the impetus for starting this journal, AI in Precision Oncology. As a clinician, I love this stuff, but we have 59 other doctors in our building, most of whom don't know the difference between deep learning, machine learning, and natural language processing (NLP). They don't have time, they're doing a fantastic job taking care of patients every day, but they're overwhelmed at the same time. Industry is hurdling forward; our industry partners are 100% all in on rapid development, sometimes for commercial gain, sometimes for the greater good, but I don't feel like the two groups are talking.My hope for AI in Precision Oncology is to combine those two forces. I've recruited about 25 people on our editorial board right now — about 40% academic heavyweights, about 40% industry heavyweights and 20% that are both. I'm really enjoying the dialogue between the two groups as they discover unique skill sets and perspectives and start to blend them. The articles that are starting to come in reflect those two teams communicating, which is exciting.Doherty: How does the procurement for new technology work at St. Elizabeth? There must be tech companies wanting to sell you transformative AI solutions. How do you decide what's relevant, what's necessary, or that this is a tool that we need to look at?Flora: We are a forward-leaning system that cares about this technology and we are looking into it heavily with very bright IT teams and very accommodating C-suite and board members who believe in what we're trying to build at St. Elizabeth from a cancer perspective. We are in the process generation phase: how do you handle governance? Who is on the committee that will adjudicate this?Everybody in the industry is approaching St. Elizabeth's as an early adopter and we can't buy 200 programs at once. We don't have the IT muscle. So we have to determine that carefully. I think there's a user case right now for the things that have been validated.We're looking at things like NLP to remove documentation burdens for doctors. I think there are some things going on in that world with Microsoft, Nuance and Epic that were announced recently. Our radiologists have pushed through mammography — AI augmentation of their reads that are highly accurate and reduce workloads. We're dipping our toes in, trying to gain experience.I have been almost heretical here and I hope people aren't getting turned off. The velocity of change is not what we've seen before. Suddenly, the world was upended and you had to build everything new. We went to virtual health, to quarantine, and people working from home and the whole system had to adapt immediately.I think 18 months from now, we're going to find ourselves immersed in AI and we should be vetting these tools carefully. But we should view them as a tool that we can use, like a stethoscope or a CT scan, to help the patients.Doherty: I'm glad you mentioned NLPs because there seems to be a paucity of institutions that are still using them to alleviate that administrative burden. I assume you're also implementing AI on the digital pathology side as well?Flora: Yes. Our pathology colleagues are digitizing all our slides this year. We're not quite there with NLP for voice recognition. We use a product — Nuance — that we've used for many years for dictation and that's been NLP from the beginning. But it's refining now with the advent of generative AI coming to the masses. The next round of products is going to be hands-free. It will be able to take large unstructured data sets and make sense of them. We're not there yet, but I'm going to be asking for pilots and trials and, please, let oncology have it first. I'd love to do that with my own division. My doctors are ready.Doherty: Another important part of AI and precision medicine is education. Many physicians weren't trained in genomics. And there's still a huge education gap, even in residency. It can be confounding for physicians to know what test to order, and which panels to use? Do I do the whole genome or exome? How do I interpret variants of unknown significance? How have you approached that educational side at St. Elizabeth?Flora: I hope they're teaching it to our new medical students because it is half of my life as a cancer doctor. The other half might be immunology, which we also didn't have heavy training on either.We're blessed in our system. We have a dedicated center for precision medicine and genomic health, led by a very bright, dedicated medical oncologist, Dr. Brooke Phillips. She trained in cancer genetics at City of Hope and at Cleveland Clinic and has been leading our charge. The director of our center, Jaime Grund is also extremely involved in providing education. It's really important for me, as an early adopter, to listen to their counsel and say, maybe what's being promised isn't quite ready.Doherty: Let's talk about the new journal. How are you getting on with submissions and preparations for launch?Flora: There will be some interesting front matter in terms of education. One of our goals is to help oncologists get caught up. One of our editors, Scott Penberthy, is Managing Director of Applied AI for Google, and he will present instructional front matter each month — definitions, what is NLP? What is multimodal, unimodal? We'll be doing multimedia and webinars as well.We have a good piece coming in from Dr. Lee Hood (Co-founder of the Institute for Systems Biology [ISB], based in Seattle, WA). Dr. Hood has a 50-year perspective on this field and has been talking about personalized medicine for half of my life. He's seen everything from the original automated DNA sequencer that he helped design to where we are now. He launched a company that's digging into gigantic sets of data to introduce these concepts.As a working clinician, I want digestible, easy-to-use tools that make my life easier. Every month, there will be a section called “Prompt Assistance” — how to construct a generative AI prompt that helps you do your job to fight an insurance company's denial or to write a letter of recommendation for a fellow or a resident. How can we use these tools to use our voice, but accelerate the efficiencies with which we work? So there'll be a lot of user-friendly content in the journal as well.Doherty: What would you perceive to be a measure of success? And what would you like your legacy to be when you hang up your white coat?Flora: I have accomplished most of the goals in my career that I always dreamed of doing, and now I'm trying to build something that is more impactful. Each day I think, what levers can I pull that will reduce suffering the most or save the greatest number of patients with screening and detection or education? I might save more cancer patients as an administrator, building screening programs, or as an editor, educating clinicians on tools that they could use to take better care of patients or make better clinical decisions. So 5–10 years from now, I hope I will have added to the Global Happiness Index because we have reduced the burden of cancer on society.These [AI] tools have incredibly high potential. I'm an eternal optimist, and I think that these things are here to help, but we need guardrails. We need strong legislation. I think some of the leaders who understand this technology the most are the ones asking for help to rein it in before it becomes unwieldy. I think we're in a critical phase in that too, where we're going to figure this out in the next year or two.FiguresReferencesRelatedDetails Volume 0Issue 0 InformationCopyright 2023, Mary Ann Liebert, Inc., publishersTo cite this article:Douglas B. title_key: stimulate don t replace how ai design shapes human creative effort the cinecoach case and recommendations for european policy|bakshi
title: Stimulate, Don't Replace: How AI Design Shapes Human Creative Effort. The CineCoach Case and Recommendations for European Policy
abstract: Films from the 27 Member States of the European Union, counted with their predecessor states, have won 52 of the 79 Academy Awards for Best International Feature Film and are credited on 54 of the 102 winners of the Palme d'Or. The festivals of Venice, Cannes and Berlin are European. Some 8.9 million Europeans work in culture in 24 official languages. Generative AI now touches every one of these fields. The European Commission is preparing an AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors on the principle that AI should complement and not replace human creativity. We ask what the evidence says about how that principle can be built into a tool and what it implies for public policy. We review seven bodies of research (neural and cognitive models of creativity, the generation effect, motivation and evaluation, deliberate practice and feedback, tutoring and Socratic instruction, guided discovery and human–AI co-creation) and report only findings from sources we opened with their statistics as stated. Human–AI co-creation raises individual output and lowers collective diversity (meta-analytic g = 0.27 and g = −0.86 with a second meta-analysis putting homogenisation at d = 0.33). The interface decides which effect dominates – an AI that questions the person about their own idea preserves diversity and ownership while an AI that rewrites the idea loses both (d = 0.76 and 0.57). In learning an answer-giving AI raises assisted performance and lowers unassisted performance (−17%) while a hint-giving AI does no harm. High-information feedback has twice the effect of corrective feedback (d = 0.99 against 0.46). We also report the findings that cut against a simple Socratic thesis – a randomised trial in which a strategy-giving AI coach left users worse off than no AI at all, another with no difference between Socratic and non-Socratic tutors and the absence of any reliable neural signature for divergent thinking. Used wrongly AI will flatten the plurality that makes European creativity unique. Used rightly it will augment and accelerate European creativity. We describe CineCoach (a coaching system encoded from one cinematographer's method and running in fifteen languages, eleven of them official EU languages, each with its own natively analysed film curation) as one working example of the augmenting design and we state its limits. We close with an agenda for the strategy – fund the design rather than the technology, measure output diversity as an outcome and put artist-facing AI under the control of the schools and studios that use it.

title_key: the impact of artificial intelligence on scholars an interview with juan d machin mastromatteo|machinmastromatteo
title: The impact of artificial intelligence on scholars: an interview with Juan D. Machin-Mastromatteo
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing the way knowledge is created, discovered and disseminated with a possible impact on the role of digital libraries, including the professional work of the digital librarian, which remains controversial and difficult to predict. In this context, what seems to be possible is to anticipate the impact on areas of scholars’ work, to offer adequate digital library services to the new needs. In particular, Generative AI can speed up the writing and research processes, improve cooperation, teaching and learning and provide fresh perspectives for the academic world. However, the introduction of Generative AI into academia can also present potential downsides, and this interview aims to explore the positive and negative impacts of AI on scholars as a food for thought for digital librarians.We chose to interview Juan D. Machin-Mastromatteo who with his young age represents a new generation of scholars in Library and Information Science (LIS) who are experimenting with AI.Juan D. Machin-Mastromatteo is a full-time professor at the Autonomous University of Chihuahua (UACH, Mexico) and member of the National System of Researchers (Level II). He is a Doctor in Information and Communication Science (Tallinn University), Master in Digital Library Learning (Oslo University College; Tallinn University; and Parma University) and Bachelor in Librarianship (Central University of Venezuela). He is a specialist in information literacy, action research, bibliometrics, open access and digital libraries.He has published over 150 scientific publications; has facilitated more than 40 courses; has participated in more than 120 international events as a speaker, panelist, organizer or moderator; and has facilitated over 20 workshops for training researchers. He is the Associate Editor of Information Development (SAGE), the Information Studies Journal (UACH) and until 2023 he held this position for Digital Library Perspectives (Emerald). He is also a member of the editorial advisory boards committees of The Journal of Academic Librarianship (Elsevier) and IE Revista de Investigacion Educativa (REDIECH). He has conducted peer reviews for 17 scientific journals within the fields of information science and education, for which he has evaluated over 300 manuscripts; and has also edited four special issues for various scientific journals. In Information Development he published, from 2015 to 2020, the column Developing Latin America. In 2019, he created the Juantífico Project: videos on scientific information, research and publication. From 2022, he co-hosts InfoTecarios podcast. Since 2023 he publishes the School of Editors section in the Information Studies Journal.He has excelled in different roles: as Editor, Reviewer, Author, Researcher, Educators and in particular well known for a series of tutorials (videos) to explain scholarly communication to interested researchers.Nowadays, it seems that a researcher might assume different roles. It might not be enough anymore just to conduct research, write and publish. For different reasons, we must conduct various activities related to research and teaching to improve our visibility and growth opportunities, and in each of these roles, different rules apply regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI).I teach at the university. I am also a researcher, and thus I am also the author of scientific publications. I also conduct peer reviews for scientific journals, and I am involved as an associate editor in two journals. Finally, I also produce educational videos related to my research and teaching topics.The use of AI in each of these roles may vary, specifically regarding how acceptable it is to use AI and under which conditions. In teaching, it might be acceptable to produce images through AI to accompany my presentations for lectures, also for finding reading materials more quickly and writing creative case scenarios for the students to solve problems. Something similar happens when I prepare a conference presentation – nowadays, a large part of the graphic content of my presentations corresponds to AI-generated images.As an author and researcher, you must be more careful about how you use AI because there are certain guidelines that you should follow. Most major publishers (including Emerald) have already set policies regarding the use of AI in research and publishing, and if you analyze those policies, it turns out that there are very few acceptable uses of AI. The only thing you can use it for is to improve your writing. These policies also point out that AI cannot be used in any case to generate content, especially for data analysis or to draw conclusions.Why is it acceptable to improve writing? The reasoning behind this seems to be that the content being passed through AI for this purpose has already been human-generated, so there’s no problem with that; the AI is just acting as a more sophisticated spelling and grammar review function than the one available in word processors. One reason why it would not be acceptable to generate content and put it in an article is related to the fact that most people use AI tools through the free versions, which give you very few options to customize the AI’s behavior. An alternative to this would be, for instance, to use OpenAI’s ChatGPT system by paying the premium subscription, which grants you access to customize ChatGPT’s behavior by configuring an assistant. For example, you can disable its ability to connect to the Internet to find responses, and you can also set very strict rules for its operation and prevent it from using sources and behaving in ways that you do not want it to.There could be other acceptable uses, such as helping in the information-seeking process. There are very useful tools such as Consensus, Scite, Connected Papers and ResearchRabbit, which help identify literature that you may have missed or literature that you must check if you’re starting a new project, and some of these offer interesting features to navigate the literature and explore the relationships among authors and publications. There are also tools that provide summaries and help in reading or even tagging the literature that you are using to have the AI help you identify topics within full texts, such as Scispace. AI tools may help review the literature in a faster way; however, you must not use the content that the AI generates for you as is, without confirming its validity and without substantially transforming it.My main concern with AI-generated content is that I simply don’t trust how AI works, e.g. it seems to be somewhat lazy and not comprehensive. Also, its responses tend to be very enumerative; its analysis might not be as deep as I would like it to be. In any case, the tool cannot guess what the human wants or how the human will make a proper analysis. These considerations, I feel, are especially valid within the humanities and social sciences, where analyses and meanings are so complex.For journal editors and reviewers, other sets of rules apply. Under both roles, you must be aware that you are handling original manuscripts, which are, of course, not published, and hence, these are confidential works that must be treated accordingly. If you check them with an AI, you do not know how AI tools might be ingesting these manuscripts that you want to process through it. While the AI might not publish the manuscripts or upload them to public servers, the contents of manuscripts checked through AI could be used to further train the language model and become part of its knowledge base. This raises serious privacy and confidentiality concerns, as the authors might not authorize the use of their intellectual property in this manner.There is the recent example of the publisher Taylor and Francis, which sold access to publications under their banner to Microsoft AI, and authors are not too happy about it. The current issue being discussed is: do we, as authors, want this to happen? The publisher has made a financial deal with an AI company, and as authors, we are not profiting from that, nor do we know the extent to which our intellectual property is being used. I doubt the publisher asked authors for their permission to use their publications in this manner, and older publishing agreements do not include provisions about this usage of authors’ intellectual property (do current agreements include this?). Of course, there could be alternatives in the near future where we can install local AI solutions (meaning, they are not online, and there are some currently available options) that might be tailored in a way that allows us to screen new manuscripts and perform some automatic evaluations on them while at the same time preventing the use of these contents in any other way.Regarding the production of videos as part of a scientific dissemination process and to extend my reach as an educator in the topics of scientific information, research and publication, I am a bit more free to experiment and use AI. Many people will have seen some videos that are fully generated with AI by now. I feel that these kinds of videos are, to say the least, dry. They might be unnecessarily long, and they often develop arguments in circles, not even getting to the main topic. The human touch is very important when communicating anything, and this fact is relevant to any of the roles we have discussed.The main question here might be: if I use AI to produce content, why should I pretend to have a human audience for it? If I was not able to produce content with my human intelligence, why should other humans bother to follow me?In any case, for the purposes of producing videos, I have found some AI support, particularly to help create video covers or thumbnails with image generation tools, e.g. with DALL-E, which is included in ChatGPT’s premium subscription. However, human input is crucial, so the resulting images originate from sophisticated prompts, and I edit them further. For instance, I can add my own picture or other elements to compose a better thumbnail, such as adding some text to make it more informative and draw users to click on it.I have also experimented with using AI to act as a marketing officer for my content. Making videos, promoting them, managing the channels and other social media sites is a lot of work – and it is something that I do entirely on my own, with the few resources I can afford and with my own skills. title_key: world cornea congress ix 2025 abstracts|
title: World Cornea Congress IX (2025): Abstracts
abstract: Publications Rates and Characteristics of Registered Cornea Transplant Trials: An Analysis of Clinicaltrials.gov Leo Meller1, Ibrahim Abboud2, Steven Anderson2, and Natalie Afshari3 1Shiley Eye Institute, San Diego, CA; 2UC Riverside School of Medicine, Riverside, CA; and 3UC San Diego, San Diego, CA. Purpose: To characterize all registered corneal transplant (CT) trials. Methods: Information of all registered CT trials was extracted from Clinicaltrials.gov. Results: A total of 164 CT trials were identified with no time limits with the oldest from 1986, to which the majority were interventional (123, 75%), early phase or uncategorized (139, 84.8%), focused on adults only (142, 86.6%), non-industry sponsored (151, 92.1%). Principal investigators were predominately male (106, 64.6%), based internationally (114, 69.5%), and led by MD only (94, 57.3%). Interventional trials were more likely to be late phase (P = 0.002) and industry sponsored (P = 0.02) compared to observational trials. Among completed trials, 74 (63.2%) were published. International trials and trials focused on adults only were associated with publication (P = 0.003, P < 0.001, respectively). Conclusions: Less than two-thirds of completed CT trials were published in peer reviewed journals. Industry played a more significant role in interventional trials and international trials were associated with publication status. Increasing efforts is needed to improve rates of publication for timely dissemination of the latest advances in CT. “Needle” Keratoplasty Delivery of Endothelial Donor Grafts with a Novel Needle Delivery System Eric Abdullayev, and Arthur Kurz Lions World Vision Institute, Tampa, FL. Purpose: To introduce the first delivery device for the eye bank prepared/preloaded endothelial grafts to be delivered into the recipient's anterior chamber through the puncture. Methods: Donor corneas with healthy endothelium were used. 5 DMEK and 5 UT-DSAEK grafts were prepared loaded in the new delivery device with a needle insertion tip and stored for 5 days in Optisol-GS at 2 to 8 C. Then grafts were unloaded and endothelial viability was evaluated using specular microscopy and a new cell staining method. Images are digitally processed by the “ImageJ” image processing program. The percentage of the damaged cells was calculated. An artificial chamber with mounted donor corneas was used to recreate graft insertion through the puncture. Results: Mean preparation donor endothelial cells density was 2593 ± 89 cells/mm2 and post load - 2655 ± 95 cells/mm2. On the first day following preload, the mean endothelial cell loss was 5%, which remained stable at day 5. Endothelial specular microscopy and staining confirmed viable endothelium. All grafts were inserted through the needle puncture without difficulties. No fluid leaks were observed from the puncture wound. Conclusions: Eye bank-prepared pre-loaded DMEK and UT-DSAEK grafts in the new delivery device with a needle insertion tip survive storage for several days and can be successfully inserted for transplantation through puncture without prior blade incision. Ocular Features of Severe Vitamin Deficiency in Autistic Spectrum Disorder Children in the USA Anas Abuseif, Oliver Beale, and Ken Nischal UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA. Purpose: To describe 3 patients with autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) and peculiar restrictive diet who presented with severe vitamin A deficiency in the USA. Methods: Retrospective chart review. Results: Two (males) presented with blepharospasm, photosensitivity and night-blindness. Only at exam under anesthesia were bilateral corneal melts found in both. Both were treated with Amniotic Membrane Transplant with tarsorrhaphy; one underwent bilateral Gundersen flaps as a secondary procedure. One female presented with severe bilateral punctate epithelial erosions and blepharospasm. All patients had severe xerophthalmia, conjunctival ulceration, and Bitot's spots and received vitamin A intramuscularly along with aggressive lubricating eye drops. Behavioral therapy was needed together with continued oral Vitamin A to improve diet. All patients improved significantly. Conclusions: The possibility of severe vitamin A deficiency should be considered in ASD patients who present with photophobia and blepharospasm. Corneal Densitometry in Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy: A Novel Attempt to Re Classify Corneal Clouding Muralidhar Ramappa1, Divya S. Achanta1, Anthony Aldave2, Deepak Edward3, and Sunita Chaurasia4 1L V Prasad Eye Institute, Hyderabad, Telangana, India; 2Stein Eye Institute, Los Angeles, CA; 3Department of Ophthalmology, Illinois Eye and Ear Infirmary, University of Illinois, Chicago, IL; and 4L V Prasad Eye Hospital, Hyderabad, Telangana, India. Purpose: To objectively grade corneal cloudiness in children with CHED and correlate it with clinical findings. Methods: This retrospective case-controlled study included 55 cloudy corneas from 32 CHED children, compared with 35 clear corneas from 18 age-matched healthy controls. Corneal densitometry (CD) was assessed using the WaveLight Oculyzer II, while central corneal thickness (CCT) was measured using anterior segment OCT. Corneal cloudiness was subjectively assessed via slit-lamp images and correlated with central 4 mm area densitometry. Objective corneal clouding grades were mild (28 eyes), moderate (16 eyes), and severe (5 eyes). Results: Combining clinical and imaging modalities, corneal clouding was graded as mild (52 eyes), moderate (25 eyes), and severe (9 eyes). The median age at the imaging time was 7.6 (5.3–10.1) years, with 58.3% being male. More advanced cases presented higher backscatter (P <0.0001). Mean central 4 mm area densitometry was significantly higher than age-matched healthy controls (P < 0.0001). Corneal grading comparisons showed a significant correlation between slit-lamp findings and densitometry measurements (P < 0.0001). CCT and LogMAR visual acuity were significantly correlated with area densitometry (P < 0.0001 and P = 0.004, respectively). Age at investigation and gender did not correlate with area densitometry (P = 0.32 and P = 0.19). Significant differences were observed for densitometry measurements across 4 annuli (P < 0.0001) and 3 corneal layers (P < 0.0001). Conclusions: A densitometry program is valuable for assessing corneal clouding in CHED patients. Densitometry measurements were significantly correlated with CCT and Log MAR visual acuity, indicating the program's utility in accurately evaluating corneal cloudiness in children with CHED. abstract: Medical School Personal Statements: A Comparison Between Artificial Intelligence-Generated and Human-Authored Essays Matthew J Vaccaro, BS*, Ishpriya Sharma, PhD, Andrea Paola P Espina Rey, MPH, CPH, Nicole Lyman, BS, Christian Palacios, MPH, Yu Zhang, MS, Aashna Mehta, MD, Angelo Leto Barone, MD, FACS, Brian Kellogg, MD University of Central Florida College of Medicine, Orlando, FL; Nemours Children’s Hospital, Orlando, FL; Dr Kiran C Patel College of Allopathic Medicine (NSU MD), Nova Southeastern University, Davie, FL Introduction: With over 67.7 million ChatGPT users in the US, nearly half of college students report willingness to use artificial intelligence (AI) in their application essays. This study investigates the quality of AI-generated medical school personal statements and whether medical school application reviewers can distinguish them from human-authored essays. Methods: Using medical school personal statements from 2019 (before OpenAI), corresponding AI-generated (ChatGPT) versions were created using experiences from each essay. Experienced application readers blinded to essay authorship were randomly assigned essays and asked to rate quality (7-point Likert), postulate authorship (Human vs AI), and report confidence in authorship postulations (5-point Likert). ZeroGPT (AI-detection tool) also analyzed the essays. Statistical analyses included Fleiss’ Kappa for inter-rater reliability, Mann-Whitney U test for perceived authorship bias, and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test for scoring differences. Results: Seventeen readers completed 325 ratings across 309 essays. Readers demonstrated fair interrater reliability (Fleiss’ Kappa = 0.211) and showed 55% accuracy, 51% sensitivity, and 61% specificity in determining authorship. ZeroGPT demonstrated 91% accuracy, 85% sensitivity, and 97% specificity in determining authorship. Higher-quality essays were more likely assumed to be human-authored (p < 0.001), and AI-generated essays scored better than their human-authored counterparts (p = 0.020) with mean scores of 5.02 (SD = 1.33) and 4.67 (SD = 1.21), respectively. Conclusion: AI-generated essays demonstrated increased quality and were essentially indistinguishable from human-authored essays. Despite ZeroGPT’s higher accuracy, its detection rate is not reliable enough to be heavily relied upon in the admissions process. The utility of personal statements in medical school applications requires urgent reconsideration to ensure a fair application process. ePosters Clinical Momentum: An Observational Study Identifying Latent Forces Driving Surgical Interventions for Older Adults Near the End of Life Melanie Fritz, MD, Michael Jaeb, BSN, RN, Sarah Zaza, MD, Alex Dudek, RN, BSN, MPH, Kristine Kwekkeboom, PhD, RN, FAAN, Anne Buffington, MPH, Leah Gober, MD, Gretchen Schwarze, MD, FACS University of Wisconsin - Madison, Madison, WI *Excellence in Research Award recipient Introduction: Older adults often undergo surgery near the end of life, in contrast to generally stated preferences. Systems forces that promote intervention may produce non-beneficial treatment despite advances in communication. We conducted an observational study to understand how a conceptual model of clinical momentum might apply to patients with life-limiting illnesses having surgery. Methods: We interviewed 31 clinicians caring for 8 patients age 65+ with life-limiting illness who received an unplanned surgical intervention. We evaluated physical, cognitive, and social behavioral processes related to the course of care. We used content analysis to code interview transcripts and higher-level analysis to understand the empirical fit of the conceptual model. Results: We found evidence of model components, including “fix it” and “recognition primed decision making” that promoted a default of surgical intervention followed by an accumulating “cascade” of subsequent interventions that generated a perception of “sunk costs.” We identified novel contributors to momentum including binary options and care fragmentation. Clinicians expressed concerns that surgery was non-beneficial, but were unable to disrupt this momentum in the moment of decision making around surgery. We identified one momentum disruption where a second operation was not offered because the patient’s abnormality could not be “fixed” with surgery. Conclusion: Clinical momentum is a model that characterizes systems forces leading to acute surgical intervention for patients with life-limiting illnesses despite surgeon concerns that the treatment does more harm than good. These forces are difficult to disrupt and may require interventions beyond improved communication to reduce non-beneficial therapy. Data Governance Ethics and Patient Confidentiality with Robotic Surgical Technologies Baddr A Shakhsheer, MD, FACS, FAAP, Peter Angelos, MD, FACS, Sean C Wightman, MD, FACS University of Chicago, Chicago, IL; Keck School of Medicine - University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA Introduction: Robotic platforms generate and store a tremendous amount of data: video recording of operations, surgeon-specific metrics such as economy of motion and tissue handling, and metadata metrics such as operation volume and average case length. We elucidated surgeon perspectives and understanding of data generated by third-party robotic surgery platforms. Methods: This study was approved by The University of Chicago institutional review board (IRB24-1635). A survey was advertised to a closed social media group of confirmed robotic surgeons. The survey was administered via REDCap. Results: 38 board-certified surgeons responded to the survey. 84% of surgeons had a personalized login for the robotic platform. 63% of respondents reviewed their personal data from the robotic platform. 76% did not know if their institutions had DUA with the robot manufacturer, and of those who were aware, 29% had read the DUA. When queried regarding which parties had a stake in the data collected by the robotic platforms, respondents stated positively for the following entities: the surgeon - 26%, the robot manufacturer - 26%, the institution - 34%, and the patient - 63%. When asked if data is collected via the robotic platform, 50% said yes, 5% said no, and 45% were unsure. 95% did not discuss this data collection with patients. Conclusion: This study raises concerns regarding data generated in robotic surgical practices. This data calls attention to the need for surgeons to work towards appropriate involvement in management and oversight of this data. Evaluating Patient and Caregiver Satisfaction on the Informed Consent for Surgery in a Tertiary Care Centre of Nepal: A Cross-Sectional Study Sujan Paudel, MBBS, Prajjwol Luitel, MBBS, Nischal Neupane, MBBS Maharajgunj Medical Campus, Institute of Medicine, Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu, Nepal Introduction: In Low and Middle Income countries (LMICs) like Nepal, informed consent (IC) is frequently obtained from caregivers and parents, with minimal involvement of patients to alleviate the patient’s anxiety. This raises concerns about whether the patient’s autonomy is respected, and whether family involvement aligns with the patient’s preferences. Thus we aim to evaluate the quality of information received by patients and their caregivers, their perceptions of the IC process, and assess whether the current practice is acceptable or warrants change. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted at tertiary-level hospital of Nepal. It included 368 patients undergoing major elective surgeries across surgical departments. A structured, pretested questionnaire was used to assess the components of the IC process, satisfaction, and understanding among patients and caregivers. Regression analysis was used to identify factors influencing patient satisfaction. Results: 86.4% of patients and 90.8% of caregivers were satisfied with the IC process. Caregivers had a significantly higher understanding of the nature (95.1% vs 88%), indication (98.9% vs 82.1%), and potential complications of surgery (87.5% vs 68.5%) compared with patients. Patients with primary education or higher had significantly higher satisfaction scores than illiterate patients (p = 0.019; 95% CI: 0.16 to 2.61). Conclusion: The current practice of obtaining IC, primarily from caregivers, can be continued. However, efforts should be made to encourage active participation from patients. Initial Results from a Novel Surgical Ethics Curriculum for General Surgery Residents Steven Char, MD, Rosamond Rhodes, PhD, Alexandra Agathis, MD, Celia Divino, MD, FACS Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY Introduction: Despite growing enthusiasm for a national surgical ethics curriculum, no such program yet exists. We created a novel resident-led curriculum for general surgery residents to address this deficit. Methods: We conducted a needs assessment to characterize baseline confidence with key ethics topics, measured on a 5-point Likert scale, then designed six modules to address the identified deficits. Modules consisted of a twenty-minute didactic on an ethics principle led by a surgical resident in conjunction with a faculty ethicist, followed by a small-group discussion of a case pertaining to that principle. To date, three of six modules have been taught. We conducted an interval assessment to assess the impact of the curriculum on resident confidence thus far. Changes in confidence were assessed using t-tests. Results: 50 residents completed the needs assessment. Residents reported highest confidence with dilemmas pertaining to obtaining informed consent, communicating a serious prognosis, and disclosing a medical error. Residents felt least confident with dilemmas pertaining to treatment over objection, requests for medically unindicated interventions, and disagreements with more senior colleagues. There was strong agreement that the curriculum has been valuable (71%) and relevant (88%). We identified significant improvement in confidence in each of the topics discussed thus far: methods to analyze a novel dilemma systematically (p < 0.001), capacity assessment (p = 0.005), and treatment over objection (p = 0.007). Conclusion: We identified the ethical challenges that our residents find most vexing and designed a longitudinal, resident-led curriculum that has been successful in increasing confidence in these domains.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Health: Real-world Insights and Implementation Challenges
abstract: Just 28 years ago, Deep Blue − the first IBM’s supercomputer − defeated Garry Kasparov in the chess match of the century.[1] At that time, we were far from imagining that artificial intelligence (AI) could drive our cars, recognize complex patterns in medical diagnostic images, or write code in sophisticated programming languages like R or Python. Today, AI has evolved to such an extent that the leaders of major software companies have called for a pause in its development so that humanity can assess the risks posed by such advanced AI systems. This breathtaking advancement has undoubtedly compelled all fields to turn their attention toward AI, and of course, medicine is no exception. AI is defined as the capacity of machines to imitate human intelligence and behavior. As a broad discipline, it encompasses numerous subfields and types. Key subfields include machine learning, where systems learn and improve from experience; natural language processing (NLP), which enables machines to identify and interact with a human language; Computer Vision, allowing systems to interpret visual data; and Robotics, focusing on the design and use of machines to automate tasks. AI further encompasses distinct types, including Narrow AI, designed to perform specific tasks such as voice recognition; General AI, which can perform any intellectual task that a human can do; and superintelligent AI, which outperforms humans in most economically valuable work. Each of these subfields and types plays pivotal roles in the vast AI landscape, driving innovation and advancement in numerous sectors.[2] However, after the release of software like ChatGPT (OpenAI, San Francisco, USA), Bard (Google, San Francisco, USA), and DeepSeek (DeepSeek, China), large language models (LLMs)-based chatbots have emerged as powerful AI tools for health care, boasting broad capabilities that are truly awe-inspiring. Historically, managing multisystem disorders such as cancer or autoimmune diseases has been challenging due to their complex and often non-specific presentation. However, AI is sparking a revolution in health care now. For several years, research has been conducted on the usefulness of the various AI subfields in the medical arena. This includes areas such as diagnosing and classifying diseases, image interpretation, and optimizing research and logistical processes, such as data extraction and cleaning.[3] With its unparalleled ability to analyze vast amounts of patient data, AI has the potential to streamline disease identification by analyzing intricate patterns invisible to the human eye,[4] predict treatment outcomes,[5] and interpret and categorize clinical notes efficiently.[6] Thus, this groundbreaking technology could revolutionize healthcare delivery and transform the patient experience [Figure 1].Figure 1: Key domains in the real-world implementation of artificial intelligence in healthcare. This figure summarizes the core challenges and opportunities identified in the editorial, including (1) data fragmentation and interoperability limitations, (2) the role of natural language processing in handling unstructured clinical data, (3) model generalizability and risk of bias across populations, (4) ethical and legal frameworks related to privacy and consent, (5) barriers to clinical implementation, and (6) future directions such as AI-assisted diagnostics and multidisciplinary collaborationAt the heart of this transformation lies big data, amassed through multicentric clinical registries, acting as treasure troves for the NLP algorithms. The concurrent growth of clinical data warehouses and national-level initiatives to standardize observational clinical data and make them available centrally is an important point to emphasize.[7] AI needs data, and clinical data are now at a stage where AI can exploit that data. With millions of patient records at their disposal, AI can decode complex disease pathways and refine diagnostic accuracy for several diseases. Currently, we are able to detect dozens of ophthalmological diseases and conditions in retinal photographs automatically using deep neural networks with a sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) above 0.97.[8] NLP approaches will allow us to extract and summarize information from clinical records which are still unstructured, empowering clinical decision support systems. However, as AI progresses at an astonishing pace, concerns regarding its risks and ethical implications have garnered the attention of industry leaders. The call for a pause in AI development reflects a collective recognition of the need for humanity to assess and address these risks proactively. Protecting patient privacy and data security, addressing biases and ensuring fairness, promoting transparency and explainability, maintaining human oversight, obtaining informed consent, and ensuring equity and accessibility are crucial. By engaging in careful evaluation and risk assessment, we can ensure that AI systems are developed and utilized to maximize their positive impact while minimizing potential harm. AI systems are only as good as the data they are trained on. Biases in data collection or algorithm design can result in a system serving only a limited subset of the population, exacerbating healthcare disparities.[9] For example, in the field of ophthalmology, a deep learning model developed to identify diabetic retinopathy (DR) on color fundus photographs had a notable disparity in diagnostic accuracy (73% vs. 60.5%) between lighter and darker skin individuals.[10] Therefore, to ensure fairness and efficacy, it is crucial to ensure that the data training these systems reflect the diversity of the global population.[10] Ethnicity, age, sex, and socioeconomic status influence disease manifestation and response to treatment. Omitting these factors can lead to skewed algorithms that fail certain groups. Therefore, overcoming this challenge will require rigorous efforts in data collection and algorithm design, embracing the full spectrum of patient demographics [Figure 1]. The impact of AI in health care is not monolithic – it differs depending on whether the consumer is a patient or a provider. For patients, AI tools enhance autonomy, access, and health literacy. Applications range from symptom checkers to virtual assistants and wearable-based monitoring tools. NLP-based interfaces help patients interpret lab results, medication instructions, and chronic disease management plans.[6] Yet, the benefits are not universal. Risks such as misinformation, misdiagnosis from unverified AI apps, and the digital divide pose real threats to safety and equity. Healthcare providers, on the other hand, could benefit significantly from AI-augmented tools that support diagnostics, clinical decision-making, and administrative efficiency.[11] From radiologists using computer vision to detect malignancies, to NLP systems that automate clinical documentation, AI promises to reduce cognitive and clerical burden.[12] However, these gains come with caveats: explainability remains a key concern, as black-box models challenge traditional standards of medical accountability. Overreliance on automated tools also risks deskilling the clinical workforce. On a systemic level, AI promises transformation toward predictive, preventive, and personalized medicine. But unless regulatory, infrastructural, and training frameworks evolve in tandem, the sector risks further fragmentation and inequality. Some even argue that AI is reshaping not only labor dynamics but also ethical values and the fabric of healthcare relationships.[13] Addressing these multidimensional challenges thoughtfully will be essential as we integrate AI deeper into the healthcare ecosystem. One particularly promising but complex application of AI in health care lies in community-based eye screening. With an increasing number of regulatory-approved AI tools in ophthalmology – ranging from DR and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to glaucoma and anterior segment pathologies – AI is poised to transform early detection and triage systems. Deep learning models have achieved remarkable performance metrics, such as an AUC of 0.98 for referable AMD,[14] and have shown capability in quantifying tear breakup time,[15] detecting preclinical keratoconus,[16] and segmenting optic discs for glaucoma evaluation.[17] Yet, implementing these tools in real-world, resource-limited community settings reveals substantial gaps. Unlike controlled clinical environments, health camps often deal with patients who present with multiple co-existing conditions. Current AI tools are frequently trained and validated for single-disease detection, which limits their utility in comprehensive screenings. A person with cataract and DR might only receive attention for one, leaving the other unaddressed. In a recent community screening study led by our team, technician-led triaging enhanced with AI assistance was tested. Over three days and 393 patients, we observed a >20% increase in screening sensitivity as technician familiarity with the AI tool improved –highlighting the importance of the learning curve in human-AI collaboration. Despite promising results, several pragmatic barriers emerged: variability in image quality due to suboptimal equipment, language barriers affecting informed consent and instructions, short patient interaction time, and logistical issues in follow-up coordination (unpublished data). These insights reaffirm that AI’s success in healthcare will depend not only on algorithmic accuracy but also on system integration. For example, our triage framework used a combination of AI image interpretation and basic clinical signs (visual acuity, duration of diabetes, anterior segment assessment) to guide referrals. Patients were flagged for referral based on retinal hemorrhages, optic disc changes, or lens opacities detected by AI. Such multi-pronged approaches reinforce AI’s value as an assistant–not a replacement–for frontline healthcare workers (unpublished data). Furthermore, implementation must be accompanied by robust ethical, regulatory, and infrastructural frameworks. Key concerns include data privacy, transparency of decision-making processes (the “black box” problem), liability in case of AI errors, and the risk of clinicians becoming overly reliant on AI outputs. There is also a need to educate both healthcare professionals and the public on how to interpret and interact with AI-generated insights safely and meaningfully. Equally important is ensuring that patient pathways postscreening are not left incomplete – diagnosis and treatment must be accessible following AI-flagged referrals [Figure 1]. As part of our PROTON initiative,[18,19] we envision developing an integrated data ecosystem – “the PROTON Data Lake” – that combines clinical phenotypes, imaging biomarkers, and patient-reported outcomes to train and validate future AI models. Such a resource, enriched by real-world annotations, will be instrumental in bridging the gap between AI research and its deployment in public health systems. In conclusion, the powerful synergy between AI and medicine holds the key to a transformative future of enhanced diagnosis and management of complex medical conditions. LLMs such as ChatGPT, Google Barts, or DeepSeek could become helpful tools in the daily lives of healthcare professionals. However, responsible and ethical development and deployment of AI are essential to harness its transformative power for the benefit of humanity. The journey toward this future must be marked by diligence, prioritizing diversity and inclusion, and preserving the sacred doctor–patient relationship. By navigating these challenges thoughtfully, we can embrace AI’s potential while safeguarding against potential risks. With these paramount considerations driving us forward, the fusion of AI and medicine emerges as a boundless frontier, poised to revolutionize health care for the greater good.

title: От «учебного инструмента» к «партнеру по творчеству»: наблюдения о том, как генеративный ИИ меняет логику преподавания в области изобразительного искусства
abstract: Трансформация педагогической логики в сфере изобразительного искусства под воздействием генеративных технологий искусственного интеллекта отражает фундаментальные изменения в понимании творческого процесса, авторства и профессионального становления художника в условиях цифровой среды. Наблюдается постепенный переход от восприятия генеративных моделей преимущественно как вспомогательных средств визуализации идей или генерации референсов к их осмыслению в качестве полноценного партнера по творчеству, способного вносить элементы неожиданности, стимулировать рефлексию и расширять границы стилистического экспериментирования. Анализ динамики взаимодействия демонстрирует, что на начальных этапах обучения преобладают сценарии замещающего характера, когда технологии применяются для получения итогового изображения, в то время как по мере продвижения к старшим курсам и магистратуре усиливается ориентация на итеративный диалог, предварительное эскизирование, критический анализ композиционных и колористических решений, создание вспомогательных текстур и элементов, что свидетельствует о формировании более зрелого профессионального подхода, при котором технология обогащает, а не подменяет авторский труд. Педагогические установки обнаруживают значительную дифференциацию в зависимости от дисциплинарной принадлежности и педагогического стажа: представители академической традиции изобразительного искусства чаще придерживаются ограничительных позиций, тогда как в областях дизайна и визуальных коммуникаций превалирует интегративный взгляд, предполагающий включение генеративных инструментов на различных стадиях работы. Оценки степени авторства в смешанных формах творчества выявляют общую ценностную основу, объединяющую преподавателей и обучающихся, согласно которой максимальная творческая субъектность сохраняется при существенной ручной доработке, а минимальная – при простом формулировании запроса без дальнейшего вмешательства, хотя студенты проявляют несколько более либеральное отношение к гибридным практикам по сравнению с педагогами. Пересмотр критериев оценивания учебных работ становится неизбежным, поскольку традиционные параметры технического мастерства и оригинальности требуют дополнения такими аспектами, как прозрачность применения технологий, качество взаимодействия с моделью и способность к осознанному выбору между инструментальной, диалогической и партнерской моделями сотрудничества. Эти модели сосуществуют в индивидуальных профилях взаимодействия, актуализируясь в зависимости от контекста задачи, что подчеркивает необходимость развития рефлексивных компетенций, позволяющих художнику сохранять контроль над творческим высказыванием в условиях ускоряющихся технологических изменений. Асинхронность между стремительной эволюцией генеративных систем и обновлением институциональных норм образовательных программ создает зону педагогической неопределенности, требующую содержательного осмысления места технологии в логике художественного образования без отказа от фундаментальных компетенций ручного мастерства, визуальной грамотности и концептуального мышления. Представленные наблюдения позволяют установить основное содержание статьи, оценить ее значимость для переосмысления методических подходов в художественной педагогике и принять обоснованное решение об обращении к полному тексту для углубленного ознакомления с конкретными тенденциями и их педагогическими импликациями. The transformation of pedagogical logic in the field of fine arts under the influence of generative artificial intelligence technologies reflects fundamental changes in the understanding of the creative process, authorship, and the professional formation of the artist in a digital environment. A gradual transition is observed from the perception of generative models primarily as auxiliary tools for the visualization of ideas or the generation of references toward their interpretation as a full-fledged creative partner capable of introducing elements of surprise, stimulating reflection, and expanding the boundaries of stylistic experimentation. Analysis of interaction dynamics demonstrates that at the initial stages of training, substitutive scenarios predominate in which technologies are used to produce a final image, whereas progression to senior courses and master’s programs strengthens an orientation toward iterative dialogue, preliminary sketching, critical analysis of compositional and coloristic decisions, and the creation of auxiliary textures and elements. This testifies to the formation of a more mature professional approach in which technology enriches rather than replaces the author’s work. Pedagogical attitudes exhibit significant differentiation depending on disciplinary affiliation and teaching experience: representatives of the academic tradition in fine arts more frequently adhere to restrictive positions, while fields of design and visual communications are dominated by an integrative perspective that presupposes the inclusion of generative tools at various stages of work. Assessments of the degree of authorship in hybrid creative forms reveal a shared value foundation uniting instructors and students, according to which maximum creative agency is preserved with substantial manual elaboration, and minimum authorship occurs with simple prompt formulation without further intervention – although students demonstrate a somewhat more liberal attitude toward hybrid practices compared with educators. Revision of the criteria for evaluating academic works becomes inevitable, as traditional parameters of technical mastery and originality require supplementation by such aspects as transparency in technology use, the quality of interaction with the model, and the ability to make conscious choices among instrumental, dialogic, and partnership models of collaboration. These models coexist in individual interaction profiles, becoming salient depending on task context, which underscores the need to develop reflective competencies enabling the artist to maintain control over the creative statement amid accelerating technological change. The asynchrony between the rapid evolution of generative systems and the updating of institutional norms in educational programs creates a zone of pedagogical uncertainty requiring substantive reflection on the place of technology in the logic of artistic education without abandoning fundamental competencies in manual craftsmanship, visual literacy, and conceptual thinking. The observations presented make it possible to establish the article’s main content, evaluate its significance for the rethinking of methodological approaches in art pedagogy, and make an informed decision about consulting the full text for in-depth acquaintance with specific trends and their pedagogical implications.

title: Artificial Intelligence is Changing Your World – Is it Dystopian?
abstract: This month’s issue is dedicated to artificial intelligence (AI). As researchers and educators, we all need and safe guidelines for acceptable use of AI. Artificial intelligence has the potential to make our lives significantly more efficient. With its use, software engineering specialists can shorten the average development time of a program from 6 months to just 3 weeks.1 Software engineers could also write code in 4 days, rather than 5, suggesting that AI could further support the transition to a standard 4-day work week within the next 10 years.2 But there are concerns that this new efficiency will decrease brain power and that students may lose the capacity to think for themselves (cognitive offloading). Natalie Wexler,2 an American education commentator, has expressed unease with the overemphasis on AI skills instead of content in the absence of critical thinking, which leads to a mechanical writing exercise that replaces intellectual processing of new knowledge. Carl Hendrick,2 a professor at Academica University of Applied Sciences, has coined the terms “pseudo-proficiency,” the ability to mimic but not possess knowledge, or “AI ventriloquism,” meaning that students write correct answers but for the incorrect reasons. Skeptics of AI remark that learning is traditionally built on exerting effort to acquire knowledge and then reflecting on that new knowledge, a process that generative AI cannot supply.2 Artificial intelligence is a technology that has been all around us for years now. When you ask your phone a question or use other voice-activated search engines, you are using AI. Google uses AI technology in many of its services such as Google Search and Google Maps. Google now has Artificial Intelligence Overview (AIO), referred to as Google Zero, which keeps users within the Google ecosystem.3 A summary of the content you are searching for appears at the top of the page results, eliminating the need to click on the source websites. Initially launched in May 2024 in the United States, by October 2024 it had rolled out to more 100 countries. As a result, click-through rates have dropped an average of 35% (range 15-64%).3 Articles from this issue feature an exploration of the strengths, weaknesses, and future considerations for AI. An excellent article by Nelson and team investigate AI in the field and how large language and machine learning models can enhance wound diagnosis and treatment. The authors caution that these tools support clinical decision-making but do not replace expert clinicians. Despite many benefits (patient empowerment/accessibility, provider-accelerated care, and enhanced continuity of care), there are several limitations, particularly AI’s inability to physically sense a patient’s temperature, tenderness, subtle lumps, or tissue fibrosis. The quality of the data collected to use in large data can be from several input sources with variable clinical expertise. Coşkun and colleagues collected qualitative opinions from 23 neonatal intensive care nurses on neonatal AI-assisted skin assessments. Common themes included the potential for AI to enhance diagnostic accuracy, standardize assessments, and reduce inter-observer variability. They were concerned with algorithm reliability, professional autonomy, and ethical consideration. The nurses also wanted transparency, training, and safeguards against over-reliance on AI. For AI to be used in prospective clinical practice, several variables need to be optimized. Puttur et al demonstrated in patients with leprosy skin wounds (each of 5 patients had at least 2 wounds as a same patient comparison) the value of an AI-enabled multispectral imaging device to enhance management over traditional measuring devices. There are 2 articles in this issue on pressure injuries (PI). The study by Demir Üçtepe and colleagues used 2 datasets to collect 1663 images, with 121 selected for training clinicians to stage PIs. The accuracy was 76.99% overall with highest accuracy for Stage 1 at 87.35% and 64.72% as a lower identification rate for Stage 3 injuries. All patients had light skin tones; those with deep tissue injuries, along with unstageable ulcers, were not included. We still need clinician verification and higher accuracy of evaluation before relying on this without expert assessors for corrections. Kirkland-Kyhn et al interviewed 202 nurses in a qualitative exploration of nurses' acceptability and readiness for patient-centered AI systems in PI prevention. They concluded that current nurse-led risk assessment systems must be improved for specific patient groups, so that safety and care quality are not compromised. Artificial intelligence-based systems can provide more accurate risk predictions and personalized interventions, improving clinical outcomes, but further education is essential for full integration. Society, scientific studies, and patient care have all been altered by AI. The next time you write a paper, AI guidance is available. Wolters Kluwer Health and its publishing imprint Lippincott have produced a document on Ethical Best Practices in Scholarly Publishing, which details several AI-specific policies.4 Of note: Authors need to declare if AI was used in writing the manuscript, production of images, or data collection or analysis. Authors must disclose in the methods how AI was used and what program was used. Authors are fully responsible for the content of their manuscript, even those parts produced by an AI tool, and are thus liable for any breach of publication ethics. abstract: Abstract This study explores the dynamics of customer satisfaction in chatbot interactions, with a focus on how chatbot performance influences users’ trust in technology. Conducted in Bangalore City, Karnataka, the research targets customers of both private and public sector banks. A multi-stage random sampling method was used, beginning with all banks in the city and narrowing to four major institutions: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, State Bank of India, and Bank of Baroda. Data were collected from 350 customers across selected branches of these banks. The study applies advanced statistical techniques, including Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) and moderation analysis, to examine the relationships among key variables. The findings highlight the critical role of chatbot performance in shaping customer satisfaction, with technological trust acting as a mediator and technical literacy serving as a moderator in influencing overall customer experience in digital banking. title_key: from data to decisions harnessing artificial intelligence for smarter faster and more resilient financial systems|belhaoua
title: From Data to Decisions: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Smarter, Faster, and More Resilient Financial Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence has emerged as a transformative technology capable of reshaping modern financial systems by enabling faster data processing, improved financial decision-making, and enhanced operational resilience. This study investigated the role of artificial intelligence in supporting smarter and more efficient financial systems through data-driven analytics and automation. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were collected from 312 professionals working in financial institutions, fintech organizations, and financial service companies. Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and regression analysis to examine the impact of artificial intelligence adoption on financial decision-making, operational efficiency, and financial resilience. The findings indicated that artificial intelligence adoption significantly improved financial decision-making efficiency (β = 0.42), operational efficiency (β = 0.38), and financial system resilience (β = 0.35). Descriptive results further revealed high levels of agreement among respondents regarding the effectiveness of artificial intelligence technologies in financial operations, particularly in AI-based financial analytics (M = 4.07), decision-making efficiency (M = 4.05), and financial resilience (M = 4.02). These results suggested that artificial intelligence technologies enabled financial institutions to analyse complex financial data more efficiently and respond proactively to financial risks and market uncertainties. The study concluded that artificial intelligence represented a critical technological enabler for developing smarter, faster, and more resilient financial systems. The findings provided valuable insights for financial managers, policymakers, and technology developers seeking to enhance the performance and stability of modern financial ecosystems. abstract: Bladder Exstrophy Iliac Osteotomy: 3D Modeling Comparative Analysis of Current Approaches’ Impact on Intrapelvic Volume and Acetabular Version Neal Mukherjee, BA, BS, Scott B Drapeau, MA, Michael Bunker, MS, Jenny Tai, BS, Joshua Cobbett, BASc, Eliana Delgado, MD, MPH, Ishaan Swarup, MD University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA Introduction: Bladder exstrophy is a rare congenital ventral wall defect often surgically corrected with an iliac osteotomy to allow for urologic repair and correct acetabular retroversion due to pubic symphysis diastasis. There are 3 common approaches described for pelvic osteotomy: superior to anterior inferior iliac spine (anterior), superior to the anterior superior iliac spine (oblique), or over the posterior ilium iliac (posterior). However, there is no consensus on which approach maximizes intrapelvic volume for urologic repair and acetabular version for gait abnormality correction while closing the pubic symphysis. This study used 3-dimensional (3D) modeling to investigate changes in intrapelvic volume and acetabular version for each approach. Methods: A bladder exstrophy model was used to create a virtual, 3D model. After virtual osteotomy, volumetric and vector analysis were to determine intrapelvic volume and acetabular version respectively. Results: Intrapelvic volumes measured 462.2 cm3 preoperatively and post-anteversion, measured 373.2 cm3 for the anterior, 395.3 cm3 for the oblique, and 437.9 cm3 for the posterior approaches. Final acetabular version was similar for all 3 approaches but the osteotomy gap measured around 1.7 cm for the anterior osteotomy and 2.3 cm for the oblique and posterior osteotomy (Figure 1). Conclusion: The posterior osteotomy maximized intrapelvic volume while also anteverting the acetabulum to a similar degree as the anterior osteotomy albeit over a larger osteotomy gap. Therefore, the posterior osteotomy may require more osteogenesis than other approaches but could be superior for urologic repair, minimize risk of soft tissue complication, and still correct acetabular retroversion: resulting in superior clinical outcomes.Figure 1ChatGPT-4o Fails to Reliably Assess Evidence Quality but Shows Moderate Agreement in Recommendation Strength for 2024 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Carpal Tunnel Guidelines Eve R Glenn, ScB, Eric Mao, BS, Emily M O’Connell, BS, Indeevar R Beeram, MD, Dawn Laporte, MD Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD Introduction: Large language models like ChatGPT show promise in medical applications, particularly in patient education. However, their ability to accurately interpret clinical guidelines, such as quality of evidence (QoE) and strength of recommendation (SoR), remains uncertain. This study evaluates ChatGPT-4o’s performance in classifying QoE and SoR for the 2024 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) Carpal Tunnel (CT) Syndrome guidelines, addressing a gap in its broader applicability in evidence-based medicine. Methods: AAOS CT guideline statements were neutralized and assessed by 3 raters using ChatGPT-4o for QoE and SoR. Outputs were compared with AAOS reference ratings. Analyses included weighted kappa, bootstrapped CIs, Spearman’s rank correlation, and permutation testing, with agreement levels interpreted using the Landis & Koch scale. Results: ChatGPT-4o demonstrated poor to slight agreement with AAOS guidelines for QoE (Output A: κ = -0.0277; Output B: κ = 0.122; Output C: κ = -0.0101) and no to weak meaningful relationships (ρ = -0.0878 to 0.2474, p > 0.05) (Table 1). For SoR, agreement was slightly higher (eg Output B: κ = 0.1273, ρ = 0.4450, p = 0.0432). Overall reliability was poor for QoE (κ = 0.0538, p = 0.502) but moderate for SoR (κ = 0.4968, p = 0.555). Conclusion: For CT guidelines, ChatGPT-4o struggles with QoE assessment, possibly due to evidence grading complexity. However, it showed moderate consistency in SoR, indicating its potential utility as a supplemental tool for recommendation grading. These findings suggest a need for further refinement, such as structured training on evidence hierarchies and expert judgment integration, to improve the accuracy and reliability of artificial intelligence applications in clinical decision-making. Patients increasingly rely on online resources for information, with artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tools like ChatGPT offering an alternative to traditional search engines such as Google. This study evaluates the correctness and completeness of HV-related information provided by ChatGPT 4.0 compared with Google. Methods: A comparative analysis was conducted using the top 20 frequently asked questions (FAQs) about HV correction sourced from Google and ChatGPT 4.0. Questions were categorized using the Rothwell classification system, and responses were assessed for readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level), correctness, and completeness. Three independent reviewers evaluated the responses, with interobserver reliability measured using Fleiss’s kappa. Statistical analyses were performed using Student’s t-tests. Results: ChatGPT responses were significantly more complete (p < 0.0001) and more correct (p = 0.0068) than Google responses. However, Google responses had a lower Flesch-Kincaid reading grade level (p = 0.02072), indicating greater readability. Fleiss’s kappa analysis demonstrated strong interobserver agreement for response classification (κ = 0.541), completeness (κ = 0.678), and correctness (κ = 0.515), confirming reliable scoring. The findings suggest that while Google is more accessible, ChatGPT delivers more precise and comprehensive medical information. Conclusion: ChatGPT 4.0 outperformed Google in providing accurate and comprehensive HV-related information, suggesting its potential as a valuable tool for patient education. However, concerns regarding AI-generated misinformation necessitate further oversight. Future research should explore the broader role of AI in healthcare education and its impact on patient outcomes.
