Artificial Intelligence for Documentation Data entry, a crucial but time-consuming task for nurses, can be streamlined with AI-powered voice recognition systems and smart electronic records interfaces. Artificial intelligence tools can automatically input patient data, update charts, and even provide reminders for necessary assessments. This reduces the risk of documentation errors, increases the accuracy of patient records, and allows nurses to focus on higher level clinical care. One example of this in practice is the use of NLP to transcribe and analyze clinical notes. An investigative group found that NLP systems could automatically transcribe physician and nurse notes in a manner that was as accurate as manual entry, saving substantial time and reducing errors in data entry[11]. As a result, AI-supported documentation including voice-to-text tools allows nurses to spend less time on administrative tasks and more time engaging with patients. Artificial Intelligence for Patient Monitoring Artificial intelligence has also been integrated into patient monitoring systems. Artificial intelligence algorithms can analyze continuous data streams from wearable devices or bedside monitors to detect trends and deviations from normal ranges, such as abnormal heart rhythms or vital signs, in real-time. In cases where nurses may not personally observe these changes, the AI system can alert the nurse immediately, helping to promote early intervention and avoid complications. This type of real-time decision support has been particularly beneficial in intensive care units (ICUs) where patients are at increased risk for acute changes in clinical condition. Artificial intelligence tools used for monitoring ventilated patients in the ICU significantly reduced the number of missed alarms and false positives, leading to improved nurse response times and better patient outcomes[12]. This demonstrates the potential of AI to enhance safety by providing support in clinical decision-making. Artificial Intelligence for Risk Stratification Artificial intelligence-powered risk stratification transforms cardiovascular nursing by enabling proactive identification of high-risk patients through predictive analytics. Unlike traditional monitoring that responds to isolated readings, AI analyzes patterns across multiple data streams—vital signs, laboratory results, medication adherence, and patient history—to predict clinical deterioration before symptoms manifest. A practical example of AI in managing complex cases is the use of predictive algorithms in heart failure management. AI systems can analyze patterns in vital signs and lab results to predict potential decompensations, prompting early interventions such as adjustments in medication or patient education[13]. Another example is AI-powered predictive analytics to identify patients at elevated risk for sepsis while caring for hospitalized patients with CVD. A recent study demonstrated that AI algorithms could predict sepsis up to 12 hours before clinical signs become apparent, enabling early intervention, and improving patient survival rates[14]. For population health management, AI addresses the challenge of monitoring large patient cohorts with limited nursing resources. With ongoing staffing shortages and a growing chronic disease burden, healthcare is shifting toward value-based, population-level care models. In this context, AI can help a small team of clinicians efficiently manage large cohorts by flagging unmet best-practice measures, identifying patients at risk, and reducing the need for full chart reviews of stable patients. For example, a cardiovascular nurse could use AI-driven dashboards to monitor trends in heart failure patients across a region or health system, flag those showing signs of decompensation, and initiate early interventions, thereby reducing hospitalizations and improving outcomes at scale. Transition of care programming is an excellent area to pilot these initiatives/tools. Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Decision Support Artificial intelligence technologies enable nurses to efficiently access and analyze large volumes of patient data to support clinical decision-making. For example, AI algorithms that integrate patient history, lab values, and imaging can assist nurses in recognizing patterns and guiding timely interventions, particularly in managing chronic conditions such as diabetes or heart failure. By leveraging these technologies, nurses can make more informed, collaborative decisions within complex care teams[15,16]. Furthermore, AI in clinical decision support systems integrates with EHR, helping nurses to access relevant evidence-based guidelines through decision prompts and apply them to patient-specific data in real-time. Artificial intelligence can also be used to assess the likelihood of adverse events, enabling nurses to prevent errors and take timely corrective actions for complex clinical management. For instance, the use of AI in assessing medication interactions and identifying potential drug errors has shown to reduce medication-related adverse events[17]. In addition, AI tools can also support nurses in case management. For example, AI-powered case management systems can track patient progress and predict potential barriers to recovery, such as social determinants of health or missed follow-up appointments. This predictive capability enables nurses to proactively address challenges in a patient’s care plan, improving overall outcomes and reducing hospital readmission rates. Artificial Intelligence for Cardiovascular Patient Education Artificial intelligence is transforming cardiovascular patient education. For cardiovascular nurses, AI tools offer a powerful way to deliver personalized health information and support behavior change. These systems analyze a patient’s data, learning preferences, and health literacy to create tailored educational content. Artificial intelligence-driven chatbots and virtual health assistants are especially promising. They provide 24/7 access to reliable health information, medication reminders, and coaching. For instance, a chatbot can guide a heart failure patient through daily symptom monitoring and provide personalized dietary advice[18]. These platforms can also adapt to a patient’s learning style, offering infographics for visual learners or detailed text for others[19]. They track comprehension through quizzes and adjust content complexity as needed. Predictive analytics within these platforms can identify patients at risk of not following treatment plans. This allows for targeted interventions, such as extra medication counseling for those showing declining adherence[20]. Artificial intelligence-enabled patient portals further empower patients by summarizing complex clinical data—such as lab results and vital signs—into easily understandable trends. Crucially, AI’s language processing capabilities may help to overcome communication barriers. By providing real-time translation and culturally appropriate content, these tools may enhance equitable access to high-quality health education for diverse patient populations, thereby closing health disparity gaps. Challenges and Barriers to Artificial Intelligence Implementation in Cardiovascular Nursing Integrating AI into cardiovascular nursing holds significant promise to not only enhancing clinical care and improving patient outcomes but to streamlining workflows and optimizing administrative tasks[21]. However, as AI gains momentum, there are challenges and barriers that must be addressed to ensure adequate delivery of AI tools and the adoption of these technologies in clinical and nursing practice. The challenges include such issues as data quality and standardization, integration within existing healthcare settings, ethical and legal concerns, regulatory issues, and of upmost importance user acceptability and training[5]. As noted previously, AI plays a critical role in cardiovascular nursing, including supporting informed clinical decision-making, interpreting data, and detecting early warning signs in patients. It also enhances workflows by streamlining nurse-patient interactions, generating clinical notes, and populating electronic health records[5]. The main challenges and barriers of AI are highlighted in the next section to ensure that most issues are addressed in ensuring the safety and adequacy of these systems. Data Quality and Standardization Artificial intelligence needs diverse, large data sets to function properly. Often, due to inadequate documentation and varying terminologies, data formats across health care systems can hinder the process of developing accurate predictive models. All AI applications must be designed to address biases and potential disparities, and regular audits and ongoing monitoring must occur to mitigate biases and disparities[22]. Integration Within the Existing Healthcare Setting Another barrier to implementation is the need to integrate AI into existing healthcare workflows, which often requires substantial redesign of clinical processes. This transformation demands time, resources, and a strong commitment to change across the organization. Ensuring interoperability between AI systems and the EHR, which may require infrastructure upgrades, is another challenge that must be overcome in clinical practice settings[23]. Ethical and Legal Concerns Ensuring the privacy of patients, nurses, and others in developing AI systems is of upmost importance[24]. To ensure privacy, encryption systems are built into AI systems, patient consent must be obtained, and guidelines for the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act must be followed[25]. Regular audits must be performed to ensure privacy is achieved, and health care professionals must understand how algorithms reach conclusions and make decisions. Finally, these systems must be developed to address biases and ensure disparities are addressed[22,26]. An AI Bill of Rights handbook has been developed by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, which may help nurses familiarize themselves with privacy needs and concerns[27]. Regulatory Issues Artificial intelligence systems lack prospective research and clinical trials to validate their safety and effectiveness. It is essential that AI systems use standardized platforms to report predictions and scaling findings. One of the main challenges in nursing is the quality and standardization of data. The current healthcare system often suffers from inconsistent, incomplete, and nonstandardized documentation across systems and institutions. Developing regulatory frameworks, standards, and pathways for AI technologies is crucial to ensure safety and effectiveness in clinical practice[28]. Nursing User Acceptability and Training Accepting AI as a solution to many issues in nursing and medicine comes with some lack of acceptability of this new technology[29]. This is often due to unfamiliarity of AI and the threats that many clinicians feel in observing their traditional roles. Thus, comprehensive training and education of all healthcare professionals is essential to help mitigate concerns within nursing and to promote acceptance. To help cardiovascular nurses accept AI, training must be thorough. Cardiovascular nurses can engage in ongoing education about AI through workshops, webinars, and courses focused on AI in healthcare. Fundamental to training is having nurses develop an understanding of AI concepts, which includes ML, NLP, and data analysis[5]. Nurses need to interpret and analyze large datasets to aid decision-making, like researchers. Managing EHRs and AI interfaces is crucial for accurate data input and effective use of AI in clinical settings. Nurses also need to be aware of privacy issues, algorithm biases, and the need to maintain human oversight in AI-assisted care. Finally, there are numerous stakeholders involved in AI development and implementation, which require nurses to communicate with interdisciplinary colleagues including computer scientists, ethicists, physicians, and other health care professionals[5,30]. Communicating with patients is also vital to ensure successful implementation and organization of AI tools in nursing practice[5,30]. While AI has both challenges and barriers to implementation, the early adoption of AI in clinical practice is here to stay. As cardiovascular nurses gain expertise in the use of AI, we will see gains in clinical practice expertise, employee efficiency, and better patient outcomes with the potential to revolutionize nursing practice and enhance patient care. Call to Action in Cardiovascular Nursing The rapid advancement of AI presents a pivotal moment for cardiovascular nursing, demanding proactive engagement to ensure these technologies enhance, rather than nursing practice and care. Cardiovascular nurses must spearhead the integration of AI, leveraging their indispensable clinical expertise and patient advocacy to guide the development, implementation, and ethical oversight of AI systems. title_key: emerging innovations and trends in academic libraries of pakistan in the 21st century|lakho
title: Emerging Innovations and Trends in Academic Libraries of Pakistan in the 21st Century
abstract: This research paper explores the new technology, emerging trends and challenges that academic libraries in Pakistan tend to encounter in the 21st century. It seeks to evaluate the ways in which the digital transformation is transforming library operations, user services as well as professional functions and also determine where it is heading to in terms of sustainable development. A quantitative descriptive study design was adopted with a structured questionnaire to be given to 200 library professionals in the public and the private universities in Pakistan. The data were interpreted through descriptive statistics (frequency and percent) to generalize the perceptions of the respondents on technological adoption, service innovations and institutional challenges. The findings show that there has been a drastic change towards digitalization as majority of libraries have embraced automation in cataloguing, OPAC and cloud based services. Digital literacy training, provision of virtual reference services and utilization of social media in engaging libraries are also emerging practices that have been adopted by libraries. Nevertheless, certain obstacles like lack of sufficient funding, ineffective ICT, ineffective infrastructure, and institutional support remain in the way. There was a great deal of optimism about the future, which included professional development, collaboration, and national policy support as respondents thought that innovation can continue to flourish. The results indicate that there is a requirement to invest in ICT infrastructure strategically, continuous professional training, and development of policy frameworks to facilitate equitable technological development within academic institutions. Innovation and quality of service can be even improved through strengthening institutional support and collaboration. The given research offers the detailed data-driven information on the technological revolution in the field of the Pakistani academic libraries, which is acute considering the lack of information about the situation on the ground in Pakistan and in the context of the digital era, in general. title_key: the editor in chief is gone long live the editor in chief|scerbo
title: The Editor-in Chief is Gone: Long Live the Editor-in-Chief
abstract: My time as editor-in-chief (EIC) of Simulation in Healthcare has come to an end. I succeeded David Gaba, the Founding EIC, in July 2016. After serving for 8 years, I felt it was time for new leadership and for me to pursue other opportunities. Last summer, a call went out for interested applicants and by January of this year, the SSH Board had selected Nicole Harder, RN, PhD, CHSE, CCSNE, as the third EIC for the journal. Dr. Harder officially began her term on February 15, 2025, but she and I have been sharing the responsibilities. I will serve as EIC for all manuscripts submitted before February 15, and she is responsible for all manuscripts that have come in after that date as well as the day-to-day management of the journal. In addition to selecting a new EIC, the SSH Board approved some changes to the leadership structure of the Editorial Board. There will be an additional Associate EIC along with a new position, EIC Emeritus (EICE). The new EICE position gives the prior EIC the option to stay on and assist the new EIC during the transition period and handle some of the workload tied to new initiatives. So, although I am leaving the journal in the capable hands of Dr. Harder, I look forward to working with her and the rest of the editorial team in my new role as EICE. Looking back, I was a bit uncertain how the journal would build upon the foundation and record of success set by David Gaba. However, opportunities and challenges presented themselves quickly. I was struck by how much changed during my time at the helm in the simulation world, in publishing, and in the world itself. First, submissions to the journal steadily increased from 290 in 2016 to a record 436 in 2020. They have remained high with 381 submissions last year—underscoring the continued strong interest among authors to publish in the journal. Consequently, the size of the editorial team needed to change as well to handle the increased volume in submissions. In 2016, we had 9 associate editors and 15 editorial board members, but that increased to the 12 associate editors and 38 editorial board members we have now. As the journal matured, we took several steps to ensure the publication of high-quality, accurate, and ethical research. First, we formally adopted the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors' Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals and are now listed on their Web site as one of many journals that follow their recommendations. Second, in 2016, Simulation in Healthcare and other simulation journals published modifications to 2 research reporting guidelines: the Consolidating Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines that address randomized control trials and the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines intended for observational studies. These guidelines provide a standardized framework for the essential elements that should be included in reports of specific research designs. The modifications prepared by Cheng and colleagues1 are aimed specifically at simulation-based research in healthcare and became a formal requirement for submissions in 2021. Since then, we have added requirements for literature reviews, Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), and qualitative studies, Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR). Most recently, you undoubtedly noticed that articles in this issue of the journal look different. The article title page has been reformatted to remove previously unused space along the left margin. In addition, the editorial staff page has been reformatted and reduced to fit on a single page. These changes were implemented to free up page space for article content. THE 2021 JOURNAL IMPACT FACTOR During my time as EIC, the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) for Simulation in Healthcare reached 2.69, the highest in the journal's history. The most recent JIF has receded to 1.7. In fact, many journals saw a decline in their JIF in 2023 attributable in part to a decline in research output in 2022 compared to previous years. In addition, the Journal Citation Report began awarding JIFs to journals in the Emerging Sources Citation Index. As a result, the number of journals in the Healthcare Sciences & Services category alone (where our journal is included) increased from 106 journals in 2022 to 175 in 2023. Our current 5-year JIF remains a respectable 2.5 and our rank within the Healthcare Sciences & Services category increased from the 38th percentile the previous year to the 50th percentile this past year. These are impressive numbers given the diversity of clinical, educational, and engineering communities the journal serves. DIGITAL REACH The JIF is an index based on citations, but that does not capture interest in a journal's content among those who do not cite it. Thus, digital reach is becoming another important index of a journal's impact. Readership of the journal extends far beyond the membership and online-only subscriptions (approximately 5000 annually). Access to the journal via the Web site or through Ovid databases has become the more common way for readers to reach us. In recent years, we've typically had more than 200,000 annual Web site page views, and institutional usage via Ovid reached 100,000 article views in 2024. Moreover, nearly 60% of individual and online access comes from outside the United States. In an effort to build and maintain a greater digital presence, many medical journals have added social media editors. In 2023, Jennifer Arnold, MD, MSc, FAAP, was added as our social media editor to engage readers, enhance article visibility, and promote authors' work to a broader audience. She now helps promote journal content via LinkedIn and Instagram. SPECIAL ISSUES/ARTICLES The Society for Simulation in Healthcare (SSH) has held 3 Research Summits since its inception to capture the state of the science as healthcare simulation evolves. Content from each Summit has been published in special issues of the journal in 2011, 2017, and 2024, respectively. The most recent Research Summit was convened to conduct a review of the simulation-based training and methodology literature and generate a set of evidence-based guidelines for simulation training in healthcare This was a significant milestone for the journal, publishing the first set of formal guidelines in a special issue complemented by 11 literature reviews offering more detailed analyses of the literature that were the foundation for the guideline effort.2 Interest in this special issue has been intense. In fact, the article, Debriefing Methods for Simulation in Healthcare: A Systematic Review, by Duff and his colleagues3 received 2445 full-article views on our Web site in 2024, the second highest of any article published in the last 10 years. This year, we published a first-of-its-kind special issue: Simulation-based Mastery Learning Curriculum Development Workbook (and Appendix).4 This is a hands-on guide for educators interested in developing their own mastery learning curricula, made freely available to anyone as an open access special issue of the journal. We also published 3 important high-visibility articles with other journals: Raemer et al. Simulation safety first: an imperative5 was published along with Advances in Simulation, and Journal of Surgical Simulation. Diaz-Navarro et al., Global consensus statement on simulation-based practice in healthcare,6 was published with Clinical Simulation in Nursing, Advances in Simulation, and International Journal of Healthcare Simulation. Lu, Pian-Smith, et al., Call to action: quality and simulation professionals should collaborate,7 a joint publication with Joint Commission Journal on Quality and Patient Safety. Last, we introduced a new article type in 2020, Reflections on Simulation,8 to offer authors a forum for sharing their personal stories or perspectives on healthcare simulation. Elaine Meyer has served as the editor of this narrative feature since its inception and has helped bring more than a dozen unique and poignant stories to our readers. COVID-19 CONTENT Without question, the most significant impact on the journal during my tenure was the COVID-19 pandemic. Essential emergency medicine personnel worked long hours under the most trying conditions while almost everyone else sheltered in place. Three years before the pandemic took hold, the journal had published a collection of articles on the potential benefits of simulation for dealing with highly communicable disease in response to the 2014 West African Ebola outbreak.9 The pandemic reignited the need for that kind of material. We received our first manuscript related to COVID-19 in March 2020 and decided to open up the pages of the journal to publish simulation-based research and solutions aimed at patient and provider safety, alternative uses of simulation equipment, and virtual solutions for training and assessment. In July 2020, we introduced the COVID-19 Brief Reports, established to expedite the publication of pandemic-related content, and made freely available to the public for 2 months after publication. The pandemic created unprecedented demand for simulation centers and staff to help train healthcare providers to treat COVID-19 patients while maintaining their own safety. I often look back on this time as the point at which simulation became a necessary component of healthcare training and education. GENERATIVE AI Perhaps the biggest challenge or opportunity facing this journal and scholarly publication in general is the proliferation of generative AI (eg, ChatGPT, Bard, etc.). It is a disruptive technology that is already having profound effects on how people prepare and disseminate written, visual, and auditory information. It is being used to emulate the writing style of authors, the vocal style of singers, and the likeness of celebrities in videos. It is also being used in a variety of ways in simulation. This journal entertains manuscripts describing research and applications of AI in healthcare simulation and we regularly receive submissions on topics such as scripting simulation scenarios, generating simulated patient responses, or analyzing student notes or learner responses. In 2023, I published an editorial describing many of the merits and concerns surrounding the use of generative AI in scholarly publications.10 It can quickly generate well-articulated, grammatically correct written text, but the accuracy of what it generates is still suspect. At present, this journal does not permit the assignment of authorship to AI. Authors of a manuscript are fully responsible for its content, even portions produced by AI; thus, as a nonlegal entity, AI cannot be an author because it cannot take responsibility for its output.

title_key: journal related activities and other special activities at the 2024 american society of anesthesiologists meeting|avram
title: Journal-related Activities and Other Special Activities at the 2024 American Society of Anesthesiologists Meeting
abstract: As in previous years, Anesthesiology will sponsor several sessions at the annual meeting of the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA), ANESTHESIOLOGY® 2024. The meeting is being held in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Details about the format and meeting attendance can be found on the website, asahq.org/annualmeeting. Secrets of Successful Manuscript Preparation, from the Editors of Anesthesiology Saturday, October 19, 2024, 9:45 to 10:45am Room 119AB The editors of Anesthesiology have organized this session to inform authors how to write and prepare a manuscript by providing a clear understanding of what is expected of both research that is considered the best and the manuscript describing it. The goal is to help authors create the best clinical and basic science research for publication. title_key: response to automation driven labour displacement adaptive universal transaction tax and request based universal basic income|kriger
title: Response to Automation-Driven Labour Displacement: Adaptive Universal Transaction Tax and Request-Based Universal Basic Income
abstract: Boris Kriger¹² ¹ Information Physics Institute, Gosport, Hampshire, United Kingdom ² Institute of Integrative and Interdisciplinary Research, Toronto, Canada Overview This paper presents a formal mathematical model of an Adaptive Universal Transaction Tax (AUTT) — a single, low-rate levy applied automatically to all electronic financial transactions, with a rate that adjusts in real time via feedback control to meet a democratically approved budget target — coupled with a request-based Universal Basic Income (UBI) that replaces fragmented social welfare programmes and provides the income floor necessitated by automation-driven labour displacement. The AUTT is defined as a dynamical system with three core variables: the aggregate transaction volume V(t), the target budget B, and the adaptive tax rate τ(t). The paper establishes formal conditions under which the system converges to its fiscal target, proves stability under economic shocks, and derives the critical rate threshold below which behavioural distortion remains negligible. The Central Proposition All existing taxes — income tax, corporate tax, capital gains tax, payroll tax, sales tax, and VAT — are replaced by a single, invisible, automatically collected transaction levy of approximately 0.3–1.5%, applied at the point of electronic settlement by licensed financial intermediaries. No individual or corporation files any tax return, faces any audit, or bears any direct fiscal obligation. The fiscal relationship between citizen and state is severed entirely: the obligation falls exclusively on a small number (~10²–10³) of already-regulated financial institutions, enforced through the existing financial licensing regime. The resulting fiscal capacity funds: universal basic income, universal insurance (life, property, liability, disability, legal aid), universal healthcare (including dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and pharmacare), and universal AI-enabled education (tuition-free, debt-free, lifelong, at any level). Key Formal Results (89 pages, 23 formal definitions/propositions/theorems) Convergence Theorem. The AUTT rate converges to the budget target under stated conditions on transaction volume and the EWMA smoothing parameter. EWMA Error Bound (Proposition 5.1). The relative estimation error of the transaction volume estimator is bounded by |(v̂ − v)/v| ≤ (1−λ)γ/λ, providing an explicit smoothing-responsiveness tradeoff. Recovery Condition (Proposition 5.2). After a volume shock of magnitude δ, the system recovers to within ε of the budget target if τ_max · V_post > B, with explicit time bounds. Cascade Multiplier Theorem. The effective tax burden through a supply chain of length n at nominal rate τ is τ_eff = τ · (1 − (1−τ)^n)/τ ≈ nτ for small τ. At operational rates (τ = 0.3–1.0%), effective cascade burdens of 0.9–2.5% are below all major VAT rates globally. Critical Rate Threshold. Behavioural distortion becomes significant only when τ exceeds the threshold τ* = 1/(ε · m), where ε is the aggregate elasticity and m is the cascade multiplier — yielding τ* ≈ 3–5% for real-economy transactions, far above operational rates. Spiral Stability (Proposition 17.1). The endogenous volume-rate feedback spiral (rising τ deters transactions, reducing V, forcing τ higher) is self-limiting if and only if ε · τ* < 1. At operational parameters (τ* = 0.5%, ε = 5), ε·τ* = 0.025 ≪ 1. UBI Sustainability Theorem. The request-based UBI is fiscally sustainable when the AUTT revenue exceeds the budget inclusive of UBI costs, with the request-based mechanism reducing actual disbursement to 35–65% of the theoretical maximum (calibrated against the Canadian CERB precedent: 8.9 million recipients of 20+ million eligible). Multi-Country Calibration (6 economies) The paper provides detailed calibrations for the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Canada, and Japan, computing for each: GDP, government budget, estimated taxable transaction volume V_T (after financial-sector exemptions at φ ≈ 0.75–0.85), the required AUTT rate τ, and the effective cascade burden at representative supply chain lengths. Required rates range from 0.72% (Japan) to 2.91% (France). Even in the worst case (France), the effective cascade burden at m = 3 (8.7%) is below the French VAT rate (20%), while being collected with near-zero compliance cost and structurally zero fraud. Intermediary Obligation Principle A foundational contribution: the paper formally defines and legislatively codifies the principle that the fiscal obligation falls exclusively on licensed financial intermediaries — not on individuals, not on corporations. The enforcement mechanism is licence revocation, not taxpayer prosecution. This inverts the fundamental architecture of taxation: instead of monitoring 10⁷–10⁸ taxpayers with imperfect information, the system monitors 10²–10³ already-regulated financial institutions whose core business depends on maintaining their licence. Structural Critique of VAT The paper provides a data-driven critique of value-added tax as an architecturally flawed system that entrusts revenue collection to private businesses — entities whose incentive is to minimise tax payments, not maximise state revenue. EU member states lost €128 billion in VAT revenues in 2023 (9.5% of total VAT liability). Missing trader fraud (MTIC/carousel fraud) alone costs €13–60 billion annually. The AUTT eliminates this structural vulnerability: automated intermediary diversion replaces voluntary business remittance, reducing the compliance gap from ~10% to approximately zero. Distributional Incidence A formal 10-decile distributional model demonstrates that the combined AUTT-UBI system is strongly progressive: the lowest income decile receives a net transfer of +159% of income; the highest decile's net contribution is less than 0.4% of income. The UBI's strong progressivity overwhelms the AUTT's mild regressivity as a flat-rate transaction levy. Dormancy Levy and Cryptocurrency Impact The paper introduces a complementary dormancy levy on idle capital (0.01%/month beyond a 12-month threshold), with mandatory exemptions for pension accounts, education savings, disability savings, and sovereign reserves. The combined AUTT-dormancy system structurally disadvantages cryptocurrency as a store of value: fiat currency in regulated accounts carries zero holding cost for active participants, while crypto carries volatility, exchange hacks, and lost keys — with zero compensating fiscal advantage. Universal Safety Net The paper establishes and legislatively codifies a foundational principle: no person legally residing in the jurisdiction shall be left in a situation of material distress, for any reason, under any circumstances. This is operationalised through five pillars: UBI (income floor), universal insurance (catastrophic protection), universal healthcare (including dental, vision, hearing, mental health), universal education (lifelong, tuition-free, AI-enabled), and emergency supplementary authority. The safety net is universal, automatic, unconditional, and available to all legal residents regardless of citizenship, immigration status, or national origin — with a 6-month residency threshold. The paper demonstrates that inclusive eligibility for migrants is fiscally superior to exclusion: remittance transfers generate AUTT revenue that exceeds the cost of UBI provision, while exclusion drives workers into cash channels, losing the entire transaction stream. Fiscal Savings The paper quantifies $425–565 billion in annual US government savings from eliminated programmes: tax enforcement apparatus ($195–205B including 6.1 billion hours of private compliance), workforce development and retraining programmes ($49–69B), welfare administration and means-testing ($53–85B), poverty-related incarceration and policing ($82–105B), and downstream social costs ($35–70B). These savings offset 85–100% of the net additional cost of the AUTT-UBI transition. Middle-Class Capital Liberation and Economic Stimulus A median US household earning $80,000 currently pays approximately $24,100 in combined federal, state, and local taxes (effective rate ~26%). Under the AUTT, total tax burden drops to approximately $5,500 (municipal property tax + invisible cascade), liberating approximately $18,600 per year in disposable income — a 33% increase. If one adult claims UBI, total household resources rise from $55,900 to $98,500 (+76%). Across 67 million middle-class US households, aggregate capital liberation is approximately $1.17 trillion per year. title_key: review of artificial life the quest for a new creation by steven levy|waldegrave
title: Review of Artificial Life: The Quest for a New Creation by Steven Levy
abstract: In the 30 plus years since the publication of Steven Levy’s Artificial Life, the field has developed extensively in many different directions. However, it is still very much worth reading the book that first brought this subject to the attention of a wider public. Not only did it increase understanding and awareness of ALife research but it was also arguably instrumental in defining the field in the first place, unifying a wide range of disparate research efforts under this heading. Its comprehensive account of the development of the field is an invaluable guide to students just starting out on ALife research and a useful summary for experienced researchers. Indeed, the multitude of familiar names that populate the pages sometimes makes it feel like a university reading list for a course in the subject, but with the additional benefit of providing engaging explanations of the research and discussions of its significance. The broadly historical approach that the author takes allows us to see the gradual emergence of the field through both the individuals and the institutions involved. Levy personalizes the story with memorable portraits of some of the characters—one is left with the impression that ALife research tends to attract mavericks!Early chapters on cellular automata (CAs) take us from von Neumann’s original idea of creating a self-replicating automaton, via Stanisław Ulam’s game-changing idea of representing this machine on a grid of cells, to John Conway’s Game of Life, Stephen Wolfram’s comprehensive cataloging of elementary CAs, and, finally, Langton’s tunable CAs and his realization of the importance of the “edge of chaos” region in dynamical systems. Although readers of this journal will of course be familiar with this history, it is enlivened with anecdotes of the process of discovery. Conway and his colleagues are described manually applying the rules of Life to black and white counters and shells laid out on (and spreading over the sides of) a common-room coffee table. The final fate of a famous “Methuselah” starting state, the R-Pentomino, is worked out over months of coffee breaks. Many less well-known early systems for self-replication are also outlined, including Roger Penrose’s set of wooden blocks that, when shaken together, can link up to create crystal-like configurations (it is well worth watching the YouTube video of this system in action).Lest the reader is ever in danger of thinking some of the research described is “merely” an amusing game, Levy frequently reminds us, through the impassioned voices of his subjects, of what is at stake: nothing less than the creation of new forms of life that would be, in Conway’s words, capable of “evolving, reproducing, squabbling over territory. Getting cleverer and cleverer. Writing learned Ph.D. theses” (p. 58).In contrast to von Neumann’s intricately designed universal constructor in a 29-state CA, Levy then introduces us to one of the major themes of ALife research, namely, self-organization and the spontaneous emergence of order. The significance of Stuart Kauffman’s work on random Boolean networks is thoroughly explained, as is the motivation behind the work: As Kauffman says, “I’ve always wanted the order one finds in the world not to be particular, peculiar, odd or contrived—I want to be, in the mathematician’s sense, generic. Typical. Natural. Fundamental. Inevitable. Godlike” (p. 128).Throughout the narrative, Levy works in a discussion of the aims of ALife, which fall into two broad categories: the “biological alchemy” of creating systems that are in some sense actually living and the simulation of life’s processes to help us understand life as it is, or as it could be (for instance, on other planets). Both aims shade into origins-of-life research: how does nonliving matter (or information) become organized into a system that can be said to be alive? In addition to these high-level aims, Levy highlights the practical contributions made by ALife research. The chapter on genetic algorithms (GAs) is full of examples of evolution-inspired approaches to solving real-world problems, as with David Goldberg’s early use of a GA to allocate gas pipeline flow. In an era when large-language models have arguably passed (or perhaps rendered obsolete) the Turing test, some people have argued that artificial intelligence (AI) making new scientific discoveries will be the mark of true intelligence. So it is good to be reminded that one of the first major achievements of Koza’s genetic programming approach more than 30 years ago was to rediscover the equations for Kepler’s third law of planetary motion from empirical data.There follow chapters on the importance of coevolution and open-endedness and the efforts to place artificial organisms in environments or ecosystems that could allow them to develop behaviors like the Red Queen phenomenon of runaway complexification in some direction and the Baldwin effect of evolving better learning abilities.A chapter on physical instantiations of Artificial Life research in the form of robots, and particularly swarm robots, is interesting not only for a discussion of a wide variety of systems but also in bringing to the fore one of the central tensions of ALife research. In the words of Patty Maes, an MIT roboticist, “do we want to be engineers and come up with systems that are useful, or do we want to study behaviours as a biological thing?” (p. 291). On one level, this can become a philosophical question, but on another level, it is highly relevant to the more prosaic necessity of securing funding.The field of ALife has developed in parallel to its sometimes more glamorous cousin AI but has probably benefited from being largely shielded from the cycles of hype and despair that have accompanied AI. Levy quotes Doyne Farmer as saying, “Right now it’s kind of nice that artificial life is underground, because it means we can keep a low profile and just do what we want” (p. 339). However, he goes on to express concern about the potential for exponential growth in the abilities of ALife systems, in a discussion very similar to current debates about the risks of AI. Nevertheless, ethical considerations about ALife must be framed rather differently from those about AI: The worry is not that an intelligent system designed to do one thing will do something we don’t want it to do—a truly living artificial system would not have human-imposed goals in the first place; its only aim would be the most basic aim of life—to stay alive and produce more of itself.The only frustration of the book is that so much progress has been made since its publication that the story inevitably feels incomplete. The chapters on CAs obviously don’t include exciting recent developments: from continuous CAs, such as Bert Chan’s Lenia, to neural CAs being trained to generate predefined patterns (work by Mordvintsev and others). There is no discussion of artificial chemistry, a subfield of ALife that perhaps brings the field full circle to von Neumann’s original (pre-CA) idea of self-replicating structures in a huge reservoir filled with the necessary raw materials. If the book were written today, it would probably also include large sections on “wet ALife” and the cross-fertilization of the field with biotechnology. Nevertheless, it remains an excellent introduction to the field, seamlessly combining discussion of the high-level concepts and their philosophical implications with detailed descriptions of specific pieces of research and the people behind them.

title_key: entrepreneurship in the era of artificial intelligence redefining opportunity recognition labour substitution and innovation processes|latif
title: Entrepreneurship in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Redefining Opportunity Recognition, Labour Substitution, and Innovation Processes
abstract: This study examined the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in entrepreneurship, focusing on opportunity recognition, labour substitution, and innovation processes. Rapid advancements in AI technologies altered traditional entrepreneurial practices by enabling data-driven decision-making, predictive analytics, and automation of routine tasks. Using a quantitative research design, data were collected from 350 entrepreneurs and managers of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) who had adopted AI in their business operations. Descriptive statistics, reliability tests, regression analysis, and structural equation modelling (SEM) were employed to analyse the relationships between AI adoption and entrepreneurial outcomes. The results revealed that AI adoption significantly enhanced opportunity recognition by enabling entrepreneurs to identify emerging market trends, assess risks, and make informed strategic decisions. AI also facilitated labour substitution by automating repetitive tasks, allowing human resources to focus on creative and analytical roles. Moreover, AI-driven innovation processes accelerated product development, improved operational efficiency, and supported experimentation, thereby strengthening entrepreneurial performance. Despite these positive outcomes, challenges such as workforce displacement, ethical concerns, and limited access to AI technologies were identified as barriers to full adoption. The study concluded that AI functions as a strategic enabler that reshapes entrepreneurial practices, labour dynamics, and innovation strategies. The findings provide valuable insights for entrepreneurs, policymakers, and academic institutions to implement adaptive strategies for sustainable and inclusive entrepreneurial growth in the era of artificial intelligence. title: CASE: THE EVOLUTION OF ISLAMIC STATE KHORASAN PROVINCE (ISK)
abstract: Author: Lynn Frederick DsouzaEmail: lynn.dsouza@espiridi.comAffiliation: ESPIRIDI LLPCase Reference: 20251209002 (Updated 2025)Industry: Counter-terrorism and Security StudiesRegion: South Asia, Central Asia, Middle East, EuropeKey Issues: Terrorist organization adaptation, digital radicalization, transnational security threats, AI-enabled propagandaYear of Research: 2024–2025Last Updated: December 2025Keywords: Terrorist adaptation, digital radicalization, AI-enabled propaganda, transnational networks, Central Asia, security innovation EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The Evolution of Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISK): A Case Study in Modern Transnational Terrorism Prepared For: Advanced Security Studies, Policy Analysis, Strategic Leadership OVERVIEW The Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISK), the Afghanistan-Pakistan affiliate of Islamic State (IS), presents a compelling case study in modern terrorist organizational adaptation. Originally formed in January 2015 with territorial ambitions in Afghanistan, ISK faced an existential crisis with the Taliban's takeover in August 2021. Rather than collapse, the organization underwent a dramatic strategic transformation, pivoting from territorial insurgency to a globally-focused, digitally-enabled transnational network responsible for mass-casualty attacks in Iran, Russia, and beyond its original Afghan theatre. As of 2024–2025, Islamic State and its affiliates, with ISK as a key contributor, were responsible for approximately 1,805 deaths across 22 countries in 2024. More significantly, ISK has expanded its operational footprint from a single-country focus (2020) to operations across multiple continents with propaganda output in nine languages. The organization demonstrates sophisticated integration of artificial intelligence into its media apparatus, use of encrypted communications for remote attack coordination, and the development of a largely Tajik-national external operations contingent now active across Europe, Russia, and Central Asia. KEY LEARNING OUTCOMES Students completing this case study will be able to: 1. Analyze how terrorist organizations adapt to conventional military defeat and leverage technological innovation to enhance operational resilience 2. Evaluate the role of digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence in enabling transnational terrorist operations 3. Assess implications of franchise-based terrorist networks for international security and the adequacy of current counterterrorism approaches 4. Synthesize insights into broader trends in modern terrorism and the emergence of technology-enabled, distributed networks 5. Examine how regional vulnerabilities (Central Asian instability, diaspora disaffection) feed transnational recruitment networks CORE ARGUMENTS AND INSIGHTS 1. Adaptability as Organizational StrengthISK transformed a strategic defeat, loss of territorial control, into an asymmetric advantage by building a decentralized, digitally-coordinated network. The group became more elusive and operationally dangerous precisely because it abandoned the geographic and hierarchical infrastructure that made it vulnerable to conventional military force. 2. The Digital Battlefield is Primary Operational DomainFor ISK, the internet is not merely a propaganda tool but a virtual battlespace where recruitment, coordination, and attack planning occur. AI-generated content enables rapid, audience-targeted messaging; encrypted platforms provide secure command and control; cryptocurrency facilitates anonymous funding. Traditional security frameworks focused on physical geography increasingly miss this critical domain. 3. Transnational Terrorism Remains Regionally AnchoredWhile ISK operates globally, its operational success depends on exploitation of regional vulnerabilities: ungoverned spaces in Afghanistan, state weakness in Central Asia, diaspora communities in Europe, political-sectarian tensions in Iran. Counterterrorism strategies addressing only the digital dimension while ignoring regional root causes will prove insufficient. 4. Emerging Technologies Create Novel Terrorist CapabilitiesISK's 2024–2025 integration of AI-generated news bulletins with synthetic presenters, guides on secure use of generative AI, and targeted digital radicalization represents a qualitative shift in terrorist media capabilities. This evolution poses unprecedented challenges for content moderation, counter-narrative strategy, and intelligence collection. CASE SIGNIFICANCE FOR POLICY AND SECURITY For Security Policymakers: Demonstrates limitations of traditional counterterrorism focused on leadership targeting and territorial disruption; illustrates necessity of transnational intelligence coordination; highlights emerging role of technology companies. For Academic Researchers: Provides rigorous examination of organizational adaptation theory applied to modern terrorism; offers framework for understanding technology-enabled transnational networks; documents evolution of terrorist use of AI. For Military and Defense Institutions: Clarifies how regional stability affects transnational threat emergence; demonstrates importance of Central Asian policy; shows how geopolitical competition affects counterterrorism efficacy. For Technology Policy: Addresses terrorist misuse of encrypted communications, cryptocurrencies, and AI; raises questions about security-privacy balance; examines role of private technology companies. INSTITUTIONAL USE CASES This case study is appropriate for: · University security studies and international relations programs · Military war colleges and defense academies · NATO and allied defense education institutions · Think tank and policy institute research seminars · Corporate security and risk management training · Executive education programs · Professional certification programs in security and counterterrorism NEXT STEPS FOR INSTRUCTORS 1. Review the complete case study (Parts A–D) 2. Adapt the 120-minute class structure to your institutional context 3. Select discussion questions and assessment options appropriate for your students 4. Consult the resource list for background reading assignment options 5. Plan periodic updates as ISK's threat profile evolves

abstract: A Comparison of Burnout Between Residents in High-Income and Low- and Middle-Income Healthcare Systems Edward A Joseph, MBBS, Muhammad Muntazir Khan, MBBS, Shusheel Kumar, MBBS, Christopher Sherry, MD, Muhammad Anees, MBBS, David L Bartlett, MD, FACS, Casey J Allen, MD, FACS Allegheny Singer Research Institute, Pittsburgh, PA; Indus Hospital and Health Network, Karachi, Pakistan; Allegheny Health Network, Pittsburgh, PA; Allegheny Health Network Cancer Institute, Pittsburgh, PA Introduction: Despite extensive recognition resident-physician burnout, differences among residents within economically and culturally distinct healthcare-systems remain unexplored. This study compared burnout among resident-physicians from a high-income (HIC) and low-and-middle-income country (LMIC). Methods: We used the validated Mini-ReZ survey to evaluate the etiological factors contributing to burnout, through subscales for supportive work environment (WE), workplace and electronic medical record stress (WP), and resident experience (RE) among trainees at multiple institutes in a HIC (United States) and LMIC (Pakistan). A positive learning experience was defined as a total score ≥60.0. Results: We received 112 responses (51.8% HIC, 48.2% LMIC) from 8 institutions. Respondents were 31.1 ± 4.2 years old, 56.3% female; 59.6% medicine residents, and 87.5% (n = 98) trained in tertiary facilities. LMIC-residents were younger (29.8 ± 3.1 vs 32.6 ± 4.7 years, p < 0.001) and predominantly female (68.5% vs 44.8%, p = 0.037). LMIC-residents reported lower WE (18.4 ± 3.9 vs 16.2 ± 4.4, p = 0.007) and WP (14.0 ± 3.8 vs 11.9 ± 3.4, p = 0.002), with comparable RE (15.6 ± 4.2 vs 15.0 ± 4.5, p = 0.412). Although HIC-residents reported higher total scores (47.9 ± 10.4 vs 42.9 ± 10.0, p = 0.013), neither cohort met the threshold for a positive learning experience (Figure 1a). Workplace support was associated with improved resident wellness across all subscales (Figure 1b). More LMIC-residents felt that burnout was poorly recognized (38.9% vs 5.2%, p < 0.001) and lacked systems to help manage burnout (83.3% vs 27.6%, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Trainees in both HIC and LMIC settings experienced significant wellness challenges. While workplace support positively influenced well-being, residents in LMICs reported higher rates of burnout and fewer resources available. Addressing these deficiencies may improve trainee wellness globally.Figure 1A Comprehensive Framework for Strengthening Health Security and Surgical Care Delivery in Armed Conflict: Empowering Local Healthcare Workforces and Enhancing Humanitarian and Non-Governmental Organization Response Kathryn K Campos, BA Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA Introduction: The urgent need to strengthen global health security programming in armed conflict settings extends to surgical care delivery. Despite extensive humanitarian efforts, critical gaps persist in surgical care delivery within armed conflict zones, underscoring the need for a structured, evidence-based framework for capacity-building. This study presents a framework to bridge gaps by strengthening healthcare workforces, optimizing coordination, and expanding surgical capacity. It categorizes workforce training, resource allocation, surveillance, emergency preparedness, and infrastructure development to enhance surgical care and mitigate health security threats. Methods: A systematic review (2002-2022) assessed global health security and surgical strengthening interventions in armed conflict settings. From 2,581 records, 25 reports met predefined inclusion criteria on surgical capacity-building and emergency response. These were analyzed to develop a structured global health security framework for humanitarian surgical care. Results: Key surgical capacity-building and health security interventions were categorized into strategic domains, including civil-military medical collaboration, workforce integration, emergency response preparedness, and resource mobilization. Findings reveal that civil-military collaboration enhances emergency response effectiveness, yet workforce integration remains critically underdeveloped, limiting sustainable surgical capacity in conflict settings (see Table 1 for framework details). Conclusion: Global health initiatives lack a unified approach for surgical capacity-building in armed conflict. This framework offers a structured, locally informed model designed for adoption by WHO, MSF, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and local health organizations. To ensure sustainable surgical interventions for conflict-affected civilians, global health organizations must urgently pilot and implement this framework in high-risk regions, with iterative improvements based on frontline data. Table 1.A Decade of Change: Declining Inguinal Hernia Severity Through Sustained Surgical Missions in Ghana Maximilian F Munoz, MD, Shahenda Khedr, BA, Aayushi Chechi, BA, Konstantin Khariton, DO, FACS, Albert Y Benneh, MD, Ziad C Sifri, MD, FACS Rutgers - New Jersey Medical School, Newark, NJ; Weill Cornell Medicine, New York-Presbyterian Hospital, New York, NY; Tetteh Quarshie Memorial Hospital, Mampong Akuapem, Ghana Introduction: Inguinal hernia is a significant surgical burden in low-resource settings, often presenting at advanced stages due to limited healthcare access. Recurrent short-term surgical missions (STSMs) help bridge this gap. This study evaluates changes in inguinal hernia severity over a decade of STSMs, assessing whether sustained efforts have led to earlier intervention and reduced disease severity. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair during 9 STSMs by the International Surgical Health Initiative (ISHI) at Tetteh Quarshie Memorial Hospital in Mampong-Akuapem, Ghana, since 2013. H-scores (hernia complexity score) were recorded using a standardized grading system, and patient demographics, including age, sex, and symptom duration, were analyzed. Characteristics were compared across 3 cohorts: 2013-2016 vs 2017-2019 vs 2023-2024. Results: Since 2013, 218 inguinal hernia repairs have been completed by the ISHI team. The mean patient age was 46.2 ± 17.6 years, with the majority being men. A significant reduction in mean H-scores was observed (p < 0.001), decreasing from 2.95 (95% CI: 2.66-3.23) in 2013-2016 to 2.26 (95% CI: 2.05-2.47) in 2017-2019, and 2.04 (95% CI: 1.78-2.31) in 2023-2024. The proportion of high-complexity hernia (H3-H4) declined, while low-complexity hernia (H1-H2) increased over time. Symptom duration did not significantly differ between cohorts (Table 1). Conclusion: Over the past decade, there has been a measurable decline in inguinal hernia severity, suggesting that sustained STSMs improve early surgical access and intervention. These findings suggest the critical role of sustained surgical outreach and capacity-building efforts in reducing the burden of advanced disease in resource-limited settings. title_key: executive summary of the 2025 ashp commission on goals preparing for the evolving healthcare landscape|mehta
title: Executive Summary of the 2025 ASHP Commission on Goals: Preparing for the Evolving Healthcare Landscape
abstract: Hybrid Live/Virtual Meeting March 18, 2025 Each year ASHP convenes a Commission on Goals, composed of thought leaders in healthcare and related fields, to review societal and healthcare trends and developments that may affect ASHP members and the patients they serve and to provide guidance to the ASHP Board of Directors about potential strategic areas of focus for ASHP.1-7 The March 18, 2025, Commission meeting focused on 5 topics: advanced therapeutics, artificial intelligence, changing environmental conditions, cybersecurity, and health policy changes. Members of the Commission (Appendix) were selected from key leaders in academia, government, healthcare associations, industry, medicine, nursing, and pharmacy for their unique ability to review healthcare industry and technology trends and identify challenges and opportunities that will impact pharmacy practice and patient care. This report is intended as a general overview of the discussion among participants and does not represent the official position of any of the individuals or organizations involved. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) describes cell and gene therapies (CGTs) as therapeutic approaches that seek “to modify or manipulate the expression of a gene or to alter the biological properties of living cells for therapeutic use.”8 As of March 2025, there were 46 FDA-approved CGT products and over 4,000 gene, cell, and RNA therapies in development.9 CGTs show immense promise for conditions like cancer, neurological disorders, and rare diseases.10 These new drugs use novel and different mechanisms of action, including CRISPR genome editing technology and viral vector gene delivery vehicles. Multiple Commission members described CGTs as nothing short of “science fiction,” redefining modern medicine. Simultaneously, they expressed concern about barriers to and implementation of these high-cost therapies. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has introduced an innovative payment model predicated on the idea that CGTs are expensive up front but should decrease spending over time by reducing healthcare use. In this CMS voluntary model, manufacturers will negotiate pricing with state Medicaid agencies, which will include rebates if predetermined outcomes are not met.11 Commission members discussed layering together different innovative payment models and warned that traditional insurance mechanisms such as high-risk pools for self-insured entities may not work with CGTs. They recommend establishing market-based incentives, such as tax credits, to promote better solutions like reinsurance, which is a form of insurance designed to protect insurance companies. Similarly, the current system of reimbursement to hospitals based on diagnosis-related groups (DRGs) must be re-evaluated for CGTs because the cost of the therapy would far exceed hospital reimbursement for a given DRG. A question was posed as to whether CGTs might become less expensive at some point in the future, to which a Commission member commented that a move from autologous to allogeneic cell therapies might do so because they shorten manufacturing time and preclude the need for apheresis. Beyond cost and affordability, the discussion covered the preapproval to approval of CGTs as they become commercially available, emphasizing the need for early dialogue among manufacturers, payers, and healthcare providers. This collaboration would help define key factors such as patient eligibility and follow-up duration, shaping clear expectations when CGT products are commercialized. The point was raised that patients who enroll in clinical trials may not fully represent the patient population at large, and real-world evidence will be necessary to bridge study data with clinical care. Additionally, healthcare providers will need specialized training, infrastructure, and mechanisms to monitor safety and efficacy. All healthcare professionals, including nurses, pharmacists, and physicians, need to be part of the conversation as they will be key players in CGT delivery and monitoring. Best practices should be documented and shared, such as a hub and spoke model in which an academic medical center creates protocols and provides clinical and process expertise to satellite hospitals in more rural and underserved geographical areas. Additionally, commission members spoke about the patient experience, specifically how patients should be part of shared decision-making, need comprehensive supportive services, and engaged in the follow-up process of monitoring long-term outcomes since “data collection” could span a lifetime. In summary, while CGTs hold a potential for curing rare diseases, their successful implementation will require innovative payment models, robust healthcare infrastructure, interdisciplinary collaboration, and a patient-centered approach to ensure both affordability and successful implementation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the healthcare field and will greatly impact both patients and the workforce. While the technical definition of AI can vary, FDA defines it as “a machine-based system that can make predictions, recommendations, or decisions based on a combination of machine and human-based inputs.”12 In healthcare, AI is often referred to as “augmented intelligence” or “intelligence-based medicine,” emphasizing its assistive role rather than its being a replacement for human intelligence.13 Commission members described the promise of AI a decade ago, when the healthcare community thought it was the ultimate solution to solve the problem of medical errors.14 While its impact has evolved in different ways than originally envisioned, there are now some impressive examples of its application, particularly in the more visually driven specialties of medicine such as radiology and pathology. A 2020 study described the use of machine learning techniques to detect intracranial hemorrhage on computed tomography scans. The AI tool flagged abnormal examinations for neuroradiologists to prioritize in their workflow, which shortened their time in queue.15 Additionally, deep learning has been applied in computational pathology to automate cancer detection, grading, and subtyping by integrating histological features with biomarker data, enabling the stratification of patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups. This approach improved diagnostic accuracy, with less variation compared to the current standard of practice; however, it needs to be validated in a real-world clinical population and combined with patient factors such as comorbidities and treatments received.16 While there is great promise, there are challenges as well. Commission members noted concerns such as lack of transparency of machine learning algorithms, propensity for bias, and risk of privacy breaches.17,18 Risk of bias can be mitigated with clarity about collected data and use of mathematical approaches to debiasing, among other methods.19 The Commission members noted the need for AI governance in health systems, which, among other things, will need to ensure AI applications improve clinical care, minimize biases, ensure fairness, and establish a way to shut down an AI system upon malfunctioning. Commission members commented that AI will serve as an extension of the healthcare workforce by complementing a team-based approach and filling in gaps, and while AI will replace certain functions, it will also create new roles in healthcare, such as medical information consultants and AI ethics and bias auditors. The argument was made that AI will allow healthcare providers to work at the top of their education and training by spending more time doing clinically meaningful tasks, including direct patient engagement. For example, another good test case is the use of AI to clear inbox messages to clinicians in the electronic health record. People are exploring ways to measure the extent to which an AI tool can reduce the daily administrative workload on healthcare professionals, a key contributor to burnout. Preferred performance indicators that might reflect a reduction in clinicians’ cognitive burden include EHR event log data and time-motion observations, as opposed to methods that add to their workload, such as surveys or self-reported time tracking.20 The reliance on AI alone made some commission members concerned. However, a study published in Journal of the American Medical Association in 2024 compared diagnostic accuracy of physicians with and without large language model (LLM) tools such as ChatGPT and found a statistically better diagnostic accuracy with LLM tools alone.21 The authors cautioned that their study was small and not “real world,” and that LLMs should not be used for diagnosis without physician oversight. Indeed, other studies have shown that LLMs perform worse than clinicians when recommending treatment plans.22 Commission members saw potential for AI to work alongside humans and considered how team-based approaches such as combining nurses and pharmacists with AI could help address care gaps in healthcare deserts and support a shift from fee-for-service medicine toward more value-based care. Commission members commented it will be up to healthcare practitioners and public health workers to work with stakeholders from government and industry to safely deploy AI. Education initiatives in coursework, training, and continuing education could guide use of AI to improve patient safety outcomes and practice efficiency. Patients are watching how their healthcare providers use AI before forming an opinion, but they generally welcome its use for administrative tasks if it means their clinicians can spend more time with them. Engaging patients by giving them visibility into how AI is used in their care and the benefits it can bring will help build trust as we navigate the emerging world of AI.23 In summary, while AI holds great promise for enhancing healthcare, its successful integration will require careful governance, collaboration among stakeholders, and a commitment to ethical, transparent, and patient-centered implementation. Changes to the natural environment pose threats to human health, impacting the physical environment as well as every aspect of planetary and human systems. A 2020 Health Affairs article highlighted that US healthcare greenhouse gas emissions are among the highest among industrialized nations, with pharmaceuticals and chemicals as major contributors, leading to a health impact on a scale comparable to that of preventable medical errors.24 The National Institutes of Health has identified outdoor air pollution as a contributor to reduced lung function, asthma, cardiac problems, and emergency department visits, with an elevated risk of death linked to specific air pollutants.25 Greenhouse gases are just one type of environmental pollutant; others include air and water pollution, as well as plastic and hazardous waste. Commission members recognized the healthcare industry’s role in environmental degradation, including medication waste, some of which contains persistent toxic chemicals, as well as greenhouse gases, emitted through manufacturing, transportation, administration, and waste disposal processes. A commission member spoke about a mitigation approach hospitals and health systems know well—stewardship. In September 2024, Hurricane Helene damaged an intravenous fluid manufacturing plant in North Carolina, resulting in a shortage of critical intravenous fluids. Health systems were forced to alleviate the shortage through conservation efforts, but when the shortage was resolved, many relinquished strict stewardship efforts. The Commission proposed the idea that we should treat the disease burden from pollution like medical errors, re-evaluate wasteful practices (eg, excess donning and doffing in IV rooms), and create environmental stewardship committees in hospitals. The Choosing Wisely Canada initiative was mentioned. That initiative provides a national voice for reducing unnecessary medical tests and treatments.26 Numerous Choosing Wisely Canada recommendations are applicable across borders, including pharmacy-focused lists, with a few examples being: Don’t prescribe greenhouse gas–intensive metered-dose inhalers (MDIs) for asthma and/or COPD where an alternative inhaler with a lower carbon footprint (eg, a dry powder inhaler, soft-mist inhaler, or MDI with a low greenhouse gas potential propellant) containing medications with comparable efficacy is available and where the patient has demonstrated adequate technique and patient preference has been considered. Don’t continue an intravenous medication when it is clinically appropriate to step down to oral therapy. Don’t use disposable gloves when standard hand hygiene disinfection practices are safe and sufficient. Don’t use desflurane when other anesthetic drugs and techniques are equally effective and less harmful to the environment. Commission members noted that stewardship is not a new concept for US hospitals and health systems, particularly for antimicrobials, so extending this effort to other medications and supplies seems plausible. The Commission also discussed being resilient in the face of environmental disasters, including keeping buildings tolerant to heat waves and storms, creating mechanisms to allow clinicians to get to work during evacuations, and providing educational resources to communities to prepare for such events. One commissioner spoke of an unprecedented heat wave in 2021 in the Pacific Northwest, where record-breaking temperatures of 116 °F warped doorjambs and window frames of a hospital building while challenging the chilling system to maintain adequate cooling.27 Some buildings in the region didn’t have air conditioning, so the health and safety of patients and employees were imperiled. In health systems, environmental stewardship often falls under quality improvement. Tracking emissions reductions, including those related to pharmaceuticals and their delivery systems, is essential for driving evidence-based environmental performance improvement. Even when emissions data is limited, reducing waste can still help lower pollution and should be incorporated into guidelines and aligned with cost-reduction initiatives. Numerous healthcare organizations are thinking about the interface of healthcare and environmental sustainability, including the National Academy of Medicine and American Nurses Association.28,29 In summary, addressing the environmental impact of healthcare requires a comprehensive approach to ensure protection of both public and planetary health. Advances in technology and care delivery broaden vulnerabilities to cyberattacks, putting patient care and public health at risk.30 In 2023, more than 250 distinct organizations in the US were targeted by cyberattacks, making a 128% increase compared to 2022.31 The financial impact of cybersecurity breaches on healthcare is immense. The average cost of a single cyberattack is in the millions of dollars, though larger incidents, such as the Change Healthcare attack, have reached into the billions in estimated costs.32,33 Healthcare is particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks given the staggering amount of sensitive health information with high monetary and intelligence value, and the American Hospital Association reports that stolen health records may sell for up to 10 times or more than stolen credit card numbers on the dark web.34 The question about cybersecurity is not if threats will occur, but rather when. Most commission members believe our healthcare system is ill-prepared for this threat and should not bear the burden of planning and preparation alone, emphasizing the need for federal support. CMS requires participating facilities to have emergency plans for all hazards, including cyberattacks, which may include antiviral programs or other electronic security systems to detect malware and viruses.35 Under HIPAA (the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act), hospitals and health systems bear the responsibility to implement “reasonable and appropriate” safeguards, a flexible standard that can lead to widely variable approaches, and potential gaps, in protecting patient information. Commission members noted that most cybersecurity threats occur through third-party vendor relationships, and yet, hospital and health systems are held accountable for the infrastructure failure resulting from cyberattacks. Commission members agreed that these impacts create ripple effects on financial systems, patient safety, and public health, framing cybersecurity as a national security issue rather than merely a business disruption. In addition to the call for policy change, commission members raised practical considerations for individual hospitals and health systems, including making a list of what actions should be prioritized
