title_key: paul pierre broca birth bicentenary|tandon
title: PAUL PIERRE BROCA: Birth Bicentenary
abstract: “Probably neither before nor since, has there been one man with such anatomical and physiological knowledge of the nervous system with such surgical skill and daring has existed in the lamented Broca” - Stone 1991 Pierre Paul Broca, son of Jean “Benjamin” Broca, a surgeon in Napoleon’s Service and Annette Thomas, was born on 28 June 1824 in Sainte-Foy-la-Grande near Bordeaux, France[1]. It is an occasion to celebrate the 200th birth anniversary of this genius, whose pioneering contributions on establishing cerebral cortical localization of function starting with speech and language, remains in daily parlance among neuroscientists, both basic and clinical. He has been immortalized by the acronyms, “Broca’s Area” and” Broca’s aphasia”. Most of us believed that he was a trained and practicing neurologist, which surprisingly he was not, even though he made many valuable contributions to neurology.[1-3] Most of the practicing clinical neuroscientists, that I have interacted with during my more than half a century of academic career in the field were not aware of his full credentials. In fact, “ Broca was a noted 19th century Surgeon - anthropologist who by modern standards could have been considered an able neuroanatomist, neurologist, pathologist, craniologist, genetist, ethnologist, evolutionist, statistician and a liberal minded politician”.[4,5] To this may be added his expertise in comparative anatomy, human evolution and diversity, oncology and therapeutics”. He was instrumental in merging laboratory science and medicine.[6] To each one of these fields, he made distinguished contributions. (For confirmation see his own numerous publications, as also by his many biographers listed in this text). In this somewhat detailed review attempt has been made to highlight Broca’s contributions in the diverse fields which are generally not well known. A detailed note of Broca’s Aphasia is provided in a monograph on “Speech and Language (‘Tandon’ In Press) and hence not included here. To understand the diverse contributions of Broca it is best to follow his early career development. He received his early basic education in a school in his home town, earning a bachelor’s degree at an early age of 16. He then joined a medical school in Paris when he was 17 years and graduated at the age of 20 years, much earlier than his contemporaries. Following graduation from the medical school Broca did extensive internship in urology, dermatology, psychiatry ending up as a Professor in Anatomy at the University of Paris Medical School. By age 30, He was awarded a medical doctorate. Soon after He became Professor agrége and appointed surgeon to the hospital. He was later elected to the chair of the external pathology in the Faculty of Medicine and a year later Professor of Clinical Surgery, a position he retained till his death. It is obvious from the above that because of his most well-known pioneering contribution-localization of speech in the left frontal lobe most clinicians believed him to be a neurologist. Notwithstanding his many contributions in the field of nervous system (see below). He was formally a surgeon and not a neuroscientist. This is further confirmed by his initial scientific contributions, which consisted of the following: As mentioned earlier during the first 10 years after graduation his work was mainly in pathology which soon shifted to Anthropology and ethnography in addition to comparative anatomy of mammalian brain.[7,8] Broca first made a name for himself by using a microscope to study normal anatomy and human diseases. His strong belief was that laboratory and clinic should come together to improve the state of medicine[9] Whether this belief was influenced by a similar pronouncement by his some years senior compatriot, Claude Bernard (1813-1878), who in 1865 had published his “Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine”. Bernard a reputed physiologist is reported to have proclaimed, “ The hospital, the library provide the opportunity for making and recording observations but only the laboratory provides the area where these observations can be tested by carefully designed experiments.”[10] His contributions in various subdisciplines of biology and medicine though overlapping, are summarized below under individual sub-specialities. Anthropology One of Broca’s work on physical anthropology was on classifying racial groups using geographic location than colour of the skin. In his support he quoted studies from USA to be consisting of brown, black, white, red and yellow races. Similarly he referred to Malayo- Polynesian- types races comprised of colour as various as those belonging to American types.[11,12] According to a review of the Samanth Ashok (2017) in The History of Race in Anthropology: Paul Broca and the Question of Human Hybridity, Broca spent much time at his Anthropology Institute studying skulls and bones.[13] He unfortunately utilized these studies as his main criteria for ranking groups is order of superiority - which has been called “Scientific racism”. This led to the unfortunate theories of sociologically maligned racial groups and human species. title_key: presidential address to the 2025 annual meeting of the congress of neurological surgeons|hoh
title: Presidential Address to the 2025 Annual Meeting of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons
abstract: Good morning and welcome to Los Angeles for the 75th Annual Meeting of the Congress of Neurological Surgeons (CNS). In 1951 at the end of World War II, a group of neurosurgeons forged by the adversity of war came together to connect. To share experiences and build a community that was the origin of the CNS. Seventy-five years later, the spirit of connection remains at the heart of who we are today. However, we face different challenges now: administrative burden, barriers to care, cuts to research funding, physician burnout. All demand a renewed connection to our community, our leadership, our peak individual potential, and our pursuit of innovation. This week, we celebrate neurosurgery and the people who make it extraordinary. Today, I reflect on these four enduring themes that define us and the CNS: community, leadership, peak performance, and innovation. First, let us talk about community. Dr Steven Miller was a pediatric emergency room doctor when I was in medical school at Columbia. Sadly, he died later in a tragic plane crash. In his time, he was an early pioneer for an emerging movement: humanism in medicine. Dr Miller said, “we must find ways to permeate each and every aspect of medicine with humanism.” He taught us humanism through the radical, but seemingly simple act of listening. Humanism is asking questions but then to stop and truly listen. Listen for two uninterrupted minutes. It is deceptively simple. A small, marginal yet innovative act of open listening: to build trust, connect, and heal. As neurosurgeons, how deeply are we connecting with our patient community? I was a neurosurgery resident here at Los Angeles General Hospital. Nearly half of this community is non-English speaking preferred. I saw firsthand the importance of meeting patients where they are—language-wise, culturally, emotionally. Doctor–patient connection is a challenge. Studies show that patients remember less than half of the informed consent. Lisa Ling, our Dorothy Nash lecturer, said, “it requires time and energy to get invested in other people's stories, but… you emerge a better and smarter human as a result of taking that time.” This is not simply a communication issue; it is about investing in human connection. Technology such as artificial intelligence (AI) will not replace us—it will help us connect more meaningfully. AI-assisted language translation, transcription, decision support tools, patient education, and counseling. AI will minimize administrative burden such as prior authorization. These tools will free us to connect more humanistically. But community is not just our patients. We are a community that connects through shared learning even and especially through difficult experiences—to uplift us as individuals and elevate our community. This early CNS meeting symposium shows we recognized early on the value of discussing our complications for learning. Today decades later, we are still connecting in the same way through our CNS Complications courses. We learn from each other through listening and sharing experiences from our most challenging cases. The cover of the May 2001 issue of Neurosurgery is a visual representation of the isolation we have all felt after a complication. It looks like what today we call burnout. But the path to improvement is not through isolation. Improvement requires community. As Gandhi said, “Freedom is not worth having if it does not include the freedom to make mistakes.” We must protect that freedom by supporting systems that foster learning. Colleen Fogarty says, “It is the practice of medicine because we must build mechanisms to prompt reflection on our work… seeking and incorporating feedback from others on our team. Effective systems protect time for practice and learning.” Our national organizations, including the CNS, empower us by reinforcing these systems for learning throughout our career. Maya Angelou said, “Do the best you can until you know better. Then when you know better, do better.” Beverly Walters and CNS Past President Mark Hadley taught us this through their pioneering work in guidelines. We build community through efforts like guidelines: asking the right questions, generating science, interpreting data, and sharing knowledge to elevate our practice standards. Advancements in data science—efforts such as the CNS Data Science scholarship—accelerate these processes. Soon, guidelines will be living documents updated in real time. Our community is connecting broader and faster virtually. CNS NEXUS is a digital library of hundreds of peer-reviewed neurosurgical cases—crowd sourced by our members. The CNS+ app has an AI chatbot that generates knowledge from NEXUS cases, CNS webinars, journal articles, and guidelines. Our Editor-in-Chief, Doug Kondziolka, and Eric Oermann are developing technology that will allow us to interact with the neurosurgical literature in innovative ways. Our advocacy work, celebrating 50 years through the CNS/American Association of Neurological Surgeons Washington Committee, is another expression of community. Thank you to past director Katie Orrico, current director Charlotte Pineda, and CNS Past Presidents Russ Lonser and Alex Khalessi for connecting our specialty to national policy. Community is a connection that breaks barriers to care, elevates our clinical practice, and affects lives. Our community is built on neurosurgeons connecting as leaders to shape our future. As a spine neurosurgeon, I am proud to stand on the shoulders of a leader like Sanford Larson. Larson fought for neurosurgeons to perform complex spinal instrumentation. Dr Larson led by training the first generation of spine neurosurgeons through workshops like this one at the 1980 CNS Annual Meeting. Leaders like Albert Rhoton, the 28th CNS President and my institution's first chair. Dr Rhoton, most known for leading microsurgical anatomy of the brain, also recognized the importance of spine surgery as a distinct community. Dr Rhoton had the vision to call upon the first joint spine section in 1978. Leaders who faced resistance and overcame adversity. Volker Sonntag and others who stood firm when orthopedics challenged our role in pedicle screw instrumentation. And those who led the effort with our industry partners to fight against the pedicle screw litigation of the 1990s—as detailed by Rusty Rodts in his 2010 CNS Presidential Address. Leaders opening doors and leveling the field. Dorothy Nash, our first woman neurosurgeon, is memorialized by the CNS Nash Lectureship. And neurosurgeon Frances Conley who championed women's rights with exceptional courage, dignity and resilience. The American Board of Neurological Surgery, the organization that certified Frances Conley as just the fifth woman neurosurgeon, is now led by Marjorie Wang and Judy Huang. A testament to the progress their leadership made possible. Leadership is shared vision. It is the CNS Pathways program which opens doors for under-represented minorities. Essential for our community, where less than 5% of neurosurgery residents are Black. It is groups such as the American Society of Black Neurosurgeons and the Neurosurgical Pride Alliance. They are building community for neurosurgeons to be welcomed and to be the next generation of leaders. It is also building future leaders. The CNS Leadership Institute celebrates its 10th year. A program that has trained nearly 200 neurosurgeons in skills such as team building, negotiation, project and change management. Starting with those in early career to those at the executive level, many alumni of the institute—myself as one of the first participants—are now division chiefs, department chairs, program directors, and health system executives. Neurosurgeons are being called up to leadership positions that we previously witnessed from the sidelines. Leadership is a connection to building community, mentoring, opening doors for the next generation, and shaping our future. I love the sport of cycling. Exercise, being outdoors, mental well-being. I love watching the Tour de France and seeing pro cyclists at the highest level—with their dedication to the science of peak performance. The relentless optimization of peak individual potential: fitness, recovery, nutrition, the psychology of winning. Cycling, such as neurosurgery, demands the absolute individual best. What might optimizing peak performance look like for neurosurgery? Our Walter Dandy Orator, Dan Buettner, studies the Blue Zones—communities around the world with different genetics, geography and culture. But they share one thing in common: human longevity and well-being. As we will hear from him, peak human potential is not about a single factor. It is about purpose, connection, and balance. Yet modern healthcare works against these values. Today's healthcare is like Frederick Taylor and his industrial engineering approach to organizational management—structure work in the simplest way to maximize efficiency at any cost. In healthcare, this is hyperstandardization without meaningful thought. Electronic health record templates that are essentially billing widgets. RVU targets. Operating room block utilization. These quantify output, but do not capture humanism in neurosurgery. Consolidation of large health systems eliminating job competition. Scope creep by non-neurosurgeons. Commoditizing neurosurgery. “The sum total of hundreds and thousands of tiny betrayals of purpose—de-valuing the neurosurgeon” (Richard Gunderman). Organizational psychology teaches us that these efficiencies do not drive performance and individual potential. Psychologists Hackman and Oldham demonstrated that to drive performance, we must find in our work skill complexity, autonomy, meaningfulness, identity, and feedback. We must connect with neurosurgery on a multifaceted deeper level to enhance our individual potential. Vital to our future is to preserve these very characteristics of neurosurgery that drive and sustain performance. We must balance efficiency with humanity. And ensure our systems empower, rather than constrain neurosurgeons. I am grateful for neurosurgeons like these who serve at executive levels: college of medicine deans, enterprise leaders. They have the appreciation for the value of the neurosurgeon in an enterprise—the true value of the neurosurgeon as presented by Council of State Neurosurgical Societies Chair Luis Tumialan at the 2023 CNS Annual Meeting. Our neurosurgeon leaders can affect health systems at an enterprise level to protect that which drives motivation, professional satisfaction, and peak performance. We cannot accept burnout as our defining narrative. Instead, we should approach the study of human performance with the same rigor we apply to neurosurgical training. Let us understand the physical, cognitive, and psychological factors that enhance individual potential. Like CNS Past President Joseph Maroon, who at age 85 years, is a vice chair of neurosurgery, researcher, ironman triathlete, and author. Joe teaches the equal balance of work, family, health, and personal growth. Enhancing peak performance requires a balance of purpose, well-being, continuous learning, mentorship, and community. These are the cornerstones of longevity. Ultimately, it is these connections, community, leadership, and individual potential that naturally propel us toward innovation. At the University of Florida, innovation has long defined our culture from Dr Robert Cade inventing Gatorade, William Friedman and Frank Bova's advances in LINAC-based radiosurgery, Richard Fessler and the first in human stem cell transplant, and Brian Hoh's National Institutes of Health funded multicenter CAPTIVA trial. This CNS meeting is another showcase for innovation: over 5000 submitted abstracts, over 900 oral abstracts, nearly 1000 unique speakers, 185 industry partners, and 3 incredible finalists for our CNS Innovator of the Year competition; we will decide this year's winner on Wednesday. Like last year's winner Alexandra Golby who developed a low cost, open-source navigation system for low-income countries. This scale speaks to our neurosurgical community connecting to innovation. Today, we are at an inflection point with the rapid development of artificial intelligence. AI will process massive data to predict disease and model outcomes. This will undoubtedly drive the pace of innovation at an incredible cadence. I had a recent conversation with Rich Byrne, Society of Neurological Surgeons President, about the potential of AI. We started by talking about chess. Rich has a master rating. We talked about my son Carter, whose chess team won first place at the 2023 national team competition. Rich says he first became interested in AI from his love for chess. Grandmasters like Bobby Fisher dedicated their lives to memorizing thousands of game scenarios. But chess has an estimated 10123 scenarios. A computer, DeepBlue, in 1996, did what humans could not. DeepBlue mastered chess and then beat grandmaster Gary Kasparov. Kasparov described his match with DeepBlue at the 2021 CNS meeting. Go is a 4000-year-old game from Asia with 10170 possible scenarios. Google's DeepMind learned it in days and then beat South Korean grandmaster Lee Sedol. Games such as chess have distinct rules. AI can do what humans cannot—process every potential scenario to generate a win. There is no need for imagination. But could a computer trained on thousands of open aneurysm clippings imagine endovascular coiling? Could AI ask the relevant questions: Who do we treat? What is a better outcome? To paraphrase Fredrik Pohl, AI undoubtedly can predict the traffic jam, but could AI have predicted the automobile? We should embrace AI for what it can do that we cannot. But AI has limitations. Current AI large language models can generate near pitch perfect language that itself does not understand—not in the way we understand, like true listening. Large language models generate text by predicting the most likely next token based on the prior set of tokens. Best fitting to statistical patterns—not actual understanding. Cognitive scientist Gary Marcus says about the limits of AI, “Neural networks of various kinds can generalize within a distribution of data they are exposed to, but their generalizations tend to break down beyond that distribution.” “You can't think we are close to artificial general intelligence once you realize that as yet we have no general solution to the outlier problem.” Often it is in the outliers that we find our greatest discoveries. It is the outliers where true breakthroughs emerge. Could AI have imagined Picasso from Michelangelo? Or innovators like Spike Lee—who we heard from yesterday—who disrupted and redefined cinema? We must listen to patients for the outliers, the nuance beyond their data. Ask better questions. What else is possible? And from there, imagine better solutions. D. Graham Burnett writes, “There is more to humanism than the accumulation of facts. AI only knows, but it has not lived. No dataset can resolve the central questions that confront every human being. How to live? What to do? How to face death?” Consider brain tumor scientist Elias Sayour. At the University of Florida, he is developing an AI approach to analyze tumor mRNA data to design personalized immunotherapy. But AI cannot ask: How do we face disease? How do we give hope? As Burnett suggests, the answers to these questions are not out there waiting to be machine learned. They are not resolved simply by knowledge generation. title_key: from fiction to reality the wall e paradigm in modern ai ethics and society|noman
title: From Fiction to Reality: The ‘WALL-E’ Paradigm in Modern AI Ethics and Society
abstract: INTRODUCTION “WALL-E” was a far-sighted cinematic paragon that, though set in a fictional, dystopian far future, impactfully reflects some of the challenges and potential dangers that our society might face as we dive deeper into the potential of artificial intelligence (AI). The movie was released in 2008; at that time, the story line seemed too far-fetched. In the movie, the earth has become uninhabitable due to overexploitation of the earth and its resources, leaving it in ruins and a pile of garbage, devoid of plants and other forms of life. Humans have left desolate uninhabitable Earth, surviving in an outer space habitat where their every need and desires are served for by advanced AI technology and robots controlled by AI. This dependency has led to a profound loss of physical capabilities, health, thinking, and, more importantly, a detachment from the very essence of human experience: the tactile, the effortful, and the authentically interpersonal.[1] Current scenario As we have arrived in the era of a technological revolution, with AI poised to revolutionize every facet of our lives, this movie’s storyline seems more relevant than ever. Advancements in AI at such magnanimous levels promise untold benefits, from revolutionizing healthcare with personalized medicine to transforming education and industry. However, there is a thoughtful question that “WALL-E” brings to the mind: In our pursuit of convenience and efficiency through AI, are we at risk of losing our identity, health, and some integral parts of our humanity?[2] TALE OF AI IN THE LENS OF WALL-E The scenario depicted in “WALL-E” might sound extreme, but it serves as a powerful warning for the potential consequences of an overdependence reliance on AI. The humans in the film have given over not only their responsibilities but also their passions, curiosities, and joys of physical exertion to machines. This brings us to a critical turning point in our real-world scenario on AI: the importance of maintaining a harmonious balance where technology enhances rather than supplants the human experience.[1] This gives an impression of one of the many catastrophic possibilities that could occur due to the overuse and dependence on AI and technology. BALANCING AI AND HUMANITY The ethical consideration of AI’s growth is vast, complex, and beyond control. As AI becomes more integrated into our daily lives, how do we ensure that it augments rather than diminishes our human capabilities? How do we preserve the qualities that define our humanity, curiosity, resilience, and the capacity for physical and intellectual effort? Moreover, how do we ensure that AI does not increase societal divides but rather works toward an inclusive and equitable future for all?[3,4] These issues open a Pandora’s box of issues as who will monitor and restrict AI development, implementation, and use. Also, there is a possibility that generative AI itself can become competent enough for its own development and progression to catastrophic levels without human intervention, supervision, or control. Also considering all weapons of mass destruction are under the control of technology, if somehow AI takes control of these, it could lead to unimaginable destruction. DECEPTIVE POTENTIAL OF AI In this thought-provoking review, contemporary manifestations of AI’s ability to deceive are evident, highlighting recent research findings and the ethical implications therein. It emphasizes the dual nature of AI deception, elucidating both its perilous risks and potential benefits across various domains.[5] Wisdom gleaned The lesson from “WALL-E” is clear: Technology, in all its awesome potentials, should not overpower the fundamental aspects of humanity; it should not diminish our physical health, nor should it impede our ability to engage deeply with our world and with each other. It should not hamper our power of thinking. As we navigate this new era, it is important that we approach AI development with a keen eye of ethical responsibility, ensuring that these technologies are utilized to enrich human life, not to detract from it. A common body like UN should be formulated with worldwide participation. This body should lay down strict rules for moderation of AI development and implementation to prevent unwarranted, unwanted events in future. There should be a clear line on how much and by whom what modalities of AI can be used. Its use should be restricted significantly in schools and colleges to prevent use by students. Over-use of AI for mental work can make the students lose the abilities of brain like thinking, creativity, and logical reasoning. What we already are seeing is use of AI in doing calculations, homework, statistics, creative writing, and so on. CONCLUSIONS “WALL-E” is a story set in a far, imaginary future; the questions it raises about our relationship with advanced technology and AI are of significant concern and pressing. It is a call to take into account for all stakeholders in AI, developers, policymakers, and users to moderate the development of AI, which fosters a future where technology serves humanity and not the other way around. title_key: smartphone based digital ruler for automated strabismus measurement in clinical and remote settings|habib
title: Smartphone-based digital ruler for automated strabismus measurement in clinical and remote settings
abstract: Dear Editor, Strabismus, a prevalent ocular motility disorder, affects approximately 2%–4% of the global population and is characterized by misalignment of the visual axes due to neuromuscular imbalance or cranial nerve dysfunction. It can lead to diplopia, amblyopia, and impaired depth perception, particularly in pediatric patients, if not diagnosed early.[1] Traditional diagnostic methods, such as the Hirschberg test, cover–uncover test, and prism alternate cover test, require trained personnel and clinical infrastructure, limiting access in underserved or remote settings.[1] These limitations have prompted the development of automated, accessible tools to improve early detection and monitoring of strabismus. A recent innovation, a smartphone-based digital ruler (DRS), offers automated measurement of ocular deviation using deep learning and three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction algorithms. This tool analyzes short video recordings of cover tests to quantify horizontal and vertical strabismus angles with ophthalmologist-level accuracy, eliminating the need for manual prism bars. Beyond strabismus, this technology holds diagnostic potential for conditions such as thyroid eye disease, cranial nerve palsies, convergence insufficiency, and myasthenia gravis, where precise ocular alignment assessment is essential for clinical decision-making.[2,3] Recent multicenter validation studies have demonstrated strong translational promise. Wang et al. reported in NEJM AI that the DRS achieved 95% agreement with manual prism testing across pediatric and adult cohorts, including esotropia, exotropia, and paralytic strabismus.[4] Complementing this, Kurdthongmee et al. validated artificial intelligence (AI)-based strabismus detection in monocular eye images for telemedicine applications, confirming feasibility in resource-limited MDPI. Together, these findings illustrate complementary strengths: smartphone-based tools can reduce interobserver variability in clinics while enabling scalable screening in teleophthalmology programs.[5] Validated in a 2025 multicenter study (NEJM AI), the DRS achieved 95% concordance with prism alternate cover testing across pediatric and adult cohorts, including esotropia, exotropia, and paralytic strabismus.[4] Beyond strabismus, similar AI-based ocular alignment tools have shown promise in: Thyroid eye disease: Automated detection of ocular misalignment and activity scoring Cranial nerve palsies: Quantifying deviation angles for diagnosis and monitoring Convergence insufficiency and myasthenia gravis: Tracking subtle motility changes critical for treatment decisions. Yarkheir et al. demonstrated that deep learning analysis of facial images could classify strabismus with high accuracy, supporting telemedicine applications.[2] Shin et al. validated AIbased assessment of thyroid eye disease using facial images, reinforcing the broader applicability of ocular alignment algorithms.[3] Together, these studies highlight that smartphonebased tools can extend beyond strabismus, offering scalable diagnostics for multiple ocular motility disorders. The ubiquity of smartphones makes the DRS particularly feasible in low-resource settings. Unlike prism bars or synoptophores, which require specialized equipment and trained ophthalmologists, the DRS can be deployed by community health workers or school screening programs. Offline inference allows use in areas with limited internet connectivity, while teleophthalmology platforms enable remote specialist review. Despite its promise, limitations remain: accuracy may be affected by poor lighting, unstable fixation, or low-resolution video capture, and performance in complex strabismus patterns such as dissociated vertical deviation is still under investigation.[4] Nevertheless, feasibility in developing countries is strengthened by portability, cost-effectiveness, and integration with telemedicine platforms.[5] The smartphone-based digital ruler represents a significant advancement in accessible, AI-assisted strabismus diagnostics. Future directions should include algorithm refinement for complex motility patterns, integration with electronic health records, and deployment in school screening and primary care settings. Cost-effective implementation and clinician training will be essential for widespread adoption. Accurate strabismus diagnosis is well established as critical for preventing amblyopia and visual dysfunction.[1] What is new here is the introduction of a smartphone-based digital ruler that utilizes AI and 3D reconstruction to provide automated, ophthalmologist-level measurements of deviation. Recent validation shows high concordance with prism testing and reduced variability, supporting its role as a scalable, noninvasive tool to enhance early detection, teleophthalmology, and equitable access to care.[2–5] Author contribution statement E.H: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Data curation, Writing Original draft preparation, Reviewing and Editing; S.N.U.S: Writing Original draft preparation, Reviewing and Editing. abstract: AI at the Forefront: Navigating Oncologic Care for Six Gastrointestinal Cancers According to the NCCN Guidelines Utilizing Gemini-1.0 Ultra and ChatGPT-4.0 Tamir Bresler, MD, Tyler Wilson, MD, Tadevos Makaryan, MD, Shivam Pandya, MD, MS, Kevin Palmer, MD, MPH, Ryan Meyer, MD, Zin M Htway, PhD, Manabu Fujita, MD, PhD Los Robles Regional Medical Center, Thousand Oaks, CA; General Surgical Associates, Thousand Oaks, CA Introduction: We explored the ability of public-domain large language models (LLMs) ChatGPT-4.0 (ChatGPT; OpenAI, San Francisco, CA) and Gemini 1.0 Ultra (Gemini; Google, Mountain View, CA) in guiding clinical decision-making for six gastrointestinal cancers using the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Clinical Practice Guidelines as a framework. Methods: We reviewed the NCCN Guidelines for Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Small Bowel Adenocarcinoma, Ampullary Adenocarcinoma, Biliary Tract Cancers, Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma, and Gastric Cancer. Clinical questions were designed for each decision-making page and categorized by type. LLMs were queried with up to 3 follow-up questions. Responses were rated on a Likert scale: 5) Correct; 4) Correct following clarification; 3) Correct but incomplete; 2) Partially incorrect; 1) Absolutely incorrect. Subgroup analysis was conducted on Correctness (scores 1-2 vs. 3-5) and Accuracy (scores 1-3 vs. 4-5). Descriptive statistics were used, and significance was tested with Mann-Whitney U-test. Results: A total of 270 questions were generated (range-per-cancer 32-68). ChatGPT vs. Gemini score frequency distribution was: 5) 45.56%-vs-41.85%; 4) 19.26%-vs-15.56%; 3) 12.96%-vs-18.52%; 2) 13.70%-vs-13.33%; and 1) 8.52%-vs-10.74%. The score difference was not statistically-significant (Mean Rank [MR] 278.30-vs-262.70, p = .222). Correctness was seen in 210-vs-205 responses (77.78%-vs-75.93%), and Accuracy in 175-vs-155 (64.81%-vs-57.41%). There was no statistically-significant difference in Correctness or Accuracy between LLMs in terms of question or cancer type (Figure).Conclusion: Both LLMs demonstrated a limited capacity to assist with complex clinical decision-making in six gastrointestinal cancers. Their current Accuracy level is below the acceptable threshold for clinical use. Future studies exploring LLMs in the healthcare domain are warranted. Analyzing the Biologic Behavior and Malignant Potential of Mixed-Type vs. Branch-Duct Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms (IPMNs) Using High-Risk Mutation Patterns in Cyst Fluid Next Generation Sequencing (NGS): A Large Multicenter Study Amudhan Kannan, MD, Tarek Sawas, MD, Nisa Kubiliun, MD, John C Mansour, MD, FACS, Amer H Zureikat, MBBCh, FACS, Herbert J Zeh III, MD, FACS, Aatur D Singhi, MD, Patricio M Polanco, MD, FACS University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX; University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Sewickley, PA Introduction: Mixed-type IPMNs (IPMNs with MPD dilation ≥5 mm) carry a greater malignant potential compared to BD-IPMNs. To study the underlying reason for this increased propensity, we examined the mutation patterns in mixed-type and BD-IPMNs using cyst fluid NGS. Methods: Prospective NGS analysis on cyst fluid samples from 31 centers was conducted between January 2018 and February 2020. Patients with IPMNs were diagnosed based on KRAS/GNAS mutations and were categorized into two groups (based on EUS): mixed-type IPMNs (MPD ≥5 mm) with BD-IPMNs (MPD <5 mm). High-risk mutations included mutations of TP53, SMAD4, MTOR, and CTNNB1 genes. Advanced neoplasia was defined as IPMNs with HGD or PDAC. The primary outcome was the rate of high-risk mutations in the two groups. Results: Out of 674 patients (mixed-type IPMNs = 202, BD-IPMNs = 472), 106 (15.7%) had high-risk mutations. Mixed-type IPMNs had a higher rate of high-risk mutations (31% vs 9%; p < 0.0001) and co-occurrence of mutations (12% vs 3%; p < 0.0001). Within the cohort of resected patients (n = 158), the rate of advanced neoplasms was higher in mixed-type IPMNs also compared to BD-IPMNs (62% vs 42%). On multivariate logistic regression analysis, mixed-type IPMNs showed an independent association with high-risk mutations (OR = 3.42; 95% CI = 1.72-6.82; p < 0.0001) (Table). Conclusion: Mixed-type IPMNs are more likely to harbor high-risk mutations associated with advanced neoplasms. The rate of advanced neoplasms was also higher in mixed-type IPMNs. Therefore, NGS should be recommended for patients with mixed-type IPMNs regardless of the presence of additional worrisome features. Several guidelines stipulate that a minimum of 12 regional LNs should be assessed to achieve accurate nodal staging. We examined temporal trends and prognostic associations of LNA at our institution. Methods: Consecutive patients who underwent resection of a primary CRC at a high-volume center between 1997 and 2016 were identified from a comprehensive clinicopathologic database. Patients were grouped into 5-year time periods according to date of surgery. Results: The entire study cohort comprised 2137 patients (929F:1208M; median age 64 y, range 16-98). There were no observed differences across time periods for patient (sex, age) or tumor (TNM stage, resection margin) features. Adequate LNA markedly increased over time, regardless of primary tumor site or neoadjuvant therapy status (p < 0.0001, Figure 1A,B). Inadequate LNA during the 2007-2016 time-period was strongly associated with inferior DSS, but this trend was not observed during the 1996-2006 time-period (Figure 1C,D). title_key: mules and tightropes embracing paradox thinking in anesthesiology|sherrer
title: Mules and Tightropes: Embracing Paradox Thinking in Anesthesiology
abstract: Paradoxes abound in our personal and work lives. Human relationships are often initiated by complementary differences that spark interest. But over time, opposites that attract can be the source of tension and conflict. Businesses often face paradoxical challenges like the need for stability and the necessity of change, which pit tradition squarely against modernization. While these paradoxes can send our brains into an infinite loop, embracing and engaging contradictions can increase human creativity and bring about solutions. In their book “Both/And Thinking,” Smith and Lewis suggest that humans tend to adopt an either/or approach when contradictions are present (Both/And Thinking: Embracing Creative Tensions to Solve Your Toughest Problems. 2022). However, our most challenging problems require an understanding of the complex paradoxes that underlie them. To understand how to navigate paradoxes in a way that fosters creativity, Smith and Lewis give the example of mules and tightrope walkers. Mules are created by breeding horses with donkeys. The resulting hybrid is more patient and hardier than a horse, and smarter and less stubborn than a donkey. The “mule” approach to paradoxical conundrums requires creative integration of opposite sides of a paradox to identify a synergistic “win-win” solution. By framing contradictions not as oppositional, but instead as opposing yet interdependent paradoxes, creative solutions emerge. Another option for navigating paradoxes is by making small “microshifts” between alternative poles of a paradox. Think of tightrope walkers who never achieve static balance but instead remain dynamically balanced by making small shifts to the right or the left. Rather than getting stuck by choosing between big either/or choices, microshifts between seemingly opposing choices can sustain continuous forward movement – making a small decision for one pole of a paradox now, then making a different choice for the other pole later. By shifting back and forth between poles, a big picture balancing pattern begins to emerge that avoids falling into ruts of indecision. The most complex problems often demand a balance of creative integration and consistent inconsistency – a proverbial “mule walking a tightrope” (Both/And Thinking: Embracing Creative Tensions to Solve Your Toughest Problems. 2022).Image created by Microsoft Copilot®. Prompt used: “Create image of making small ‘microshifts’ between alternative poles of a paradox balancing stability and change.”Paradoxes in anesthesiology Anesthesiologists can fall into ruts of indecision as we ponder the complex issues that challenge our specialty, including production pressures and workforce shortages. These challenges can manifest in the form of harassment, incivility, and disrespect (HID), where anesthesiology is an ignominious leader (ASA Monitor 2025;89:12-3). Addressing this problem requires an investment in workplace culture through training and education. How does a practice enduring the current business and workforce stresses make additional investments in training existing and new clinicians? How does that practice embrace educating residents or students when its clinicians are already burned out? These complex decisions can present as either/or conundrums and lead to indecision. We feel pressure to choose either one path or the other, but both/and options exist. Lurking beneath these dilemmas are paradoxes of stability and change, of tradition and modernization, and of new and old. Implied in this argument is the anesthesiologist's perceived career choice of “either academic or private practice.” However, hospital consolidation, financial pressure, and workforce shortages are causing these lines to blur. Private practice anesthesiologists are thus now frequently asked to be both private practice clinicians and teachers and mentors. Similarly, an increasing emphasis on clinical service can diminish the nonclinical time needed to fulfill the educational and research missions of academic anesthesiologists. The conundrum of creating new anesthesiology residency positions to bolster the workforce in an era where federal funding is limited further complicates the matter. Rather than waiting on federal dollars, innovative practices are now partnering with hospital systems to fund residency positions in novel ways. One hospital system has discovered that labor costs for anesthesiology residents offer a financial advantage, and that expanding anesthesiology residency spots allows for parallel expansion of other residency positions in lucrative surgical subspecialties. These new anesthesiology residency positions also offer a recruiting advantage by retaining graduating anesthesiology residents who already understand the culture and workflow of the institution (asamonitor.pub/3ON9aSz). In another example, a large anesthesia practice has partnered with numerous health systems in creating several new anesthesiology residency programs, accepting whatever federal or state funding it can obtain while subsidizing the balance of funding internally (asamonitor.pub/3ODCr2d). These creative integrations offer residents both an academic experience and exposure to the nuances of private practice. The tightrope between obtaining federal funding when possible, state funding where available, and internal funding as needed is dynamically balanced to avoid ruts of stagnation.Image created by Microsoft Copilot®. Prompt used: “Create cartoon image of a mule dressed in surgical scrubs walking a tightrope.”These creative integration models led to the development of a multidisciplinary collaboration that brings together a CAA program, CRNA programs, a medical student pathway to anesthesia residencies, and a college of business to educate anesthesia professionals on the business, operational, and strategic aspects of anesthesia practice, including workplace culture (asamonitor.pub/4u8trlF). This partnership allows the practice to be “better prepared to lead teams, innovate, and adapt to the evolving health care environment” – while also supporting and solidifying its supply of future clinicians and leaders. By embracing both/and thinking – both continuing longstanding practices and tinkering with new solutions to the most vexing problems – this group has avoided vicious cycles and built dynamic balance between tradition and modernization while expanding strategic workforce options through creative integrations. It is true that the specialty of anesthesiology faces complex challenges that one could call problems. But it could also be said that we have a problem with the way we think about these problems. Reductionist “either/or” thinking may sometimes be the answer, but often “both/and” thinking is needed to foster creative solutions. As a specialty, we can be as hardy as a mule and as balanced as a tightrope walker.D. Matthew Sherrer, MD, MBA, FASA, FAACD, Associate Professor, Department of Anesthesiology and Perioperative Medicine, University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, Alabama.Moeed Azam, MD, MBA, FASA, Head of Innovation, US Anesthesia Partners, AdventHealth Orlando, Member, Board of Directors, Florida Society of Anesthesiologists (FSA), and FSA Co-Director of Legislative Affairs, Orlando, Florida.

title_key: pioneers of plankton research easter ellen cupp 19041999|dolan
title: Pioneers of plankton research: Easter Ellen Cupp (1904–1999)
abstract: Easter Ellen Cupp (Fig. 1) authored a book familiar to many of us, Marine Diatoms of the West Coast of North America. It was published in 1943 and is today still regularly cited. Lesser known to most of us is that Cupp was also a remarkable figure in the history of Oceanography. In 1934, she was the first woman to earn a PhD in Oceanography in the United States, and probably the first in the world. Perhaps most remarkably, Cupp was very likely the first oceanographer to lose her job because she was a woman. Here an introduction to the life of Easter Ellen Cupp (Fig. 1), with a focus on her short but significant, and singular, career in plankton research will be provided based largely on the works by Day (1999, 2002) and Russell (2000). Easter Ellen Cupp in 1938, at age 34. She was the first woman to earn a PhD in oceanography in the United States and the author of Marine Diatoms of the West Coast of North America. Easter Cupp was born on Easter in 1904, hence her first name. She grew up in Whittier, in Southern California near Los Angeles, and attended Whittier College (Fig. 2), graduating with a Bachelor's degree, with a major in Zoology in 1926. After Whittier College, Cupp and her lifetime companion, Dorothy Rosenbury, went to University of California in Berkley to pursue Master's degrees. Cupp worked on protists and graduated in 1928 with a Master’s thesis in Zoology on the flagellate gut symbionts of termites. At some point, Regina Woodruff, Cupp's Professor of Biology at Whittier College, contacted Winifred Allan at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO), advising him that Cupp would be an outstanding PhD student to take on. Allen's field was phytoplankton ecology. He was concerned at the time with the lack of knowledge concerning the characteristics and distributions of individual species (e.g. Allen, 1929a,) as well as statistical analyses (Allen, 1929b). Allan wrote to Cupp asking her to apply to the doctoral program at the University of California and work with him at SIO in La Jolla. Allan would prove to be both a fortunate and unfortunate choice as a PhD advisor. Easter Ellen Cupp in 1925, at age 21, as a 3rd year student at Whittier College, majoring in zoology (left panel) from the Wittier College yearbook for 1925 and in 1935 at age 31 in an SIO portrait as a Research Associate and Instructor at work (right panel). Allen was an “old-timer” of SIO, having begun working on plankton in La Jolla during the summers from 1917 onward when he was a high school teacher. Allen was recruited by Thomas Waylan Vaughn in 1919 to work on plankton and also to write reports for the newly re-named institution he directed. For Cupp, Allen was a fortunate choice as a PhD advisor as he had a wide range of interests, published extensively and was active in scientific societies such as the Ecological Society of America and the American Microscopical Society. Allen was an unfortunate choice as he did not hold a PhD and so was not well regarded by some members of the faculty. Allen retired in 1943 with the rank of Associate Professor; he was never promoted to full Professor. Cupp arrived in La Jolla in 1928 and began working on phytoplankton, focusing on problems of identification and analyzing samples that had been taken years earlier for Allen. She quickly became recognized as a productive member of the staff of SIO. In the publications summarizing the research carried out at the SIO by the director Thomas Wayland Vaughn. Cupp was specifically mentioned and associated, in general, with Allen's work on field studies of phytoplankton, as well as with some of Claude ZoBell's experimental work on marine microbiology (e.g. Vaughan, 1930; Vaughan, 1933). In 1930, Cupp's first publications appeared, one from her Master's thesis on a new flagellate species found in a termite (Cupp, 1930a). Recently, in honor of that work, a new genus of flagellates was named for her, Cuppa (Taerum et al., 2020). Cupp's other 1930 paper was her first on diatoms and dinoflagellates. She analyzed 391 samples taken from the surface waters in the North Pacific in a variety of locations between 1924 and 1928 (Cupp, 1930b). Echoing a problem many of us have encountered, in the conclusion, she admitted that her attempts to correlate temperature and salinity with community characteristics had “yielded no positive results!” Cupp soon began the culture work on diatoms that would form the basis of her PhD dissertation. On 8 May 1834 at the University of California (UC) in Berkley, she defended her thesis in Biological Oceanography, entitled “A Critical Study of Certain Distinguishing Characters in Three Closely Allied Plankton Species of the Diatom Genus Nitzschia and their Relationship to Certain Environmental Conditions”. All of the members of her examining committee were biologists of very considerable renown. The committee was chaired by Cupp's advisor Winifred Allen at SIO and composed of the UC phycologist William Setchell, the UC botanist Alva Davis, the bacteriologist of SIO, Claude ZoBell and the UC protozoologist and Zoology Department Chair, Charles Kofoid. Cupp's PhD in Biological Oceanography in 1934 was the first PhD in Oceanography granted to a woman in the United States and possibly in the world. For SIO, Cupp was only the second PhD in Oceanography and the fifth doctoral dissertation since its inception in 1919. It would be quite some time before another woman earned a PhD in Oceanography at SIO. It was not until 1957 that June Pattullo earned a PhD in Oceanography at SIO. It is fair to state that women PhD students were exceedingly rare at SIO for many years. From 1919 to 1966, out of a total of 103 PhD degrees granted, only 4 went to women (data from Raitt and Moulton, 1967). With her dissertation defended, she became Dr Cupp and was promoted from Research Assistant to Research Associate and Instructor. She worked, as before, on analyzing samples taken from open water sites and reporting on the occurrences of diatom and dinoflagellate taxa (Cupp, 1933; Allen and Cupp, 1935). With her cultures of diatoms, she also collaborated with other SIO researchers. For example, Cupp worked with ZoBell who was beginning to study biological film formation and Fox who was investigating the biochemistry of “heavy water”. However, she devoted most of her time to working on her monograph, Marine Diatoms of the West Coast of North America. Cupp did all of the drawings, many of which are quite striking (e.g. Fig. 3), and took the photomicrographs herself. The left panel shows some of Cupp's detailed illustrations from her monograph Marine Diatoms of the West Coast of North America: various aspects of Biddulphia dubia. The right panel shows the number of times the monograph was cited in publications by year from 2017 to 2022. An average of about 40 citations per year for a work published 80 years ago is clear evidence of contemporary value. Thomas Waylan Vaughn retired as the director of SIO in 1936. Cupp's activities were well in place when the new director, Haruld Sverdrup, arrived in August of 1936. Sverdrup, trained as a meteorologist, had little familiarity with biology. He had a 3-year contract with the University of California and his goal was to transform SIO, which he judged to be a laboratory of "marine research", into a laboratory focused on oceanography, especially physical oceanography. Sverdrup, at first, appeared to be appreciative of Cupp's work. He noted, in his first report of SIO activity, her efforts to work out methods for analyzing nanoplankton and her ongoing work on the diatom monograph (Sverdrup, 1937). Thus, it was a surprise to Cupp, and the staff of SIO, when he summoned her to his office in December of 1938 and told her that she should seek employment elsewhere. Sverdrup told her that taxonomy did not fit within the future research program of SIO. However, according to Sverdrup's letter to the head of the University that same month, Sverdrup simply wanted to replace Cupp with Marston Sargent (Rainger, 2003). Sargent was not trained as an oceanographer. His PhD thesis concerned culturing blue green algae (Sargent, 1934). Replacing Cupp, with her degree in Oceanography and thesis on culturing diatoms, with Marsten makes little sense absent the consideration that Marsten was a man and Cupp was a woman. Later, Sverdrup would outright tell a female student, considering oceanography as a career (Margaret Robinson) that oceanography was a man's field: “My Dear Mrs. Robinson, this is a man's field. You would never be accepted” (Oreskes, 2000). Sverdrup's statement reflected reality with regard to going to sea at SIO. At the time, women were not allowed to go to sea except on day cruises. A taboo against women at sea was as a matter of official policy, not only at SIO but other institutions as well, such as the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (Day, 1999). A goal of having sea-going faculty likely was behind Sverdrup's action of replacing Cupp with Marsten. Sadly, none of the accounts of Cupp's dismissal mention that Allen or any other SIO staff interceded in her behalf. As remarked by Legg et al. (2023), “Women have been able to pursue an education in oceanography for longer than they have been able to go to sea”. In this regard, it is interesting to note that excluding women from expeditions at sea were the policies of oceanographic institutions (up until the 1960s), but did not extend to all institutions. For example, women did participate in the oceanographic expeditions of William Beebe of the New York Zoological Society (see images in Dolan, 2020). Although Cupp's work was supposedly not within the SIO research program in Sverdrup's view, this did not prevented Sverdrup, as Editor of the Bulletin of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, from publishing her study of arctic phytoplankton in 1937 (Cupp, 1937) nor did it dissuade him from publishing Cupp's monograph “Marine Diatoms of the West Coast of North America” in 1943. It appeared in March of 1943. However, it had been “in press” since December of 1940, a year after Cupp was told her contract at SIO would not be renewed. Cupp left SIO in 1940 and worked as an Assistant Biologist at the Naval Biological Laboratory in San Diego working on studies such as the “fouling of ship's bottoms” (Whedon et al., 1943) until 1943. In 1944, she left science entirely. She became a teacher of Science and English at the Woodrow Wilson Junior High School where her companion, Dorothy Rosenbury, was already a teacher. Cupp retired in 1967 and passed away at the age of 95 in 1999. Easter Cupp's legacy is 3-fold. First, there is her place in the history of Oceanography as the first woman to earn a PhD in Oceanography. Second is that because she was a woman, she lost her job as an oceanographer, an event that appears remarkable today. The third part of Cupp's legacy is her detailed diatom monograph. Cupp's first accomplishment has been highlighted in histories of the early years of SIO with the second fact simply not mentioned (Raitt and Moulton, 1967; Shor, 1978). However, in more recent studies that consider gender in ocean sciences, the ultimate fate of Cupp has been highlighted (Oreskes, 2000; Legg et al., 2023). The role of Cupp in the history of Oceanography has overshadowed, and left somewhat neglected, the third and most important legacy of Cupp in plankton research, her Marine Diatoms of the West Coast of North America. According to Google Scholar it has been cited a phenomenal 1446 times. One could say that Cupp's posthumous revenge for being fired by Sverdrup is that her work became the most cited item ever published in the journal Sverdrup edited, the Bulletin of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography. The monograph of 237 pages is today in free access (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/922945w8). It begins with a detailed introduction to the basic biology of diatoms. The bulk is given over to illustrations (approximately illustrations and 5 plates of photomicrographs) and text descriptions of diatoms. The enduring value of Cupp's monograph can easily be demonstrated by a simple tabulation of recent citations (Fig. 3). Most of us would be quite happy to have a work we published still cited 80 years from now about 35 times a year! Apart from her role of “first woman” of Oceanography, Easter Cupp deserves a place in the history of plankton research, if only for her magnificent monograph.

title_key: love gadgets apps and innovative ideas mhiz is the place to be|zagorski
title: Love Gadgets, Apps, and Innovative Ideas? MHIZ is the Place to Be
abstract: Back to table of contents Previous article Next article APA & MeetingsFull AccessLove Gadgets, Apps, and Innovative Ideas? MHIZ is the Place to BeNick ZagorskiNick ZagorskiPublished Online:26 Feb 2024https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.pn.2024.03.3.3AbstractFrom panel talks to product demos to pitch contests, the Mental Health Innovation Zone will provide a host of exciting learning experiences and insight on emerging advancements in mental health care. And this year—double the MindGames competitions.The Mental Health Innovation Zone (MHIZ) will once again be the APA Annual Meeting's premier location to learn more about technological advancements related to mental health. From Saturday, May 4, through Tuesday, May 7, MHIZ will feature a variety of panel sessions and sponsored discussions that will highlight the new tools and resources that are shaping the psychiatry field. For this year's go-around, attendees can learn how to use ChatGPT, launch a start-up venture, integrate artificial intelligence (AI) tools into practice, and more.The Mental Health Innovation Zone, APA's showcase and catalyst for the advancement of technologies in psychiatry, is dedicated to answering the question "What's next in mental health technology?"Oscar & AssociatesIn addition to the expert-led discussions, the MHIZ stage will host a trio of competitive events: the Psychiatry Innovation Lab, MindGames, and —new for this year—MindGames Masters.MindGames (Sunday, May 5, 5:30 p.m.-7 p.m.): This Jeopardy-style competition for psychiatry residents is one of APA's most popular events. Three teams of three residents will have the opportunity to assess their knowledge on patient care, medical terminology, and psychiatric history while earning bragging rights for their program. Don't miss the opportunity to stop by, root for your favorite team, and test your own psychiatric knowledge.MindGames Masters (Monday, May 6, noon-1 p.m.): Why should residents have all the fun? The inaugural Masters trivia event will give three experienced psychiatrists the opportunity to showcase their knowledge in five psychiatry subspecialties: geriatric psychiatry, addiction psychiatry, forensics psychiatry, consultation-liaison psychiatry, and child and adolescent psychiatry. The finalists will be chosen based on their scores on a 100-item self-assessment related to the five subspecialities. In addition to the live competition, MindGames Masters will host an expert-led course on Sunday, May 5, from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. that will review these five topics ($300, space is limited). For those interested, the deadline to complete the self-assessment for a chance on stage is March 15. However, the assessment will be available online until December 31 for anyone to take for educational purposes.The Psychiatry Innovation Lab (Tuesday, May 7, noon-1:30 p.m.): The "pitch meeting" game that started it all, the Innovation Lab (led by the APA Innovation Committee) will give a select group of innovators a chance to sell their ideas at improving patient care with technology. The contestants will compete in front of a panel of judges and the audience, with a chance to take home the Most Promising Innovation or Audience Choice award, along with some seed funding to help get their projects up and running.Even when the stage is quiet, the MHIZ lounge will offer attendees something to do. They will have the opportunity to directly connect with companies that are leading innovators in mental health care and perhaps see demonstrations of new products, ideas, and methods in technology.As the meeting gets closer, be sure to check for updates here. ■ ISSUES NewArchived

title: GENERATIVE NEURAL NETWORK APPROACHES FOR ADAPTIVE BUILDING ENERGY FORECASTING AND CONTROL: A REVIEW OF METHODS AND MICROSERVICES ARCHITECTURES
abstract: Phishing attacks remain one of the most widespread cyber threat vectors, as they combine technical mechanismsfor compromising information systems with social engineering techniques. At the same time, existing phishing detectionapproaches are primarily focused on analyzing the technical parameters of an attack and do not provide a formalizedtransition from detection results to identifying the characteristics of the attacker, which complicates cyberattackattribution, cyber threat intelligence, and information security incident response. The aim of this study is to develop amethod for constructing a social engineer profile based on the analysis of a detected phishing attack on an informationsystem. The proposed method is based on extending a generalized tuple by integrating a set of attacker profile featuresformed according to the set-theoretic classification model of modern social engineering attack implementation approachesand the parameters of the detected phishing attack. The method consists of four main stages: constructing a formalizedrepresentation of the phishing attack, determining the characteristics of the social engineer profile, constructing anintegrated social engineer profile, and visualizing the resulting profile. Unlike existing approaches, the proposed methodprovides a formalized transition from the parameters of a detected phishing attack to the construction of an integratedprofile of its perpetrator. The proposed method was validated using a representative phishing attack, resulting in theconstruction of a social engineer profile, identification of its key characteristics, and generation of a diagram that providesa graphical representation of the resulting profile. The obtained results can be used to support cyberattack attribution,cyber threat intelligence, information security incident response, and the development of countermeasures against socialengineering attacks.Keywords: phishing, social engineer profile, attacker profile, social engineering, cyber threat intelligence,information security. title_key: integrating the slavevoyages databases the database of combined slave trade voyages|evans
title: Integrating the SlaveVoyages Databases: The Database of Combined Slave Trade Voyages
abstract: Dataset CreatorsRichard Evans, SUNY Maritime CollegeThe Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, the Intra-American Slave Trade Database, and the African Origins Database have been described in this journal and are available as downloads on the SlaveVoyages.org website.1 Those datasets were combined and modified to create the Database of Combined Slave Trade Voyages (DCSTV). The DCSTV was designed to make it easier for scholars to explore and analyze the SlaveVoyages.org data in ways that their website is not set up for using advanced statistical methods and software. By combining the African Origins database with the Trans-Atlantic and Intra-American databases, the DCSTV is both event-centric and person-centric.In a sense, the DCSTV is not new because it uses existing digital databases. On the other hand, it is new in the sense that by modifying and rearranging the databases into one, new insights into the transportation of enslaved Africans are easier to obtain. An analogy for conceptualizing the DCSTV might be a marine archeologist studying a shipwreck. First, photographs of parts of the ship are examined because the ship is too large to be photographed in one image. Next, a researcher prepares and assembles the photographs into a mosaic of the entire ship, which the archeologist then studies as a whole. The ship is still the same ship, and the photographs are the same photographs, but the ensemble can be used to get different views of the shipwreck. I have prepared the databases, like a mosaic, to make it easier to model relationships among variables and create hypotheses or draw conclusions within and across the databases.The objective was to create the DCSTV in a reproducible way while encouraging further software development.2 To that end, it is part of a GitHub repository along with the free and open-source R code used to create it from the downloadable SlaveVoyages.org databases. That way, the code can be cloned, improved, and potentially updated by anyone. When SlaveVoyages.org updates its downloadable data, the version control provided by Git will allow for organized updates of the code used to combine and modify the databases.The modifications to the SlaveVoyages database are described in the methodology section below, but they are generally the data preprocessing that statisticians do before analyses (e.g., label date variables as being of date class for easier date arithmetic). The database is an R dataframe and is exported as a .CSV file so that it can be analyzed with other statistical software.3 From a technical perspective, the DCSTV should facilitate making composite regions or voyage routes, or new constructed variables, modeling relationships among variables, and modeling uncertainty about estimates and imputed values. Also, the DCSTV uses R dataframes, which are used in machine learning and AI. Moreover, by connecting the African Origins database directly to the other databases, all the voyages can contribute information to the voyage record of a known enslaved person, and vice versa. For example, it is possible to impute (with appropriate measures of uncertainty) the language groups of enslaved persons aboard Trans-Atlantic ships that were not captured and whose cultural identities were not recorded.The DCSTV has 131,416 rows and 326 variables. It has more rows than the sum of rows of the Intra-American and Trans-Atlantic databases because the persons from 280 African Origins voyages were included with their Trans-Atlantic voyages. For example, in 1819, the Dutch ship Virginie (voyage id 2728) was captured by the British Navy and disembarked 32 liberated Africans, ages 3 to 38, in Freetown. So, that voyage added 32 rows to the database because the information of each liberated African has a unique row and is joined with the other information about the voyage (e.g., ship tonnage and captain’s name). Of course, much of that information is available through the SlaveVoyages interface but not if a scholar wished to, say, account for the variation in the Virginie’s imputed values using multiple imputation.4 Note that only the records from the African Origins dataset that correspond to voyages in the Trans-Atlantic database are in the DCSTV.The DCSTV is in long format, so that voyage-level data for a single voyage may be repeated over multiple records. Data analyses of voyage level data (e.g., counts of embarked persons, tonnage, port of embarkation) must appropriately account for this duplication to avoid erroneous results.This means that for any analysis focusing on characteristics of the voyages themselves (rather than individual enslaved Africans), the data should be aggregated or de-duplicated to ensure each unique voyage is represented only once. One approach to de-duplication is to select only the first occurrence of each voyage ID when performing voyage-level counts or summaries.The principal files in the GitHub repository are defined in Table 1. Note that the .csv files are not automatically updated when new downloads are available for the Intra-American, Trans-Atlantic, or African Origins databases. The commit messages in the repository should indicate if and when the .csv files were last updated and with what new databases.2024English, Spanish, PortugueseAfrica, Europe, North America, South America1514-1866Digital Data RepositoryTrans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database: https://www.slavevoyages.org/voyage/trans-atlantic#voyagesIntra-American Slave Trade Database: https://www.slavevoyages.org/voyage/intra-american#voyagesAfrican Origins Database (previously African Names Database): https://www.slavevoyages.org/past/enslaved/african-origins#peopleA large group of international researchers has contributed individual records and entire databases to the SlaveVoyages.org databases. Their names are listed on the SlaveVoyages.org website and in the three JSDP papers describing the databases (listed in footnote 1 above), and their impact on our understanding of the European enslavement of Africans cannot be overstated.Although David Eltis describes the SlaveVoyages.org website as “Much of the site was built with classrooms and non-academic users in mind,” an informal Google Scholar search of the term “slavevoyages.org” (as a rough proxy for citations) gave over a dozen results for 2023 alone.5 Also, informally, it would appear that the data is most often used to report summary statistics, such as total numbers of slaves, total voyages, or averages.6To take the next step beyond data summaries, the DCSTV was built with digital scholars in mind. Eltis noted the importance of this when making their data downloadable: “To make the imputed variables as transparent as possible and to facilitate refinements, alternative assessments, and corrections that users might think necessary, we have included a download page which makes the database available to users in various formats.”7The DCSTV has prepared those data for easier analysis. The R code in the DCSTV repository combines the three databases and then modifies the format. In short, the Intra-American and Trans-Atlantic voyages databases were combined row-wise and then left-merged with the African Origins database using voyage ID as the keyword. After combining the databases, modifications are as follows.Replacing the numeric codes facilitates making tables for previously coded variables. For example, using the DCSTV, one line of R code can produce Table 2, the ten most common rigs by route:To make Table 2 using the Intra-American and Trans-Atlantic databases directly, the two tables would first have to be combined, and then Table 2 would look like Table 3, where the second column represents rig codes. A researcher would then have to reference the SPSS codebook to look up those codes and enter them by hand into the table. That is not hard for a table of ten rows, but there are many more rig types and ways of looking at RIG. For example, the tables get larger if, say, the decades of the voyages are included on the table to see how rigs changed over time. Tables with region or ports data can be even larger. Although researchers may wish to avoid publishing a large table, they can be useful during exploratory data analysis.One disadvantage of using names rather than codes is that names are not unique. For example, for the principal place captives were landed, “not specified” could refer to an unspecified port in Rhode Island, or in Virginia, and so on. Data analysts should use caution; filter by “broad region,” “specific region,” and “place”; and verify their results.Figure 1 is another example of the strength of the DCSTV. This is a plot of the median non- missing slave ship tonnage by year, with interquartile range error bands. (It is important to plot medians, as the average tonnage is skewed by outliers.) The plot is not meant for inference, rather it is used to understand the database—where data are missing, where there are few points, where there is large variation, and so on. The key idea is that this plot was made fairly quickly using the DCSTV with R code that was generated, as a demonstration, by ChatGPT 4.0.9 The code was cut-and-pasted into RStudio, checked, and then the plot saved as a jpeg.After examining Figure 1, a data historian could first verify the veracity of parts of the plot that may not make sense (i.e., a data checking step) and then focus on regions of interest for a more detailed, inferential analysis.Data Repository: GitHub, https://github.com/revans011/database-of-combined-slave-trade-voyages.git

title_key: understanding how academic libraries in the united states navigate uncertain times results from ithaka s r s 2025 us library deans and directors survey|bergstrom
title: Understanding How Academic Libraries in the United States Navigate Uncertain Times: Results from Ithaka S+R's 2025 US Library Deans and Directors Survey
abstract: Over the past year, research libraries across the United States have faced severe budget reductions coupled with personnel hiring freezes. Underlying these challenges is a political climate increasingly antagonistic to the independence of higher education and the scholarly record. As a result, library leaders are making difficult decisions around how to safeguard users’ fundamental rights to access knowledge, where to restructure staffing, and how to sustain or strategically reduce collections. These compounding pressures raise critical questions about the contemporary role of the research library in a nation grappling with profound social and political change. While such dynamics are currently acute in the United States, the challenges they reflect are shared globally. Thus, understanding how library leaders in the United States are navigating these conditions can offer insights that translate across national contexts. This presentation will share key findings from Ithaka S+R’s 2025 US Library Deans and Directors Survey, with a particular focus on evolving perceptions of the core values that underpin academic libraries and the changing nature of library work. Since its inception in 2010, this triennial online survey has provided foundational data on both longstanding and emerging priorities for library leaders. Each cycle offers longitudinal insights into libraries’ core services and responsibilities while introducing new questions that address novel strategic concerns. This cycle, fielded Fall 2025, explored several new areas, including library leaders’ confidence in their ability to guide their organizations through times of change, how libraries are adapting services and workflows in response to operational budget cuts, the perceived role of the library in protecting academic freedom and access to knowledge, and the function of the library within the third role of the institution to engage broadly with the community. The survey was distributed to all deans and directors of four-year, not-for-profit academic libraries in the United States, yielding responses from 36 percent of all such leaders (n = 492). Respondents indicated their views using 5- and 7-point Likert scales across a battery of measures aligned with the aforementioned topical areas. We will present results derived from descriptive statistics and a suite of inferential techniques, including independent-samples t-tests, correlation analyses, and one-way ANOVAs with Tukey’s HSD post-hoc comparisons to examine variation across libraries of different sizes and institutional profiles. Where applicable, we will draw on longitudinal data from prior survey cycles to illustrate how library leaders’ perceptions and strategies have shifted in response to acute organizational, social, and political change. In addition, we will present findings by region, highlighting how library leaders are responding to real and potential political threats across the United States. The findings reveal a library environment characterized by significant operational strain, organizational change, and growing uncertainty. At the same time, the data also reveal emergent areas of innovation, most notably the adoption of generative AI tools to augment traditional library work. We highlight functional areas in which AI is being integrated and the resulting changes to staff workflows. Taken together, the survey data illustrate how myriad interconnected factors are accelerating change within the working environments of research libraries. We will conclude the presentation with a discussion of the global implications of these findings, situating them within the international circulation of scholarship and students and highlighting how library leaders in other national contexts might leverage these insights to anticipate and respond to similar pressures.
