title_key: what is artificial life today and where should it go|dorin
title: What Is Artificial Life Today, and Where Should It Go?
abstract: The field called Artificial Life (ALife) coalesced following a workshop organized by Chris Langton in September 1987 (Langton, 1988a). That meeting drew together work that had been largely carried out from the 1950s through to the 1980s. A few years later, Langton became the founding editor of this journal, Artificial Life, which started its life with Volume 1, Issue 1_2 in the (northern) winter of 1993/1994.1 This current issue therefore begins the 30th volume and 30th year of Artificial Life. We think this is a milestone worth celebrating!In the proceedings of that first workshop, Langton famously defined ALife as the study of “life as it could be,” of “possible life,” in contrast to biology’s study of “life as we know it to be” (on Earth). His stated aim was to derive “a truly general theoretical biology capable of making universal statements about life wherever it may be found and whatever it may be made of ” (Langton, 1988b, p. xvi).Central to ALife is a debate that has continued sporadically since the field’s formal inception. This explores what should be properly counted as living phenomena and what should not. As a field, ALife has sustained a diverse range of opinions on this topic and has simultaneously investigated even contradictory perspectives. As the field gained attention in the mid-1990s, this was partially responsible for criticism that ALife had a lack of focus, a looseness with metaphor and the use of terminology, and a lack of grounding in fundamental biology (Horgan, 1995; Smoliar, 1995). Such risks were explicitly preempted by Nils Aall Barricelli (1962) as he pioneered digital evolution in the 1950s and 1960s. Similar criticisms, however, have also been leveled at biology for failing to agree on the necessary and sufficient characteristics, hence a definition, of life itself. This is something considered even by Aristotle; countless books, including those by Schrödinger (1944), Monod (1971), Rosen (1991), and Morange (2008), have been written on the subject in the 2,300 years since that time. Hence it is hardly surprising that ALife, a relative newcomer to the debate, has struggled with the same issue, especially because it proposes to broaden biology’s definition, whatever that may be.Possibly as a result of ALife’s diversity, the field resembles more a tangled bramble of subdisciplines than some neat “Tree of Life” (Figure 1). Most of its current topics build directly on work published in the earliest workshop proceedings (Langton, 1988a; Langton et al., 1992) and the first double issue of this journal. Indeed, we recommend that newcomers to the discipline, and even more established members, (re-)read those early works. They reveal that the relationships between the topics were as tangled then as they are now. Arguably, this is because tight classification seems less interesting to the community as a whole than exploring links between fields; the nodes of this complex network are less important than its edges.We venture to claim that ALife is an outlet for the parts of ourselves that are “scientific misfits,” the parts that do not fit naturally into a single academic discipline. This does not undermine the field’s validity, the quality of its practitioners, or the rigor with which ALife research can be conducted; rather, it highlights a strength, namely, that we cherish the opportunity to be creative, to think outside the silos that today’s science can inflict regarding “value”: departmental foci and territorial stakes, government funding priorities, industry needs, financial reward, initiation of hot topics and trends, promotion paths, employment opportunities, and publication citation metrics. ALife is arguably not a straightforward way to meet such goals.We have found anecdotally during decades of ALife conferences, meetings, and email exchanges that a diversity of views and explorations is a key feature that maintains individuals’ interest in the ALife research community. As a community, we prize novelty, innovation, and open-endedness in approaches to our work as much as we prize them in the outcomes of our research. We have also been historically accepting of a wide range of opinions, have been willing to openly debate them, and have welcomed explorations made by hobbyists or professional academics in their spare time beyond that devoted to “serious” research in traditional and better-supported fields. As a result, ALife remains fresh and fun at 30 plus years, and attendance at an ALife conference can be as exciting as entering a new field, even for those of us who have been involved a long time.But, if the field is so diverse, does it have a common goal? Yes, and this does not seem to have changed much in the last 30 years, as the word cloud from 1993–1994 (Figure 1) illustrates. We would add, though, that it is not simply to study life as it could be using a diversity of approaches; it is also to design it, build it, play with it, and enjoy it from a variety of perspectives. The playful aspect has been criticized repeatedly, especially but not exclusively in the contexts of synthetic biology and cloning, where the manipulated media match those of natural biology. One criticism leveled at practitioners in this subdomain is a perceived need to “play God” (Douglas et al., 2013), usually a male one (throughout Helmreich, 1998), with Frankensteinian connotations of upsetting the natural order (Kember, 2003, p. 56). There may be some elements of this in ALife. But our (one male and one female) editors’ sense of the dominant engagement between world builder and worlds here is one of curiosity and wonder, rather than a drive for control or mastery. As pointed out in some accounts of the God-likeness of ALife world builders (Kember, 2003, p. 97), a lack of control is in fact frequently encountered; it may even be desirable (Brooks & Flynn, 1989; Kelly, 1994). Hence the sense of exploration and playfulness not only endures; arguably, it is fundamental.Playfulness is something we frequently see in submissions to the journal. In fact, we wish that some projects and submissions were less “tinkering” and better structured! We need our journal’s submissions to follow at least the main requirements of rigorous science, including well-stated hypotheses; clear context setting; reproducability; careful analysis; and detailed exploration of outcomes, benefits, and their implications. Yet even in the more formal submissions, playfulness and enjoyment need not be diminished; they underpin thoughtful and well-contextualized research in a collective and individual effort to (a) understand the aspects of biological, ecological, and societal systems that facilitate or generate interactions or behaviors typically understood to be characteristics of living systems and (b) replicate the interactions and behaviors of life in media other than those from which natural organisms are constructed.Ultimately, then, our journal’s scope remains more or less constant after 30 years. Studies of life’s behaviors and interactions realized through technology are always welcome. The media might change. There may remain long-standing disagreement in the community whether something is “really alive” (Pattee, 1988). There is sometimes a tendency even to ignore or set aside this question and delve recklessly into biological metaphors; we have been warned repeatedly. But all of this has been shown over the years to matter far less to our community than whether our novel study systems behave in ways we deem to be relevant and engaging.With the design of engaging systems a high priority, it is little wonder that ALife continues to be enthusiastically embraced and broad: compare Figure 2, a title-term plot (1993–2023), and Figure 1, a keyword cloud (1993–1994). Its topics have been surveyed before (Aguilar et al., 2014), even since the early days (Farmer & Belin, 1992), but here we attempt to manage ALife’s bramble of subdisciplines with a simple taxonomy and 30 years’ hindsight. We then discuss the articles published in this issue of the journal, before concluding with a discussion of some important ethical and practical concerns for future ALife technologies.Today’s interdisciplinary study of ALife covers a variety of aspects.2 Not all researchers in these areas would consider themselves to be studying ALife per se; nevertheless, here we describe a simple taxonomy of research topics in this context. As noted, these topics do not form a neat hierarchical tree but rather form a tangled meshwork of interconnected and interrelated aspects that encompass ALife activities. Our classification is not exhaustive. A complete and detailed scope would be short-lived, because the field shifts with changes in technology, understanding, and culture; its boundaries are ill defined, and as subareas mature, they may calve off, form new (sub-)disciplines; and acquire new names.This topic considers individual artificial entities that represent or behave like artificial organisms. It can be roughly broken down into three areas: wet, robotic, and virtual ALife (Bedau, 2003; Farmer & Belin, 1992).Wet ALife covers artificial entities made from “wet” chemicals and their reactions. Examples include chemical systems like motile droplets (Čejková et al., 2017); minimal protocells constructed either bottom-up, from biochemical components, or top-down, by stripping out nonvital components from natural cells (Rasmussen et al., 2009); and natural organisms modified by synthetic biology techniques, such as gene engineering (Hanczyc, 2020).Robotic ALife covers artificial entities engineered from “dry” components. The robot bodies may be “hard,” mostly rigid, stiff mechanical components with relatively few degrees of freedom, or “soft,” mostly pliable, elastic components with very many degrees of freedom (Lee et al., 2017; Yasa et al., 2023). The “brains” of these systems are often some form of neural controller implemented in a standard computer. The area includes evolutionary robotics, especially when allowing body and brain to coevolve (Doncieux et al., 2015; Nolfi & Floreano, 2000); swarm robotics, a population of homogeneous or heterogeneous robots cooperating to achieve a task, from nano-scale to macro-scale systems (Schranz et al., 2020); and cognitive robotics, focusing on the intelligence, learning, and adaptation of robots (Cangelosi & Asada, 2022).Virtual ALife covers artificial entities that exist in a virtual environment as software running on a computer or over a network of computers. The research goal is for these entities to actually live, not to be mere simulations of life (Pattee, 1988). What this means, and whether it is possible, has been a subject of some philosophical debate, especially in the early days of ALife. Life is a dynamic process; “life is a verb, not a noun” (Gilman, 1904, chap. X). Does that process need to be physically realized in carbon-based chemistry, or can it be realized in different material substrates undergoing different physical processes—or can it even be virtual? Does the matter matter? The computational viewpoint tends to say that it does not (Langton, 1986; Ray, 1992); the biological viewpoint tends to disagree (Maturana & Varela, 1980; Morange, 2008; Rosen, 1991). Pattee (1988) explored criteria for realizations of virtual life.Some of the issues around virtual ALife are sidestepped by simulated ALife, which makes no claims about the simulation being alive, and by embodied ALife, which focuses on embodiment and situatedness as necessary components of a living entity (Clark, 1997); a form of embodiment may be possible even in virtual systems (Stepney, 2007). Consideration of embodied ALife includes aspects of growth, morphogenesis, and development (Doursat et al., 2012) and more generally of self-construction, self-assembly, and autopoiesis (McMullin, 2004; Varela et al., 1974).In addition to these of the material or of the and computational aspects of the and are also of the whole living the in a through its and in to and population behaviors and and on to intelligence, all have an computational aspect (Stepney, and all of the subareas can be for in evolutionary swarm et al., & might be at the of and swarm ALife, the individuals’ bodies and swarm collective can result from swarm et al., the tangled of the that is for all parts of our not only for artificial organisms do and in complete They exist as and in of including some and in This of ALife of artificial its with artificial organisms of organisms undergoing with and in the context of use simple of these to for of their use can often have and surprising et al., natural evolution is much more in of population of from gene to gene the of development and interactions between and defined more natural of evolution are the of ALife evolutionary as of in the including the articles by et et et and also such as collective in or and & of biological like these can drive in swarm simulations can these behaviors can from only in of their other and an environment of entities and all of which of different ways of making a that can themselves and & 2008; et al., This of different to and through and & and & and et al., as the can facilitate and interactions et al., and all which to of and & and are also fundamental to biology. title_key: the deposed queen a reflection on crises in religious studies1|imhoff
title: “The Deposed Queen”: A Reflection on Crises in Religious Studies1
abstract: When I started to think about how the field of religious studies has changed over the last 50 years, I read through quite a few essays on the state of the field. Religious studies can be an almost obsessively self-reflective field, and it appears I am guilty of this solipsism, too. The Talmudist Saul Lieberman once famously said, “Nonsense is nonsense, but the history of nonsense is scholarship” (Ozick 2002, 143). I hope that, like nonsense, the history of solipsism is scholarship. In reading the history of the state of the field, two dynamics stood out to me. One of these dynamics remains the tendency to think of the field as both in crisis and in good times. The other dynamic has changed: imagining the field in terms of gender and power. When Religious Studies Review was first published 50 years ago, it was a great time to study religion. College and university departments in religious studies had grown throughout the late 1950s and 1960s, and new departments and programs were still being added into the 1970s (McLean 1957). Claude Welch's 1970 American Academy of Religion (AAR) presidential address discussed the “great upsurge in the academic study of religion,” including greater student interest, especially in public and nonsectarian colleges and universities (1971, 4). Pressing questions about democracy, the Cold War, the war in Vietnam, and race in the United States—all of which included matters of religion—animated both academic pursuits and dinner conversations. Clyde Holbrook wrote about the mid-1960s: “Religion was ‘in the air’ so far as popular culture was concerned” (1963, 67), and students had big questions. Richard Wentz observed in 1970 that the growth of religious studies departments was “little short of phenomenal” (463). Religious studies scholars felt buoyed by the institutional growth and cultural relevance of their field. Later decades were also very good—or at least very important—times to study religion. In the 1990s, as cultural assumptions about the decline of religion and advance of secularism were crumbling, scholars of religion addressed pressing questions about religious trends in the modern world in both the classroom and their scholarship (see, e.g., Berger 1999. For a later reflection on the relevance of these topics for teaching, see Britt 2006). After the events of September 11, 2001, many scholars and nonscholars alike pointed to the necessity of studying religion. In his analysis of the events, Bruce Lincoln pointed to the necessity of returning to the question, “What do we mean by religion?” (2010, xi). Stephen Prothero averred that in a post-9/11 world, Americans “are not equipped for citizenship” if they lack religious literacy, which the field of religious studies helps provide (2008, 148). Today, political trends and events across the world have spawned a widespread interest in understanding religion in its relationship to nationalism, phenomena that religious studies scholars can help illuminate. In short, there is always something that makes religion feel very culturally relevant, whether that is the Cold War, conscientious objection during Vietnam, fundamentalism after 9/11, or the role of religious right in politics today. As nearly every conversation I have had with a neighboring airplane passenger in the past 20 years can attest, every time is an interesting time to study religion. Everybody concedes that grave troubles beset the higher learning and its institutional stewards in America. Analyses of the malaise usually include the financial squeeze, leveling or declining enrollments, curricular anomie, surging vocationalism, pedagogic tendentiousness, rampant specialization and compartmentalization, turning tenure into sloth, and converting academic freedom into partisan license. And each new diagnosis sends academics running for the stale nostrums of innovativeness, interdisciplinariness, and relevance. (1975, 264) The doom continued into the next decade. In 1986, philosopher of religion Carl Raschke wrote in the Journal of the American Academy of Religion: “The study of religion academic venture is pitching headlong toward an eleventh hour confrontation with its own legacy” (131). “The field now must face the wincing fact” of the disappearance of the factors that had allowed religious studies to grow, including, according to Raschke, the breakdown of a Protestant establishment, ample funding for higher education, and the viability of “studies” departments without “underlying conceptual architecture” (132). The field's past had been characterized by growth and abundance, but the present and future were grim. Without a central disciplinary method, religious studies, like women's studies and Black studies, would not have a future. These factors, he wrote, “in which the operative assumptions of the ‘discipline’ have been embedded from the beginning, have been quietly erased, particularly in the last four years” (132). The scare quotes around “discipline” signaled his suspicions about the possibilities for the future of the field. The 1980s, then, were also particularly dismal. As were the 1990s. J. Z. Smith wrote in 1995: “If 1963, the year of the U.S. Supreme Court decision on School District of Abington v. Schempp marks the mythical year of the founding of the present state of religious studies in the United States, then some apocalyptic-minded mythographer may yet point to 1993 as the year of the portent of its demise” (411; on the popularity of this false origin story of religious studies, see Imhoff 2016). Even the nonmythographers must recognize the unfortunate “economic forces” and religious studies' inability (or unwillingness) to adapt. In the 2000s, scholars lamented “departments closing and undergraduate numbers falling” (see, e.g., the conversation in the conference proceedings in Bunt 2004, 161). Throughout these decades, the doomsayers included presidents of the AAR and intellectual titans in the field. These scholars here were neither marginal voices nor spiteful critics. Sometimes, scholars even described a crisis at the same time as extolling the virtues of religious studies in higher education. For example, in their full-throated defense of religious studies, Margaret Mitchell and Jodi Magness weave both of these threads: “Informed and reasoned inquiry into religious traditions, texts, rituals, and practices is an essential component of civic life, on both individual and public levels. This is acutely the case in the present moment, even as religious studies faces significant challenges in the contemporary climate, both in higher education and our wider culture.” They conclude: “We urge its protection and support into the future” (2022, 166–179). Scholars of religion have been lamenting the crisis, the grave troubles, and the withering of the field of religious studies ever since its arrival in US colleges and universities. Many of these troubles and crises seem constant: declining funding, declining enrollment, and a dearth of jobs for graduating PhDs appeared as concerns in every decade. I do not mean to suggest, however, that the issues these scholars describe are mirages or that they do not merit attention. Nor do I think that the troubles are identical: the political landscape with respect to higher education is different, the demographics of college attendance are different, the academic job market is transformed, and even today's financial problems have different contours than those of past decades. We can and should attend to these particulars. But we should not mistake our current set of crises as the first time the field has been “in crisis.” Although the “best of times/worst of times” dynamic is one that has characterized the field of religious studies for the past 50 years, other dynamics have changed. While I was reading through these earlier decades of reflections on the field, another dynamic stuck out to me as I read through past state-of-the-field essays—one that seemed to have changed in recent decades. There are two parts to that dynamic: First, the overwhelming majority of scholars who offered meta-reflections on religious studies were men. Not all (in 1951, Virginia Corwin, e.g., contributed a chapter about the teaching of religion that counted religious studies programs; see 169–196), but the vast majority. Women scholars became better represented in these pieces as the decades went on, as one would expect, given the increasing numbers of women faculty in religious studies over the past 50 years. Second, and perhaps facilitated by the male-dominated nature of these reflective works of scholarship, many authors personified the field as female, especially its past as the “queen of the sciences.” This image of the queen is almost always invoked as part of a declension narrative: once theology was held in the highest esteem, and then secularization (or another villain) came and displaced those big, important questions and modes of thought.2 These authors often see religious studies and theology as closely related, either with religious studies as growing out of theology or even as properly the same thing (e.g., Vance-Trembath 2006). Here, I have only quoted articles that discuss religious studies as a field (although many discuss theology, too) rather than those that are dedicated to theology alone. The narrative of the dethroned queen was popular in the second half of the 20th century, but it did not originate there. “The queen of the sciences is deposed from her throne,” the theologian Francis Greenwood Peabody wrote in the first issue of Harvard Theological Review in 1908 (1). Francis X. Clooney cited the same passage in his 2008 article, noting how the same description of decline seemed to describe his own time (2008, 339–349). References and meditations on religious studies as a deposed or historical queen continued to appear throughout 20th- and into 21st-century appraisals of the field. In 1975, Ninian Smart wrote “Theology was once looked upon as the queen of the sciences; now it is often regarded as the knave of the arts” (1). Later the same year, biblical scholar Raymond Abba wrote about the “fall of the queen of the sciences” and repurposed another scholar's phrase to refer to religious studies as “‘the harlot of the arts’” (1975, 355). Religious studies should be understood as a fallen woman—one who echoes biblical tropes of a sinful people turning away from their god. A 1990 article emphasized the importance of abjection: “Of course, she cannot come imperiously to demand the place of the ‘queen of the Sciences.’ She knows that the Middle Ages have passed. But if she comes humbly to subject herself to the discipline of scientific and critical method on the same terms as the other departments of study, then she has a valuable contribution to make” (Ross 1990, 7–8). Queen Religious Studies recognizes her fall and should subject herself if she is to contribute to the enterprise of knowledge. Less dramatic personifications to describe the supposed decline of the field abound. “Christian theology will [not] be re-enthroned as ‘queen of the sciences.’ Quite to the contrary, religion is now being subjected to the norms of the ‘secular’ world,” a 1974 AAR roundtable declared (Huntsberry 1974, 734). An ethicist wrote in 2019: “Once hailed as the ‘queen of the sciences,’ its status has been questioned ever since” (van den Brink 2019, 442). A 2014 article about political theology narrated the history of religious studies: “There was a time when theology was the queen of the sciences . . . that time has long past” (Hawley 2014, 1631). These images make religious studies into a woman who has lost her power. In this way, these queen of the sciences narratives share characteristics with the crisis narratives—romanticized past, dim future, often a call to do something to save ourselves—and indeed, some articles do both. As Tomoko Masuzawa has recently shown, even this historical idea of theology as preeminent within the university has only tenuous historical evidence (2022, 1262–1285). Yet the narrative appeals to many scholars who write about the field of religious studies, perhaps because it creates an image of a golden age to which one might return, justifies the felt sense of the importance of the field, or serves as a past with which to chastise a field gone awry. The queen of the sciences references are not the only religious-studies-as-woman portraits of the field. Others similarly personified religious studies as a woman who was not in a position of privilege. Ronald Cottle wrote about the marriage of religious studies to the modern university: “Has it occurred to any of us that perhaps it is not only religious studies that should ‘make up her face’ for this wedding but that the groom, too, might be in need of dressing himself up a little?” (1973, 387). Even Cottle, who argued that the field of religious studies had something unique and important to teach the university, painted “her” as a woman who knew she should make herself pretty for others. Few of these authors focused their research on women as religious subjects or wrote sustained analyses of gender or femininity. But others who did focus on women and religion had different observations and critiques of the field. In 1976, in an early feminist critique of the field of religious studies, theologian Valerie Saiving asked, “Is scholarship in religious studies androcentric?” Yes, she answered, and at least as importantly, “That the question is being asked is a sign of a profound paradigm shift now underway in Western culture” (1976, 177). In recent decades, women scholars published many more state-of-the-field and history-of-the-field essays (for a few examples, see Coakley 2005; Jakelić and Starling 2006; Fredericks 2017; McClymond 2020; Magness and Mitchell 2022). They rarely personify the field's history as a queen, and when they do, it is usually to reject its resemblance to the present.3 Male scholars, too, have increasingly left it aside or rejected it (or, perhaps for authors of all genders, not known of it in the first place), though it remains as an occasional reference to a declension narrative (e.g., Olson 2010, 13). The paradigm then established and perpetuated in ever more virulent forms in successive epochs of our history is the paradigm of domination—the coercive control of men over nature and of some men over others. Domination has taken many forms in the history of the West: nation over nation, rulers over the ruled, the wealthy over the poor, the rape of the environment; and (on another level but governed by the same paradigm) the domination of mind over body, will over passion, intellect over feeling, competition over communion, and a patriarchal God over his subjects. (1976, 178) Yet other parts of Saiving's argument describe one of the most significant trends in religious studies scholarship over the past couple of decades: attention to power dynamics as central to the study of religion. Feminist studies of religion were some of the first to point to these issues, but they have hardly been the only. Scholars have both critiqued and built on those early studies to think in terms that now perceive domination (or power, in a Foucauldian mode) as central. The paradigm shift that Saiving pointed to may not have developed in precisely the way she imagined (or hoped), but the cluster of ideas she labels domination has become central to the field. Religious studies now regard issues such as colonialism and empire as not only important topics but as primary analytics. Many scholars study the constructions of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality as central questions—and even those studies that do not foreground these questions are at least expected to note their influence. While the class has played a somewhat smaller role in religious studies scholarship, it also plays a recognizable role in the field. Perhaps one could say that the deposed queen has a useful vantage point from which to observe. In this interpretation, religious studies occupies a subordinated space that attunes it to other modes of subordination. Yet, I'm hesitant to endorse any narrative that paints the field as a woman defined only by her lost power or the need to make herself subservient. Instead, if we jettison the personification and instead see ourselves as a community of scholars (admittedly not romantic or metaphorical), we can sustain our investment in big questions and unequal relations—while also attending to the particulars of the crises of our moment.

title_key: the coming age of interdependence|epner
title: The Coming Age of Interdependence
abstract: Today, health system fragmentation has led the clinical laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, and other departments to operate somewhat independently of each other, increasing risks to patients (1). This situation should improve substantially as artificial intelligence (AI) drives the need for interdependence. In this paper, we present one version of healthcare’s future, which will expand the laboratory’s domain to the clinician’s mind and the patient’s home. We envision a more engaged patient who will initiate care via an AI assistant (AI-A) provided by their primary care physician. AI-A will manage screening reminders, monitor chronic conditions and wellness indicators, with testing as appropriate, and assist with decision-making (with clinician oversight) for new complaints. When a new complaint occurs, AI-A will collect history and patient-generated data from wearables and home tests. It will then advise the patient, using their preferred language and health literacy level, whether to treat themselves at home with continued self-monitoring or to seek medical care (urgently, quickly, or nonurgently). During each primary care physician encounter, an AI-enabled decision support system (AI-DSS), with in-office listening capabilities, will record visit notes including physical findings and integrate them with historical digital data, laboratory or otherwise, and previsit notes. The AI-DSS will prompt the clinician for potentially missing information and confirm immunizations, comorbidities, and medication utilization, both prescription and over the counter. A probability-ranked differential for the patient’s new complaint will be generated. Interactions between the clinician, the patient, and the AI-DSS will lead to a diagnostic strategy [i.e., testing, “wait and see,” or treatment (presumptive diagnosis)]. The AI-DSS will then monitor next steps, including the timely ordering, completion, and review of test results. Whole-genome sequencing, age, gender, sex, and so on will allow the AI-DSS to create a personalized test-result interpretation instead of a standard reference range. If the diagnosis is still unclear, the AI-DSS suggests next steps, and timely completion is monitored. Following an accepted diagnosis, the AI-DSS will propose a treatment plan with follow-up. The patient will be queried periodically by their home AI-A under the supervision of a clinician about their health status and satisfaction. Does this sound like nirvana or a disaster—a healthcare boon or a recipe for deskilled clinicians (2), patient safety hazards, and hard-wired, obsolete, biased data? The necessary enabling technologies exist (3); thus, the opportunity for improved, equitable care is here. It will be driven especially by more timely and accurate diagnosis, itself heavily dependent on laboratory information. However, substantial patient risk also exists (4). How will laboratory physicians and scientists (laboratorians) meet the needs of this new world? Will they remain largely disengaged from individual patient care, merely turning out results, or will they assume the role of key “knowledge manager” on an integrated healthcare team that helps govern the AI system? Most importantly, if they accept that role, resultant needs will emerge across four domains: patient care, laboratory operations, AI governance, and population health. Patient care often requires testing, whether for diagnosis, treatment selection, monitoring, prognosis, or screening. And many clinical laboratories practice “lab stewardship” with the goal of ordering the right test at the right time for the right patient. However, current stewardship initiatives fall short when they rely on gross process measures that primarily target overuse of tests (5) but do not address the appropriateness of a test order at the individual patient level. AI will shift the paradigm from process to outcome and from retrospective analysis to concurrent analysis, promoting “patient-value stewardship.” Laboratorian’s value will shift from performing assays to providing patient-specific actionable information in real time. A successful shift will require integration of, and access to, disparate data systems (i.e., lab, pharmacy, imaging, and electronic health records). It will require a comprehensive knowledge system that understands how the interpretation of data from one source (e.g., the lab) is affected by data from a second source (e.g., radiology) in the context of a specific patient. The knowledge system, likely a commercial product, will utilize nationally developed algorithms, locally modified and applied (6). Laboratorians will need to consider how the test result interpretation changes based on patient factors (longitudinal trends, normal variation, extrinsic factors), analytical methods (laboratory-developed tests, point of care, send-outs), and the acceptability of patient-generated data. New quality measures will have to be developed within and between departments. Prominent among them will be quantifying how often clinicians vary from recommended AI-proposed personalized care plans, replacing rates of guideline compliance. Other outcome-oriented measures will become possible (e.g., time to diagnosis). Lab operations will also evolve. The lab already uses advanced technologies to perform its assays, assess quality control, and support productivity. Automated checks for sample quality (e.g., hemolysis) or acceptance of results (e.g., autoverification) will remain common. AI analysis is likely to support new opportunities for the lab (Table 1), such as improving the prediction of assay interferences based on access to the patient electronic health records, identifying intravenous fluid contamination (7–9), or using AI-enabled lookbacks to determine whether laboratory test results were optimally utilized for patient care. Emerging opportunities in the lab-driven by AI-enabled surveillance, data linkage, and advanced algorithms. An active interdepartmental governance body will certainly be needed to support AI-enabled care plans (10), and the laboratorian’s role should be central. The interdepartmental governance body’s first task will be to prove the safety and efficacy of the system. This will not be a trivial task given the current state of knowledge regarding validation and verification. Commercially available AI systems could take different approaches. Various national organizations (e.g., CLSI, Joint Commission) will need to take a leadership role in establishing quality standards for vendors and their customers. Laboratory and radiology professional societies, among others, should replace their guideline development work with intersociety algorithm development and provide guidance on local implementations, including methods to establish surveillance processes to confirm the system performs safely and reliably. Any new or modified data elements (new tests, test methods, reference intervals, or knowledge) will need to be assessed for their impact on AI systems either nationally or locally and verified prior to being used with patients. System surveillance will be complex and require people’s time, especially those department experts who fully understand the complex interrelationships of data from different departments to ensure appropriate safeguards are in place and the system continues to perform as expected (6, 10). A separate and unique AI application will be used to automatically identify and address patient safety incidents and near misses (AI QC), as well as other quality checks. If the AI system learns through use and dynamically changes its performance over time after validation, new strategies to more tightly monitor safety and performance locally will be needed, and the notion of continuous validation will have to be considered (6). New capabilities to manage distinct populations will also become available. Imagine the ability to identify reduced screening rates and being able to link them to facility or personnel availability or having the system notice an uptick in an infectious disease and automatically notify schools, increase emergency department staffing, and dynamically adjust pretest probabilities in diagnostic algorithms. And when a chronic disease, treatable by modifying behaviors such as diet or testing, increases in prevalence, the system can call for increased classes or additional educational materials. If the disease benefits from more active management, AI-DSS can order tests, building on existing practice in some systems (11, 12), or monitor medication treatment compliance with data from pharmacies. Screening regimens will no longer be modified based solely on age and sex but instead will be based on results of whole-genome sequencing at birth (or later) and updated as appropriate. Other “omic” data will be used for these purposes and also to more generally manage wellness (13). AI will also be able to assess undiscovered correlations between laboratory and other data and subsequent patient outcomes. However, it will take joint efforts from all departments and researchers to discover these relationships. This new knowledge can be used to risk-stratify populations and direct diagnostic efforts and treatment to patients at the highest risk. As new opportunities emerge and are implemented in the system, AI will be used to monitor the effects of these changes. Laboratorians have always been comfortable with and expert at using data. Frustrations about their undervalued expertise typically point to the importance of the data they produce and less often to the expertise of the professionals producing it. Missed opportunities for laboratory data to improve outcomes often go unrecognized (14, 15). Laboratorians have long wished to be less siloed. Their wish is about to come true, triggering new responsibilities and reframing their domain well beyond the laboratory’s walls. Success will require uncovering and managing interrelationships of lab data, data generated by other testing specialists, and patient-generated data and patient-specific factors and then applying this rich information to clinical processes. It will require national efforts to understand and define algorithms but also local efforts to adapt and implement those algorithms to optimize patient care in a specific population. Failure to meet these needs will not prevent commercial companies from introducing “good enough” products, but patients deserve better. It is incumbent on laboratorians to recognize that direct links to patient outcomes are coming and to embrace interdependence with other departments for patients to realize the best outcomes. title_key: language is a virus|modern
title: Language is a Virus
abstract: Identifying emotions during information processing is crucial for marketers and businesses to generate an effective customer experience. The emotions involved in our collective and sustained dalliance with our own annihilation are messy. At the time of this writing—indeed, in the very act of this writing and thinking through—a feeling of doom is palpable. Dread has become exhilarating as we doomscroll the headlines (Salisbury 2023). Fantasies of victimhood and revenge proliferate and provide cold and complicated comfort to the masses. Whether we are addicted to exaggerations of our own ending, or the smoothness of the algorithmic delivery system, or their particular, potent, and poetic combination, the so-called difference between reason and emotion has shown itself to be rather muddled. Something solid melts into air as we are instructed to think about and “feel our feelings” (Beckner 2023). The difference of secular reason loses its luster as we are willingly and repeatedly trained to value our feelings as legitimate political resources and essential expressions of our (well-) being. Which is to say that in this long century of the self, the politics of agency are of a convoluted piece with the feelings involved.1 New advertising copy is necessary. Sentio ergo cogito ergo sum. In Wild Experiment: Feeling, Science, and Secularism after Darwin (2022), Donovan O. Schaefer leans into these complex loops between affect and politics. Schaefer argues against efforts to immunize reason and learning from emotion and for the transformative politics that might result from recognizing the passions of rational inquiry. Over the course of the book, Schaefer weaves together two major threads: a comparative history of affect within rarefied intellectual circles and the lens that affect theory provides in understanding the epistemic practices of religion and science in this shitshow of a secular age. In its insistence that scientific rationality is ever more than mere computation, Wild Experiment is relevant to a staggering number of conversations across the humanities and social sciences. First and foremost, Schaefer’s is a necessary reminder to be suspicious of those approaches to religion, or anything else for that matter, whose explanatory purchase depends on narrowly defined rational actors and their atomistic sociality. In his refusal to portray belief or practice as merely cognitive phenomena, Schaefer’s monograph is an original critique of rational-choice theories and the politics of objectivity that have long marginalized the material and embodied and sensational. Such theories and related fictions of autonomous human cognition have been disastrous for the planet and its species. They have advertised the promise of heaven and secular flourishing both, even as they undergirded colonial and technocratic aspirations. Their testament to the inalienable right to be buffered has also provided ideological cover for practices of exploitation of workers and extraction of capital. The myth of agentive reason has long given emotional support to those living through the degradations of techno-capitalist advance. Such degradations haunt the pages of Wild Experiment. In a passage startling for its pathos, Schaefer writes of the catastrophic machinery our species has built to rake the planet. This catastrophe—broad-based ecosystem collapse, resource scarcity, mass migration, war isn’t going to be like the swift-but-gentle snuffing out of a candle. It won’t produce redemptive misery—the romantic myth of apocalypse trafficked by chic fatalists across the religio-secular spectrum. It will be a long, exhausting endgame. It will mean mayhem, violence, and starvation for every human alive and for our animal kin. No one wants the pain that climate chaos has already started to distribute around the world—starting with those who are least responsible for it—let alone the even more frightening landscape we are leaving to our descendants. (236–37) Despite evoking, with bracing prose, the prospect of decay, distress, and inevitable decline, Schaefer is committed to tacking toward the necessity (and charismatic potential) of optimism. As Schaefer argues, his book is constructive—a corrective to the hyperbolic (and nihilistic) responses by (mostly humanistic) scholars and citizens alike to the bad news of modernity (the violence, the lies, the failed promises, etc.). For Schaefer, detecting the flaws in human idealizations of their own rationality is but the first step in a reparative project that addresses the role that emotions have (and have not) played in the present environmental crisis and, in particular, the lackluster and often cynical responses it. The urgent task in front of humanists, Schaefer continues, is to learn a thing or two from science, that is, “learning how to move with confidence through a world where certainty is impossible, but resolute action is vital.” For “most scientists,” he writes, “have moved on from positivism and are bustling away in their laboratories, making discoveries and crafting tools to try to heal this planet. And they’re making mistakes—in part because they often borrow concepts, like the reason/emotion binary itself, that are the residue of thousands of years of humanistic conversations. Humanities scholars can help correct those errors” (236). So rather than breathe “the fallout of science wars fought generations ago,” Schaefer claims that “the gamble [] is that taking the role of feeling in thinking seriously will allow us to chart new bridges and build new conversations.” The interdisciplinary bridge is what Schaefer calls “cogency theory” (236–37; 20). For Schaefer, something has been lost in all of this squabble between extremists on different sides of the “science wars.” Indeed, what has been lost is the plot of science itself! Whither the promise of an empirically driven and humanistic science when reality is reduced, before the passions of inquiry may begin, to either the certainty of numbers or the uncertainties conjured by self-defeating deconstructions? In Wild Experiment, Schaefer movingly writes that “Academics, for our part, can reaffirm a commitment to truth as central to scholarship. In many places, this is already happening, with a thoughtful postpositivist approach underwriting interesting research in every department. But disavowing the search for truth altogether is just as dangerous as embracing the naive view of reason as untainted by feeling” (236). There is a jeremiadic tone built into Wild Experiment. From 1660 to 1690, the jeremiad became a common sermonic and literary form in New England amid struggles over land ownership, natural disasters, and the perception of moral deterioration among second- and third-generation Puritans. With a long afterlife in the American grain, the jeremiad was both a political sermon delivered by Puritan clergy and a ritual response to perceived weakening of social cohesion.2 Schaefer, for his part, is grieving the failure of humanists and scientists both to live up to a commitment to face a reality that is many-splendored, present, and orienting. And if a full accounting of reality remains an impossibility or perennialist fantasy, there is still work to be done. For as chaos builds outside the scholar’s study, Schaefer laments the fact that the “feeling/thinking binary still has the power that it does in the humanities (and is also why we’re still spiraling in a bottomless pit of debates about relativism)” (17). Schaefer’s urgency to reaffirm a “commitment to truth” stems from what he sees as the need to repair the damage wrought by social constructivism, paranoid readings, and discursive analysis of power coursing through the institutions and practice of science. We are in trouble, suggests Schaefer, and the last thing that the world needs now is another argument that effectively silos off the best qualities of the humanities from the best in the sciences. The key, moving forward, is the pursuit of knowledge about reality, an approach that is nimble and on the move and resists the pull of naive positivism, the seductions of nihilism, and the false comforts of apathy. At the very end of this passionately argued book, Schaefer hints at the connection between climate denialism, the science wars of the 1990s, and the reactionary critics who still insist that particular sciences and particular scientists are not only out to lunch but, at the end of the day, affecting those around them negatively. He then cites Bruno Latour, approvingly: In a blend of lamentation and caricature, Latour writes that entire Ph.D. programs are still running to make sure that good American kids are learning the hard way that facts are made up, that there is no such thing as natural, unmediated, unbiased access to truth, that we are always prisoners of language, that we always speak from a particular stand-point, and so on, while dangerous extremists are using the very same argument of social construction to destroy hard-won evidence that could save our lives. We can’t just teach our students the impossibility of certainty over and over again. title_key: large scale electron microscopy to find nanoscale detail in cancer|riesterer
title: Large-Scale Electron Microscopy to Find Nanoscale Detail in Cancer
abstract: Sadly, cancer will touch every person at some point in time. Unfortunately, this collection of diseases is still not understood enough to provide adequate treatment to all patients. Investigating the structure-function, a.k.a. genotype-phenotype, linkages within cancer cells and the tumor microenvironment is a critical undertaking involving many forms of imaging and computational data. To facilitate this effort, not only do microscopists need to collect large amounts of data, large teams of researchers are needed to provide a complete story of the disease. Here, we will describe the unique challenges and key advantages when trying to apply Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)-based imaging to aid in this effort. The OHSU Serial Measurements of Molecular and Architectural Responses to Therapy (SMMART®) clinical trials aim to find more durable and tolerable treatments for metastatic cancer. Measurements from longitudinal biopsies include biomarker measurements, -omic profiling, and imaging data scaling from whole-body MRI to nanoscale SEM [1]. While not directly impacting clinical decisions, large-format and volume electron microscopy (vEM), including focused ion beam- and serial block face-SEM. has assisted in understanding crucial aspects of breast, pancreas, and prostate cancers, and has identified additional potential therapeutic targets. Next to biomarker monitoring, SEM can identify cellular perturbations with the earliest ultrastructural changes due to the high resolution available over the entire tissue landscape. This level of detail is not found with other imaging modalities and is an important complement to immunohistochemistry (IHC) and cyclic immunofluorescence (cycIF). Our work with the SMMART and Cancer Early Detection Advanced Research (CEDAR) programs has compiled the largest known repository of human cancer data using SEM. At time of submission, 285 samples have been collected and imaged, with at least 50 more expected this year. High-resolution montages at 4nm/pixel have been collected on every specimen, with vEM being collected on targeted areas to gain a deeper understanding of interesting ultrastructural features. All imaging was completed using readily-available standard microscope configurations: FEI/TFS Helios NanoLab™ G3 and UC5 Dualbeams, TFS Apreo Volumescope 2™, and Zeiss Gemini 2 Crossbeam 550. In order to preserve tissue quality, biopsies, and resections are placed into fixative in the operating suite within 5 minutes of collection [2]. Specimens are processed quickly and reproducibly using a Microscopy Innovations, LLC mPrep™ ASP-1000™ automatic specimen processor, enabling raw data generation to keep up with patient treatment schedules [3]. As one can imagine, dealing with this large amount of data can be tricky. Datasets range between 50–75 Gigabytes each, requiring large storage capacity and GPU capabilities. We recognize that imaging each sample at this depth may be considered excessive. However, human tissues are difficult to get and precious, so we collect at the highest resolutions possible, recognizing that down-sampling may be needed and in anticipation of better computational methods available in the future. Efficient and accurate deep learning models to enable automated annotation and segmentation of this data are ongoing development, and are a necessity in order to generate meaningful, clinically-impactful statistics from this large cohort [4–5]. Yet, ground truth must be generated first. Crowd-sourced annotation has been shown to be an effective method of ground truth generation, but takes too much time to be clinically relevant and requires extra quality control due to annotators’ inexperience. In addition, HIPAA privacy concerns may not allow data to be shared publicly. For this work, a CloudFactory managed workforce is employed to ensure timely, high-quality, and secure manual annotation and segmentation [6]. Not only is the data large and unruly, but these large projects also require a different way of working than what most electron microscopists are used to. Data described above is also submitted as part of the National Cancer Institute’s Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN), a national consortium part of the Cancer Moonshot Initiative [7]. These programs require working with large teams including clinicians, making de-identified data publicly available, managing large budgets, and fighting the “light microscopy and omics can do it all” mentality. Accurate metadata reporting is critical for reproducibility and clinical accountability as well as findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) guiding principles [8–10]. Cross-consortium collaboration for SEM imaging of irreplaceable samples is difficult but can be successfully accomplished. An early-detection and early-stage cancer effort as part of OHSU’s CEDAR program is currently being ramped up, and these large-scale considerations are being implemented as we progress. Whether internal or external, these efforts require specific infrastructure needs requiring interdisciplinary assistance. Implementation of something as simple as data access has proven to be time-consuming. Going forward, this “large-scale microscopy” workflow will be needed to tackle not just cancer, but all diseases requiring a personalized-medicine approach. Additional correlative and vEM techniques, such as Array Tomography, will assist in this effort. Of course, one cannot overlook the need for skilled human resources to assist in sample collection, imaging, and data post-processing [11].

title_key: the role of emotional intelligence during stressed and demoralized environments inside organizations|raisani
title: The role of Emotional Intelligence during Stressed and Demoralized Environments Inside Organizations
abstract: Various issues regarding stress and demoralization of employees working in organizations have been noted while dipping the attention of the workforce, However, emotional intelligence is a pivotal role in the stress and demoralization of employees/workforce. The requirement for the judgment of managing emotional intelligence, an optimistic relationship with stress management, and demoralization of employees seems mandatory. The study examined two frameworks/hypotheses that examined the quantity of emotional intelligence as a forecaster during the handling of a stressed and demoralized environment inside an organization. In this regard, 120 (86 males and 34 females) various ethnic employees, professionals, and managers were nominated from the banking sector (Including National Bank, HBL, Askari Bank, Khyber Bank, UBL & Meezan Bank) in Pakistan as respondents for the survey to measure variables including, Emotional-intelligence, stress environment, and demoralization of employees. Resultantly, a substantial association between emotional intelligence, Stress, and demoralized environment were found. Stress and demoralization emerge as statistically significant components concerning the relationship with emotional intelligence. The experiment proves that the role of EI is essential for leaders while leading an organization, especially in stressed and demoralized environments, to cope with any unforeseen problems and enhance the productivity of the organization with high morale of the workforce. title: General Surgery
abstract: WITHDRAWN A Structured End-of-Shift Handoff System Improves Information Transfer and Staff Experience in 2 General Surgical Departments: Findings from the SIPS Surgical Handoff Prospective Cohort Study Jessica M Ryan, MRCSI, Therese Lynn, PhD, Jan Sorensen, MS, MA, Anastasija Simiceva, MCh, Walter Eppich, PhD, Deborah A McNamara, MD, MB, BAO, BCh (Hons), FRCSI Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, Dublin, Ireland; Tallaght University Hospital, Dublin, Ireland; Department of Medical Education & Collaborative Practice Centre, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia Introduction: Poor handoffs lead to patient harm, yet no gold standard exists for safe and effective practice in surgery. This multisite interventional study aimed to improve general surgical handoff using a novel system. Methods: Teams who participated in the emergency general surgery handoff were included. The SIPS Surgical Handoff System was designed using our previous findings and is a structured 4-step approach to the handoff meeting (Figure 1). This effectiveness-implementation hybrid study assessed both the clinical effectiveness of the intervention and the feasibility of the implementation strategy. Patient, staff, handover, and implementation outcomes were assessed. Results: During a baseline assessment, n = 26 handoff meetings were evaluated. After implementation, n = 92 meetings were evaluated. The intervention was used on 93% (n = 200) of days. Introduction of the intervention led to a significant increase in the number of attendees present (4 (2-7) vs 5 (2-12); p = 0.00374), sick patients highlighted (n = 1, 4% vs n = 69, 95.8%; p < 0.0001), priority lists given (n = 5, 20.8% vs n = 73, 79.3%; p < 0.0001), and summaries provided (0% vs n = 80, 86.9%; p < 0.0001). After the intervention, interns reported significantly fewer daily patient safety issues (n = 14, 18.2% vs n = 3, 3%; p = 0.0008) and less patients missed on morning ward rounds (n = 8, 10.4% vs n = 2, 2%; p = 0.0182). Assessment of length of stay, mortality, transfer to ICU, and change in vital signs is in progress. Conclusion: Successful implementation of the SIPS Surgical Handoff System led to an improvement in the content and structure of handoffs with a staff-reported reduction in patient safety events. The SIPS system is simple, easy to teach, and requires no additional equipment or information technology, making it adaptable for use in even resource-limited circumstances.Figure 1Academic Center and Federal Grants Exceed Industry-Based Funding for Surgery Clinical Trials: A National Analysis of Trial Sponsorships Justin Bauzon, MD, Allan Siperstein, MD, Fadlullah Ba’th, MD, Melody Y Zhou, BASc, Gustavo Romero-Velez, MD Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Cleveland, OH; Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine, Cleveland, OH Introduction: Clinical trials represent the highest tier in the evidence-based research hierarchy, but surgical fields have historically trailed medical trials in quantity and methodological rigor. This lag is attributed to multiple factors (standardizing surgical techniques, time constraints), but less clear is the role of trial funding. We aimed to evaluate funding sources of modern US-based clinical trial activity. Methods: This is a cross-sectional study of ClinicalTrials.gov, a trial registry maintained by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). We identified all active Phase I-IV studies (accessed January 1, 2025) represented in 5 surgical specialties: general (hernia, gallbladder disease, appendicitis), hepatobiliary (pancreatic/liver cancer), bariatric, robotic/minimally-invasive, and endocrine (thyroid/parathyroid/adrenal diseases). Using available sponsorship data, trial funders were categorized into “academic centers”, “NIH/government”, “industry”, and “private-public” (both industry and academic/NIH support). Descriptive statistics were used. Results: A total of 150 active US-based surgical trials were identified. Most (45%) were funded exclusively by academic centers; few (9%) were industry-only trials. Trials supported by NIH/government grants (23%) and private-public partnerships (23%) were equivalent in number. Of industry-sponsored studies, most were in phase II-III (71%). NIH/government (82%) and dual private-public sources (86%) chiefly funded phase I-II trials. Hepatobiliary surgery trials received most industry and private-public support (Figure 1). Conclusion: Almost half of all US surgical trials are funded by academic centers with variability among specialty. Sponsorship collaborations between academia and private sectors were not uncommon. Interestingly, industry only funded less than 10% of modern trial activity. Potential changes in federal funding would most likely impact early-stage surgical trials.Figure 1Artificial Intelligence in Surgical Decision Support Systems: Enhancing Clinical Decision-Making and Patient Outcomes Harendra Kumar, MBBS, Daniel Shlyak, MD Dow University of Health Sciences, Karachi, Pakistan; Department of General Surgery, Larkin Community Hospital, South Miami, FL, USA, Coral Springs, FL Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled clinical decision support (CDS) tools are revolutionizing surgical decision-making by delivering real-time data analysis and suggestions. These technologies increase clinical judgment, decrease bias, and improve patient outcomes. Methods: A meta-analysis of 5 research studies comprising nearly 2,500 surgical cases investigated the usefulness of AI in surgical decision assistance. Data sources included radiography, pathology, intraoperative imaging, and real-time physiological information. The study focused on preoperative risk assessment, intraoperative monitoring, and postoperative patient treatment. Results: AI-enabled CDS systems demonstrated a significant improvement in surgical outcomes. AI models predicted surgical risk with an average accuracy of 92% (95% CI: 88%-96%). Real-time AI analysis reduced intraoperative complication by 30% (95% CI: 25%-35%), while AI systems identified postoperative complication early, reducing the hospital readmission rate by 24% (95% CI: 19%-29%). AI-driven CDS systems boost pattern detection and efficiency in surgical decision-making. These technologies enhance hospital productivity via data extraction, documentation, and real-time insights. However, issues such as ethical considerations, data privacy, and clinical validation persist (Figure 1). Conclusion: AI-enabled CDS systems considerably enhance surgical outcomes by increasing clinical decision-making and minimizing complication. Future research should concentrate on overcoming ethical problems and verifying AI solutions in varied healthcare situations to enable universal implementation.Figure 1Automating Feature Selection and Generation on Unprocessed Tabular Data Using Large Language Models for Surgical Risk Predictive Models Yun Xing, PhD, Nathan Wolfrath, BS, Adhitya Ramamurthi, MD, MS, Anjishnu Banerjee, PhD, Yongwoo D Seo, MD, Rachel Morris, MD, FACS, Patrick Murphy, MD, FACS, Anai Kothari, MD, MS, FACS Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, WI Introduction: LLMs excel in handling text data and demonstrate potential for improving tabular data analysis by automating pre-processing, modeling, and reporting. The objective of this study was to test the capabilities of LLMs in automating feature selection using an unprocessed real-world surgical dataset for surgical risk prediction. Methods: The 2023 NSQIP Participant Use File was used as the tabular source dataset. A composite outcome of any surgical adverse event that occurred within 30 days was used as the target variable. The unprocessed dataset was provided to OpenAI’s GPT-4o using a HIPAA-compliant cloud environment. GPT-4o was prompted to perform feature selection. Features were compared with those used in the publicly available NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator (NSQIP Calculator). Selected features were used as inputs of a light Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) model to predict the target variable. abstract: Artificial Intelligence Can Facilitate Application of Risk Stratification Algorithms in American Urological Association (AUA) Guidelines to Patient Case Scenarios Max S Yudovich, MD, Ahmad Alzubaidi, MD, Jay D Raman, MD, FACS Milton S. Hershey Medical Center, Hershey, PA Introduction: Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (ChatGPT) has been shown to accurately predict colon cancer screening intervals when provided clinical data and context in the form of guidelines. The AUA has published a guideline on the management of microhematuria (MH). This guideline includes criteria for risk stratification into low, intermediate, and high risks groups based on patient and disease characteristics. We evaluate the ability of ChatGPT to apply the AUA guideline to risk stratify theoretical patient scenarios with MH. Methods: Forty-six patient scenarios related to MH were created and submitted to GPT3.5 and GPT4. The models were initially asked to risk stratify without any additional context provided. Custom instructions were then provided as textual context using the written version of the MH AUA guideline, and risk stratification was repeated. GPT4 was then provided with an image of the MH management algorithm, and the risk stratification was again performed. Results: GPT3.5 correctly assigned risk groups to 61% of MH scenarios without context, slightly decreasing to 57% with textual context. GPT4 had an accuracy of 70% for MH without context, reaching 100% with textual context. GPT4 with image context maintained similar accuracy to GPT4 without context, with an accuracy of 72% (Figure 1). Conclusion: GPT4 can accurately risk stratify patients with MH when provided with textual guideline context. With further testing and validation, GPT4 could become be a tool to facilitate risk stratification of MH in clinical practice.Figure 1Exploring the Access to Care: Nationwide Analysis of Sacral Neuromodulation Utilization for Overactive Bladder Lakshika Tennakoon, MD, MPhil, Ruoxue Wu, MPH, Susanna Gunamany, PhD, Shada Sinclair, BS, Ekene Enemchukwu, MD, FACS Stanford University, Stanford, CA Introduction: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a prevalent condition that significantly impacts quality of life. Despite its prevalence, OAB management varies widely. Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is an effective treatment for patient’s refractory to pharmacotherapy. We aimed to evaluate access to SNM. We hypothesized that hospital size, type, and location would be associated with lower utilization. Methods: We queried the 2020 Nationwide Ambulatory Surgery Sample (NASS) for patients ≥18 years with OAB using ICD-10-CM codes. The primary outcome was SNM utilization, defined using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes. Results: Among 144,649 ambulatory surgery patients diagnosed with OAB, 15.3% (22,175) were treated with SNM during the study period. Patients who had SNM were more often younger (63 vs. 65 years, p < 0.001), female (85% vs 39%, p < 0.001), with Medicare (60% vs. 55%, p < 0.001), and White race (85% vs. 78%, p < 0.001). SNM was more common among patients in the South region (44% vs. 39%, p < 0.001). There was no significant association between SNM and hospital type (teaching vs. non-teaching), hospital size, and hospital location (urban vs. rural). Adjusted analyses revealed greater odds of SNM management among female patients (aOR 3.5, p < 0.001) but lower odds of SNM utilization in non-Whites (aOR: 0.5-0.83, p < 0.001). Conclusion: During the study period, the size, type, and location of the hospital were not associated with SNM utilization, suggesting these factors are not significant barriers to utilization. However, non-White race, ethnicity, and male gender were associated with lower SNM utilization. Fournier’s Gangrene Patients Reside in Disadvantaged Neighborhoods as Measured by Area Deprivation Index Bryn M Launer, MD, Kate Dwyer, MD, JD, Matthew W Cole, BA, Andria N Li, BA, George Koch, MD, Niels V Johnsen, MD, MPH, FACS Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN; University of Washington Medical Center, Seattle, WA Introduction: Fournier’s Gangrene (FG) is associated with poorly-controlled chronic illness. Neighborhood socioeconomic status impacts healthcare access/utilization, as well as morbidity and mortality. Area Deprivation Index (ADI) is a composite score of 17 neighborhood-level social determinants of health. We investigated if increased neighborhood deprivation was associated with delayed-presentation or outcomes in FG. Methods: Patients were queried from our FG registry from 2018 to 2022. Demographics, clinical data and outcomes were stratified by ADI, obtained from the University of Wisconsin Neighborhood Atlas. ADI scores are normalized to a national percentile, with higher values representing more disadvantage. Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Pearson’s Correlation. Results: Fifty-three patients were included, with mean age of 52.7 years. 47% had private insurance, 26% had Medicare, 9% had Medicaid, and 17% were uninsured. Mean BMI was 34.2 (SD 9.6) and 40 (75.5%) patients were diabetic. Neighborhood socioeconomic evaluation showed the vast majority of patients presenting with FG come from more disadvantaged neighborhoods, with a median ADI of 72 (IQR 47, 87; Figure 1). Median ADI was similar for those who did and did not see a healthcare provider within 30 days of FG presentation (73.0 vs. 66.0, p = 0.86). There was no correlation between time from symptom onset and ADI (p = 0.74).Figure 1Conclusion: Most patients admitted for FG came from socioeconomically disadvantaged communities. While our data did not show significant differences in patient presentation or outcomes stratified by ADI, our analysis may be underpowered. Results highlight population-level risks for FG and resultant health services utilization. Incidence and Survival of Extramammary Paget Disease from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Database Edouard Nicaise, MD, Maeve S McNamara, BS, Benjamin Schmeusser, MD, MS, Gregory S Palmateer, BA, Dattatraya H Patil, MBBS, Philippe E Spiess, MD, FACS, Kenneth Ogan, MD, Keith A Delman, MD, FACS, Viraj Master, MD, PhD, FACS Emory University, Atlanta, GA; Indiana University School of Medicine Department of Urology, Indianapolis, IN; Moffitt Cancer Center, Tampa, FL Introduction: Extramammary Paget’s Disease (EMPD) is a rare intraepithelial neoplasm that often presents in anogenital regions, primarily affecting older, female, and Asian patients. This study sought to investigate survival and incidence trends in a contemporary analysis across sexes. Methods: Data from 22 SEER registries were queried for all patients diagnosed with EMPD from 2004-2020. Cases were categorized by disease site: non-anogenital skin, perianal and rectum, penis and scrotum, and vulva. Data included disease stage, treatment type, and time to treatment. Age-adjusted incidence rates were calculated from 2000 to 2020. Kaplan-Meier curves estimated survival and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models examined factors associated with all-cause mortality. Results: 1179 male and 2429 female patients were included. 76.2% of patients received treatment with 32.4% experiencing a 3+ month delay. Incidence has increased with an annual percent change (APC) of 1.27% in males and 1.23% in female patients. Incidence was greatest among Asian patients, 2× greater than White patients, however, the APC was only significant among White patients (+1.22%). On multivariable analysis, older age (75+: HR 5.92; p < 0.001), advanced stage (distant: HR 12.45: p < 0.001), and treatment delay (3+ months: HR 1.29;p = 0.047) were associated with worsened overall survival, while surgery alone (HR 0.73; p = 0.043) decreased the risk of mortality in comparison to no cancer-directed treatment (Figure 1). Conclusion: Over 20 years, the incidence of EMPD has risen across sexes, with survival worsened by older age, advanced stage, and treatment delay. Primary surgical treatment alone decreases the long-term risk of mortality, potentially secondary to early, complete resection of disease.Figure 1Prognostic Value of Preoperative Paraneoplastic Syndromes in Renal Cell Carcinoma Edouard Nicaise, MD, Benjamin Schmeusser, MD, MS, Gregory S Palmateer, BA, Dattatraya H Patil, MBBS, Shreyas Joshi, MD, FACS, Vikram M Narayan, MD, FACS, Kenneth Ogan, MD, Viraj Master, MD, PhD, FACS Emory University Department of Urology, Atlanta, GA; Indiana University School of Medicine Department of Urology, Indianapolis, IN Introduction: The prevalence of preoperative paraneoplastic syndromes (PNS) in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is poorly understood. Many laboratory abnormalities representative of PNS have demonstrated prognostic value when incorporated into predictive survival models in RCC. We characterize the relationship between baseline prevalence of PNS with overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) in RCC patients following nephrectomy. Methods: Our prospectively maintained nephrectomy database was retrospectively reviewed for any stage, major histology RCC patients that underwent surgery from 2000-2022. Baseline laboratory values within 90 days (closest used) were required. Presence of PNS was defined according to established laboratory cutoffs. Kaplan-Meier curves estimated survival rates, and multivariable COX Hazards models examined the association between PNS with OS and CSS following nephrectomy. Results: 2596 patients were included with listed staging: 1494 Stage I; 180 Stage II; 616 Stage III; 306 Stage IV. Proportion of patients presenting with >1 PNS significantly increased from stage I (31.3%) to stage IV (74.2%) RCC (p < 0.001). Elevated C-reactive protein was the most prevalent PNS (45.4%). On multivariable analysis, the presence of >1 PNS was associated with higher risk of all-cause (HR 2.09; p < 0.001) and cancer-specific mortality (HR 2.55; p < 0.001). Figure 1 demonstrates 10-year OS estimates: 65.2% (no PNS), 52.3% (1 PNS), 36.6% (>1 PNS); and 10-year CSS estimates: 88.3% (no PNS), 79.3% (1 PNS), 61.6% (>1 PNS).Figure 1Conclusion: Increased prevalence of PNS in major histology RCC was associated with a significant increase in the risk of all-cause and cancer-specific mortality even when accounting for patient and disease characteristics. Sepsis and Septic shock on admission can be associated with obstruction by renal calculi but data is lacking.
