title_key: chatbots and zero sales resistence|succi
title: Chatbots and zero sales resistence
abstract: Not a day goes by without we hear of the latest AI breakthroughs, such as chatbots that write up texts or generate images increasingly harder to tell apart from their human-made counterparts. These headlines come with a heavy load of hype, but even with hype factored out, a highly seductive promise stands tall, the promise to capture levels of complexity largely out of grasp for our best theories, models and simulations. Briefly, AI would supplant the time-honored Scientific Method, as we know it since Galileo's time [1,2].While heavily pumped up, this promise is not empty, addressing as it does, among others, one of the most vexing Achille's heels of the scientific method, the infamous Curse of Dimensionality (CoD) [3]. Indeed, CoD compounds with a profound hallmark of Complexity, namely the fact that complex systems are sneaky: they inhabit ultra-dimensional spaces but don't fill them up [4,5,6]. To the contrary, "interesting things" take place in ultrathin and often highly scattered portions of the huge state space available to them. Nature likes to play hide and seek and big time so. An illuminating example can be found in the book of Frenkel and Smit [7], where we learn that the chance of making a sensible Monte Carlo move in the state space of hundred hard-spheres (please note, hundred, not Avogadro's) is about 10 -260 ! The golden nuggets are well hidden indeed.Computational science has devised a number of clever techniques to visit the regions hosting these preciously rare golden nuggets without waiting many ages of the Universe [8]. Yet, the CoD still remains a very tough cookie for the scientific method to the present day.Artificial Intelligence, mostly powered by Machine Learning (ML), promises a new and unprecedently powerful angle of attack to Complexity in science and society. And again, the promise is largely overblown but not empty, as witnessed by a number of success stories: chess and GO winnings, self-driving cars, Deep-Fold mapping of protein structure, stand out as some the most spectular(ized) cases in point [9].It is worth discussing where this "magic" comes from in some little more detail.The basic idea of ML is to represent a given D-dimensional output y (target) through the recursive application of a simple non linear map [10]. For a neural network (NN) consisting of an input layer x, L hidden layers z 1 . . . z L , each containing N neurons, and an output layer y, the update chain x → z 1 . . . → z L → y reads symbolically as follows:x = input(1)z 1 = f (W 1 x -b 1 ), . . . z L = f (W L z L-1 -b L )(2)y = f (W L+1 z L -b L+1 )(3)where W l are N × N matrices of weights, b l are N-dimensional arrays of biases and f is a nonlinear activation function, to be chosen out of a large palette of options.. The output y is then compared with a given training target y T ("Truth") and the weights are recursively updated in such a way as to minimize the discrepancy between y and y T (Loss function), up to the desired tolerance. This latter task is pursued by changing the weights along the direction of maximum change of the Loss function. In equationsW ij = W ij -γ ∂L ∂W ij(4)where L[W ] is the loss function, which depends on the full set of weights W , and γ is a numerical parameter in control of the convergence of the overall process.The idea is that with enough (big) data for training, the combination of (1+2+3) and ( 4) can reach any target, with no need of any model/theory aimed at capturing the causal structure of the problem at hand. Whence the alleged demise of the scientific method [1,2].Put down in such simplistic and bombastic terms, the idea is readily debunked, based on well-known properties of complex systems [11,12]. Yet, it is true that neural nets prove sometimes capable of representing "sneaky" functions in hyperdimensional spaces which would be extremely hard to attain by any other method.So, where does such magic come from?The key point is that for a DNN (deep neural network) of depth L (number of layers) and width N (numbers of neurons per layer), there are P = N L possible paths connecting any single item x i in the input layer to any another single item y j in the output layer. Hence a DNN with N = 10 3 and L = 10 2 features N 2 L = 10 8 weights and P = 10 30 paths. Moreover, the search for the target can proceed in parallel across all of these paths. If you think that this is sci-fi, please think again, as current leading edge ML applications, such as DeepFold or Large Language Models motoring the most powerful "ask-meanything" chatbots are using up to 100 billions weights, basically the number of neurons in our brain. Except that our brain works at 20 Watt while the largest ML models are now sucking up at least ten million times more energy, a point to which we shall return shortly.These numbers unveil the magic behind ML: DNN duel the CoD face up, by unleashing an exponential number of paths, and adjusting them in such a way as to sensibly populate the sneaky regions where the golden nuggets are to be found.This strategy is an opinion splitter: pragmatists are enthusiastic at the conceptual simplicity of this black-box and, speaking of weights, to them "too much is not enough". Scientists fond of Insight, are horrified at the diverging number of parameters, their "prejudice" being that parameters are fudge factors concealing lack of understanding, so, to them the motto is rather "the least the best". There are of course many nuances to be considered between these two opposite fronts, but here we shall focus on just two interconnected ones: Explainability and Sustainability.Besides the exponential number of weights, in order to converge, the ML procedure needs correspondingly huge training datasets. Alas, training does not come for free: it is estimated that new generation chatbots will come near to the Gigawatt power demand, in excess of most existing power plants. The comparison with the 20 some Watts of our brain is embarassing. Given the energy-devouring nature of the large-scale ML procedure, the obvious question is: is it really worth sacrificing a substantial share of the total energy budget worldwide to the totem of chatbots?This may make Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, the richest man on Earth, but still it hardly looks like the way to go for the rest of us, apart the super-elite who may be able to afford extra-terrestrial life for the decades to come. The point is that, even when it works, ML is hardly Explainable, it offers little clue on the physical meaning of the parameters: Control but little Insight. And with Insight out of the game, there's no guarantee that what works for seen data will keep working again for the unseen ones (extrapolation).Of course, one can close eyes and keep going on steroids with weights, but, given the power bill discussed above, this sounds reckless at best. There must be better ways. An interesting clue in this direction is that the overwhelming majority of the weights, the experts tell me, are close to zero, meaning that they do not contribute significantly to the success of the ordeal. This is scientifically very interesting and it begs for understanding, not just because this is what science is all about, but also because understanding here means saving oceans of Gigawatts.Recently Elon Musk advocated the need of putting AI on a rigorous scientific basis, in his own words "Join xAI (Explainable AI) if you believe in our mission of understanding the universe, which requires maximally rigorous pursuit of the truth, without regard to popularity or political correctness." Yann LeCun, one of the most respected computer scientists worldwide and Turing awardee, promptly countered that "Musk wants a maximally rigorous pursuit of the truth but spews crazy-ass conspiracy theories on his own social platform." And, upon being questioned by Musk about his recent science, LeCun goes on by quoting his some 80 papers, as opposed to Musk's zero entries in this ballgame. Now, it is ironic enough to hear one of the most muscular and hungriest AI energy consumers on the planet to advocate the rigorous pursuit of scientific truth. And despite his towering status in computer science, it is only slightly less ironic to see LeCun taking up the role of the guardian of science. Indeed, LeCun, incidentally also Chief AI Scientist at Zuckerberg's Facebook, is a champion of that kind of computer science where the dismissal of Insight in favor of Control is largely tolerated, see [13,14].But let's give Musk the benefit of doubt and assume he's genuinely interested in understanding the Universe. The tip is fairly simple: stop leveraging the muscular power of ML with legions of GPU's and surprise us with more understanding and less weights. The name of the game being causal AI or explainable AI, acknowledging the fact that whenever Correlation can replace Causality, what we are talking about is not Science but Control. This is the biggest lie which has been served to us by AAI, where AAI stands for Aggressive AI, in order to distinguish it from the many important contributions of AI to technology and society. But the king is now hopefully naked, since the pursuit of Control regardless of Insight comes with a energy price tag that planet Earth just cannot sustain. Incidentally, many scientists (most physicists and mathematicians) much less visible than Musk and LeCun, are already doing this out of the limelight [15,16,17].Musk's glorious statement about xAI calls for another comment, mostly related to a strategy that, back in 1944 in his prophetic book "The abolition of man", CS Lewis dubbed Zero Sales Resistence, ZSR for short [18]. Pursuing financial/economic interests under the glorified veil of world-saving intentions is a well-known strategy since long. What is new, though, is the unprecedented power of the modern AAI lords. Here comes the point. The speed of modern technology has basically collapsed spacetime: a single message can reach any (connected) individual on this planet in virtually no time. The result is that a well-crafted message, suitably conveyed by your most seductive influencer of choice (maybe a chatbot?), can win billions of brains in a single swoop, a process called brain condensation [19]. The associated profits go with some square root of this condensation ratio, as reflected by the four-five orders of magnitude gap between the salary of top executives versus their least paid employees [20]. Under the ZSR light it is hardly a surprise to hear Zuckerberg proclaiming that "connectivity is a human right" (to which Bill Gates allegedly returned "Have you ever heard of things likewater and bread?).The next interesting step is to realize that steering the "sentiments" of human beings amounts to controlling a comparatively small number of high-level "psychological variables". This is piece of cake for the most powerful ML algorithms, no point of Insight, Control is all that matters [19].Trying to cure Alzheimer with ML shows a very different movie, one where CoD hits hard, Correlation cannot replace Causation and Control cannot replace Insight [21], on pain of providing to society a cure far worst than the disease it is meant to relieve. Yet, the tools are the same, it is basically the very same machinery described by the equations (1+2+3+4) above! That's why Science is so easily served as a strawman for Control. This is where AAI becomes as dangerous as never before in the history of science: it just trickles into our habits, step by step, pretending to ease all our pains without asking anything in return, "other than" data on all sorts of penchants of ours, food, movies or mating patterns alike. A silent but relentless conquer of our brain towards the ZSR goal. And please, make no mistake, the main item on sale with ZSR is not the commercial product but our brain instead.The motto Why learn if you can look it up? speaks loud for the above. A perfect echo to the comment we find in Domingo's book, where we are informed that the Master Algorithm will do "anything we want before we even ask"! So, while science occasionally gets significant contributions from ML, hardly ever in proportion to the bombastic headlines, what the Master Algorithm does for sure is secure sky-rocketing sales.CS Lewis says it best, quoting verbatim: "What we call Man's power over Nature turns out to be a power exercised by some men over other men with Nature as its instrument" . In more mundane and actual terms, "If something is free, you are the product" (anonymous).What to do then? In the recent years there have been increasing calls to "Algorethics", the idea being of injecting "ethical constraints" into the ML algorithms [22,23]. This is certainly a commendable goal, one which makes the object of high-level agreements between Institutions and AI companies.The question is: will it really fix the ZSR issue? Will it stop AAI from promising master algorithms which do "anything we want before we even ask"? I sincerely doubt it, no matter how good and well meant the law, history shows that the smart villain always manages to find the next loophole. More effective, I think, is to pursue the inherent spiritual drive of Science (and capital R Religion, of course), namely the pursuit of Insight for the pleasure of finding things out, period. The rest will follow, as it always did. Control without Insight, on the contrary, is a sure recipe for major failure of society.

title_key: artificial intelligence for animal science from applications to integrated knowledge systems|niu
title: Artificial intelligence for animal science: from applications to integrated knowledge systems
abstract: AI is shifting from discrete tools to a system-level integrator, requiring a holistic approach to manage farm ecosystems rather than isolated disciplines. Advanced AI transforms farms into real-time living laboratories, accelerating knowledge creation and positioning AI as a co-producer of scientific discovery. The next frontier is a multiscale vision for AI, integrating data across molecular, animal, herd, and environmental levels to sustainably manage agricultural ecosystems. Responsible AI deployment requires co-developed frameworks for ethics, data governance, and equity to protect animal welfare, ensure farmer agency, and build trust. Practitioners should view integrated AI as a long-term investment. Emerging evidence shows measurable productivity and environmental gains over 3–5 year periods, but return of investment timelines will vary by farm. Animal science is at a critical juncture, faced with the challenge of providing sustainable nutrition for a growing global population. Against this backdrop, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful transformative force, offering the potential to enhance efficiency, improve animal welfare, and reduce environmental footprints (Distante et al., 2025). To date, the application of AI has largely taken the form of discrete, stand-alone solutions, with specific tools successfully addressing challenges in areas such as health monitoring and feed optimization. This toolbox paradigm has yielded significant gains and demonstrated the clear value of data-driven management (Cabrera, 2024; Menezes et al., 2024). However, a fundamental leap in the technology itself now invites a more ambitious vision. Whereas early AI was primarily analytical, tasked with identifying patterns in existing data, contemporary generative approaches, driven by large language models, vision models, and AI agents (systems that can perceive their environment and take autonomous actions), have begun to demonstrate synthetic reasoning and proactive planning capabilities (Li et al., 2025). Such a qualitative progression, from analytical to generative AI, has the potential to transform the concept of an integrated knowledge system from a distant aspiration into an attainable reality. It is this transition and its profound implications that this review seeks to explore. We articulate how AI is evolving beyond a passive farm management tool to become an active co-producer of scientific knowledge and a cross-disciplinary system integrator. This article argues the revolutionary impact of AI in animal science lies not in isolated tools but in its emerging role as a systemic driver, with the potential to advancing the entire field from disparate applications toward an integrated knowledge and decision-making ecosystem. However, realizing this vision requires addressing fundamental challenges in validation, reproducibility, and responsible deployment. To understand the paradigm shift currently underway, it is necessary to review the evolution of AI in animal science from both a technological and a conceptual standpoint (Ghavi Hossein-Zadeh, 2025). The application of AI has progressed through four identifiable stages, each representing a significant increase in analytical sophistication and operational autonomy (Figure 1). The initial phase was characterized by sensor-driven analytics, where technology was used to monitor discrete variables, such as an animal’s temperature or activity level. These systems were largely reactive, designed to trigger passive alerts when a predefined threshold was crossed, signaling a potential issue for human intervention. Evolution of AI in animal science from data points to digital ecosystems. A significant advancement came with the application of machine learning (ML). As sensor data accumulated, ML algorithms enabled a shift from simple reactive alerts to predictive tasks (García et al., 2020). These models could analyze historical data to forecast outcomes, such as the likelihood of disease, predict milk production, or optimize feed formulations to improve management efficiency. The next leap in capability was driven by the advent of deep learning, particularly through computer vision. This technology unlocked the potential to analyze complex, unstructured data, such as images and video, enabling more sophisticated and noninvasive phenotyping (Okinda et al., 2020). Through image analysis, it became possible to monitor intricate animal behaviors, estimate body weight, and even identify individual animals within a herd automatically. The current frontier marks another fundamental shift, defined by the rise of generative AI and agent-based systems. This fourth stage moves beyond analysis and prediction into the realm of synthesis and autonomous action. Powered by large language and vision models, these systems possess advanced capabilities for reasoning, simulation, and proactive decision-making (Ferreira and Dórea, 2025). More importantly, this technological progression has enabled an equally profound conceptual evolution. Early AI applications were constrained by both a scarcity of on-farm data and the computational power needed to process it. The proliferation of Internet of Things sensors solved the data generation problem but often resulted in information being stored in isolated data silos. Concurrently, the rise of cloud computing and deep learning provided the immense power required to analyze these vast and disparate datasets. The convergence of these two trends, which are widespread data generation and massive computational capacity, has made a holistic systems approach practically achievable for the first time (Kaur et al., 2023). This represents a fundamental change in mindset, moving from reactive, problem-specific solutions (e.g., identifying a sick animal) to proactive, systems-level optimization (e.g., adjusting the herd’s environment to minimize future disease risk). This shift from viewing the farm as a collection of data points to understanding it as an interconnected digital ecosystem provides the foundation for AI’s emerging role as a true system integrator. The next revolutionary step for AI in animal science is its function as a system integrator (Figure 2) capable of understanding of complex interactions. For example, a change in a feed ration may have cascading effects on an animal’s reproductive health and methane emissions, but these connections can be difficult to quantify when data is not integrated. AI provides a unifying computational layer. This layer should not be envisioned as a single, monolithic model (e.g., a specific GPT), but rather as a sophisticated architecture that allows multiple, specialized AI models (such as computer vision models, forecasting models, and generative agents) to interoperate. This is that architecture ingests diverse data streams from these areas, placing them within a single analytical framework to reveal previously hidden interconnections and enable proactive, cross-domain optimizations. AI as a system integrator connects siloed domains of dairy science into a digital twin framework enabling proactive, cross-domain optimization. The ultimate expression of this integrated approach is the digital twin, a dynamic, virtual replica of a physical entity (such as a single animal or an entire farm) defined by a continuous, bidirectional flow of data between the physical and virtual worlds (Escribà-Gelonch et al., 2024). Real-time information from sensors on the physical entity constantly updates the virtual model, while simulations and optimizations run on the model provide decision support to directly guide actions in the real world. This capability allows managers to conduct complex hypothetical analyses and elevates farm management from descriptive, backward-looking assessments to proactive, predictive optimization. To make this abstract concept concrete, the pioneering effort to connect the DairyBrain project (Cabrera et al., 2020; Ferris et al., 2020; Cabrera, 2024) at the University of Wisconsin–Madison with the Ruminant Farm Systems (RuFaS) model (Kebreab et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023) illustrates the practical pathway toward this vision. DairyBrain functions as a data integration hub, using an application programming interface to automatically pull, clean, and standardize data from previously disconnected on-farm software systems, including herd management, feeding, and milking parlor data (Wangen et al., 2021). The RuFaS model, in turn, is a next-generation, open-source simulation tool designed to assess how different management practices affect systemic outcomes like economic profitability, environmental footprint, and animal welfare. The explicit goal of the collaboration between these projects is to create a data pipeline where the unified stream from DairyBrain can feed the RuFaS model, thereby laying the groundwork for a complete loop from raw data collection to sophisticated, cross-disciplinary knowledge generation. This level of deep integration and virtualization gives rise to a powerful new concept: the computational phenotype. This is not merely a collection of metrics but a high-dimensional, data-driven expression of the animal, derived from the unification of its extensive behavioral, physiological, and production data. In practice, this expression manifests as a series of quantifiable novel derived traits (Brito et al., 2025). This computational phenotype can capture subtle, complex patterns, such as minor behavioral changes preceding clinical disease, resilience calculated from the raw data of milk yield fluctuations or fertility traits defined through activity monitoring data, that are difficult or impossible to measure with traditional methods. It provides a new language for animal breeding and management, suggesting a future where selection goals may include not only traditional genetic traits but also the optimization of these comprehensive, data-defined derived traits. While the vision of AI as a system integrator is compelling, translating it from research prototypes to widespread on-farm reality requires navigating a significant gap. The path to adoption is not merely a matter of refining algorithms or scaling infrastructure. It involves overcoming fundamental barriers that determine whether these powerful tools will be accepted, trusted, and used effectively in the real world (Dibbern et al., 2024). Addressing these challenges within agriculture, informed by the valuable lessons learned from other high-stakes industries, provides a constructive path forward. The widespread adoption of integrated AI systems is hindered by an interconnected set of technical, socioeconomic, and human-centric barriers (Baldin et al., 2025). The technical challenges are rooted in the lack of data standards and interoperability between systems from different vendors, which prevents the seamless data fusion necessary for a true digital twin (Cabrera et al., 2025). Furthermore, while low-earth-sorbit satellite providers are solving historic issues of low speed and latency, they introduce new adoption barriers, including high initial hardware costs, reliance on proprietary technology, and a lack of local technical support (McMahon et al., 2025). From a socioeconomic perspective, the high initial investment and switching costs are significant deterrents for farmers, particularly as the return on investment has historically been difficult to quantify. However, concrete, longitudinal evidence is beginning to emerge. For example, a life-cycle assessment of intensive dairy goat farms implementing an integrated smart-farming platform found significant environmental benefits over 4 years, including an 11% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and a 9–16% reduction in other impacts. These gains were driven by improved resource efficiency, lower replacement rates (−20%), and higher annual milk productivity (+11%; Pardo et al., 2022). Despite this emerging evidence, adopting these systems also requires new technical skills, creating a potential labor gap that the industry must address. The third, and perhaps most critical, barrier relates to human trust and governance (Barton et al., 2025). Farmers are often cautious about ceding critical decision-making authority to opaque black box algorithms. This issue is particularly acute with the deep learning models that power many advanced AI tools. title_key: the challenges and promise of ai for clinical documentation in pediatric inpatient care|levitties
title: The Challenges and Promise of AI for Clinical Documentation in Pediatric Inpatient Care
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into health care is occurring rapidly with the potential to transform clinical practice and patient outcomes. Among the most promising applications is the use of AI to improve clinical documentation. Ambient AI scribes, which use speech recognition, natural language processing, and machine learning to convert clinical conversations into clinical notes, offer the potential to streamline documentation,1 but their effects on health care quality and patient safety remain unclear.Most existing research on AI scribes focuses on outpatient care, with limited data on inpatient use, especially in pediatrics.1–3 Hospitalized children receive care rooted in their clinical course, which is focused on achieving multiple goals for discharge. During morning rounds, multidisciplinary teams discuss daily plans with families who influence clinical decisions. All of these need to be concisely but clearly communicated in clinical notes. Given these unique challenges, AI-assisted documentation must be thoughtfully implemented.In this article, we present physician perspectives from our pilot experience implementing an ambient AI clinical documentation system in the pediatric medical intensive care unit and pediatric intermediate care unit at Boston Children’s Hospital, a quaternary referral freestanding children’s hospital and teaching hospital. We reflect on the impact of this technology on clinical documentation quality, physician workflows, and cognitive reasoning and provide recommendations for tailoring AI to fully support documentation for hospitalized children without compromising care quality.We piloted a commercially available ambient AI scribe technology that uses a medically tailored automated speech recognition system to produce a transcript of rounds and natural language processing to transform the transcript into a draft clinical note. The pilot (December 2024–March 2025) aimed to optimize the AI system for inpatient settings, as it was initially developed for outpatient use. Six attending pediatric intensivists used the AI scribe to listen to rounds and generate admission and daily progress notes. Families and clinical staff were informed and given the opportunity to opt out. At that time, the AI platform operated independently of the electronic health record (EHR); thus, physicians copy-pasted generated notes from a secure external program onto the patient’s medical record. Physicians retained full control over final documentation, reviewing and editing the AI-generated note before signing.Ambient AI can capture clinical conversations in real time, meeting or exceeding clinician standards for inclusion of critical data in notes.2 However, AI systems can mishear information and introduce confabulations (factually incorrect information),4,5 posing risks to patient safety.6 AI note accuracy also declines with increasing case complexity and note length,7 raising concerns for children with medical complexity who often have detailed histories and multiple problems. In our pilot, the AI scribe captured most essential information accurately and was able to correctly differentiate team members speaking during multidisciplinary rounds. However, physicians also reported documentation errors. Many were misheard words/phrases easily fixed during editing, but others were confabulated tests or treatments that were not discussed at all or being used. Such serious errors obligate clinicians to review notes at a granular level, undermining expected efficiency gains.8High-quality clinical notes are not merely transcripts—they should reflect clinical reasoning, the patient/family’s values, and the appropriate clinical context.9 One of the known limitations of our pilot was the lack of meaningful integration of AI with the EHR, precluding consideration of the patient’s clinical course and relevant data in writing notes. Thus, during rounds, a short clinical summary needed to be verbalized to ensure that context was considered. Clinical reasoning was also inconsistently captured because this was often not explicitly discussed.EHR documentation burdens contribute greatly to clinician burnout.10 AI-driven tools can potentially address this by improving clinician efficiency.11,12 Early data show promising reductions in cognitive demand and better clinician engagement with patients,1,3,13,14 although benefits to long-term clinician wellness are still unknown. In our pilot, physicians found the user interface intuitive and noted the platform’s remarkable ability to capture and summarize information. However, potential time savings were counteracted by the considerable need to edit notes. Perspectives also varied regarding the technology’s impact on cognitive load, with some experiencing better engagement during rounds without the need to remember minute details, while others felt that line-editing notes and adding clinical reasoning documentation offset initial reductions in cognitive burden. Still, physicians recognized ambient AI’s potential for more efficient note-writing, potentially increasing time for clinical care and teaching and improving work-life balance.As with EHR adoption, ambient AI systems will likely shift not only how clinicians write notes but also how they reason through clinical problems.9 For many physicians, note-writing is a crucial part of synthesizing information and refining diagnoses or care plans. Some worry that delegating this process to AI might reduce critical thinking time.9,15,16 Similarly, physicians in our pilot expressed concern that overreliance on AI could erode the development of clinical reasoning skills for trainees and hinder optimal care for patients with medical complexity whose problems are often clarified during note-writing.Key concerns relevant to AI scribes include data privacy,11 informed consent, and transparency in documentation practices.4 In our pilot, concerns were raised about how protected health information was recorded, stored, and transmitted, even though staff were notified that recordings would be destroyed after 30 days. Some physicians noted that conversations during rounds were more guarded, with staff delaying sensitive discussions or questions until the recording was off. In contrast, families were generally accepting of the new technology, with all those approached allowing AI to be used.Based on our experiences, we offer the following recommendations for AI scribes to meet the specific needs and challenges of pediatric inpatient documentation.Developers must train models to become more adept at general and subspecialty-specific pediatric terminology, including norms for pediatric data. Confabulations must be addressed aggressively, as they threaten documentation fidelity, patient safety, and trust in AI technology. Safeguards for catching inaccuracies should be built into the system rather than relying solely on physician vigilance.8Aside from greater ease of note creation, meaningful EHR integration of ambient AI systems is crucial for incorporating relevant information not discussed on rounds and providing richer context for decisions. While some AI programs are already incorporated into EHRs in that they can add notes directly into the medical record, many still lack the ability to contextualize notes within patients’ overall clinical trajectory using prior documentation and data.In academic settings, resident physician or advanced practice provider notes are usually detailed with systems- or problem-oriented documentation, while attending physician notes provide a broader view of the plan and expected outcomes. Having AI systems that can be adjusted to generate detailed to more summative notes would give clinicians control over how the clinical story is presented and may eventually eliminate the redundancy of separate note-writing efforts. Moreover, AI systems can be trained to support clinical documentation improvement efforts for best billing practices.AI-generated notes must include more comprehensive documentation of clinical reasoning to achieve a shared mental model for clinical staff and patients/families. EHR integration can help by providing the necessary context for clinical decisions. Rounding scripts may need to be altered to include information justifying care plans so these can be included in notes by the AI scribe. Additionally, graduate medical trainees’ use of ambient AI tools should be closely supervised. Trainees’ clinical reasoning skills must be developed and evaluated through other means in addition to documentation.We must ensure the ethical use of AI systems despite lagging legal standards for implementation. Patients/families should be informed when ambient AI systems are in use and given the opportunity to decline. Rigorous standards for Healthcare Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance, robust data encryption, and secure data storage by AI must be clearly established.17 Ethical issues regarding secondary data use for further AI research must be addressed.17 Clinical staff and patients/families should be educated on data security and safety measures to promote comfort in implementation. Increased transparency about AI- vs clinician-generated sections of notes and mapping of note contents to source rounding transcripts can further support trust. Finally, institutional policies must be clear that clinicians hold responsibility for final documentation.To be successful, AI developers, clinicians, and patients/families must collaborate to implement and evaluate these recommendations. Throughout our pilot, we worked closely with the AI system developers, resulting in iterative improvements contributing to the development of an EHR-integrated system supporting inpatient-specific notes.Ambient AI for clinical documentation in pediatric inpatient settings promises to be a transformative technology that can improve documentation, increase workflow efficiency, and support cognitive reasoning. Current limitations allow for ample opportunities to tailor this technology to enhance care. Future improvements will require collaboration across stakeholders and rigorous evaluation to ensure effectiveness without adversely affecting safety and quality.The authors thank Dr Chase Parsons and Ms Yiyao Barnoon for leading the implementation of ambient artificial intelligence documentation systems at Boston Children’s Hospital and for reviewing this manuscript.
authors: ["Nathan Levitties", "A K Sinha", "Kathleen Cullion", "Daniel P. Kelly", "Poornima Pandiyan", "Michael S. D. Agus", "Christina L. Cifra"]

title_key: collaboration and engagement to support public protection|chaudhry
title: Collaboration and Engagement to Support Public Protection
abstract: This past year at the FSMB we have continued to focus on engagement with our member boards and partner organizations. Our engagement initiative is principally led by our Vice President of Engagement and Member Services, Andrea Ciccone, JD. Andrea liaises with all FSMB departments and many constituencies and is doing an excellent job of identifying and implementing strategic initiatives that ensure valuable, high-quality engagement experiences for our member boards and targeted stakeholders.The FSMB continues its very active engagement and collaboration with the National Academy of Medicine (NAM), on two critical issues for public protection and health care: the worsening drug overdose epidemic, and the need to support clinician wellness. FSMB Past Board Member Barbara Walker, DO, now serves as FSMB's board liaison to NAM's Action Collaborative on Combatting Substance Use and Opioid Crises. The Collaborative aims to facilitate a cohesive, systems-based response to better meet the needs of those most impacted and improve outcomes for all. It is working in parallel with the Opioid Regulatory Collaborative pioneered by the FSMB that includes our regulatory colleagues in nursing, pharmacy, and dentistry.On a related note, the FSMB Workgroup on Opioid and Addiction Treatment, chaired by FSMB Past-Chair Sarvam TerKonda, MD, continued its work in 2023 to evaluate all current FSMB policies, terms, and definitions related to opioids and develop a report and policy recommendations for consideration by the House of Delegates in 2024. The draft recommendations include an update and finalization of Strategies for Prescribing Opioids for the Management of Pain. This document reflects comments received during the first comment period in 2022 and strengthens language related to health equity and the importance of medical recordkeeping. The Workgroup also created a document related to OUD Treatment that provides information on major legislative and regulatory changes that have occurred in the OUD treatment space since the formation of the Workgroup, including the removal of the “X-Waiver” and updated DEA telemedicine prescribing rules. The document also provides a list of principles that can be utilized when evaluating treatment for patients with OUD and an extensive set of resources for state medical boards and prescribers.We are also continuing our involvement with NAM's Action Collaborative on Clinician Well-Being and Resilience. FSMB's Past Chair Art Hengerer, MD, has served as FSMB's liaison to the Collaborative from the beginning, in 2017, and the effort relies on a network of more than 200 organizations committed to reversing trends in clinician burnout. In 2022, the group created a meaningful National Plan for Health Workforce Well-Being.Given the pace of advancement in generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the fact that some physicians are already using AI tools in their practices, it will be challenging for state medical boards to stay current on key AI trends while also advancing thoughtful legislation to better protect the public. The FSMB hopes to fill knowledge and regulatory gaps in this dynamic space in a variety of ways. Our Ethics and Professionalism Committee, chaired by Board Member Mark Woodland, MD, has been tasked by FSMB Chair Jeffrey Carter, MD, with identifying ethical principles to help inform potential medical regulatory considerations for state medical boards as they begin to encounter the application of AI in clinical practice. We held a successful symposium for our member boards on “AI in Health Care and Medical Regulation” in Washington, DC in January, to discuss AI with stakeholders from government, industry, and academia. The FSMB will keep a watchful eye on developments in AI for state medical boards and continue our own analysis of how AI might advance quality health care while limiting patient harm.After a robust search, I am pleased that Mark A. Bechtel, MD, a Professor and Chair of the Department of Dermatology at Ohio State University College of Medicine, was appointed as the next Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Medical Regulation. Dr. Bechtel began his 5-year term of service on May 1, 2023, and is working diligently to ensure that JMR continues to serve as a primary vehicle through which the US and international medical regulatory community exchanges new knowledge and best practices about physician licensure, discipline, and regulation.In November 2023, alongside several FSMB leaders and staff, I had the privilege of attending the 15th Biennial Conference on Medical Regulation in Bali, Indonesia, the first in person meeting of the International Association of Medical Regulation Authorities (IAMRA) since the COVID-19 pandemic. The theme of the conference was “Regulation in a Disrupted World: Challenges and Opportunities.” IAMRA members and partners from around the world came together to share their experiences in a disrupted world. The conference marked the first time that a member of the staff of a state medical board in the United States was elected Chair-elect. We extend our heartiest congratulations to Nicole Krishnaswami, JD, Executive Director of the Oregon Medical Board, as she undertakes this exciting role.In 2023, the FSMB initiated a strategic communications and branding project to enhance our messaging to more clearly articulate the resources and services we offer our member boards and customers. This work was done in tandem with the work of FSMB's Strategic Planning Committee to ensure that the mission, vision, and future direction of the organization are reflected in the recommendations about messaging and communications for the organization. Over the course of 2024, FSMB will be delivering a revamped brand platform and messaging to better meet the needs of our members, as well as a refreshed visual identity to ensure a seamless experience across all FSMB service areas, communications materials, and digital platforms.The FSMB and Administrators in Medicine (AIM) have collaborated to develop a Certified Medical Board Licensing Specialist (CMBLS) training program. The program was developed for licensing specialists in our state medical and osteopathic boards. It is comprised of six virtual modules and one in-person, full day meeting that culminates in participants earning a certificate as a Medical Board Licensing Specialist. The content includes education on various aspects of the licensing process, including licensing related documentation (eg, primary source verification credentials), and organizations that support the licensing process (eg, NME, FSMB, and NBOME, and accreditation organizations for UME and GME in the US and Canada). Participants have the opportunity to network with their counterparts in other states and have monthly assignments that require collaboration with a partner in another jurisdiction. The inaugural program began in November 2023 and concludes in July 2024. Currently, there are 22 participants from 17 different member boards.The FSMB recognizes that physicians may take a temporary leave from practice for a variety of reasons, and that physician re-entry can be a normal part of a physician's career. Decisions about re-entry, however, are often challenging for state medical boards as questions arise about how long a physician can be away from practice before needing additional training, what type of processes should be involved in each individual case, what factors are relevant for maintaining competence while out of practice and many more. To address these challenges, Dr. Carter established the Workgroup on Physician Reentry to Practice, chaired by Board Member George Abraham, MD, to review and update current FSMB guidance, bringing it in line with the experiences of state medical boards and making sure it is informed by expert opinion, while also removing stigma around physicians’ decisions to take leaves from practice.Resident training licenses were the subject of another workgroup created by Dr. Carter, the Workgroup on Physicians in Training, that was chaired by Board Member Andrea Anderson, MD. Not every jurisdiction requires licensing of medical residents and fellows, but the workgroup has made some helpful draft recommendations about their value. The workgroup is also recommending support for the advancement of resident training licensure portability, to enable residents to cross state lines and obtain knowledge and skills otherwise not available in their training programs.Finally, I'd like to take this opportunity to say that I am very grateful this past year to Dr. Carter, who has worked tirelessly in his role as FSMB Chair to champion actions and services that directly and indirectly benefit our member boards and the public they protect. It has been an honor to work along-side him with our passionate and energetic board of directors and staff.

title_key: catering to today s need for new human capitalism|sampson
title: Catering to Today's Need for New Human Capitalism
abstract: You might have seen the reel on social media: Some Gen Xer reflecting on their childhood to humblebrag that they basically raised themselves and survived some near-death experience that seemed like a jolly good idea at the time because, in their defense, they were left unsupervised. Sure, but that was a very different time. One feature of that freedom was that, sometimes, we were fortunate to be present (actually, held hostage) in adult settings and observe because, back then, we were seen but not heard. Those observation-only interactions are where I learned how to be a good host because my mother loved to host a good party. I know now that the best experiences are carefully planned to cater to people's unique needs in spaces where they can relax, be themselves, and just be present. And the secret to any good gathering is the right mix of people. At our human core, we want to be ourselves and belong to something. We desire close friendships, a happy family, a sustaining community or collective, a high-performing team. Healthcare leaders realize this while navigating school years. Yet, as we rise in the profession, we may have set aside these carefully honed social skills in pursuit of organizational goals. We may even have asked our employees to leave their home lives at the door once they come to work. Then, four years ago with the arrival of COVID-19, we all quickly reckoned with a different reality. Times changed. Facing burnout, attrition, costly quick fixes to fill work schedules, and union organizing, we eagerly agreed that our people matter and we must cater to their needs. The task has become delivering on that promise for every employee at every level of the organization—mass customization over one-size-fits-all. Enter new human capital strategies. Maslow's theory of human motivation comes to mind. It is based on five rising levels of needs: physiological, safety, social, ego, and self-actualizing. As applied to the workplace, the theory suggests that employees ascend to different levels that must be satisfied so that they can stay fully engaged and productive. Appreciation for the levels of Maslow's pyramid is mandatory for employee engagement success. The physiological needs on the bottom translate to the minimum work requirements of a fair salary, a safe work environment, and the tools and resources to do the specified job. Employees at this level are not engaged and are primed for the next opportunity that will better satisfy these basic needs. Once met, safety and security needs translate to protection from discrimination and harassment, clear expectations, and consistent feedback. Still unhappy, these employees are disengaged from the organization and could well be job searching. The personal need for belonging translates to the workplace need for positive relationships with colleagues, managers, and patients, as well as team spirit and collaboration. Although not actively searching, they are not yet engaged. Once met, the need for esteem translates to recognition and respect in the form of appreciation, praise, rewards, and growth opportunities. It is only here that engaged employees believe that they are an essential part of the organization. The apex of Maslow's hierarchy—self-actualization—is achieved after the lower-order needs are satisfied, and that is precisely where employees are highly engaged and deliver the innovation to advance the field. The effort is not easy, but it is doable. This issue of Frontiers of Health Services Management includes examples of successful strategic human resources management. We asked contributors in healthcare to share how they were creatively solving workforce issues at their organizations. In This Issue One persistent challenge in the wake of clinician shortages—registered nurses (RN), in particular—is enabling team members to contentedly practice at the top of their licenses in team-based models. Kathleen D. Sanford, FACHE, executive vice president and CNO at CommonSpirit Health, outlines the system's evidence-based approach to collaborative team-based models. She shares plans to surmount the barriers posed by complex factors such as culture, laws, regulations, and reimbursement systems. Given the breadth of CommonSpirit's operations in 23 states, her story highlights how these approaches must vary for different markets. Kecia M. Kelly, FACHE, senior vice president and CNO at Legacy Health, describes strategies to coach new nursing graduates and support the development of current employees. Legacy Health's comprehensive approach has netted strong gains in nurse residents hired in the past four years and scored reductions in RN turnover and vacancy percentages in the same period. In her words, “[Legacy Health leaders] have not yet won the war but have been able to enjoy solid wins through collaboration and innovation.” A key piece of this puzzle is employee engagement. Ron C. Werft, FACHE, president and CEO of Cottage Health in Santa Barbara, California, describes the “what” and “how” efforts that Cottage Health leadership emphasizes to build the core competencies that are crucial to good care. “Each of these ‘what’ initiatives has been effective in recruiting and retaining certain staff categories. However, the most valuable investment has been the ‘how’ through system-wide shared governance, the creation of a culture of engagement, belonging, and alignment,” he writes. Byron Hunter, FACHE, executive director of population health strategy and innovation, and colleagues at JPS Health Network explain how JPS Health is working to advance health equity with the development of a collaborative community-based pilot program. They leverage Agile principles (the topic of our Winter 2023 issue) to engage stakeholders and rapidly deploy programs to support healthcare beyond the walls. Pulling this off requires strategic workforce development. Finally, we revisit the archives as we continue to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Frontiers. It appears we were talking about diversity management 30 years ago! Consultants Lee Gardenswartz and Anita Rowe outline a practical application for diversity management. They remind us that workforce engagement was no walk in the park in 1994, either. “[The] organization is analogous to a human system whose primary function is to sustain and perpetuate itself. Any outside intervention is viewed as threatening, so the system closes to protect itself from intrusion,” they write. “Sheer inertia will keep the system moving on its own steady course; hence, organizational and personal responses to change almost guarantee that reversing or changing direction will not happen easily.” Continuing the Conversation Strategic human resources management understands that having the right people with the right skill set in the right number cannot be taken for granted. The flow of trained health professionals is crimped all along the workforce pipeline. Early retirements and career changes exceed the inflow as well-trained individuals opt for new opportunities that do not require long hours away from home and family. Yesterday's capitalism, notably human capitalism, no longer holds sway for many of them. Thus, there is not one simple problem for which we derive a single solution but rather tensions that must be delicately balanced. What are today's healthcare leaders to do? Just for fun, I asked BingChat (powered by GPT 4) what leaders should do to engage healthcare employees. It did not fare too badly in its generative ideas, although the responses required some editing for me to share here: Communicate the vision, mission, and goals of the organization and how each employee contributes to them. Provide clear and specific guidance, feedback, and expectations for each task and role. Communicate frequently and transparently with employees, especially during times of uncertainty and change. Listen to their concerns, suggestions, and feedback, and involve them in decision-making processes. Support employees' learning and development by providing coaching, mentoring, and training opportunities. Encourage them to pursue their passions, interests, and strengths, and work toward new goals and experiences. Foster a positive and inclusive work culture that values diversity, collaboration, and innovation. Promote a sense of belonging and community among employees and celebrate their achievements and successes. Reward employees fairly and generously for their performance and contributions. Offer nonmonetary incentives, such as recognition, praise, feedback, and time off, that align with their preferences and motivations. True to the AI nature of BingChat, most, if not all, these points could have been lifted from this or previous issues of Frontiers. After you peruse the articles in this issue, let's continue this conversation at [email protected] or at the 2024 Congress on Healthcare Leadership March 25–28 in Chicago.

title_key: aapor presidential address aapor presidential address 2026 bearing witness to this moment|peugh
title: AAPOR Presidential Address AAPOR Presidential Address 2026: Bearing Witness to This Moment
abstract: When I first became AAPOR’s vice president/president-elect in 2024, I thought I might focus my presidential address on something like “the business of research,” reflecting my perspective as chief business officer of a research company and considering how the association might think about its financial stability and growth. Then in 2025, a little something happened… A new administration arrived and took a chainsaw to the statistical and scientific institutions of this country. A national leader sued and threatened some of the most public faces of our industry. And the economic fallout of these and other actions shook our industry to the core. Once I got out of the fetal position, I had to grapple with new priorities for my AAPOR presidency. So today, what I want to do is bear witness to this time we are living through and provide hope for the future. There are four things I will reflect on: the moment we are in; the work we do; the community that makes that work possible; and how we respond to these times. I want to present not just my own voice, but those across our community. To do so, I have talked to members from a wide variety of fields, experiences, and circumstances. I share their views, along with my own, and I thank them for the honesty, vulnerability, and inspiration they gave me. We are living through a period of profound instability in the systems that produce and protect evidence. The federal statistical system—one of the pillars of how we understand this country—has faced extraordinary pressure. Programs have been halted. Funding has been threatened or withdrawn. Statistical leaders have been dismissed. Institutions designed to operate independently have faced increasing political pressure. Many of us have lost our jobs or found our work threatened. The American Statistical Association reported that all 13 federal statistical agencies lost staff in 2025, with some, like the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)—at least temporarily—almost totally demolished (American Statistical Association 2025). The shuttering of USAID halted critical research projects and is projected to lead to a staggering number of avoidable deaths (Cavalcanti et al. 2025). These systems were built over decades. The people who have dedicated their lives to these objectives have created a body of knowledge that is essential to understanding the way we live and how that changes—the statisticians and survey methodologists, analysts and researchers, project managers and directors, contractors and subcontractors. There has been messaging through DOGE actions and other high-level communications that the work of these individuals is biased, wasteful, unneeded, or worse. Many of those people are members of this community. And this rhetoric and these actions are having a profound effect. One experienced federal researcher told me she was considering getting out of the field altogether. She couldn’t see a path forward for herself. We are losing some of our greatest assets and future leaders. For those that remain, we bear witness to their integrity, persistence, and quiet professionalism as they continue to produce evidence when the environment around them is uncertain and unsupportive. We see and empathize with the “survivors’ guilt” many experience. We also recognize the disruption in the lives of many who have lost their positions and now face remaking their careers. They must do so at a time when uncertainty and trepidation have affected the entire industry, making it a less-than-hospitable place for job seekers and career changers. A displaced federal worker I spoke to said she feels a sense of grief and loss. Grieving not only for her own personal losses, but for the bigger picture of what is happening to federal government data collection, to public health research, and to the scientific community. I spoke to a small business owner who saw critical work that she and her colleagues had done shelved, to possibly never see the light of day. A graduate student shared with me the challenges she has experienced—having her research funding terminated, seeing fewer placements for her fellow students at universities, and being forced to grapple with new worries about her international student status. She said, “When I was coming to the US, I didn’t think that I would have to worry that scientific research could be compromised in a country like this.” Others shared: “The last 18 months have felt like a ticking countdown clock”; “The institutional knowledge we have lost will take years to recover”; and “The foundation is shakier than I thought.” I want to acknowledge the extreme stress that has characterized our field and so many of our members in 2025 and 2026 and bear witness to the professional and personal toll this has taken. Next, I want to talk about the importance of our work. At its core, what we do is deceptively simple. We ask people about their lives—how they live, think, work, and experience the world. We do so carefully, systematically, and with the goal of understanding more than just the loudest voices. The importance of that work becomes clearer in moments like this, when increasingly, we are living in a world where the idea of shared evidence itself is contested. Where data can be dismissed because it is inconvenient. Where research can be labeled fraudulent if it challenges power. Some specific examples of this are the lawsuits against Ann Selzer (Doyle 2024); the litigation threats to the New York Times (Svirnovskiy 2026), CNN (Grynbaum and Haberman 2020), and their research partners; the demand for cancellation of programs deemed focused on DEI (Exec. Order No. 14151 2025; Hsu 2025); and the removal of nonbinary gender categories from federal research (Exec. Order No. 14168 2025), to name just a few. This runs counter to everything our field stands for. We may never measure perfectly. But through rigorous methods and transparency, we highlight the experiences, hopes, and fears of everyday Americans. In a democracy, that matters. Because governing without understanding the public is governing in the dark. What we produce is not just data. It is a record. A record of what people think, what they experience, and how society is changing. We must protect that, celebrate it, and feel pride in the importance of the work that we do. A researcher at the Census told me that she was most proud to be part of a system where, despite current narratives, the goal is to “measure truth, to the best of our ability, across time, across administrations, and across events.” Through all of this, the work continues. A statistician at a large research company spoke of his pride in what we do. He said, “Linking what people are thinking and saying to policy has never been more important.” I now want to reflect on the community, because this work does not happen in isolation. It depends on a diverse and interdependent community. The work we do is the product of government, academia, nonprofit organizations, and the private sector. Each plays a distinct role. Government statisticians establish benchmarks. Academics develop and test new ideas and train future researchers. Nonprofit and election researchers help us understand civic life. And commercial researchers innovate—finding ways to make data collection more scalable and accessible. We often approach problems differently. We use different methods. We operate under different constraints. We do not always agree (looking at you, AAPORnet). We debate probability and nonprobability sampling (boy, do we debate probability and nonprobability sampling!). We debate qualitative and quantitative approaches. We debate new tools, new data sources, and, more recently, artificial intelligence. These debates can be intense. They can feel divisive. But they exist because we are all trying to answer the same questions: How do we understand people accurately? How do we do this work responsibly? And how do we do it within real-world budgetary and time constraints? Our disagreements are a sign of a healthy scientific community—a community that makes our work possible, improves it, and, at times, helps us bear it. Multiple people I spoke to talked about the importance of having people to turn to that believe in the work that we do, to bounce ideas off of, to call when we need questions answered. A sympathetic human to talk to, not an obsequious chatbot. The government employees I spoke to remarked on how important this community has been in making it possible to keep going when they felt disparaged, and in helping make connections in the search for a new opportunity. A private-sector researcher reflected on how we share expertise to improve the work for us all, even when there could be commercial reasons for not doing so. A multicultural researcher noted that perhaps our recent struggles have brought us together. She said, “I have co-pollinated with so many others that I wouldn’t have before, because we’re working through the same struggles.” A methodologist at a start-up company noted that through all this craziness, he is seeing more acceptance and creativity in our community; more openness to the wide variety of practices and innovations. I can see frustration among our ranks as we debate how to respond to today’s challenges, how to move forward, how to value and publicize what we do. Some have called for the community to have a stronger voice. Some have expressed that doing so would put their membership at risk. Some have suggested our separating ourselves based on method. Some have felt marginalized, seeing the work that they do categorized as lesser. I urge our community to recognize that what unites us is more important than our differences. Remember that your fellow researchers are seeking to do just what you are doing—increase our understanding of a given population or issue. They may be doing it with different methods, budgets, and styles, but we are united in seeking clarity, and we are family in this enterprise. Be kind to each other. Seek to understand and empathize. Show respect for your fellow researcher, even if the work that they do seems only marginally connected in our big Venn diagram of the research industry (see figure 1). Humorous Venn diagram depicting our shared commitment to research. Now, what do we do with all of this? How will we respond to this moment—not just endure it, but build a more resilient, innovative, and inclusive future for our field? This is why AAPOR is so important. Through AAPOR we can support the work and strengthen the community that makes it possible. AAPOR facilitates the critical work of public opinion research by creating task forces, providing forums for debate and discussion, educating on best practices, and evolving standards for the industry. Our work on cell phone samples and text messaging has paved the way for the wide use of new methodological tools. Our pre-election polling task forces have changed the way we conduct and talk about election research. Our reports on opt-in and probability panels have given us frameworks for transparency and a shared language for these sample sources, to name just a few examples. Our response to these times should be to keep driving forward. We must continue what AAPOR has done for 81 years—help the industry understand itself, improve what we do, and identify new challenges and opportunities. In the past 18 months, through these challenging times, AAPOR has released major resources on pre-election polling (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025a), establishment surveys (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025b), texting for research (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025c), linking survey and nonsurvey data (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025d), and, most recently, on responsible AI integration (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2026). We have updated our code of professional ethics and practices, hosted webinars and short courses, organized new workshops, and put together two major conferences. Table 1 highlights a small selection of these achievements. Selected AAPOR resources and activities produced during 2025–2026. All of this is carried out by volunteers, supported by a small staff, who work collaboratively, from their different vantage points and experiences, to express the latest information about our field. Keeping this collaborative enterprise going is what will keep our industry vibrant and resilient through these times, and it is what AAPOR does best. AAPOR’s response is also to foster the community doing this important work. We are A Meeting Place (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2020). Every year, through our conference, we provide an opportunity to come together to share ideas and network. If lately the conference has felt like a therapy session (as in figure 2), it is needed for us to support each other during these times. Cartoon highlighting AAPOR’s annual conference as a place for mutual support around the emergence of AI. Created by author using ChatGPT. We also need to ensure that our industry is expanding and inclusive. AAPOR’s commitment to diversity has helped reshape the field and made this organization stronger and better able to respond to today’s challenges. We must continue to prioritize this. The AAPOR Affinity Groups give us more ways to connect and share our challenges. As shown in table 2, today we have 11 Affinity Groups, including ConsultPOR, formed in early 2026 in part as a reaction to the movement of practitioners out of traditional employee settings into business for themselves, and the Global Research Affinity Group, inaugurated at our May 2026 Conference. List of AAPOR Affinity Groups as of May 2026. We need to provide tangible, practical support to our community as well. Last year, when so many faced layoffs, travel restrictions, and financial hardships, we rallied as a community and raised a record amount of donations to support conference travel grants. We also provide upskilling sessions, professional development, job coaching, and networking opportunities, all led by volunteers in this room and beyond. In terms of our individual responses, the people I spoke with offered a clear message: steady on, stay curious, and do this together. One academic said, “We need to keep doing what we have always been doing—learning, innovating, and using evidence-based approaches.” A business owner urged us to “lean into the unknown.” And a student reminded me that when we multiply our efforts with others, “it’s way stronger than we can imagine.” My call to action today reflects these sentiments. Stay the course, seek help when you need it, and provide a hand up to another when you can. And don’t give up. Because what we do is important. The industry has faced challenges before: shifts in methodology, new technologies, declining response rates, new forms of data, and now a double whammy of a federal administration hostile to research and the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence. What do we do? We engage with these challenges. We communicate our values. We set standards. We adapt our practices. And we continue the work. Get involved. AAPOR needs each of you. Join a committee. Say “yes” if I ask you to run for council! Ask me, or any of us on council, how to participate. Be a deeper part of this organization that provides a voice, a space, and a framework for what we do. Get involved outside of AAPOR, too. Write local op-eds, contact your representatives, reach out to colleagues in need, and support causes that support the industry, including AAPOR. Join us in this moment, in this community, and in being the way forward. As I close, I want to return to where I began. How do we bear witness to the moment we are living through? And how do we ensure that this work and this community can thrive in the years to come? AAPOR has existed for more than eight decades. Through profound change, the purpose of this work has remained remarkably consistent: to create valid and transparent data about behaviors, attitudes, and characteristics that enable informed societal decision-making. That work is not always easy. But it remains essential. Because no society can understand itself without evidence about the people who live within it. When we do this work well—carefully, ethically, and openly—we create something larger than a dataset, report, or publication. We create a record of the public’s voice. In that sense, this field helps our society bear witness to itself. One of the people I talked to said, “We are writing history right now.” How we respond to this moment is something future researchers will examine. They will seek to understand the foundations of our systems that produce evidence. They will ask how those systems were challenged. And they will ask what we did in response. Our responsibility is to strengthen what we do, improve our tools, defend our standards, and support one another. We continue by doing what this field has always done: help the public be heard, help society understand itself, and strengthen the democracy that depends on both.

title_key: challenges in antithrombotic treatment and in the management of valvular heart disease|crea
title: Challenges in antithrombotic treatment and in the management of valvular heart disease
abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Focus Issue on thrombosis and antithrombotic treatment, and valvular heart disease contains a Special Article entitled ‘Antithrombotic drugs for acute coronary syndromes in women: sex-adjusted treatment and female representation in randomized clinical trials. A clinical consensus statement of the European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) and the ESC Working Group on Thrombosis’ by Valeria Paradies from Maasstad Hospital in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, and colleagues which provides consensus-based guidance for optimizing antithrombotic treatment based on sex.1 Sex-related differences are increasingly recognized as relevant in the management of cardiovascular diseases.2–7 In particular, thrombotic and bleeding risks differ between sexes, partly in relation to distinct biology and hormonal status, but also due to differences in age, comorbidities, and body size at presentation. Women experience frequent fluctuations of prothrombotic and bleeding status related to the menstrual cycle, use of oral contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy, or menopause. Although clinical studies tend to under-represent women, available data consistently support sex-specific differences in the baseline thrombotic and haemorrhagic risks. Compared with men, women are susceptible to an increased risk of in-hospital bleeding related to invasive procedures, as well as long-term out-of-hospital bleeding events. In addition, the inappropriate dosing of antithrombotic drugs, which is not adapted to body weight or renal function, is more frequently associated with an increased risk of bleeding in women compared with men. While acute coronary syndrome (ACS) studies support similar antithrombotic drug efficacy, irrespective of sex, women may receive delayed treatment due to bias in their referral, diagnosis, and invasive treatment decisions. The current clinical consensus statement highlights the need for an increased awareness of sex-specific risks and biases in ACS management, with a focus on sex-specific bleeding mitigation strategies, antithrombotic management in special conditions (e.g. myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries), and barriers to female representation in cardiovascular trials. This manuscript aims to provide expert opinion, based on the best available evidence, and consensus statements on optimizing antithrombotic therapy according to sex, which is critical to improve sex-based disparities in outcome. In a second Special Article entitled ‘Antithrombotic treatment following revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: a scientific statement of the European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Aorta and Peripheral Vascular Diseases and the European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Cardiovascular Pharmacotherapy’, Oliver Schlager from the Medical University of Vienna, Austria, and colleagues provide a scientific statement that addresses peripheral arterial diseases.8 Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) is defined as ischaemic rest pain, or non-healing ulceration, requiring endovascular or surgical lower limb revascularization (LLR).9 Lower limb revascularization in CLTI entails a high risk of major adverse limb events (MALE) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This scientific statement addresses this risk based on a systematic review. A structured literature search was performed, and articles were independently evaluated by two investigators. In total, 1678 articles were identified, of which 34 were included in the final analysis. Only three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) addressed antithrombotic therapy in CLTI following LLR. None of these demonstrated superiority of any antithrombotic regimen over the other. Eight RCTs investigated antithrombotic therapy following LLR in populations with PAD including CLTI subgroups, and suggest a benefit of dual antiplatelet therapy on limb events. One large RCT demonstrated that dual pathway inhibition with aspirin and vascular-dose rivaroxaban reduced the risk of MALE, MACE, and unplanned target limb revascularization. Data from 22 observational studies suggest a benefit of dual antiplatelet therapy on overall survival and amputation-free survival after LLR as compared with single antiplatelet therapy. Intensified antithrombotic treatment should be proposed in patients with CLTI following LLR to reduce the risk of MALE and MACE. Randomized controlled trials on antithrombotic therapy in patients with CLTI following LLR are scarce. Dual pathway inhibition is the only regimen for which an RCT demonstrated a reduction of MALE and MACE following LLR. Dual antiplatelet therapy appears to be associated with a reduced risk of MALE in CLTI following LLR. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has revolutionized the treatment of patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS).10–14 Originally developed for patients with tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) anatomy, the procedural success and expanding indications of TAVI have spurred interest in its application to more complex aortic valve anatomies, including the treatment of AS in bicuspid aortic valves (BAVs). In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Bicuspid aortic valve disease: advancements and challenges of transcatheter aortic valve implantation’, Marco Barbanti from Umberto I Hospital in Enna, Italy, and colleagues aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of TAVI in BAV patients, including an analysis of anatomical considerations and procedural pitfalls, as well as improvements in outcomes with new device iterations (Figure 1).15 The growing interest in this specific subset of patients with AS is driven by the recent extension of TAVI indications to younger individuals, who exhibit a notably higher incidence of bicuspid anatomy compared with older populations. Bicuspid aortic valves present distinct anatomical and pathological complexities that pose significant challenges to the conventional TAVI approach. These include asymmetric calcification, aortic root dilation, and variations in cusp fusion patterns, which can affect valve deployment, transcatheter heart valve sealing, and long-term durability. Despite these challenges, advancements in imaging techniques, valve design, and procedural strategies have led to increased adoption of TAVI in BAV patients. However, surgical aortic valve replacement still retains a more prominent role in this group compared with patients with tricuspid valves. This preference is partly due to the exclusion of BAV patients from almost all previous RCTs, which limits the available evidence supporting the use of TAVI in this unique cohort. This state-of-the-art review provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of TAVI in BAV patients, including an analysis of anatomical considerations and procedural pitfalls, as well as improvements in outcomes with new device iterations.
