title_key: oral examination is a requirement for certification by the american board of orthopaedic surgery|kasser
title: Oral Examination Is a Requirement for Certification by the American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery
abstract: An oral examination is central to the certification process of many of the Member Boards of the American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS). While there have been some concerns regarding the validity, bias, and reliability of oral examinations, the Boards view this type of examination as the best way to ensure that board-certified physicians are ethical, competent, and knowledgeable. Throughout its existence, the American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery (ABOS) has relied on the oral examination to determine the suitability of orthopaedic surgeons for ABOS Board Certification. History of the ABOS Oral Examination The ABOS was established in 1934. Initial certification was granted to members of the American Orthopaedic Association (AOA), a subset of whom became examiners for nonmember orthopaedic surgeons, or for AOA members who did not gain certification during the “grandfathered” period. Inaugural members of the Board felt that an oral examination was the best method to test knowledge, decision-making ability, and ethical performance in the practice of orthopaedic surgery. The initial requirement for ABOS Board Certification was an oral examination that was partially based on the submission of 25 case histories on which an individual’s practice could be evaluated1,2. In the early years, the oral examination was given by 3 examiners for 15 minutes each, and an essay question also needed to be completed. A candidate’s “orthopaedic work” was evaluated by the examiners, who generally asked a broad array of questions, including some that effectively evaluated the submitted cases. The scoring system used for the oral examination was “BONE”: “B” for excellent, “O” for satisfactory, “N” for borderline, and “E” for failure. The minimal passing grade on the examination was 2 borderline scores and no failures. Three borderline scores or 1 failure resulted in a failure of the overall oral examination and denial of certification. The ABOS has always considered the oral examination to be the best method for evaluating an orthopaedic surgeon’s practice, but examiner reliability and fairness of testing have always been a concern1. From 1937 to 1948, the ABOS Board Certification examination consisted of 2 parts. Part I included both a written and oral examination during training. The Part II oral examination consisted of five 15-minute examinations in each of the following areas: clinical care, pathology, anatomy, cadaver dissection, and osteology. Candidates sat for Part II of the Board Certification examination, which consisted of an oral examination based on the submission of 25 to 50 case histories, after 2 years in practice. Three examiners administered the test. The candidate’s biographical information, including name, practice area, and training program as well as educational background, was known to the examiner. The examination was prone to consisting of a social discussion rather than a true assessment of knowledge or orthopaedic practice, and grading was highly variable, with some very severe and some very lenient examiners. Some examiners spent much of the examination time making the candidate feel comfortable, while others spent most of the examination time making the applicant feel miserable. The non-numerical grading system led to further concerns about the fairness of the examination. Failure rates varied from 15% to 25% during this period1. In 1949, the written portion of the Part I examination was moved to being taken after a candidate had been in practice for 2 years, and it was given in conjunction with the Part II Oral Examination. During that time, examiners who were either very severe or very lenient were identified and either “trained” or dropped from administering the oral examination in order to address examiner fairness and consistency. Subject areas of the oral examination were changed to include anatomy, fractures, pathology, congenital and acquired deformities, and static and postural defects1. Between 1950 and 1970, the oral examination format underwent progressive development. Examiners could bring their own material to use in the examination of individual applicants, and standard cases and questions were adopted in the areas of anatomy and pathology. Two examiners at each examination station caucused to determine the final grade, and the pass/fail grading system was changed to a numerical scoring system. There were continuing efforts to increase the reproducibility and reliability of the oral examination. Starting in 1961, examinations were held in booths in a common area rather than in hotel rooms1. Candidate anonymity was adopted; individuals were identified by number, and the examiners were blinded to the candidate’s training program and institution. Rather than caucusing, the examiners scored each candidate independently in an effort to increase reliability. Examiner variation was assessed by comparing the scores provided by paired examiners who independently scored the same examination. There was a continued effort to standardize the examination, which increased the reliability and validity of the results. Between 1970 and 1989, the oral examination had evolved and became focused on 4 areas: pediatric orthopaedic surgery, adult orthopaedic surgery, trauma, and interpretive skills. In 1979, there was an attempt to include motor skill evaluation as part of the oral examination, but this was dropped after 1 year because of the difficulty in scoring1. During this era, the oral examination was composed of four 30-minute sections. In 1980, the criteria for choosing examiners were modified. Rather than choosing examiners solely because of their status and hospital or medical school affiliation, a broader group of examiners was identified. The number of examiners was increased to prevent examiner fatigue, which was thought to compromise the oral examinations. The examiners were rated in terms of severity and consistency. Although examiners were paired for each examination, they scored each examinee independently. There was agreement between the examiners in 82% of cases, with a 6.5% failure rate, which was consistent from year to year. In the late 1980s, the ABOS Oral Examination Task Force recommended a return to a case-based oral examination in which the individual’s cases were the basis for the examination. In 1990, the examination was changed to consist of 6 standard cases (2 pediatric orthopaedic cases, 2 adult orthopaedic cases, and 2 trauma cases) in addition to 10 selected cases from a Case List that had been submitted from each examinee. Three panels of 2 examiners were used at that time. Starting in 1991, cases were selected from a 6-month consecutive surgical Case List that was submitted by each examinee. By 2000, the standard cases were dropped, and the oral examination was based entirely on an individual’s submitted surgical Case List. The Board was quite concerned about the validity, accuracy, and fairness of the oral examination during this time. Dr. Mary Lunz, a psychometrician and expert in testing, provided extensive consultation to the Board over many years, evaluating the performance of the examiners as well as the overall fairness and validity of the examination. Case selection from the submitted Case Lists initially included 15 cases, and the examinee could drop 5 cases. Over time, case selection became more focused and standardized, requiring the candidate to be examined on nearly all of the selected cases. A scoring rubric was developed and was accompanied by an increased effort in examiner training to improve both consistency and discrimination in scoring. Examiners were handicapped based on their harshness or leniency in scoring so that a candidate’s score would not be adversely affected by examiner severity as long as the oral examiner was consistent. Inconsistent or nondiscriminatory examiners were identified and educated about the use of the scoring rubric. If the individual examiners did not achieve the established target in consistency and discrimination, they were dropped as oral examiners. Between 2008 and 2013, with the evolution of electronic medical records and digital imaging systems, the ABOS changed to a computer-based format, digitizing images and documents for all oral examinations. The need to keep personal health information confidential complicated ABOS oral examinations in both the digital and paper environments. In addition, the validity of medical records and imaging in the digital environment was a substantial concern of the ABOS during this transition period. These issues were addressed, and the conversion to digital format was accomplished without compromising the validity or fairness of the oral examination. There was also concern about the potential effect of the communication skills of the examinee and their influence on the outcome of the examination3. In 2008, Dr. Lunz published a paper showing that the communication skills of the examinees were not correlated with performance on the oral examination. Specifically, clinical decision-making and problem-solving, as well as ethical behavior, were the factors determining performance on the oral examination rather than communication skills. During the 90 years of ABOS certification of orthopaedic surgeons, the oral examination has evolved, but with consistent concern for validity, fairness, and reliability. The current oral examination, for which a 6-month surgical Case List forms the basis, is viewed by the Board as the gold standard in candidate evaluation and peer review. The scoring rubric and the statistical evaluation of examiners are integral to the oral examination process. The validity of the oral examination for Board Certification has also been studied in other specialties, all of which have shown that examiner training has improved validity and reliability4–7, corroborating the findings of the ABOS and supporting the improvements in the Part II Oral Examination for orthopaedic surgeons. ABOS Oral Examinations During the COVID-19 Pandemic In March 2020, the Oral Examination Committee met to discuss the feasibility and potential consequences of conducting the Part II Oral Examination during a worldwide pandemic. As with any crisis, a list of goals and guiding principles was initially established: The aspirational goal of the ABOS was to set the highest standard for the practice of orthopaedic surgery to benefit the public. The goal of the Part II Oral Examination was to measure the candidates against the highest standard for actual performance in practice and assess each candidate on their own cases. As an alternative for achieving these goals, the examinations included evaluations of a series of cases that would have the same goals as the ABOS Oral Examination, but without face-to-face contact in order to maintain the safety and health of the candidates and the examiners. The Committee considered a list of contingency options regarding the possibility of conducting or not conducting ABOS Oral Examinations in 2020, given the many unknowns at that time. These included cancellation, postponement, remote examinations, and additional dates for the examinations. The Committee also developed a list of considerations from the perspective of the examiners and the examinees. These included travel issues, institutional issues and mandates, timing of the examinations, and location of the examinations. In addition, the Committee conducted a survey of other ABMS Member Boards and found that in 2020, most had canceled or delayed certifying examinations for the foreseeable future. Ultimately, the Oral Examination Committee made the decision to formulate a case-based examination format, which included the following: Developing a method to deliver the examination in 2020 while staying true to the ABOS mission, Maintaining ABOS standards while being fair to candidates and diplomates, Prioritizing the health and safety of all candidates, diplomates, examiners, directors, and staff involved in the examination process, Eliminating the risk of substantial health issues as much as possible, Using virtual practice evaluation (VPE) principles that had been developed before it was known that they would be needed (see below), Advancing the use of ABOS technology, Maintaining examination consistency and reliability for 2020 examinees, Producing an examination that was psychometrically sound, and Maintaining an immediate appeals option for examinees. The decision was made to limit the possible outcomes of the 2020 oral examinations to either “Pass in 2020” or “Take in 2021,” allowing those who did not pass to retake the ABOS Oral Examination in-person in 2021 without penalty. Fortunately, and coincidentally, the ABOS had been testing a VPE during 2018 and 2019 and had data demonstrating that this was a valid alternative to the oral examination. The Oral Examination Committee viewed its utilization as a possibility and, with consensus from the ABOS Board of Directors, provided the following 3-stage plan for the oral examination in 2020: Stage 1: Case-based VPE Pass or move to Stage 2 Stage 2: Remote virtual oral examination Pass or move to Stage 3 Stage 3: Full review of all examinees who did not pass Stage 2 Examination performed by ABOS Directors The similarities to the oral examination included: Examiner severity/leniency adjustments Scoring rubric and scoring scale The Oral Examination Committee then began discussing the 2021 oral examination. In addition to safety and health concerns, there was concern that the examinees would not have the appropriate number of surgical cases to sit for a valid oral examination. The committee developed the following plan to address those issues: Back up the surgical case collection period 3 months (to begin on January 1, 2020), Collect consecutive surgical cases for a minimum of 6 consecutive months, Stop at 6 months if ≥250 cases had been collected, or Continue collecting beyond 6 months until 250 cases were collected, or until September 30, 2020. In July and August 2020, the Stage 1 ABOS case-based VPE was carried out successfully, allowing 878 examinees to be examined. More than 10,000 surgical cases were evaluated and scored by an incredibly dedicated group of ABOS volunteers. In October 2020, the Stage 2 ABOS virtual case-based examination was conducted successfully. The oral examinations were carried out on a virtual platform using multiple Zoom accounts. The predicted and actual results for the oral and recertification examinations are shown below. Oral examination: Predicted: 78% to 88% of candidates would pass Actual: 78% to 83% (depending on the Stage 3 results) Recertification examination: Predicted: 38% to 49% of candidates would pass Actual: 28% to 36% (depending on the Stage 3 results) In November 2020, all Stage 3 scores and results were evaluated. No examinees were given the final outcome until December. The 3-stage process was successful, and the Board was able to pass 659 of the 878 examinees; the other 219 examinees took the oral examination in 2021, without having been reported as having a failing result. The returning examinees were given the options of either continuing with their existing Case List or submitting a new Case List. For the 2021 Oral Examination, the options included: Pass and become ABOS Board Certified or recertified, or Advance to an in-person oral examination in October: ○Schedule at the Palmer House Hilton, Chicago, for October 17 to 21, 2021 ○Develop a virtual option if an in-person examination was not possible ○Allow examinees to defer to 2022 with no penalty Based on continuing issues with the pandemic, the ABOS developed a 2-stage plan for the 2021 ABOS Oral Examinations: Stage 1 ○Case-based examinations ▪July 17 to July 25, 2021 ▪Document and image review ▪Pass top group (as in 2020) ▪No failures ▪Complete by mid-August Stage 2 ○Standard in-person oral examination ▪Palmer House (Chicago) ▪October 17 to October 21, 2021 ▪Four days of examinations The 2021 Stage 1 oral examination allowed the successful evaluation of 822 examinees and nearly 10,000 individual surgical cases. The Stage 2 oral examinations were given as scheduled in October 2021, with multiple modifications of protocols that had been established to ensure safety. These included masking and contactless registration for both the examiners and the examinees. In addition, briefing and orientation sessions were conducted with appropriate social distancing and without contact. An electronic vaccination verification also was required. These precautions allowed the examinations to be conducted with minimal disease transmission. This resulted in larger examination booths and more time for examiners to move from booth to booth (15 minutes versus 5 minutes), which resulted in a longer examination day (11 hours and 15 minutes). While there was success in carrying out the oral examinations during the COVID-19 pandemic, there was unanimous affirmation by the ABOS Board of Directors that going forward, the ABOS Board Certification process needed to include an in-person, face-to-face oral examination for each ABOS Board Certified orthopaedic surgeon at least once in their career, if possible. The ABOS was very grateful for the innovative work and support of all of the stakeholders who helped navigate through the pandemic to conduct the 2020 and 2021 oral examinations, including our examiners and examinees. title_key: news in astronomy geophysics december 2023|bowler
title: News in Astronomy & Geophysics – December 2023
abstract: More than 100 000 people visited the UK Space Agency's ‘Space for Everyone’ tour between June and October this year. The travelling exhibits, which included a full-size replica LauncherOne rocket, visited 13 cities across the UK, from Plymouth to Aberdeen, Belfast to Hull. The interactive activities were designed to inspire the next generation of space professionals, with presentations from organisations and companies from the World Wide Fund for Nature and Lockheed Martin, among many others. There was also a virtual tour, explored by nearly 50 000 users and an online broadcast reaching 9000 people; schools, youth groups and community organisations took advantage of tailored tours. At the same time, Imperial College worked with UKSA to highlight the range of careers in the space industry and offer resources and career tips on their website ‘I'm a Space Person’. Now that the tour has finished, the replica rocket is on loan to Spaceport Cornwall, to become part of a free exhibition. spaceperson.co.uk In October, the RAS received as a gift a valuable addition to the archive: the Gold Medal awarded to Francis Baily in 1843. Descendants of Francis Baily's brother visited the RAS at Burlington House to return the medal. The RAS is extremely grateful for this kind donation; the medal is now on display in the Library. Francis Baily is best known for his observations of the 1836 total eclipse of the Sun in the Scottish borders; he noted the bright points of light arising from the Moon's irregular surface; these have been coined Baily's Beads. Baily received his first Gold Medal in 1827 in for his reform of star catalogues; the 1843 Medal so kindly returned to the RAS was awarded for his comprehensive restaging of Cavendish's classic experiment to measure the mass of the Earth. The Lord Rees of Ludlow OM FRS, University of Cambridge, has been awarded the Copley Medal for his achievements as arguably the most distinguished theoretical astrophysicist of his generation, responsible for numerous and varied conceptual breakthroughs. Professor Michele Dougherty CBE FRS, Imperial College London, was awarded the Bakerian Medal and Lecture for her scientific leadership of the Cassini magnetic field instrument at Saturn, seminal research findings on potential life support on Enceladus and leadership of forthcoming missions to probe Jupiter's icy moons. royalsociety.org Congratulations to John Zarnecki, past president of the RAS, who was awarded the 2022 Sir Arthur Clark Award for Lifetime Achievement of the British Interplanetary Society in October 2023. The award cited his “more than 40 years at the forefront of space research and exploration, from Skylark sounding rockets, the Hubble Faint Object Camera, the Giotto DIDSY dust instrument and the Huygens Surface Science Package to Rosetta and Beagle 2”. At the same event, Prof. Giovanna Tinetti of University College London won the Arthurs individual award for research, for her work leading ESA's Ariel mission in particular. tinyurl.com/vvucyvnx The RAS award for undergraduate work in instrumentation has been won by Bradley Lewis for his undergraduate project at Liverpool John Moores University. Bradley devised a means of measuring atmospheric turbulence close to the ground, based on small temperature fluctuations. You can find out more about the project and the award in our profile, on page 43. tinyurl.com/4jkrumv9 The RAS recently took part in the annual Open House event, alongside other Courtyard Societies in Burlington House. A team of dedicated RAS staff took 267 people on tours of the building and entertained 41 young people with workshops making cyanotypes and constellation cards. The Library was open for visitors and featured the RAS quilt as well as some of our historical treasures; Caroline Herschel and Isaac Newton also dropped in to entertain our guests. tinyurl.com/4pthyhpd The UK Space Agency has signed an agreement with the Houston-based company Axiom Space to explore a commercially-sponsored UK astronaut mission. Plans are currently on the drawing board for four astronauts, with Tim Peake, who flew to the International Space Station as an ESA astronaut, leading the team. UKSA are seeking input from UK universities for experiments and technology demonstrators suitable for a two-week mission, plus ideas for space education and outreach. tinyurl.com/3kmc2rvs In a new study of supernova SN 2023ixf, researchers suggest the delayed shock break-out is direct evidence for the presence of dense material from recent mass loss. The observations revealed an unexpected amount of mass loss in the year prior to explosion. Such extreme loss is atypical of Type II supernovae, but may be related to the final stages of nuclear burn-off of high-mass elements in the star's core. A paper by Daichi Hiramatsu (Center for Astrophysics) appears in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. tinyurl.com/ywk3ud26 It's 2075 and the exploration of Mars is gathering pace. Robotic rovers are the essential tools, but then, as now, they are vulnerable to cyberattack. This was the scenario for a hackathon organised by ESA in October this year, with the aim of educating and inspiring young people in cybersecurity. The competing teams had to defend their rovers from attacks by other teams, attack competing rovers, drive through an abandoned martian base and unlock and solve ‘Capture the Flag’ challenges involving hidden code in programmes and websites. The competition was organised by ESA with Fraunhofer SIT and ATHENE-Center, and the winners were a team called SPAAAAAACE from Warsaw University of Technology and the University of Potsdam. tinyurl.com/yy466eb4 Kaitlyn Szekerczes (NASA GSFC) and colleagues have simulated a glimpse of the sky as it would appear in gravitational waves. Based on the expected distribution of ultracompact binaries (UCBs) and the form of gravitational wave signals from these systems, the team developed a way to combine the data into an all-sky view. The image shows how space-based gravitational wave observatories will enhance our understanding of the Milky Way. The findings appear in The Astronomical Journal. tinyurl.com/mrhpvnw9 Computer simulations have shown how intermediate-mass black holes could form inside stellar clusters. A team led by Manuel Arca Sedda (Gran Sasso Science Institute) computed a sequence of interactions between normal single and binary stars. Collisions formed increasingly massive stars that evolved into IMBHs. The results, published in The Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, demonstrated the rapid expulsion from parental clusters, typically within a few hundred million years. tinyurl.com/4zbx86bn This image of billion-year-old merging spiral galaxies may hold clues to the eventual fate of the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. This is a Gemini South image of the peculiar galaxy NGC7727, around 90 million light years away, made using GMOS, the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph. NGC7727 contains two supermassive black holes, one measured at 154 million solar masses, the other at just 6.3 million; they are currently around 1600 light years apart. These are inferred to have been at the centres of the two spiral galaxies; their gravitational interactions have perturbed those spiral arms into loops and trails, stirred up interstellar gas and dust into clouds like candy floss and triggered regions of starburst and bright young stars. The two black holes are anticipated to merge in about 250 million years, triggering a burst of gravitational waves; NGC7727 will probably end up as an elliptical galaxy. tinyurl.com/48nmxzut Measurements of the precession of the jet shooting out of supermassive black hole M87 offer direct evidence that the black hole does in fact spin. M87 is known for its giant jet perpendicular to the accretion disc around the black hole. Data collected by Very Long Baseline radio Interferometry around the world for 170 time intervals over 20 years have shown that the orientation of the jet where it begins precesses with a period of 11 years, changing direction by about 10°. The precession is thought to arise from gravitational interactions between the accretion disc and the spinning black hole; detecting the precession implies that the black hole spins. The results are published by Yuzhu Cui, now at Zhejiang Laboratory, Hangzhou, China and colleagues in Nature. tinyurl.com/2pvzwvjf A new massive structure in the universe, a bubble of galaxies a billion light-years wide, has been discovered. Given the name Hóoleilana (from a Hawaiian creation chant evoking the origin of structure), it encompasses many familiar structures including the Sloan Great Wall and the Hercules, Coma and Boötes clusters. Structures on this scale were predicted to arise from Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAOs), ripples in the plasma of the young universe. The team, led by Brent Tully (University of Hawaii), believe this may be the first individual structure associated with a BAO to be identified. They also say it is bigger and closer than they anticipated, suggesting a high value for the rate of expansion of the universe. The new findings are published in The Astrophysical Journal. tinyurl.com/5euj8k8f New simulations indicate that black holes ‘eat’ much faster than conventional understanding suggested. According to simulations, spinning black holes twist up the surrounding space-time, resulting in accretion disks splitting into inner and outer ‘subdisks’. Once consumed, the inner disk is repeatedly refilled from the outer disk. One cycle of the endlessly repeating eat-refill-eat process takes just months – in contrast to the century-long timescales previously proposed. The study, by Nicholas Kaaz (Northwestern University) and team appears in The Astrophysical Journal. tinyurl.com/yc2cutmp GRB230307A Kilonova Emission Spectrum, detected by JWST The JWST has detected tellurium in the aftermath of a very bright gamma ray burst from the merger of a pair of neutron stars, confirming the role of these events in forming such heavy elements. GRB230307A was first detected in March this year by NASA's Fermi Telescope, and telescopes on the ground and in space tracked the evolution of the signal; observations at gamma-ray, X-ray, optical, infrared, and radio wavelengths showed that the optical/infrared counterpart was faint, evolved quickly, and became very red – hallmarks of a kilonova, the electromagnetic signal of the merger of a pair of neutron stars. The JWST's infrared detectors NIRCam and NIRSpec showed that tellurium was present from its emission line at 2.15microns and the broadening of the line indicated that the source was moving quickly. The team also found a very red source at mid-infrared wavelengths, which they interpret as coming from the production of lanthanides. Together, these data demonstrate that the formation of such heavy elements by the r-process can indeed take place in gamma ray bursts. Andrew Levan of Radboud University in The Netherlands, and colleagues, published in Nature. tinyurl.com/5daeb2ac The launch of XRISM, the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission, took place on 7 September and the new observatory is in the commissioning phase. XRISM, a joint JAXA/NASA project, carries two instruments: Resolve, a spectrometer using microcalorimeters that offer excellent spectral resolution across the 0.3–13keV range over a field of view ∼3arcmin, and Xtend, a soft X-ray imager with a wider field of view of 38arcmin. Resolve is now cooled to working temperatures and has demonstrated better than 5eV energy resolution. XRISM replaces some of the instruments lost when Hitomi failed six weeks after launch in 2016. Hitomi's first data opened a new window into hot gas in the Perseus galaxy cluster, establishing the value of microcalorimeters in X-ray spectroscopy. tinyurl.com/ymkcfbxs India has become the fourth nation to achieve a soft landing on the Moon, with the touchdown of Chandrayaan-3 on 23 August. The Vikram lander achieved the goals of taking measurements on the surface, detecting sulphur, for example, and releasing the rover Pragyan. However, the Indian Space Research Organisation announced that the lander and rover did not survive the lunar night without solar power. tinyurl.com/z46y3rf2 The latest study of a tidal disruption event, ASASSN-14li, using data from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESA's XMM-Newton telescope and other instruments has allowed astronomers to estimate the relative amount of nitrogen compared to carbon in the aftermath of this gravitational cannibalism. This value indicates that the shredded star in ASASSN-14li was about three times the mass of the Sun, i.e. one of the largest stars ever known to be devastated in a TDE. A paper by Jon M. Miller (University of Michigan, Ann Arbor) and team, appears in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. tinyurl.com/mtd4jhxf If you dropped some antimatter, would it fall up or down? This experiment has now been performed at CERN by E K Anderson (Aarhus University) and colleagues. The team observed antihydrogen atoms escaping a magnetic trap and noted that 80% were annihilated below the trap – a result consistent with how a cloud of the more usual form of hydrogen would behave under the same conditions. Thus, they concluded, gravity was causing the antihydrogen to fall down, as theory suggested. A paper appears in Nature. tinyurl.com/3zne4s5h Researchers have found a striking link between the amount of dust surrounding a supermassive black hole (SMBH) and the of the radio emission in extremely bright galaxies. title_key: should data protection authorities enforce the ai act lessons from eu wide enforcement data|mazur
title: Should data protection authorities enforce the AI Act ? Lessons from EU-wide enforcement data
abstract: Most Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems involve some form of personal data processing, yet the role of Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) in enforcing the AI Act remains critically undefined. This article empirically investigates current DPAs’ role in enforcing regulations concerning AI-driven services and automated decision-making (ADM) systems to assess their suitability for enforcing the AI Act. Drawing on a dataset covering DPA activities relating to AI in all European Union Member States, we analyse multiple indicators as proxies for their activity level concerning enforcement associated with AI and ADM. Our findings suggest that, although many DPAs have some experience with AI-related enforcement, their activity level in this area varies significantly. Combining these results with a legal analysis of the AI Act’s provisions, we argue that, despite being heterogeneous, the expertise developed by DPAs represents a valuable resource for effectively enforcing the AI Act. Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies often rely on processing personal data. However, the role of Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) within the enforcement model of the AI Act1 remains unclear. This article investigates how actively DPAs currently enforce data protection rules in cases concerning AI-based products and services and automated decision-making (ADM) systems. It is crucial to scrutinize this issue given the AI Act’s substantive scope, which covers specific ADM systems, and the institutional solutions it foresees, which might require the involvement of the DPAs in certain enforcement aspects. Drawing on evidence from documented DPA activities across EU Member States, we develop an index to quantify their activity level, identifying concrete ways they could contribute to effectively enforcing the AI Act. Our analysis addresses explicitly three key research questions: two descriptive (1 and 2) and one prescriptive (3): What role does the AI Act assign to DPAs within its enforcement model? What is the current DPA’s activity level concerning AI-driven products or services and ADM systems? Given their experience, what is the extent to which the DPAs should be involved in enforcing the AI Act? We address these questions through an empirical and legal analysis. The section ‘The role(s) of DPAS in the enforcement system of the AI Act’ presents the AI Act’s provisions regarding the potential involvement of the DPAs in its enforcement. The section ‘Methods and sources’ describes the methods and sources used for the empirical analysis, while the section ‘How active are the DPAS in the enforcement related to AI?’ presents the results. As the enforcement of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is entrusted to the national DPAs,2 thus, decentralized,3 we analyse the enforcement practices in all the Member States. We collected and analysed a unique dataset on the activities of DPAs across all EU Member States, structured by the following indicators: (i) data protection impact assessment (DPIA) blacklist inclusions (with explicit or implicit references to AI); (ii) AI-related decisions; (iii) ADM-specific decisions (concerning Article 22 of GDPR); (iv) mentions of AI in annual reports (2021–24); and (v) website search results for search terms describing AI. We decided to include the decisions concerning ADM for two reasons. Firstly, since the AI Act incorporates a right resembling the GDPR’s right to explanation, the enforcement record of DPAs under the GDPR serves as an indicator of their likely role in upholding this right under the AI Act. Secondly, experience in the enforcement of ADM is an essential proxy for enforcing prohibitions and transparency obligations concerning high-risk AI systems under the AI Act, as these systems often entail processing personal data and ADM. Therefore, alongside the indicators directly referring to AI, we also include those concerning ADM. The results of this analysis are used to evaluate the activities that the DPAs have undertaken concerning AI-related matters. We treat the collected data as a proxy for assessing the readiness of DPAs to enforce legal norms in AI- and ADM-related cases. This assessment proposes a quantitative index based on the indicators mentioned above. Member States are then divided into four groups according to their activity level: very active, active, reluctant, and inert enforcers. We then discuss the characteristics of each group. The section ‘The potential involvement of the DPAS in the enforcement of the AI Act’ presents the results of the empirical analysis of the regulatory framework of the AI Act’s enforcement model. Assuming that a higher level of AI-specific enforcement activity indicates greater institutional learning and a stronger foundation for active future enforcement, we propose evidence-based solutions for the scope of DPAs’ involvement in the AI Act’s enforcement system. Based on this analysis, we have three targeted recommendations. We limit our suggestions to those aspects of the AI Act that are linked to the types of activities scrutinized in our study, as we take into account how different the AI Act is in terms of the regulatory approach to the GDPR (eg due to its focus on product safety). Thus, while we recognize that assigning specific responsibilities to other authorities might be recommended, our recommendations focus on the extent to which the DPAs should be involved in enforcing the AI Act due to their activity level observed in our research. First, we advocate including DPAs as Market Surveillance Authorities (MSAs) for high-risk AI systems under Annex III, points 3–5 of the AI Act, where the intersection of data protection and AI regulation is most evident. While very active and active enforcers could fulfil the role of MSAs, given their activity level, there might be doubts concerning reluctant and inert enforcers as well. title: How to Cultivate a Thriving Work Culture
abstract: Most people, at some point, have voluntarily left a job. Motivations for resigning vary widely. An employee may leave a job because of a troubled relationship with an employer or other co-workers. In other cases, the worker may find a new job offering more benefits. Some people leave a job because the work is no longer enjoyable because of a toxic work community, and even when people attempt to improve their work environments by speaking up, their complaints fall on deaf ears. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, more than 47 million Americans quit their jobs in 2021.1 This phenomenon, coined the Great Resignation,1 was partially spurred by the COVID-19 pandemic and had a significant impact on the health care workforce, with 117,000 physicians quitting in 2021 and 1.7 million health care workers resigning in 2022.2,3 According to a survey in 2021, 1 in 5 physicians planned to leave within the next 2 years, and 1 in 3 physicians reported planning to reduce their work hours in the next 12 months, leaving hospitals potentially short-staffed.4 For the health of both patients and physicians, or workplaces in general, the implementation of a thriving work culture to combat burnout and dissatisfaction in the workplace is necessary to retaining teammates. This article will focus on identifying aspects of a toxic work culture and how to do away with such toxicity for the creation of a thriving work culture. Furthermore, aside from defining a thriving work culture, we strive to provide guidance on how to build a thriving work culture that promotes not only exceptionality in the workforce, but also well-being among team members. THE PROBLEM: TOXIC WORK CULTURES Before describing the importance of a thriving work culture and the strategies to create one, it is important to understand what workplaces should avoid: a toxic work culture. A toxic work culture is an environment that supports negative behaviors and attitudes, leading to a lack of trust among team members; low enthusiasm; and poor-quality work from employees, employers, and leaders.5 Aspects of a toxic work culture include a lack of clear leadership, violating values and beliefs, toxic behavior, and resistance to change (Fig. 1).Fig. 1.: Aspects of a toxic work culture.Lack of Leadership A team needs a leader. A lack of leadership results in a nebulous direction toward an unclear goal, leaving team members confused and more likely to work ineffectively.6 Before unraveling what makes a good leader, it is important to identify certain traits of an ineffective leader, and how to avoid being or becoming one. One trait that identifies an individual as a poor leader is being a know-it-all—an attitude that indicates close-mindedness. Leaders who are close-minded do not collaborate well with team members because they resist ideas that are not their own, even if the idea from someone else is better. Ineffective leaders also lack accountability. When they are responsible for a mistake or failure, they will not apologize or accept blame. They often point the finger at others for their failures, while claiming credit for someone else’s success. Inadequate leaders also lack emotional self-control. Effective leaders remain calm and collected in even the most stressful situations. Violating Values and Beliefs Employees are less likely to find their work fulfilling and valuable if the job clashes with their personal beliefs and values.5 The population is representative of many diverse cultures, socioeconomic backgrounds, and religious beliefs. For example, a health care team should all believe in the value of honesty between each other to ensure that all possible avenues of treatment are discussed and understood when developing the best plan to treat a patient. No employee should be expected to abide by rules that contradict his or her personal beliefs. Therefore, before employees are brought onto a team, it is important to explain the team’s mission statement and ensure that their personal values align with that mission to avoid disputes, lower productivity, and increase unhappiness. Toxic Behavior Unfortunately, some individuals will encounter toxic people within the workplace who bully, manipulate, and lie to others. A toxic individual destroys a team by festering an unhealthy dynamic that not only leads to low morale and negativity, but also causes a higher employee turnover rate. It is important to make people feel they belong within a team. Employees who are bullied or isolated are less likely to enjoy their work and more likely to leave, even if they are strong workers. To address an employee exhibiting toxic behavior, it is best to pull them off to the side to explain how their behavior was not appropriate. However, if an employee continues to act in an unprofessional manner that hurts other team members, it is best to enforce consequences for such behavior.7 For example, for minor offences such as making an unintentionally rude comment, employees should be given a verbal warning; for repeated offences or major offences such as bullying and lying, employees should be given a more severe punishment such as suspension and even termination. Terminating a toxic employee ensures that the rest of the team members will work in a safer, and thus more productive environment, enticing great team members to stay. Resistance to Change Stagnant processes that do not facilitate change or flexibility—even when there is a better, more efficient manner of completing a responsibility or task—prevent growth. For example, continuing to rely on old procedures instead of branching out to try new technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT for responsibilities that do not require human critical thinking. A task that might take a human several hours to complete, such as organizing data into a spreadsheet, could be finished in a matter of minutes using AI. Implementing and handing over mundane tasks to AI gives team members more time to think creatively and critically to develop better, more innovative solutions to achieve a goal. Therefore, teams that do not think innovatively to improve their systems and find solutions to their problems more effectively will not succeed when compared with teams who are willing to embrace change. WHAT IS A THRIVING WORK CULTURE? A thriving work culture is an environment that supports positive behaviors and attitudes, leading to strong camaraderie among team members, high enthusiasm, motivation, and high- quality work from every team member in the workforce.5 Aspects of a thriving work culture include clear leadership to create attainable goals, inclusion, and diversity, radical honesty and transparency, and rules people believe in (Fig. 2).Fig. 2.: Aspects of a thriving work culture.Clear Leadership to Create Attainable Goals Unlike a toxic workplace, a thriving workplace has a clear, designated leader that understands his or her team. A good leader will create defined goals for the team to accomplish. In a thriving workplace, all employees should be treated equally and their ideas thoughtfully considered regardless of education or job title. A common framework for creating realistic goals in medicine is SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and timebound; however, it may not be sufficient for collaborative environments. CLEAR—collaborative, limited, emotional, appreciable, and refinable—is an updated framework that is tailored to creating goals for collaborative projects and goals.8 CLEAR goals are collaborative, limited, emotional, appreciable, and refinable (Fig. 3). Using CLEAR goals helps to streamline the process of solving a problem, or accomplishing a goal, in a systematic, efficient manner. To demonstrate how each aspect of a CLEAR goal should be implemented, an example task, such as how to plan a blood drive in an academic institution, is integrated with each of the points below.Fig. 3.: CLEAR goals. Collaborative: The goal should encourage team members to work together and assemble unique skills into 1 objective. To host a blood drive, each team member should contribute a skill. One member should advertise, another should schedule the venue, or another should register volunteers for the drive. In addition, a connection to a professional organization, such as the American Red Cross, should be used to access personnel who are licensed to withdraw blood from blood donors. Limited: It should be attainable in terms of skill and available time. It is difficult to run a blood drive alone; therefore, it is important to ensure there are enough members on a team (ie, volunteers, supervisor, phlebotomists) to ensure the blood drive has been organized well. Emotional: Team members should be passionate about and interested in accomplishing the set goal. There are often blood shortages, meaning it is difficult for people in need to obtain blood. Therefore, impassioning team members with the notion that the blood drive matters to people will encourage greater interest in accomplishing a successful blood drive. Appreciable: Larger long-term goals should be broken down into smaller short-term goals to encourage long-term gain. There should be many blood drives within the year. However, it is difficult to schedule and obtain all the volunteers for each scheduled blood drive for the entire year. Instead, schedule the volunteers a couple weeks before the blood drive to ensure attendance, leading to more efficient blood drives. Refinable: Set goals with a clear structure on how to obtain them. At the same time, be sure to remain flexible and willing to change the plan when necessary to achieve the goal. Say there are many no-show blood donors. To meet the blood quota, advertise to people around the blood drive to become walk-in blood donors. INCLUSION AND DIVERSITY Different people will catch and fix different mistakes. Including people from diverse backgrounds should lead to many perspectives that influence and improve work quality.9 Encourage team members to keep an open mind. Do not immediately dismiss another person’s idea but rather pause to consider all ideas to actively ensure that the best one is put into production. Similarly, a thriving workplace should enforce a standard whereby everyone is comfortable speaking up. To ensure a positive team dynamic, team members not only need to collaborate, but also should feel secure to disagree with each other and fix issues that the other did not notice. Inevitably, there will be instances where team members will feel insulted by an unintentional remark, but it is important to foster a culture where team members feel comfortable to speak up and clear up such misunderstandings. When forming a team, it is important to hire people, especially for leadership positions, from different backgrounds, to increase the diversity of ideas and perspectives in the workplace. In addition, providing diversity training, such as an online course, presentation, or workshop, not only gives the impression of a welcoming work culture, but also asserts a workplace’s intolerance toward discrimination and prejudice. Furthermore, according to the Harvard Business Review, 75% of respondents were critical of superficial language and policies that did not actually cause any significant improvement with inclusion and diversity.10 Therefore, when implementing the methods cited above, it is crucial that policies enact true, noticeable changes that employees will perceive. Radical Honesty and Transparency A productive workplace functions best with a culture of honesty, especially in terms of providing honest and constructive criticism.11 Everyone will make mistakes and have room to improve aspects of their work. For example, when writing a research paper, it is important for an editor or fellow co-worker to point out when they feel that a section of the paper is lacking, such as when there is not enough evidence to support the article’s hypothesis. Especially in research, honest reporting of one’s findings is not only important to the expansion of knowledge, but also because it could have measurable impacts on real people. It is also vital to acknowledge the overall quality of someone’s work while providing constructive feedback for personal enrichment. Emotional intelligence is required to give constructive feedback.12 The framing of the feedback is essential to ensure the other does not feel personally targeted or humiliated. For example, before handing out hard-to-hear criticism, it is a good idea to first start out the conversation by preparing the other about the unpleasant news they are about to hear by saying something like, “I need to tell you something that is going to be hard to hear.” Furthermore, emphasize that the criticism is not a personal attack, but rather toward the issue at hand. Be specific with the criticism and avoid making general statements that will be interpreted as a personal attack. For example, instead of saying, “You aren’t doing anything,” say what exactly the other did not do: “I don’t think you put enough time to develop this idea, it is lacking in detail.” Along with the criticism, it is also constructive to offer help and give suggestions to encourage the teammate receiving the criticism in a better direction. This way, teammates will feel supported and be less likely to feel defensive and unmotivated. Have Rules People Believe In Some parts of daily work life will be stagnant—sometimes even boring—for team members. Therefore, reminding individuals why their role is important motivates them to continue their work and to create effective solutions. Team leaders and members should reinforce this belief by showing appreciation for the work of their fellow team members and delivering encouragement when work becomes difficult. For example, some physicians will experience burnout. Therefore, administrators in health care should recognize that physicians also need time to recuperate and should permit physicians to rest and spend time with their families. Having rules that show care notifies team members they are valued, leading to greater appreciation for their leaders and a stronger desire to stay within their position. By integrating these aspects into the work environment, not only will employees produce high-quality work, but the health and happiness of the team will improve, leading to more people choosing to stay at their jobs. However, for true implementation of these aspects, it takes the skills of a great leader to uphold and maintain the pillars of a thriving work culture. HOW TO BUILD A THRIVING WORK CULTURE Great employees stay because of other great people—but especially because of great leaders. The way people are regarded in the workplace is a predictor of employee happiness and whether they choose to remain at their job (Fig 4).Fig. 4.: How leaders should promote a thriving work culture.Promote Respect Few employees want to work for people who are demeaning and condescending. Acting respectfully during times of conflict is especially important and a key indicator for whether employees decide to stay at their job.13,14 Leaders should always think before speaking to avoid misunderstandings or accidentally offending a team member. Asking the question, “Would I like it if someone told me what I am about to say?” is a good way to check to determine whether a statement is appropriate and respectful. Leaders should also set a precedent of showing appreciation for others and acknowledging team members who turn in quality work. A simple “thank you” is an easy yet effective way to make someone feel appreciated and motivated to continue doing great work. A perfect role model who encompasses a respectful and generous nature is the actor Keanu Reeves, who often exuberantly thanks crew members and those who contributed to the movie and will often give gifts, such as gifting a dozen stuntmen with Harley-Davidson motorcycles.15 In addition, leaders who demand positive traits from team members, such as being reliable or considerate, should also hold themselves to high standards and do what they say they will do. It is unlikely that people will want to continue to work with an unreliable person. Leaders should also exhibit emotional maturity to be considerate toward team members. Simply being mindful of one’s surroundings, such as not interrupting a co-worker who is on a phone call, is important to maintaining and boosting team cohesion. title: When Eurovision Came Out: LGBTQ+ Visibility and the Eurovision Song Contest in the “Queer 1990s”
abstract: Europe's “queer 1990s,” at least for those who put their faith in liberal activism and legal reforms, represented a distinctive, post-Cold-War turning-point, when the European integration project still attracted widespread optimism for future prosperity and social progress.1 Indeed, the very symbolic meanings of “Europe” within that liberal project shifted to encompass sexual equality in these 1990s through cumulative legislative and judicial moves by the European Union (EU) and the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). After much lobbying by Western European NGOs connected through the International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA), formalized as “ILGA-Europe” in 1996, activists harnessing the EU's ambition to become a “community of values” persuaded it to incorporate sexual orientation in the new antidiscrimination clause of the 1997 Treaty of Amsterdam.2 Significant ECHR judgements on trans people's identity documents, equalized ages of sexual consent, and gay and lesbian rights to military service showed that judges were recognizing changing attitudes and treating sexual equality within the European human rights regime in the 1990s even though that regime's creators in the 1950s had excluded it.3 In these “queer 1990s,” the Eurovision Song Contest witnessed its first openly queer performers, Iceland's Páll Óskar in 1997 and Israel's Dana International in 1998.4 Although the contest had long had an active gay following, it was in 1997–98 that LGBTQ+ politics at Eurovision entered what I elsewhere call its “visibility phase.”5Eurovision, as frequently associated with European integration as it is, is not a direct instrument of any European political institutions. It is produced by an entirely separate organization, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), an association of public service broadcasters which formed for the purposes of technical cooperation in 1950 and staged the first annual Eurovision Song Contest in 1956.6 From its Swiss base in Geneva, the historian Dean Vuletic argues, the EBU always distanced itself from the integratory supranationalism of the future EU, even though it allowed the European Commission to sponsor some “postcard” films and interval acts in 1987, 1988, and 1990.7 Eurovision's “map” of Europe has always been wider than the European political union, from Switzerland's founding participation, through Mediterranean and eastward enlargements that reached further than any EU ambitions, to Australia's incorporation in 2015. Nevertheless, even if only as a “historical fiction,” the ideas of Eurovision and European integration have overpowered archival realities and become interwoven in numerous popular imaginations of the contest.8 Moreover, both projects did emerge in a shared historical context, the political, economic, and cultural climate of early 1950s Western Europe.Eurovision had already gained a queer audience well before the Dublin 1997 and Birmingham 1998 contests, especially among gay men. By the 1970s, gay viewers in many Northern and Western European countries were already recognizing each other as fans. According to interviews with gay fans in Ireland, however, this was still “largely in terms of the closet,” that is, “a shared, open secret with other gay spectators” unseen by the heteronormative world.9 Until the mid-1990s, the contest itself continued to be “presented . . . as hugely respectable” by the standards of mid-twentieth-century European “high culture,” with a live classical orchestra, a black-tie dress code for audience members, and a peripatetic home in prestigious national theatrical/orchestral venues of each host country.10 Queer readings of camp and excess in Eurovision remained “a private affair, embedded in . . . subcultural systems” such as Eurovision parties in private homes or gay pubs/bars, or the activities of the international fan club OGAE, founded with a “largely gay” membership in 1984.11 Even before 1997–98, however, understandings that Eurovision had special meanings for gay fans were beginning to cross into wider public discourse about the contest in the 1990s. This may have been particularly so in Ireland, where Ireland's unprecedented four Eurovision wins in one decade (1992–96) coincided with the 1993 implementation of the 1988 ECHR ruling that Ireland must decriminalize sex between men.12 This sense of simultaneity might also have manifested in other national contexts, including the UK, where the gay press frequently covered activists’ strategy of pursuing legal reforms through the ECHR.Before 1997, Eurovision had known closeted queer performers, including 1961’s winner Jean-Claude Pascal, who represented Luxembourg with the romantic chanson “Nous les amoureux” (“We, the lovers”): its non-gender-specific portrayal of a couple defying community hostility to assert God is on their side has only very recently been reinserted into Eurovision's queer history.13 Óskar, however, was the first openly queer contestant, marking his performance equally as queer to any viewer who knew about his queerness through media coverage, broadcasters’ live commentary, or fandom word of mouth. Óskar's seductive performance of “Minn hinsti dans” (“My final dance”) typified the 1990s’ seeping of queer aesthetics into mainstream fashion and popular culture, and broke the mold of Eurovision performance to prefigure the contemporary contest in numerous ways. His electronic backing track was still a rarity at Eurovision; his sensual interactions with his female dancers, who wore fishnet tights and “kinky” black bodices, gloves, and boots, referenced BDSM aesthetics more daringly than any previous entry had attempted in this respectable, “family”-oriented show; his radio mic might have evoked Madonna's stage outfits; he transgressed masculine gender norms by visibly wearing make-up; his use of props, including a large white leather sofa and multiple television screens on the stage floor, was on greater scale than any previous entry; his sound resembled current chart pop music much more closely than Eurovision entries by the 1990s typically did; and from the five countries where Eurovision was piloting telephone voting (Austria, Germany, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK), it won notably more points than from the professional juries who traditionally awarded Eurovision scores.Viewed intertextually within transnational popular music culture, Óskar's image, sound, and performance might have evoked particular comparisons with George Michael, a star whose transforming public image became a major popular-cultural narrative in the queer 1990s. Michael's star image since 1990 had shifted from his early music videos’ “explicit heterosexuality” (albeit with potential alternative queer readings) towards the “sexual ambiguity” that had become central to his star “metanarrative” by 1996–97.14 It would be another year before Michael's arrest for public sex in Los Angeles first forced him to declare his sexual orientation on CNN and then inspired him to reclaim the stigma in his 1998 video “Outside,” which directly referenced the arrest, yet in queer culture he was already an object of fascination, desire, and sometimes frustration. His transnational star persona might therefore have made Óskar's more legible as queer. “Minn hinsti dans” has particular commonalities with Michael's 1996 hit, “Fastlove.” Both performances’ characters appear as bored playboys who cannot even be excited by conspicuous sexual excess; in the “Fastlove” video and in Oskar's performance, dancers wear BDSM-inspired clothing, the performer addresses the camera from a sofa, and the space is scattered with TV screens. Eurovision's first openly queer performer, employing queer popular-cultural aesthetics on stage, was thus representing Iceland less than a year after Iceland had become only the fourth European country to introduce registered partnerships for same-gender couples.15A further dimension of queer aesthetics, culture and experience—drag culture and trans femininity—gained visibility at Eurovision when Israeli television selected Dana International for Eurovision 1998. Her participation simultaneously represented a further landmark in Eurovision's queer history, perhaps even in European trans history writ large, but also a knot of contentions that force understandings of Eurovision's “queer 1990s” to confront the widely critiqued politics of “LGBTQ+-friendly” messaging in Israeli public diplomacy.16 The 1990s in Israel were a transitional phase between repression and visibility for LGBTQ+ people: same-gender sex had been legalized in 1988; certain equalities for lesbians, gays, and bisexuals had been introduced in the early 1990s, including the right to serve openly in Israel's all-important military; Israel's first Pride happened in Tel Aviv in 1993; and drag troupes were gaining crossover appeal in mainstream popular culture.17 Dana herself had broken through from Tel Aviv's drag scene into an original recording artist who had released three hit albums, replete with musical and linguistic border-crossing (her songs employed both Western dance and Middle Eastern musical elements, and shifted between Hebrew, English, and Arabic), by the time the Israeli Broadcasting Authority (IBA) selected her for Eurovision in November 1997.18Within Israel, Dana's participation was denounced by ultra-Orthodox rabbis, including the deputy health minister Shlomo Benizri who branded her an “aberration.”19 Media coverage once she was in Birmingham for Eurovision dwelled far more on her gender confirmation surgery than her creative achievements, her deadname was routinely given even in sympathetic articles, and UK newspaper columns mocking the contest were peppered with transphobic remarks. Yet “Diva,” her winning entry, marked her triumph “as a woman singing about women,” linking her own embodiment of glamorous femininity to the myths of Aphrodite, Victoria, and Cleopatra, all mentioned in the song.20 For her winner's reprise, she changed into a feathered outfit by the gay designer Jean-Paul Gaultier, whose career-defining fascination with the homoerotic mariner had earned him appreciation in 1980s and 1990s queer culture.21The “diva” figure, evoked through the nexus of image, lyrics, choreography, couture, and metanarrative in Dana's performance, had of course already enjoyed decades of “iconic” status in transnational queer culture. One of the more serious UK newspaper articles about her before the contest, in The Guardian, remarked she was “said to represent two nations—Israel and gays.”22 Her metanarrative of triumph over prejudice exemplified the “duality of stage/screen and life” that must exist for audiences to invest in diva figures with authenticity, against the background of 1990s LGBTQ+ activism.23 As such, she epitomized the kind of “underdog story” which arguably contributes to Eurovision's queer appeal: The underdog story—the person who battles against obscurity or oppression to triumph against the odds—is a classic gay narrative, through which spectators can read their own stories of fighting through bias and prejudice towards fully realised, proud gay identities. Eurovision is a treasure trove of underdog stories to be sought out and identified with or queered if necessary, year after year.24Her meanings to gay male fans in Israel, as retold to the scholar Dafna Lemish several years later, seemed to map this narrative on to late 1990s Israeli circumstances. Lemish's interviewees frequently aligned themselves with a transnational queer passion for camp, which they eagerly read into extravagant performances at Eurovision, and some perceived that Eurovision's camp let them take pleasure in “the extroverted expression of femininity,” which mainstream Israeli cultures of masculinity would heavily stigmatize.25 Connecting with the imagined “European” space of Eurovision reminded some of past travel to Western European cities where they had seen same-gender couples expressing affection more openly than they could then have done in Israel, and Dana winning Eurovision in the first year of predominantly public telephone voting (following 1997’s successful experiment) could even feel like a show of support from the gay community all over Europe.26 Hundreds of gay fans rushed to central Tel Aviv with rainbow flags, mingling with straight revelers waving the national flag and even football fans celebrating a championship win. “The community as a whole came out of the closet that night,” Lemish observes, and her example illustrates Peter Rehberg's 2007 description of Eurovision as “a rare occasion for simultaneously celebrating both queerness and national identity.”27Even before Eurovision, scholars of Israeli popular culture were recognizing Dana as a singular figure embodying fundamental religious, cultural, ethnic, political, and sexual tensions in Israeli society.28 Yet to talk of her national or international meanings today requires acknowledging how Israeli state organizations since then have instrumentalized a narrative of Israel as a uniquely LGBTQ+-friendly nation in the Middle East to win international public sympathy for the state's actions towards Palestinians, a strategy that critical scholars term “pinkwashing.”29 The scale of its repression and military violence in the occupied Palestinian territories amount, in the eyes of Palestinian activists and their supporters, to “apartheid.”30 In 1998, and when Israel hosted Eurovision 1999 in Jerusalem, the Oslo Accords peace process was still underway, the Second Intifada had not yet occurred, and Israeli forces had not yet launched the devastating operations that led Palestinian civil society to found the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement in 2005. It can be argued that this was a very different historical moment from that surrounding Israel's next, controversial Eurovision victory in 2018.31 Yet Dana's historic Eurovision victory remained a resource for Israeli public diplomacy in this later context.32 A statement by Israel's ambassador to the United States in 2012 citing it as proof that Israel was an LGBTQ+ rights “pioneer,” for instance, directly illustrates for Aeyal Gross “homonationalist discourse and ‘pinkwashing’” in Israel's diplomatic strategy.33 All this must be held together with the immediate meanings Dana's victory had inside Israel, and its revelatory impact for numerous trans people in Europe who had only ever been shown freakish or abject representations of trans femininity in mass media before.34 The politics of her domestic reception in 1997–98 do, however, suggest that LGBTQ+ equality in Israel was won much more contingently in the 1990s than the future tone of Israeli public diplomacy would imply.These two queer “firsts” in Eurovision performance, Páll Óskar in 1997 and Dana International in 1998, show that in the late 1990s queer aesthetics openly came to Eurovision for the first time, in the name of nations that were experiencing dramatic sociolegal changes around LGBTQ+ rights. Yet, performances aside, the organization of Eurovision contests themselves was also changing in the late 1990s in ways that grew Eurovision's queer audience, as a live crowd and as a fandom. this
